UPDATE 2017: tooltips on tech tree now. Didn't check anything else.
UPDATE 20 JULY 2015: Another game update. Still no tooltips on tech tree, no mouse on screen edge scrolling. I don't think they care about making the interface more PC-like at all. Either that or they are using some crossplatform framework which doesn't allow PC features so they -can't- make it palatable to pc users.
UPDATE 19 JUNE 2015: I checked the game again to update my review. Nothing has changed except there is now a full screen option.
There may be a good game inside here somewhere but I'm having trouble persevering with it due to the atrocious interface, which is exactly the same as the mobile one and makes no effort to take advantage of the PC.
The game runs in a window at a set size and you can't change it. (update there is now a fullscreen option) There are no tooltips, so you have to press buttons to find out what they do then click back. This is especially annoying in the technology tree where you have to click on everything one by one to find out what it is. It's seriously tedious. There is no mouse on edge of screen scrolling. No use is made of right click.
Just like a mobile game it has a "please review the game" button and another button to "more games".
There's quite a long time between turns after you press next turn. Some kind of progress indicator would be reassuring.
I mentioned when the game first came to PC  in early/mid September 2014 that they needed as a matter of urgency to move away from the mobile interface and make a new interface for PC and I seem to remember a dev saying they would be doing just that.
It's been nearly 6 months. It's clear they aren't going to do anything. The game has been written to make money on mobile and then as an afterthought they have dumped it on the pc to make some more money, but they aren't willing to actually put any work in beyond making it actually run on the pc.
The worst effect from the mobile interface is the tech tree, which I mentioned earlier. There are a ton of technologies on the screen and you have to click each one to find out what it is, (like Warp Drive 1 or Spanner Throwing 3 or whatever). There's no way to know just from the icon what the tech is and clicking it takes you to a whole new screen which pretty much just says the name of the tech, then you need to click back to go back.
It would be so, so easy for them to add tooltips to the tech tree and it would be remove a massive frustration from the game. They've had 6 months to do it and they haven't done it.
I have no respect for the devs at all.
I seriously suggest not buying this game.

I started playing SMITE during their beta phase, I played both LoL and Smite for quite some time but ultimately sticking with League just because most of my friends didn't want to make the switch to SMITE at that time even though I did.
Let me put it that way:
From a pure gaming standpoint: Is it "better" than League? No. It's not as well thought through into the last detail, it's not quite as balanced and tactical decisions are not as deep and impactful as in other MOBAs.
From an aesthetic standpoint: Is it better than League? No. Riot has better artists than Hi-Rez. Hands down.
Is it more fun to play SMITE than any other MOBA? Absolutely.
Why? Well,
1) The community isn't quite as toxic as in League or other MOBAs I have played. Sure I have been wished to get cancer and been asked to deinstall the game, but the density of REALLY badly behaved players is lower than in other games of that genre.
2) Community support. Riot please! While it is sometimes hard to understand the decisions of other game companies and how they treat their communities, HiRez is doing a pretty good job giving the players what they want.
3) Diversity: While Riot announces "featured game modes" a month before they come out and then have them run for two weeks and make a whole fuzz about it, there is a new featured game mode every couple of days in SMITE, usually suggested by the community via Twitter. Remember when millions of players wanted the "ultra-rapid-fire mode" in League back and had to beg in every way shape and form for a whole year before Riot made it available again for 2 weeks? Yeah ... with HiRez you just tweet them...
Summary: If you are sick of the community and poor support in League of Legends, this game is for you.

Less toxic, more action packed and more skilled based then other M.O.B.A.'s out there. I'm looking at you League of Legends.

One of the better CoD games. The single-player campaign is interesting and fun to play, and is long enough to be satisfying without overstaying its welcome. Multiplayer uses a connection mechanism similar to the Modern Warfare games, automatically matching up players into games without needing to select a server. This seems to work pretty well - better than on any previous CoD, at least. Building classes and characters has a lot more variety without being over-complicated and the actual gameplay in multiplayer is good with mostly well-designed maps that offer plenty of different tactical options. MP rounds are a little too short, though, many rounds are finished in under 5 minutes. The new abilities are a mixed bag, some of them being quite tricky to use. None of them really over-balances the gameplay, like the "noob tube" grenade launchers in earlier CoD games often did.
Long story short: If you like CoD, you'll have fun with this one.

BroForce. It's all good.
The controls are crisp & responsive, the animation & design is charming, the playability is untapped - random placing of items assists, but playing the game is as compelling as breathing. But far more fun.
Never do you feel cheated, neither does 'dying' result in punishment - just a loss of momentum at worst, but, more often than not, it rewards you with a 'Bro' that may be better skilled (or not) to re-try the area.
The random selection of 'Bro's' is welcome and adds an interesting dynamic - choosing whether to swop a currently decent 'Bro' for a random rescue can make the player hesitate (sometimes fatally) or at least force a little wince.
All in all, it just adds to the appeal, because whoever you play as, you kick♥♥♥♥♥  ..and i mean 'Kick♥♥♥♥♥♥ - Destructable ..erm, everything! to the point where 'Over Kill' can hinder you're progress.
Mix this with the Physics, exploding barrels/oxi tanks, suicide bombers etc.. & you have an exploding-sploshy-chain-reacting-death-arena-of-fun.
Being far from financially comfortable, i'm not one to flippantly recommend a purchase, but i do whole heartedly recommend 'BroForce' to anyone who wants a humourous, swift, cheeky little shooter. An interest in the subject matter is a bonus - the characters are superb & there has clearly been a lot of care & attention put into all aspects of this game.
Beta: The game (at the time of writing) is in a Beta state. Buy it anyway..    ..seriously, it looks & plays better than plenty of 'finished' games currently available. Not once have i experienced a bug, glitch or anything adverse.
Admittantly, I am kinda smitten with this game, partially because of nestalgia (it satisfies my retro sensibilities) & partially because it's genuinely sack loads of fun. Rarely does dying in games make me laugh, this title had me giggling like a school girl.
When the initial 'Free Lives' hand clap logo appears & the music kicks in, it immediately makes me smile.
It could be said that it's not difficult to complete (yet) but even so, I genuinely feel that it's more about the fun to be had whilst playing (even repeatedly) not so much the challenge, that once beaten, is rarely played again.
If 'Super Crate Box' was a teenage speed freak, then 'BroForce' is his older, millitary trained, crackhead Bro..   ..and all his mates.
And there's more to come..
EDIT: The updates have been substancial, there has been dozens of new Bro's, several new levels, features and there's even Gigers Aliens (complete with working face huggers) and Predators running around.
The party has got a whole lot wilder.
What you waiting for Bro?
I love this game! It's energetic, nostaglic, and humorous. You definitely get your money's worth with Broforce!

I don't play games for the writing, so I don't care about the meme.  Borderlands 2 is exactly what its predecessor is; a singleplayer game with aspects that play like an MMO.  You can spend all day killing the same bosses, grinding out drops to get a specific unique drop, or looking for a hot little number to replace your current gun.  Like it or not, this is why I play Borderlands, because I enjoy the make your own fun gameplay where the game doesn't force you to continue forward to the next area and bankrupts your gameplay for the current area.
Is it a well-made game?  I'm going to say no, but that doesn't mean it's not a fun game.  Does that prevent me from playing it for hours on end, grinding out and getting better gear, progressing the hot mess of a story just because I want to get to a new area with better gun drops?   No, not at all.  The game doesn't require you to care about the story, it gives you objectives, and you can fulfill those objectives to proceed to the next area to get higher level enemies.
That said, I don't hate the story of the game.  If you play Borderlands, you ought to know what you're getting, it's like a singleplayer Korean grinding MMO, which isn't a bad thing if you like the gameplay.  I happen to like the gameplay, because there's not much else like it on the market.  I don't mean "first-person shooters are a dying genre," I just mean a game which has as much FPS as it does RPG to it.  The game has 4 base classes (just like the first game), and then 2 DLC classes (the Mechromancer and the Psycho).  Obviously they all play similarly in design of being FPS characters, it's their abilities that changes up their gameplay and I feel that the abilities really do change up the gameplay by a lot.
It's not the Citizen Kane of games, it's not some pretentious navel gazing game, it's just a game where you shoot things, they drop things and you pick up those things to help you shoot more things.  If that sounds like a game for you, consider getting this game.  If you're looking for a great story with lots of dramatic moments, then I have to ask, why you would look in an FPS game and also tell you this game is not it.

Honestly the best FPS I have ever played, high replayability due to the RPG mechanics, the writing is amazing, there are Diablo-esque unbalanced mechanics which I think are really fun, the only downside in the whole game is the slag mechanic and either way it's just another challenge to play with/around. This game is timeless.

Slime rancher is one of the most disturbing games I've played. It features unique gameplay that is repetetive yet strategic. It's graphics are simply yet pleasing, and it relies on the player to "assume the story".
I hope I didn't assume wrong.
Initially, you are presented as Beatrix LeBeau, a slime rancher that attempts to gain profit. With it she is greeted by her neighbors through e-mail, and also requested to gift slimes to nearby researchers.
As the main character, you are told to round slimes, grow crops, and feed them to drop "plorts", which can be sold on what is essentially a stock market.
Eventually, when a player becomes skilled enough, they are presented with largos; a slime that has eaten a plort from another slime of a different kind.
Then comes the horrid part.
When a largo consumes another plort of a different kind than the original two, it gets consumed by greed and turns into a "tarr," a rainbow devil that immediately consumes slimes. The hunger transforms the slime into a monster, and you as the protagonist cannot save the devil inside it; you merely are given water to shoot at it, and it will disspate, leaving residue behind. Slimes that are not consumed by hunger are terrified as they see their aquantances' bodies become horribly tranformed; but they do not learn. They follow them, as a sheep will follow another, all towards an infinite doom of mutation.
You trap slimes and give them food, seperating them from the wild and family all for a needy desire for wealth. You are shown that you must selectively breed two slimes, in an attempt to gain more plorts, and more money. With this money, more land is bought, more power, and more upgrades; but these upgrades are not to help people, but rather help you gain more profit.
You are also presented with doors; man-made doors, sealing off slimes from the rest of the land, most likely in hopes to prevent them from suffering. But you, as the protagonist, are not allowed to stop there. Gordo slimes are large slimes that are one species, and too fat to move. You must force feed them, until the point they explode into regular slimes, and are given the key. It's similar to ripping a slime open for a key.
Unlocking the door expands new lands, new foods, and more subjects to torture.
Slime Rancher is a kid-friendly game with endless opportunity. It features unique gameplay and simple yet pleasing graphics.

It's not ground-breaking by any means but it's a fun little Match-3 puzzle game where ship battles are concerned, which is a bulk of the game aside from sailing around to different ports to take on missions that range from "sell this item at this port" missions, to "sink X amount of ships and bring back their flags".   Where the game sort of falls flat however is the puzzle game itself.  I would much rather prefer it to be a live versus type of puzzle combat, rather than turn-based.  Because if you score a 4-in a row or higher of any symbol you get a bonus turn.  Keep in mind that only you act during the puzzle sequence, the enemy just seems to blindly fire cannons at you ever turn and doesn't make use of any of the other actions (repairing, acquiring more cannons, boarding enemy ship, etc.).  You can also take your time as you try to find the best possible matches as there is no time penalty.
It's not perfect but it's also not an atrocity.  I mostly loaded it up just for the trading cards, but managed to get sucked into playing it for 2+ hours in one sitting.  Could the game be better?  Most definitely.  But I find the price to be reasonable for what you get.  My biggest complaint has to be the trading.  You can purchase goods in ports and sell them at other ports.  The problem with this is you have no real clue what prices are considered low or high, and the only real benefit of buying anything is to obtain the achievements linked to it, otherwise I typically just sell cargo I plunder from enemy ships.   Who this game will appeal to?  Casual puzzle gaming fans who like games such as Puzzle Quest or 10,000,000 who also love the theme of pirates.  It's a very laid back game and doesn't challenge your mind too much and pressure you to be quick on the matching.

Loot Hunter, a derivative name for a derivative game. Funny how that works.
A more appropriate title might be Puzzle Quest: Pirates, except with none of the polish and only a loose approximation of the mechanics that made that series such a hit. Loot Hunter is a hybrid RPG/match-3 game, dividing its time between sailing around picking up quests and getting into ship battles where you need to match tiles in order to defeat your enemy. It worked for Puzzle Quest which didn't even have the benefit of being stuffed full of pirates, and it should have worked here, but everything about Loot Hunter is so undeniably and disastrously bland and unexciting.
Quests are designed as if they've been ripped out of an RPG Design for Dummies handbook, either fetch quests sending you across the rather small map, or asking you to defeat a certain number of a faction's ship. Upon clearing a given quest you're presented with one that reads identically word for word, only you now have to carry even more cargo or defeat even more ships. It's so painfully mundane that it's almost laughable, so plainly uninspired that it doesn't even feel worthy of criticism.
The idea of factions and having to manage wars between them by choosing who you do and don't attack is something I'd have loved to experiment with, but it's implementation is so shallow it's hardly a system at all. The outbreak of war is always in your control, and the only reason to ever start one is because one side decided they wanted some of the other's flags. Of course you never have to debate actually participating in these meaningless declarations of war as you can simply slip some gold to the faction whose fleet you blew to hell and all is forgiven. Its only purpose is to occasionally dock you some funds and add one more checkmark to your list of pointless goals; a wasted opportunity and another tedious aspect of an already enormously repetitive game.
Finally the match-3 mechanics themselves (this may perhaps be the first time I've brought up the mechanics or a match-3 game in a review, as they seem so impossible to screw up, being this perfectly established thing) are absolutely dreadful. The lack of cascades (ie. matches made by falling gems) means you're only ever looking for groups of 4 to match, and this makes for a very dull time as it completely removes any strategy from making matches and leaves everything up to chance that you hopefully get a decent board. The power ups you can use during battle are often less effective than just making the same matches over and over, and the complete lack of any balance means you pretty much know who is going to win a battle as soon as it begins and you can see each others life bar.
I'm not sure I expected anything from Loot Hunter, but I certainly didn't imagine they could botch mechanics already proven in other games so badly. It's a throwaway experience that will eat your time in the most trivial and unrewarding way possible, constantly spurring you onward by recycling the same content and hoping you go after the carrot on the end of the stick that is the ever growing numbers seemingly popping out all over the screen. Unfortunately for Loot Hunter is seems to have misplaced any purpose for said numbers, or forgotten to create one altogether, leaving you nothing to latch onto but the escape button.

I started playing SMITE during their beta phase, I played both LoL and Smite for quite some time but ultimately sticking with League just because most of my friends didn't want to make the switch to SMITE at that time even though I did.
Let me put it that way:
From a pure gaming standpoint: Is it "better" than League? No. It's not as well thought through into the last detail, it's not quite as balanced and tactical decisions are not as deep and impactful as in other MOBAs.
From an aesthetic standpoint: Is it better than League? No. Riot has better artists than Hi-Rez. Hands down.
Is it more fun to play SMITE than any other MOBA? Absolutely.
Why? Well,
1) The community isn't quite as toxic as in League or other MOBAs I have played. Sure I have been wished to get cancer and been asked to deinstall the game, but the density of REALLY badly behaved players is lower than in other games of that genre.
2) Community support. Riot please! While it is sometimes hard to understand the decisions of other game companies and how they treat their communities, HiRez is doing a pretty good job giving the players what they want.
3) Diversity: While Riot announces "featured game modes" a month before they come out and then have them run for two weeks and make a whole fuzz about it, there is a new featured game mode every couple of days in SMITE, usually suggested by the community via Twitter. Remember when millions of players wanted the "ultra-rapid-fire mode" in League back and had to beg in every way shape and form for a whole year before Riot made it available again for 2 weeks? Are you thinking, Just give me the facts and I’ll make up my own mind?  Hopefully I can answer this question.
A blend of complex strategic development of technology, star system colonization, war and politics. The remnants of the human race must survive and hopefully flourish in the face of enemies within your society and aliens bent on total final destruction.  This is not a casual game. Where Masters of Orion and Civilization cross paths you will find Star Traders 4X Empires.
To get a small demonstration of real time game play take a look at these two YouTube videos the Developers have published.
Pros
1.  Documentation Score 5 out of 5.
All the rules are contained inside the game by clicking on the Advisor Library.  I wish more games would do this!  During this Steam holiday sale I’ve picked up inexpensive games then thrown in the deep end, especially the “oldies but goodies”.  In addition you can find the ST 4X rule book online at
The in-game rules get updated as new content is added
2.  Technology Tree 5 out of 5.
Close to 100 separate categories each one providing multiple benefits.  One box might give you access to 4 different weapons and a new ship class.  Another might give you a Spice den to increase morale while unlocking a big money making trade option.
3.  No IAP 5 out of 5
The Elite version contains all 8 of the factions and syndicates, and you don’t ever pay for new releases as the game expands.
4.  Ships 5 out of 5
You can design your own ships, name them and train captains as specialists in planetary invasion, gunnery, or repair to name a few.  The tactical battles involve whole fleets where every ship is controlled individually.  Being turn based you get a chance to really think about what will happen on the next move.
5.  Hot Keys 4 out of 5
Having them and the mouse wheel zoom functions really speeds up game play, touch screens always seem to slow me down.  More keys need to be  added so that’s why I gave it a 4.
6.  Artwork and Atmosphere 5 out of 5
It is important to compare this with games of similar type not Skyrim!  The ships are very detailed when you zoom in.  The sound effects are great.  There is an Ethereal soundtrack that currently has a bug but will be fixed soon.
7.  Game design and play 5 out of 5
You cannot play as a Tyrant warlord.  Refugees are landing all the time. The morale and political development tree are just as important as designing and launching warships.  If you can’t manage the human side the economy will crash, people will riot, syndicate rivalries can result in war, and your research will stagnate making you easy pickings for the enemy.
Cons
1. Difficulty 4 out of 5
There are multiple difficulty levels.  All Trese Brothers games set on Normal are meant to be challenging.  The game does not cheat it just opens a can of whoop♥♥♥♥♥on me every time I play.  I’m not the most skilled player in the world so it will take several months to get the hang of it.  You aren’t going to see comments like “I beat it in 4 hours at Impossible level”.  If you are looking for a solid challenge you just found it.

I'm pretty sure this is some of the most fun I've had with friends in a video game ever. After 1400 hours on my criminal character, countless quittings and returns, and a mind blowing amount of 4€ spent, I believe I can finally give an honest review. I started playing back in 2011 and had an amazing new player experience, which included me and my four friends robbing stores to gather money for a personal van. The game was in a way worse state back then, but there was still plenty to enjoy. I don't play on a regular basis anymore, but the good memories still make me visit it every few weeks.
Now, I can see what people are whining about. Not much new free content has been released in the past year. But if you are a new player, there is still plenty to experience, ESPECIALLY with friends. And yes, there are still hackers and bugs, but it seems way better than 5 years ago. The servers seem to have improved significantly, atleast on EU. While the gunplay might not be impressive for most fps players and the driving mechanics aren't on a racing sim level, the character customization and the social aspect are unlike anything I've experienced before. Starting my own clan of around 40 people, sending them all stuff to design their outfits and cars, then rolling around the district trying to approach missions tactiacally... and end up team killing everyone anyway. But looking great while doing it.
It used to be way worse than it is, and it can still be a lot better. If you are like me and are willing to ignore some of the game's flaws and learn the basics, you can be in for a lot of fun. When or if the updated engine rolls out, I recommend every player, old and new alike, to check this game out. Hopefully after that, the devs will start pushing out more new content too, because it would be a shame if such a unique concept went to waste.

The most entertaining CoD since Modern Warfare, but not better than. Unfortunetly has some serious issues:
1) The game is not optomised for AMD hardware at all. If you are running AMD then expect to switch to 'low' everything, even if you have good hardware that should run the game. Apparently this is a known issue that AMD are trying to patch, according to the DEVs.
2) No dedicated servers means that you will often spend up to 30 min trying to find a game that agrees with you. This is very frustrating.
3) The way respawns work is much like in older CoD games, in that in switches polarity when one team wipes the other from a certain area. The problem is that the maps are so tiny, and the added mobility of the exo suits with unlimited run time so great, that the spawn system cannot keep up. This often results in teams being split across an entire map with someone, somewhere, spawn camping the enemy.
4) Another problem is that the suit system is largely flawed in general. It doesn't add anything other than mobility to the game, which makes the game feel much more like Titan Fall than any of the previous CoD games. All of the abilities you can add to the suits are largely a gimmick that are either useless in some way (e.g the stealth ability can still be seen by players, hovering is useless, extra speed is minimal, and mute footsteps is very situational) or are out performed by something else in the game.
5) The new weapon selection - this ties in with the above. To make matters worse there is a distinct split between weapons that are actually useful in this suit setting and those which are not. If you cannot make a combo that works with the extreme dodging antics that the exo suit allows then you will quickly find yourself getting a high death count. As such grenades have now become largely redundant, especially with how long they take to throw. The addition of several futuristic weapon scopes also benerfit assault rifles, and one or two of the submachine guns, far more than any of the other branches, meaning that they are no brain choices. This means that despite their being a slew of new and different weaponry you will notice that most people use the same 3 or 4 guns, because they are simply that much versatile with the new add ons. You may find the odd person still trying to scope with a sniper, but with how mobile suits have made the game this has largely become a dead play style.
6) Steam does not count your game time on multiplayer as counting towards time playing the game...

At present, there are only a handful of minor complaints I have about Broforce that could easily be lumped into the personal preference pile. The only major issue I have with this Early Access gem is that it's short on levels - a problem slowly being resolved by the community and to be improved on by the developers as time goes on.
At its core, Broforce is an intense, old-school platformer. The player can take one bullet, explosion, or what-have-you, but has a slowly increasing pool of lives. Skilled timing and awareness are key to surviving and excelling in the fast-and-furious shootouts between mook and bro.
Variety, as well, plays a key role in every encounter. The player's character is randomly selected from a long list of action movie heroes with unique talents and behavior and every level presents a wealth of different ways to be completed. Did the game give you Rambo? Lob a grenade to terrify your opponents and gun them down in the confusion. Did Indiana Jones step up to the plate? Whip the guns out of your enemy's hands and wipe clear the leftovers with your devastating revolver. Every bro offers a unique experience and every situation highlights just how differently every bro handles it.
On top of the rich amount of options, from destroying terrain to bypassing enemies altogether, Broforce is a game that never ceases to surprise. A chain reaction of barrels, suicide bombers, or even just collapsing scenery can lead to unexpected victory, defeat, or simply hilarity. Over-the-top action movie heroes, dim-witted mooks, and more explosions than you can shake a stick of dynamite at make for comedy gold in the most unexpected of situations.
Broforce and its dedication to the things that make me proud to be a God-fearing, red-blooded, American patriot have helped restore my faith in Early Access games. I wish Extra Lives all the best with this title and greatly look forward to the bright, flaming, shrapnel-battered future ahead.

Tales of Valor is the third, and most likely final, part of the complete CoH experience. ToV, unlike Oppossing Fronts, does not add any new factions compared to the base game. Instead, it adds three new campaigns (Really only two campaigns; Tiger Ace is a three mission mini-campaign) and a plethora of multiplayer features to enhance playing online. Namely, it introduces new units, such as the Kangaroo Carrier or the Swhimmwagen 166. Also, there is three new game types for online play: Assault, Panzerkrieg, and Stonewall. Assault is much like CoH's Defence of the Ancients, with players being hero units fighting to destroy the enemy's base. Panzerkieg is similar to Assault, but with tanks and control points. Stonewall, however, has the player and teammates fighting together to hold back the enemy from capturing the city you are located in. In all, if you are debating to get base over ToV, I'd get ToV. The one campaign you'd miss is nothing compared to the online modes  you'd miss out on.

This is a game that combines very clever complexity and balance, within seemingly straightforward strategy of colony survival.  Unlike most 4X type games, you aren't controlling a single empire, but rather three disparate factions.  They each bring strengths to the table to help you succeed, but they often don't see the big picture, and bicker like children, hindering your chances.
I like the turn-based approach, allowing you to really think out your strategy, and the fact that the research paths are so diverse.  There isn't a "one path to success" approach in this game - trying different things nets different results, with some being equally as successful as others.
I would recommend this game to those who enjoy turnbased 4X games, and who love to challenge themselves with a brilliantly thoughtout game design.  It's hard to believe it's made by really only two brothers, who also develop multiple other games of equal quality.
If you do try the game and find some aspect not to your liking, good news, the developers  actually listen, and work tirelessly to improve the games they develop.  The community forum that they run is also fantastic because no question bad or trivial.  Learn from other players and get advice directly from the developers!

At first glance this seems to be a very simple 4X game. And while it's true that the interface, graphics, and sound are extremely simple, the game does offer a competent AI, in-depth gameplay, and its own unique twists to the formula.
If you're in the market for a simple 4X game, Star Traders delivers.
The one major missing feature which more complex games do have is a notification system. While ST4X does have advisers and alerts which can tell you if a production on a planet is complete, it will not alert you if the queue is now empty. Likewise ships require fuel which automatically is restored in owned (green) territory, but it will not alert you when a ship is beginning to run out. Thus it requires you to constantly keep track of production queues and ship capabilities.
That minor issue aside, ST4X definitely has the depth you want from a title like this, and the fact that it is a relatively simple game and of course turn based, like all 4X games, means it can easily be played on the side while you do something else.

I started playing SMITE during their beta phase, I played both LoL and Smite for quite some time but ultimately sticking with League just because most of my friends didn't want to make the switch to SMITE at that time even though I did.
Let me put it that way:
From a pure gaming standpoint: Is it "better" than League? No. It's not as well thought through into the last detail, it's not quite as balanced and tactical decisions are not as deep and impactful as in other MOBAs.
From an aesthetic standpoint: Is it better than League? No. Riot has better artists than Hi-Rez. Hands down.
Is it more fun to play SMITE than any other MOBA? Absolutely.
Why? Well,
1) The community isn't quite as toxic as in League or other MOBAs I have played. Sure I have been wished to get cancer and been asked to deinstall the game, but the density of REALLY badly behaved players is lower than in other games of that genre.
2) Community support. Riot please! While it is sometimes hard to understand the decisions of other game companies and how they treat their communities, HiRez is doing a pretty good job giving the players what they want.
3) Diversity: While Riot announces "featured game modes" a month before they come out and then have them run for two weeks and make a whole fuzz about it, there is a new featured game mode every couple of days in SMITE, usually suggested by the community via Twitter. Remember when millions of players wanted the "ultra-rapid-fire mode" in League back and had to beg in every way shape and form for a whole year before Riot made it available again for 2 weeks? Yeah ... with HiRez you just tweet them...
Summary: If you are sick of the community and poor support in League of Legends, this game is for you.

Less toxic, more action packed and more skilled based then other M.O.B.A.'s out there. I'm looking at you League of Legends.

I went into this purchase feeling optimistic and filled with nostalgia from when I used to play MW2 with all of my high school friends. It reminded me a lot of that - in fact, a little bit too much.
Call of Duty needs to give everyone a little victory. This means that, even if you take the time to become good at the game, you'll only do marginally better than somebody else. The maps are too small to incorporate any real strategy (other than keeping mental notes of spawn points). Anyone running around with a shotgun or an SMG has a good chance of being able to kill you. Because everyone dies so quickly, if an enemy sees your back, you're dead. There's more maneuverability, but it's largely overrated. The maps are slightly more vertical but they still fall victim to CoD map tropes. They all feel like the exact same map, except they differ in how unfun they are. Also, the killstreaks just feel so neutered. They're useless!
Speaking of useless, the devs didn't spend any time balancing weapons. I'll save you time; the strongest gun this time around is the BAL-27. It's an assault rifle, unsurprisingly. If you use anything else, you're automatically at a disadvantage. Although the callsigns encourage you to do novel things, that's the only real reward, and it's usually just arbitrarily done. For instance, there's one callsign for getting 200 kills with primary weapons with 2 attachments, and another callsign for getting 200 kills with secondary weapons with 2 attachments. The first one is monumentally easier, because there's a more varied selection of primary weapons, some of them are really effective, and you generally have a choice of attachments that will satisfy the 2-attachment rule. Secondaries, however...none of the secondaries are good. They deal virtually no damage, have very little range, and are just a pain to use. Moreover, some attachments cancel other ones out. For some reason, you can't use akimbo pistols with laser sights (even though you can do that with primaries). It'd make the most sense, as akimbo is hip-fire only, and laser sights increase hip-fire accuracy. No, instead the only valid two attachment setup is akimbo and silencer. Akimbo ruins your accuracy, and silencer drastically reduces your damage and range. It's literally the worst combo for a weak secondary. Nobody took this into account at any point.
In a nutshell, that's the game's balance. There are plenty more things like that that prove very little testing was done in the three year development cycle that they had.
Oh, and the exosuit - the big claim of this entry? It's OK. It gives you some more options in how you play, and it does as if you have more freedom of movement, but it literally doesn't matter when you gracefully navigate the claustrophobic maps only to die from three BAL shots.
Also, Sledgehammer (that's the dev this time IIRC, they're all the same anyway) doesn't care about improving their netcode. It's terrible. It's not getting any better.

After playing for six hours (with more to come) here's my revised review.
Note that this is a review treating the game as a larger part of the Alien Canon, as licenced by Fox. Meaning that it's being looked at taking the books, comics, movies, etc. into account, as the game was made under the Fox license.
I am VERY impressed by the design of the game. They fulfilled all my exceptions of the Lo-fi sci-fi environment they promised.
They have this filter on the game by default that subtly adds that static effect you'd get on an old CRT monitor and/or an old CRT TV. It hits the nostalgia VERY well. It holds the modern graphics, modern physics, and modern mechanics while giving it a very nice classical feel to it.
Exploring the entryway you see a handheld that looks like an old SNES controller with a screen on it. It's managed to encapsulate the whole 70's vision of the future VERY well. They hit it spot on by designing everything only in a manner that could be replicated on set of the original Alien movie.
There's the loading bar when you use a terminal, and many other things that were accepted in the late 70's/early 80's that were just accepted as part of the territory, which adds to the ambiance even more. The Xenomorph is a standard Xenomorph drone, and the AI behind it was phenominal.
Now for the only issue I see with the game. The lore and justification behind it. Yes, CA said they wanted to base the alien off of the original Alien movie, and yes they did say they wanted only one.  Therein lies the problem. You, as Ripley's daughter arrive on the space station Sevastopol after the Xenomorph has been onboard for quite some time. Even the original Nostromo Xenomorph took Dallas and Brett's body into the air shafts to create more Xenomorphs, as is customary for the Drone caste to do.
In the absence of a Queen, a Drone possesses the ability to create a complete reproductive life cycle that did not require a Queen to lay more Eggs. Rather, the Drone would cocoon a victim in its Hive, and the victim would subsequently be changed by unknown means into a new Egg containing a Facehugger. Footage of this process was shot for Alien, although it was later removed from the final print of the film. The sequence was, however, included in the novelization of the film, and the movie footage was subsequently reintegrated in the 2003 Director's Cut. Note that this is Alien, not Aliens. Meaning that the reproductive cycle is outlined in the original film, that the game should be based upon.
The entire process  would only take a few days at absolute most, meaning that there SHOULD be more Xenomorphs on the station, as they're a very hive oriented species, with reproduction being very high on the list of priorities. They should also be extrordinarily flammable and should be able to be killed by fire at the very least, although ultimately I do think the Xenomorph should be able to be killed anyways in the game. I see why CA did what they did, and they said what they want, but the Alien fan in me has a hard time following their attempted rationalization when so much of the pre-established source material, even the original Alien film, speaks against it. They used aspects of the Alien, but they ignored alot of what makes it THE Alien, and that's the only part of the game where they really fell short.
The game is fantastic, as an Alien game, it's better than most. For nerds like myself who love the entirety of the lore, there are some moments where CA sacrificed continuity for gameplay, which ultimately comes down to your own preferences. I could see why they did it, and the resulting gameplay is utterly astounding. With Dan Abnett onboard, I think they could have gone farther than they did. I don't feel that this is the ultimate Alien game, or that it's the best we'll get, but it's definitely a step in the right direction. Creative assembly made an astounding game, with solid gameplay, which resulted in an utterly superior survival horror experience. It was a shakey ride as far as the lore went, so that's the only area I can truly deduct a point from.
Overall, this game is a 9/10. I'll be playing it again and don't regret buying it.

Even if I ignore how awful the keyboard and mouse controls are, or the fact that invincibility frames and parrying are tied to your framefrate, the game is still not as good as the first Dark Souls. Enemies track, and some have infinite stamina. You'll have enemies rising from pits that, if you were to knock them back into, would kill them immediately. The coherent and connected world of Dark Souls is gone and now you get areas that can either be summed up as "That one area from Dark Souls but..." or it's an actually interesting area and it's extremely short, linear, and doesn't make any geographical sense. The story doesn't make any sense. If you wanted explanations for most things from Dark Souls, you could go read item descriptions and talk to NPCs. In Dark Souls 2, it's just a mess, just a huge mess. You start off seeking a cure, that falls through, so now you're off to be king? Being forced to talk to Emerald Herald to level up sucks too. It gives the feeling that the game is letting you level up instead of you just becoming stronger through your own experience, and no being able to teleport doesn't make up for that. In fact teleportation just allowed the B team to be even lazier with level design. Almost everywhere is extremely linear, at the most, one linear path branches off into 3 other linear paths.
I played this beginning to end and all I have to show for it is dissappointment by how close to being a decent game it is. They didn't have the old director involved in this and it shows. The games aren't about being hard, they're about being rewarding and fair, which requires challenge, not precognition. I went into this knowing about some of it's problems, but I loved the first Dark Souls and wanted more so badly that I thought "Even if all the little acts of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t add up too much, it'll still be mostly good." It wasn't worth it. If you're dead set on getting into the Souls Series and don't mind the fact that armor is entirely useless and that shields and poise are too, then play this one first, because not only will you rarely be invaded and have plenty of time to learn the basic gist of the combat system but because every other Souls game will be a major improvement in comparison. I could go on and on about everylittle thing they messed up in this game, but a general summary for Dark Souls 2 would be "One step forward, two steps back."

Best MMO in a long time.
+ No subscription fees. (compared to other MMOs)
+ Offers a lot to explore and try out. (compared to other MMOs)
+ PVP is engaging. (compared to other MMOs with the exception of GW2)
+ You don't scale down to low level when you visit old areas. (compared to GW2)
+ Using melee weapons is more responsive and less hack and slash. (compared to Skyrim)
+ Playing with friends (compared to Elder Scrolls)
+ Crafting system
+ Guild system and guild shops
+ Voice acting
- Theft and murdering npcs makes it feel more like a GTA sometimes rather than Elder Scrolls when you see a pack of player-bandits battling city guards. (compared to save-load in Elder Scrolls)
- The item shop doesn't offer anything worth interest. (compared to other subscriptionless MMOs)
- Skill system made me feel a bit overwhelmed since extensive googling didn't give me an answer on what is the "best" build since there are so many ways to build your character. (compared to other MMOs)
- Using skills requires you to aim. (compared to other MMOs)
But many of my points can be considered bad and good depending on your own view. ESO can be considered great MMO and good Elder Scrolls game. Or bad Elder Scrolls game and fine MMO.
For example I believe part of what made Skyrim so great experience for me was the fact that there was no one else to judge me, my choices or the way I play and I had no one to compare yourself to. So "Playing with friends" could also be taken as a serious negative side. But that's what you get when you play MMO and you should expect it.
PS. Oh and if you read reviews. Try to filter out those which are older than a few months. I found out that rather many of the reviews point out old information. I've noticed a huge amount of changes from beta to a few months ago to now. Pretty much anything older than 4 months is seriously outdated and everyone older than a few weeks keep pointing out that this had a subscription.

Masomenos como un DAYZ o un H1Z1, y este juego medio que reunia esas caracteristicas, asi que con los pibes le dimos una chance. Primera vez que jugabamos, nos matan unos VIRGACHOS de origen Ruso con cuenta premium, que le habian gastado toda la tarjeta de credito al viejo para gastar guita en esta poronga de juego que realmente no se merecia ni un "yyyyy...mira esta masomenos bueno tu emprendimiento".
La movida del juego igualmente medio que nos gusto y terminamos dandole mas pelota de lo que se merecia este juego, al punto donde terminamos entendiendo como carajo jugarlo. La cosa siguio bien, hicimos nuestro mega sucucho que era como la villa 31 plasmada en este juego rancio, ubicada justito en Forsaken Fort (una parte del mapa del juego) que era un punto bastante estrategico y teniamos buena relacion con los jugadores latinoamericanos que regularmente jugaban al juego (exceptuando Brasileros). Al otro dia, cae una actualizacion que cayo como si te clavaran una papita como la de los cumpleaños en el medio del higado, nos dimos cuenta que no habia mas construccion de bases para jugadores con cuenta no premium y que si querias jugar como en los viejos tiempos tenias que pagar como 20us$ en tapitas para el Garraham. I've played ESO for a while. Coming from playing TES: IV Oblivion as my first Elder Scroll's game, The Elder Scroll's Online feels EXACTLY like how you would want an Elder Scroll's MMO.
Combat is very good. It feels fun. It's not clunky, it's not overly complicated, and any situation can be treated any way a player might want. I've been able to stealth through dungeons AND storm in brandishing a giant hammer smacking around anything in my path with power attacks. It feel just like any other TES game. You left click to swing your weapon or fire your bow/staff, you hold left click to use a power attack with any weapon (Staffs have power attacks,) and you hold right click to block. The ONLY diffrence from any other TES game is the fact that power attacks don't use stamina. Instead, you have to make the choice between using quicker normal attacks or more damaging power attacks that leave you open.
Questing feel JUST like any TES game. The stores are good, the exploration is great, and the rewards are perfect.
(POSSIBLE SPOILERS AHEAD)
One of your first quests if you choose to ally yourself with the Ebonheart Pact has you going around talking to a number of mages. The Dunmer mages want to trap the ghosts around the battlefield and use them in the war as tools. The Argonian mage wants you to help her set the ghosts free so they can heal the land that the war is taking place on. I went with the Argonian's option, and the Argonians ended up sacrificing themselves to become one with the land in order to heal the land with their spirits. The story was really awesome and you actually get to see a lot of the "Druid" like aspects of Argonian magic.
(END OF SPOILERS)
Over-all. This is a great game. Play it if you're a fan of The Elder Scrolls.

Performance and visuals:
I don't know how, but this game looks and runs worse than the first dishonored, released in 2012. While the optimization problems AND ♥♥♥♥ING FRAMERATE DEPENDENT MOUSE MOVEMENT have been fixed somewhat in the beta patch, visual bugs and artifacting draw you out of the game and ruins immersion. Pop in rendering when rounding corners or turing around quickly, awful aliasing that appears on sharp shiny surfaces up close, (no matter what option you use for anti-aliasing) and worse aliasing on distant objects. Options for AA include low and high FXAA, which does little to nothing to help visuals, and TXAA, which fixes some of the aliasing problems, but makes the screen appear as if it's been smeared with vaseline, and arguably looks worse. Such a lazy way to hide aliasing. Even more bizarre is frame rate feeling jittery and choppy despite running at 60+fps. V-sync helps this marginally, but causes noticable input lag, as expected.
Gameplay:
If you've playled the first Dishonored, the gameplay feels very much the same, but somethings feel slowed down and cumbersome. For example:
*Peeping through keyholes feels like it takes twice as long as it needs to because of an animation
*The game has no options for leaning and sprinting and instead locks both on toggle, sprint of which is even more frustrating, as it actually requires you to stop moving to toggle of sprinting, and not by pressing the sprint button again.
*Picking up bodies takes about one second of holding the interact button. Not once did I pick up a body in the first game by accident. I don't need one second to make sure I don't accidentally pick up a body.
Those are minor complaints, but the UI is even worse:
*The font is garbage it might as well be cursive because of how thin, stylized and hard to read it is.
*The way the UI is animated when it pops in, like when bringing up a yes/no prompt to save, makes you wait to click on it because it's tilting on the ♥♥♥♥ing screan. Feels like the UI was designed more for consoles.
*Menus take ages to bring up. More than one second to open the pause menu, and about the same time to open up the equiptment radial menu, which---
*Is not a radial menu, as it does not put your mouse in the center for you. It instead lets the mouse move freely when you're looking around in game, and then unhides the mouse when you bring up the menu, putting it in a seemingly random place everytime. Because of this I just stopped using it, and it stead hotkeyed Items to the number row (which actually, I really like, as it's customizable in the radial menu by pressing the respective number while mousing over equiptment or abilities.
As for story, I haven't gotten very far, so I can't say if it's worthwhile. Overall though, it does seem like a good game, but I just don't recommend it in it's current state. More patches are on their way, and I would definitely recommend it when some of these problems are fixed.

The Good:
-Graphics are much improved.
-The number of interactable, and summonable NPCs have been increased.  Some have plots that last the whole game.
-Covenant rewards are much better than the first game.
The Bad:
-One of the worst gameplay mechanics ever concieved in Soul Memory. A hilariously bloated 41 multiplayer tiers which all but guarantee sparse, if any, invasions from 3 out of the 6 pvp covenants your first time through the game.  This is not, in any way shape or form, a good thing.
-Finite red/blue orbs in New Game which contributes to the problem above.  NG+ and up you can buy invasion orbs for 10k souls a piece. Oof.
-Ill-concieved world design. Elevators go up that should go down.  Disjointed level-connects that make no sense.
-Experimentation is punished.  Finite upgrade materials to start with mean you are pigeonholed into one weapon for the majority of your playthrough.  Some upgrade mechanics, and basic upgrade materials are only unlocked much too far into the game.
Overall it's a pretty major disappointment.  I mean, I'll probably play it a hundered hours or so, but that is 1/9th the amount of time I spent in the original Dark Souls.  Wait until it goes on sale.

is an excellent game and continues to show why From Software stands out from the crowd, while falling short of their previous game.
Firstly I want to say how well Dark Souls 2 runs on PC, buttery smooth framerate the whole way through and the game Alt + Tabs like a champion, which is always worth mentioning. It still looks like a PC game from past decade, but fancy graphics isn't why you play these games.
As much as I hate to say it, the core gameplay is a slight downgrade from the previous game. Some don't like the floaty movement, I'm indifferent about it. What I do have a problem with, is the botched hitboxing and bad i-frames sometimes resulting in unfair damage, which is not cool in a game like this ...and frankly incomprehensible when they had it just right in the last game.
The previous Souls games have been great at rewarding exploration and Dark Souls 2 is no different. There is a ton of content to discover and your first playthrough will probably clock a little under 60 hours. DaS 2 feels quite linear and the level design does not weave together as brilliantly as in the previous game.
From Software has superb art direction in their games. Though after Demon's Souls and Dark Souls 1, many of the places in DaS 2 feel samey and uninspiring, others like the hub area Majula are breathtaking vistas that demand you to stop and just look at them. Motoi Sakuraba has returned to compose a solid soundtrack for the game and his exquisite work make places like Majula truly memorable.
The Souls games were never straight forward with their lore but unlike Lordran, I didn't much care what went down in Drangleic as I made my way from an uninspired boss fight to another predictable boss. In the end I was left with only one memorable fight,
...I got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked over and over and it was great when I finally beat her. I wanted more of that, but after watching the credits roll, I was still waiting for that special boss fight.
I have mixed feelings about the covenants. I liked how invading worked in Dark Souls, how someone could surprise me when I least expected it. In this game I never got invaded once, apart from getting gangbanged in dedicated griefing areas. The bulk of the PvP is dueling, which can be fun for a while but quickly gets infuriating when you get unjustly backstabbed due to lag. Co-oping and helping others through difficult times has its own rewards but soon you might not be able to do it anymore thanks to 'Soul Memory'.
Following the pre-release statements saying the game would be made to 'appeal to a wider audience', many feared it would lose its Soul. Some changes were made as a lubricant to ease new players into the game, but luckily nothing too drastic. These changes include the likes of more item descriptions, the ability to fast travel back and forth as soon as you discover new bonfires and being able to deplete enemies from areas after killing them enough times. I think the 'improved' item descriptions are a welcome addition but the problematic 'Soul Memory' system, not so much.
- Amount of content
- Retains the Soul of the series
- Framerate
- Soundtrack
- Majula
- Lore/World
- Linearity
- Floaty movement
- Covenants
- Fast Travel
- Boss fights
- Level design
- Soul Memory
- Enemy depletion
- Botched hitboxing and bad i-frames
- Minor PvP lag
I liked my time with Dark Souls 2 but I would recommend the previous game over this one in a heartbeat.

I've played ESO for a while. Coming from playing TES: IV Oblivion as my first Elder Scroll's game, The Elder Scroll's Online feels EXACTLY like how you would want an Elder Scroll's MMO.
Combat is very good. It feels fun. It's not clunky, it's not overly complicated, and any situation can be treated any way a player might want. I've been able to stealth through dungeons AND storm in brandishing a giant hammer smacking around anything in my path with power attacks. It feel just like any other TES game. You left click to swing your weapon or fire your bow/staff, you hold left click to use a power attack with any weapon (Staffs have power attacks,) and you hold right click to block. The ONLY diffrence from any other TES game is the fact that power attacks don't use stamina. Instead, you have to make the choice between using quicker normal attacks or more damaging power attacks that leave you open.
Questing feel JUST like any TES game. The stores are good, the exploration is great, and the rewards are perfect.
(POSSIBLE SPOILERS AHEAD)
One of your first quests if you choose to ally yourself with the Ebonheart Pact has you going around talking to a number of mages. The Dunmer mages want to trap the ghosts around the battlefield and use them in the war as tools. The Argonian mage wants you to help her set the ghosts free so they can heal the land that the war is taking place on. I went with the Argonian's option, and the Argonians ended up sacrificing themselves to become one with the land in order to heal the land with their spirits. The story was really awesome and you actually get to see a lot of the "Druid" like aspects of Argonian magic.
(END OF SPOILERS)
Over-all. This is a great game. Play it if you're a fan of The Elder Scrolls.

This game is absolutely great so far.  Summarized concisely, it has tight controls, fast play(completing a tough level might take five minutes max), seizure-inducing particle effects, clever puns, satirizes Amurican war culture, and seems like a labor of love on the part of its developers.
In my opinion, it isn't playing through the single player campaign that shows the finished game's potential, but the custom campaigns that players make.  What is important about the custom campaigns is that they show how difficult the game can become and often give a better idea of what the game's engine is like.  To give an example of the latter in case jargon is being used wrong, there are weird custom campaigns that could be described as hardcore platforming objective-based puzzles, where attacking is impossible for one reason or another. Hypothetically, even if all of Broforce's devs vanished off of the face of the planet, I could still fire-up steam and play new custom campaigns daily that are often really awesome and hard.
The only things that really get me down when I play is that levels are seldom long enough for my taste and a few characters are *currently* too limited by their mechanics for my taste.

After receiving the still persisting development for just passed a decade and being one of the first titles to be given the Steam Greenlight, it's now finally here in an Early Access build. So the first question most would surely be asking is; "What's the difference between the mod release I can still get, and the Early Access build?"
Well, this official press kit should enlighten you:
If you can't view the contents of the link, I'll list it here for you:
In summary, you're getting the same as the mod release now with online ready multiplayer, fully integrated Steam Workshop & other Steam specific features, with the addition of improvements in audio, visuals & game stability for single-player.
What I can personally vouch for with my time with it is that the weapon audio has been given welcome improvement where needed & the animations have been drastically expanded upon, improved and/or even reworked (Especially the Crowbar), with initial pick-up animations for weapons that didn't have them and half-mag & full-mag reload animations too. And there are new voice actors whom have joined the existing cast, which fans of certain existing third-party Source games should recognise fondly.
For anyone that previously enjoyed the Black Mesa mod like myself or is keen to enjoy themselves another Half Life experience, this is extremely recommendable from myself. And with the benefit of having the free mod still available, you have the chance to evaluate for yourself if this is something you want to jump into during Early Access.

I'll admit that rally games are my guilty pleasure.  Most feature mushy controls, daft physics or ridiculously undamageable cars.  this has none of those.  The controls are crisp, the physics moderately good, and cars which will fly apart satisfyingly when you ram into a building or errant rock.   The career feature is quite well done, leaving you to decide which cars to buy to win certain races.  It does have relatively few maps (4 maybe?), but  a lot of variety of tracks round them keep things moderately interesting.  Stability-wise, there were very few glitches (I can count them on one hand, after months of play). The car addons actually feel like they're making a difference, and strategic part and tyre-selection can make an impossible stage remarkably enjoyable.
The games's only main downside is the repetitiveness.  Only four 'areas', means you get to race the same track over and over in different directions and different combinations of bits.  The openness of the career path does also lead to you making bad choices when purchasing cars and add-ons from time to time.   That means you must  race the same race 10x in a row to get the money to afford the thing you should have bought instead.    The only other small downside is the micro-stutter which occurs when a texture or sound is first loaded.  That can cause you to spin out, or miss a corner (e.g. when the game first loads the copilot voice for that corner).  A quick reload, and it doesn't happen there again.   Other than these small niggles, the game is notably bug and hassle-free.
I recommend anyone who likes Rally games to play this.. It's got satisfaction value in spades, and while it's not as polished as Colin Macrae, I think in some areas it beats it (blasphemy!!) :-)

TESO tries to bring the epic feeling of The Elder Scrolls singleplayer games to a massively multiplayer univerese.
The result unfortunately is neither a good Elder Scrolls Singleplayer game, nor a good MMORPG.
In trying to cater to both markets the game dilutes each genre to the point neither side of the game is particularly fun.
From an Elder Scrolls point of view questing is linear, mundane and non organic. You get the typical MMO style of hubs, with packs of mobs standing around waiting for you to attack them. The story is not very engaging and the cliché repetitive nature of mmorpg shopping list questing comes into play.
From an MMORPG point of view the game feels like a shell. No nameplates, poor communication options and a lack of social tools all make the game feel like it was designed from the ground up for consoles. The dungeons are boring, the PvP leave much to be desired and your actions feel like they have little impact.
All in all the game is a solid 5/10 as buy2play. Quite frankly you should save your money.

Re-reviewing after spending more time and getting used to things.
CONS:
—The big one is the performance issues. With a 1060 gpu and i7 cpu I personally haven't notived many issues, though there are framerate dips in the between mission city areas. However, it seems every other negative review is due to performance issues so hopefully something is done soon.
The rest are minor quality-of-life gripes that if fixed would improve things a lot.
—Lean/peek is toggle now instead of hold, which is a major inconvenience when one peeks around every bend.
—You can be seen when leaning/peeking, contrary to the lean feature's behaviour in Dishonored 1, and also defying the in-game tips which state you can't be seen while peeking.
—Upon loading screens, you press Enter instead of any key to continue. As someone who tries different approaches and quickloads every other minute, this is just an inconvenience. Dishononored 1's miniscule load times and click to continue approach was so fluid that you could quickload and get back in a second.
—Not so much a con, but the movement and controls felt a bit different at first, not as smooth as Dishonored 1's. Possibly performance related? It took a while to get used to but when you do it's fine.
PROS:
—The new powers, and the branching upgrade paths are an excellent addition to the game. Emily and Corvo both feel different and fun to play. Corvo has a slew of upgrades to breathe new life into his moveset, while Emily boasts an array of brand new and interesting powers.
—Alongside this, there are new moves to add variety in combat - the grab/throw feature is a whole lotta fun if you like tossing people off ledges or into furniture. There are more non-lethal methods available, allowing you to drop-KO people, or choke-hold even when in combat. New gadgets as well, such as stun mines and sting darts.
—Subtle graphical details like true reflections in shiny surfaces and mirrors, actually reflecting the room they are in and not some stock reflection image.
—The game itself, the story and characters and world are all wonderful and intriguing. That is one area where (so far, and in my experience) Dishonored 2 has not disappointed.
Price tag is still too high in my opinion (100 NZD, yikes) but if you can get it cheaper and you loved Dishonored 1, I would recommend.

UPD: Performance patch released! Now the game works much better. After finishing the game I will edit this review last time to share my full opinion about the game.

Firstly, I would like to start off by saying that I was one of the seemingly few people that didn't have too many performance issues. That being said, I will be reviewing this game based on MY experiences only.
So first off, lets address the performance issues. For me, The performance was ok until I hit the main city, but after searching a bit, I found a fix for NVidia users to basically disable Nvidia's unoptimized turd known as Ansel. This boosted my performance massively by 30-40 more fps. For a while, the Mouse Input was absolutely horrible, however with the new beta patch, it has been pretty normal. Arkane should be putting out a performance patch in the coming weeks, as well as adding New Game+ and other features. That's pretty much it for the performance side, runs pretty well for me on the following specs:
i7 6700k
16 GB DDR4 RAM
EVGA GTX 1080 FTW
(Using 1080p monitor, so I can't speak for performance on 1440p)
Alright, now for the actual game. The short answer is: this game is a ♥♥♥♥ing masterpiece. The story, in my opinion, was fantastic. I feel that this was one of the few games that lived up to its predecesor. Couple the story with amazing level design, and you have yourself a fantastic game. Not only is the game good, it also looks like a painting. The art design team really out did themselves, and how Dishonored 2 wasn't nominated for GOTY in Art Design is beyond me. Similarly to the first game, Dishonored 2 has insane replayability value. Since you can play as both Emily and Corvo, you essentially get 2 playthroughs (thats not including low chaos, high chaos, no kill, etc playthroughs). If I recall, Polygon complained that Dishonored 2 had horrible voice acting. In my opinion, the voice acting was nowhere near horrible. Infact, I rather enjoyed the majority of it. It's nice that Corvo finally has a voice actor so you are no longer a silent protagonist, even if Corvo says some pretty obvious♥♥♥♥♥♥sometimes. Another thing that really stood out to me in Dishonred 2 was the combat. Somehow they managed to make Dishonored's combat even better. The gore is also 10x better than the first game. Skillwise, Corvo's skills are identical to the original game's skills, with some new upgrades. I cannot speak to Emily's skills as I have not done a playthrough with her yet.
Overall, I feel that Arkane did a really good job on this game, but was ♥♥♥♥ed over by Bethesda pushing for their release date. Quite a shame that the game had to suffer a terrible launch because of an overzealous publisher.

I paid about $2.99 for the game and I have about 9 hours on it.
Although there are many zombie games that involve base-building and scavenging supplies out there, Survivalist still remains a unique and enjoyable game to play.
One problem, as you can guess from my relatively short time spent in this game, is replayability.  For the $3 that I paid I wouldn't penalise the game too much, but sadly once you're done with the game then there isn't much of a purpose to come back to it.  Most missions can only be completed in pretty much the same way.  The towns and resources are all pre-set (as far as I can tell), not dynamically generated, so exploration isn't a draw.
Because of the lack of replay value, the game's limited time for a playthrough is also puzzling.  One character in the game has a medical condition and is reliant on a constant supply of medication.  This forces the player to complete the game within a certain timeframe as the supply is limited.  While certainly such a mechanic introduces urgency, it also serves to shorten the game.  I would have preferred the option to build and explore, instead of being so rushed.
But Survivalist does some things very well.  Exploration is actually interesting, with towns being varied enough to make cars and houses worthwhile to explore.  You find things where you would reasonably expect them, such as water from a water tower (duh).  There is also an automated retrival system, where you can use NPCs you recruit to haul supplies back for you.  This offers a nice solution to the tedious task of resource retrival that other zombie survival games fall short on.
NPCs are probably another strong feature of Survivalist.  Whereas most other games of the genre simply feature the sole survivor versus other zombies, Survivalist gives you NPC helpers.  Some of them are decently fleshed out and created, while others have no significant backstory.  The presence of NPCs helping you out makes for a much more interesting game, because it allows for an actualy plot beyond "don't get eaten".  Getting a quick message from a NPC that they are being attacked will cause me to drop what I'm doing and sprint back to base, because I sort of actually care about what happens to them.
Co-op play is another area that has been getting more attention from the Devs.  I tried one session, which was okay.  Dropped in and took over a character.  Started running off to find supplies for the base.  Played for maybe half an hour until the other person logged off.  It's still not a very deep system and because I couldn't figure out how to communicate with the other player (say to figure out which resources I ought to be collecting) it was rather strange.
Overall, Survivalist seems like a great work-in-progress game that (very importantly) carries a price like a work-in-progress game.  Although the content could be expanded, the underlying concept is fun and solid.

I didn't play Colonial Marines, so I didn't have any positive or negative expectations for another game in the same universe.
I was going into this game very fresh. A lot of the references have gone way over my head because, while I've watched the original movie, I'm not some die hard fan. (I'm assuming that's going to put the feedback of my review at some arbitrary disadvantage). So let's be clear, I'm looking at this game as a game. Not something based off of a movie series.
With that out of the way, how do I like the game?
First off, the atmosphere can drown you. The sound is absolutely perfect, especially if you have a sound system capable of taking advantage of the excellent mixing. Sounds echo and boom where appropriate, and on louder volumes you get this perfect sense of sound immersion as you hear footsteps and voices from varying distances and directions. I feel like this is one of the first games to truly make use of my 7.1 surround sound headset.
Visually the game looks very nice. There is a lovingly crafted amount of detail in everything with trash littering the floor and tables, CRT monitors blinking and humming all around you, metallic floors reflecting light and objects, and just enough other visual details that cue you in on what might have happened here before you got there.
Gameplay is slightly hit or miss with me personally however. I understand, it's difficult to balance gameplay, especially combat, in horror games like this. On one hand, you want the player to feel terrified at the right moments, where they feel helpless and get that rush of fear and adrenaline that they sought out to feel in the first place. One the other, you don't want the player to feel too overwhelmed, and eventually frustrated enough to quit playing the game by constantly making them fail no matter how hard they try. Alien: Isolation is one of those games that really does try to balance it, and the success of this depends on your patience.
If you were hoping to get through this game with only a couple deaths and that's it, don't bother. Even on medium difficulty, enemies will spot you easily even in the dark, and shoot at you despite you sprinting diagonally further away from them. That's the only enemies that have this problem though, the humans with the guns, particularly in the segments where you're forced to stealth around them or they will shoot you on sight. This happens a couple times early on, and until you truly learn the way stealth works in this game, you'll probably die more than a few times to those same people.
However, humans are easy to kill early in the game. Just sprint at them from a corner and tap the melee buttons with two swings and they go down. And that's on the hardest difficulty. I was able to clear a whole large room by doing that.
That's the extent of the combat really. So far I've found you get a tool, a revolver, and eventually other items like a flamethrower, but each is both effective and ineffective in their own way. The melee weapon won't always work, the gun won't always work, your other items won't always work. That's what makes this a survival horror game. Not everything is in your favor. Nothing in this game likes you.
Other enemies I've encountered will just chase you down (sometimes rather slowly) until you enter a hiding spot, in which they may or may not instantly find you in that particular spot. It instantly reminded me of Outlast in that respect.
There are crafting elements, which are easy to understand. There's a handy little motion tracker, which will often save you from running straight into a partolling enemy you couldn't hear or see otherwise.
The Alien itself is obviously terrifying. Don't get me started on the booming footsteps of the alien when it spots you hunting you down as you desperately try to sprint away regreting every choice you've made. As you've probably already heard, you can't kill it. You can only stun it, or scare it off temporarily, even with freaking fire right in its face. And there's only this one Alien, no others. It is the most constant threat in the game, where you know that no matter what it will continue to chase you down when it can, and it has no pity or mercy.
Honestly, I don't much care for the character I'm playing as. Like any good game, it doesn't matter that you're playing as a woman. She will still easily bash someones face in with a tool, and fire a gun to defend herself. Most of the time, you won't even notice unless you look straight down to see the bottom of your torso, or when she speaks. Otherwise you'll be too focused on surviving to even care, assuming you did in the first place.
Overall, Alien: Isolation is an immersive, theatric, gorgeous, well crafted survival game. I won't say it negatively impacts the game for myself, but it's fair to mention that the difficutly of this game will frustrate just about anyone. You'll be starting over at the same save points over and over again, slowly making your way through the area for the 4th time hoping the AI won't spot you again from above.
