Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: Much like the somewhat divisive impact Dark Souls' launch had on the Souls community, Dark Souls II has had an equally divisive presence. For a lot of the main gameplay dynamics, they remain largely unchanged. Combat is very weighty and feels great; the controls are excellent as ever, and the game is still pretty challenging. When I wrote a review for the Xbox 360 version, I gave it a then-unprecedented (for me) 10/10, and after playing through as a shieldless mage, I can't quite call it a 10/10 game. For starters, some of the bosses have... questionable hitboxes, at best. A few major offendors being the Giant Lord, the Lost Sinner, and the Ancient Dragon. These can, of course, be fixed with tweaks (as I can only assume is being done by the Calibrations version number in the upper right hand of the main menu), but they can still be very irritating nonetheless.
Another thing that I noticed in my NG and NG+ playthroughs is the sheer amount of one-hit-kills that this game has. Admittedly, the expectation is that you have upgraded your health throughout the game, and as such, the enemies should hit harder. However, in the aforementioned bosses that don't have the greatest hitboxes, this can be especially infuriating when you get one-shotted by an attack that was clearly a miss. A system in which any hit that would one-shot you (from let's say 75% of current capped health) would drop you to 1HP for a slight chance of recovery would be an excellent addition in my eyes.
Notice how in the last sentence that I said "capped health." This game goes more of a Demon's Souls route with death in which you gradually lose a portion of your maximum HP in human form, decreasing to 50% of your maximum potential health. At first I was vehemently against this feature (in fact, this is the main reason why I never wanted to play Demon's Souls in the first place), but I've grown to accept it as a worthwhile feature. Rather than just throwing yourself endlessly at an area, you are instead punished for being careless. This is also balanced out by the design choice of enemies disappearing after you kill them about 15 times.
The enemy placement is much smarter this time around than in Dark Souls, and the enemies themselves are especially nasty this time around. Rather than staring at you slack-jawed while you chugalug on your Estus, they'll recognize your state of weakness and go in for the kill. It can be a bit frustrating at times, but it soon subsides as you realize that it was your mistake healing and leaving yourself open. That is the very core of any Souls game: when you mess up, it's almost always because of a mistake you made; either out of a lack of observation or a very poor decision. Again, I say almost to include the kinda broken hitboxes of a few bosses.
Bosses overall are much better this time than in Dark Souls. I know that some people were disappointed that the bosses were, for the most part, "dudes in armor." I don't mind that as much, as the game is much more centered around humans this time around than it is about gods and demons.  Plus, the boss fights are (again, for the most part) much better than in Dark Souls 1; the core game at the very least. None of these bosses top the Artorias of the Abyss bosses, but that's a pretty high goal to reach anyways. Also, doing a little directory digging, I found a folder named DLC. Potential DLC in the future or possibly another high-calibur Artorias of the Abyss DLC? We'll just have to see.
For one of the highest quality adventures this year, despite a few minor technical niggles here and there, I'll give this game a 9.5/10 for gameplay.
Story: Much like Dark Souls 1, your involvement in the story is entirely dependent on you. Either you can regard it as a story where you go around killing mans for souls, or you can start digging in, finding yourself in as rich of a world (perhaps even richer) as Dark Souls 1. Of course, I am nowhere near going through all of the lore, but seeing just a few of VaatiVidya's videos, as well as my own personal experiences, lead me to believe that the lore will be both debated for a long time as well as being plentiful enough to fill a novella, at the very least. The surprise in the Cathedral of Blue was certainly enough of a conversation starter as is. I do realize that I've been somewhat ambiguous while talking about the story, but this was intentional. After all, one's involvement in the story only goes so far as their interest. I'm a very interested man, and from just what I've seen in lore, I feel confident in giving this game a perfect 10/10 for the story.
Graphics: Ho boy, this is where I talk about the discrepancy between the release copy and the E3 demo. Honestly, I'm not too annoyed by it. Why, you may ask? First off, the game still looks gorgeous as-is, with some of the best views in the game being in Aldia's Keep, Huntsman's Copse, and Heide's Tower of Flame. Second, HD texture packs are a thing. Also, I think someone will eventually do a mod for the torch, making it as integral to the gameplay as it was in the demo. The lighting engine is already there; it probably just needs some tweaking to get it to work as intended. Speaking of tweaks, just playing the launch copy from Steam leads me to say that this game could still use a few more tweaks. There's still some texture pop-in whenever you pan the camera and it's still kind of silly to see a spear go flying halfway across the map because the physics engine herp'd. Nevertheless, the game still looks gorgeous, and these technical things can be buffed out. Plus, the game ran flawlessly at 1080p max settings on my GTX 760, not topping 60degC once. For just a few minor technical quibbles, I give this game a 4.5/5 for the graphics.
Music: Motoi Sakuraba sure is a good composer. There was also a new guy on this time around as well (Yuka Kitamura). I'm not entirely sure who did what song, but given Sakuraba's contributions to the series, I can make good guesses. Kitamura probably composed some of the more ambient tracks, such as the Lost Sinner's theme and potentially Mytha's. Nevertheless, the soundtrack is still as excellent as the one from Dark Souls 1. The sound design is just as fantastic as well. For example, I missed so much of the ambiance of Black Gulch with my TV's crappy speakers (since I played DaSII on 360 first). Pretty much excellent all-around. 5/5.
Overall scores are: 9.5/10/4.5/5; total score of 9.7/10. Hey, that came out to the same exact score DaS1 had. Again, a lot of the things that I wasn't happy with can be fixed with patches and calibration updates. While I won't be playing this again for a few months, hopefully these issues are fixed. Maybe this game can reclaim its 10/10 from me.

Singleplayer is typical CoD, nothing special but fun enough to go trough. The multiplayer has to many issues making it more or less unplayable. There is the infamous lag, which seems standard in every CoD game, but there are more flaws in the mulitplayer which can be considered as design errors.
You can say that the maps are large enough but the unlimited sprint and the exo abilities makes the player move too fast for the size of the map to have decent spawns causing a lot of spawnkilling. Another consequence is that most kills are shots in the back.
Another huge design error is the inconsistent soundeffecs. It is unrealistic and undesirable that the footsteps and exo ability sounds of your teammates are louder than those of your enemies. An enemy can exo jump in the sky landing right behind you, walking to you and knife you in the back without hearing him.
Weapon balance is always a discussion in FPS but not in CoD AW. Most guns are just useless in the game. Most players use the same guns for the simple reason that there is no advantage using the others.
There is whole concept error in the design of the game. The developpers wants a different CoD game. They increased the pace of the game with the exo abilities and the unlimited sprint. The pace looks more like a Unreal Tournament or a Quake game. In those games it takes more bullets to kill a man, except for a sniper rifle. In CoD it takes three to four bullets to kill a man. The pace works in Unreal Tournament but not in CoD AW. If a developer choose for a FPS with realistic weapon damage and map design than the pace of the game should be developed according to it.
The result of the developers non ability to think trough about the concept is that skills are non existent in CoD AW.  Two players are facing each other with their guns. In a normal FPS the person with the fastest reaction time and aiming skills would win the shootout. Not in CoD AW. First there is the lag. Second, the person can be killed by someone spawning in his back. Third the person can be killed by someone knifing him in his back without hearing him because it is not possible to hear him. Fourth the other person can make an exo jump, forcing the person also to exo jump otherwise you are dead and then both players just spray on each other in the sky.
To conclude, is it a good FPS? No.

For PC, Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare takes what all other previous Call of Duty's were lacking and adds in that extra oomph.  Exceedingly well optimized for PC, a sprawling options menu and nice little touches like an FoV slider and shader caching really add to the brevity at which Sledgehammer has worked to make a legitimate PC Port. Between being an excellent PC port, legitimately good additions to the game-play and the single player/Co-Op being excellent as usual, it truly is hard to deny that this year's Call of Duty might just be worth the price.

I'm not going to give a traditional review of the game given that this game is 4 years old and many reviews have been done about it. Instead, I'm going to point out initial differences in how this game is different from Borderlands 1. This is all PvE, I didn't play with anybody in co-op mode.
I not only played 160 hours of Borderlands (two play-throughs, which I just completed as recently as two weeks ago) and about 115 hours of Borderlands 2, but I also played and completed those two games recently, so it's not like I'm trying to recall something from 4-5 years ago from either game. This is still (relatively) fresh in my memory.
(Positives):
+They did away with "weapon proficiency" that was in Borderlands to encourage people to use various gun types (repeater pistols, revolvers, submachine guns, combat rifles, shotguns, sniper rifles and rocket launchers). It worked. Instead of focusing on myself trying to level up my combat rifle (weapon proficiency) for my soldier in Borderlands, with my assassin in Borderlands 2, I was far more diverse and indiscriminate with my weapon choices.
+Incentive to sell the massive amounts of items (weapons, shields, grenades, etc.) you acquire, which didn't exist in Borderlands
+No shields that recharged ammo (that I came across) like in Borderlands, which almost felt like a cheat code and made ammo chests and vending machines irrelevant
+Enemies now get injured and exhibit injuries, either by stumbling when moving (humans/skag) or crawling on their hands and dragging themselves (robots)
+In the fast travel, they mark what region you're currently in, where your active mission's destination is (something they didn't show in Borderlands and that was commonly confusing) and the various missions that are situated in that region (if you have two or three or four missions in one region-useful if you want to knock out 2 or 3 or 4 mission in one sitting)
+Realistic "fight for your life" mode. If you've recently entered fight for your life mode for the second time, you have less of a chance of survival. This sounds like a drag, but it adds realism to the game/character
+(Minor) They brought back Fyrestone town for nostalgic purposes, even if I recently finished the first Borderlands, I like tie ins like that
+(Minor) Vehicle attacks are far more fun and less frustrating than in Borderlands 1. In the first one, things were so frustrating, I would often avoid vehicles and only attack them if they were mandatory as part of a mission, here, I've often attacked them if they've attacked me or just for the exp.
+Awesome final boss. This is how you do final bosses. I'm tired of the three phases boss where you kill somebody one time, they then evolve into something stronger, and then when you kill him a second time, he evolves into something even stronger and more annoying to kill or if you kill somebody one time and they come back later on, and Borderlands was guilty of this in the first Borderlands with General Knoxx. This time around, the final boss was definitely more fun and enjoyable to play against as an assassin
+REALLY GOOD value. I bought Borderlands 2 (GOTY edition) for $10. Just on the core game alone (haven't played the DLCs that come with GOTY, yet) I got 115 HOURS of play time! That's about 3-5 times as much gameplay as the first Borderlands core game.
+Definite replayability here. I played the first Borderlands, not once, but twice-fully. That's something I NEVER do, due to my ADHD and easily attainable boredom. The question here is do I continue leveling up my assassin and going over stories and missions I missed the first time or do I play a new character and try out their skills from the skill tree to see which character I enjoy more?
(Negatives):
-(Minor, and varied between PvE and Co-op) Not a big fan of the arenas. In Borderlands, they had 2 arenas, one for skags, the other for bandits. In Borderlands 2, they have 3 (bandits, species (skags/varkids) and robots)
-Game is harder/has a steeper climb towards the end of the game, even on the first mode (and that's with me doing all of the side missions/quests of my level to level up my character)
-Leveling isn't as advantageous/noticeable as in the first game (I admit, this could be due to my change in classes between the two games, for example, leveling up my soldier in Borderlands using "points" was more rewarding and meant more than it did with my assassin)
-(Minor) Not a fan of the tired "'yay, everything is going our way and let's be happy and cheery,' but then reality/hardship sets in as soon as someone says/expresses it" trope in stories in games, movies, tv, etc. Borderlands uses it a lot
*The one thing I would like to see from the Borderlands franchise is them develop towns. We saw them do that in New Haven and a little with Tartarus Station (DLC#4-Claptrap's New Robot Revolution). They also drew more on it in Borderlands 2 with Sanctuary. I would like to see a town that is as alive as Megaton from Fallout 3 was. And that game (FO3) predates the next installment of Borderlands by at least 8 years now, given that FO3 came out in 2008.
And I know it's going to feel like I'm FO3-centric by also mentioning this point, but I feel the franchise can be more sophisticated with in-game details. What I mean by that is, there are vast amounts of space in Borderlands 1 and 2, that are open and barren and that can be used to hide various in-game trinkets or items, etc.
I'm already a fan of this franchise, I trust them and their direction. And I'm definitely looking forward to also getting the Borderlands: Pre-sequel (hopefully once its on sale).

The download file is indeed massive, it's a large game. The updates are big, the game is big, even patches seem to be fairly large. So come into the game with the expectation you're going to spend a bit downloading before you can play. This should rule out about 50% of the negative reviews.
The other 30% of negative reviews come from a general theme of 'boring mmo'. As we all know, or at least should know, a lot of time and effort goes into the ambience of the Elder Scroll games. The small side stories, the heart, the emotion around the play. The entire game is like a massive novel, there is some reading to be done and a lot of voices to listen to. I would strongly suggest that for those of us who want to get involved with a great story and fantastic lore, play this game.
If you're looking to rush and skip all dialog and just run between point to point to grind missions of course it's going to be boring. You're purposely skipping the content just to level up. Don't do that, then say the game was boring because you purposely made it boring.
The reviews for graphics, gameplay, physics, etc are all great. The game feels like Skyrim and the other ES games and in my opinion does a great job of bringing it online.
In short don't let the 'mixed' reviews fool you. The true reviews are the positive ones. Most negative reviews focus only on the file size and how grinding is boring. Don't let those fool you.

Re-reviewing after spending more time and getting used to things.
CONS:
—The big one is the performance issues. With a 1060 gpu and i7 cpu I personally haven't notived many issues, though there are framerate dips in the between mission city areas. However, it seems every other negative review is due to performance issues so hopefully something is done soon.
The rest are minor quality-of-life gripes that if fixed would improve things a lot.
—Lean/peek is toggle now instead of hold, which is a major inconvenience when one peeks around every bend.
—You can be seen when leaning/peeking, contrary to the lean feature's behaviour in Dishonored 1, and also defying the in-game tips which state you can't be seen while peeking.
—Upon loading screens, you press Enter instead of any key to continue. As someone who tries different approaches and quickloads every other minute, this is just an inconvenience. Dishononored 1's miniscule load times and click to continue approach was so fluid that you could quickload and get back in a second.
—Not so much a con, but the movement and controls felt a bit different at first, not as smooth as Dishonored 1's. Possibly performance related? It took a while to get used to but when you do it's fine.
PROS:
—The new powers, and the branching upgrade paths are an excellent addition to the game. Emily and Corvo both feel different and fun to play. Corvo has a slew of upgrades to breathe new life into his moveset, while Emily boasts an array of brand new and interesting powers.
—Alongside this, there are new moves to add variety in combat - the grab/throw feature is a whole lotta fun if you like tossing people off ledges or into furniture. There are more non-lethal methods available, allowing you to drop-KO people, or choke-hold even when in combat. New gadgets as well, such as stun mines and sting darts.
—Subtle graphical details like true reflections in shiny surfaces and mirrors, actually reflecting the room they are in and not some stock reflection image.
—The game itself, the story and characters and world are all wonderful and intriguing. That is one area where (so far, and in my experience) Dishonored 2 has not disappointed.
Price tag is still too high in my opinion (100 NZD, yikes) but if you can get it cheaper and you loved Dishonored 1, I would recommend.

There are quite a few negative reviews, and they're all coming from people that were expecting it to be something that it wasn't planned to be. So many people expected this to be "Multiplayer Skyrim", which it isn't. I'm glad it isn't.
The combat flows very nicely, albeit the weapon swings and such aren't quite as smooth as skyrim, they are still good in their own right. The classes don't influence anything that you would see in skyrim, only the new skill sets, and you can mix and match all the different armor and weapon types no matter what class you are, none of it is restricted.
There have been complaints that it isn't rewarding, but rewards come as how you see them. I'm not saying that the quests are unrewarding, or that they are he most satisfying thing ever, but I still quite happy being able to talk to an NPC and tell them that I've finished something. In some cases, you can choose who you want to turn into, or what you want to say to them, and this adds a bit of variety, even potentially changing the story.
In conclusion, don't expect it to be the next Elder Scrolls game but with other players running around, and if you do that, it's quite the good and enjoyable game.

Firstly, I would like to start off by saying that I was one of the seemingly few people that didn't have too many performance issues. That being said, I will be reviewing this game based on MY experiences only.
So first off, lets address the performance issues. For me, The performance was ok until I hit the main city, but after searching a bit, I found a fix for NVidia users to basically disable Nvidia's unoptimized turd known as Ansel. This boosted my performance massively by 30-40 more fps. For a while, the Mouse Input was absolutely horrible, however with the new beta patch, it has been pretty normal. Arkane should be putting out a performance patch in the coming weeks, as well as adding New Game+ and other features. That's pretty much it for the performance side, runs pretty well for me on the following specs:
i7 6700k
16 GB DDR4 RAM
EVGA GTX 1080 FTW
(Using 1080p monitor, so I can't speak for performance on 1440p)
Alright, now for the actual game. The short answer is: this game is a ♥♥♥♥ing masterpiece. The story, in my opinion, was fantastic. I feel that this was one of the few games that lived up to its predecesor. Couple the story with amazing level design, and you have yourself a fantastic game. Not only is the game good, it also looks like a painting. The art design team really out did themselves, and how Dishonored 2 wasn't nominated for GOTY in Art Design is beyond me. Similarly to the first game, Dishonored 2 has insane replayability value. Since you can play as both Emily and Corvo, you essentially get 2 playthroughs (thats not including low chaos, high chaos, no kill, etc playthroughs). If I recall, Polygon complained that Dishonored 2 had horrible voice acting. In my opinion, the voice acting was nowhere near horrible. Infact, I rather enjoyed the majority of it. It's nice that Corvo finally has a voice actor so you are no longer a silent protagonist, even if Corvo says some pretty obvious♥♥♥♥♥♥sometimes. Another thing that really stood out to me in Dishonred 2 was the combat. Somehow they managed to make Dishonored's combat even better. The gore is also 10x better than the first game. Skillwise, Corvo's skills are identical to the original game's skills, with some new upgrades. I cannot speak to Emily's skills as I have not done a playthrough with her yet.
Overall, I feel that Arkane did a really good job on this game, but was ♥♥♥♥ed over by Bethesda pushing for their release date. Quite a shame that the game had to suffer a terrible launch because of an overzealous publisher.

This game is absolutely great so far.  Summarized concisely, it has tight controls, fast play(completing a tough level might take five minutes max), seizure-inducing particle effects, clever puns, satirizes Amurican war culture, and seems like a labor of love on the part of its developers.
In my opinion, it isn't playing through the single player campaign that shows the finished game's potential, but the custom campaigns that players make.  What is important about the custom campaigns is that they show how difficult the game can become and often give a better idea of what the game's engine is like.  To give an example of the latter in case jargon is being used wrong, there are weird custom campaigns that could be described as hardcore platforming objective-based puzzles, where attacking is impossible for one reason or another. Hypothetically, even if all of Broforce's devs vanished off of the face of the planet, I could still fire-up steam and play new custom campaigns daily that are often really awesome and hard.
The only things that really get me down when I play is that levels are seldom long enough for my taste and a few characters are *currently* too limited by their mechanics for my taste.

Harvest Moon meets Dragon Warrior in this fun, cute little game where you gather, feed, and export the 'plorts' or waste products of various slimes. You're given a large amount of starter plots to build and get ready to farm, and then it can expand, offering a large amount of different things your plots can evolve to. I love the different slimes and learning what to do to cage them effectively. It's explained in your Slimepedia what they may need to function, and what you may need to look out for, like Tabbies jumping, Boom slimes' explosions, and Rad slimes' radiation, as well as diet. This takes a lot of the guesswork out and allows you to focus moreso on feeding these ravenous, goopy beasts.
The only problem I have is the rate Roostro's, being so rare, age. It takes about two days for them to turn into Elder Roostros, while siring a dozen Hen Hens. Then, it's a race to HOPE to find another Roostro to breed for meat, beating back every Pink slime and Tabbie that goes near it in hopes of being able to cultivate more. It would help if they didn't become Elders unless another Roostro is born, or have a higher Roostro drop the day after yours turns into an Elder. Otherwise, it's find and hope, and I can't tell you the amount of times I was entirely crestfallen, finding one that gets devoured by a Tabbie just hopping by.Overall I recommend it, fun game ^_^

Harvest Moon meets Dragon Warrior in this fun, cute little game where you gather, feed, and export the 'plorts' or waste products of various slimes.  You're given a large amount of starter plots to build and get ready to farm, and then it can expand, offering a large amount of different things your plots can evolve to.  I love the different slimes and learning what to do to cage them effectively.  It's explained in your Slimepedia what they may need to function, and what you may need to look out for, like Tabbies jumping, Boom slimes' explosions, and Rad slimes' radiation, as well as diet.  This takes a lot of the guesswork out and allows you to focus moreso on feeding these ravenous, goopy beasts.
The only problem I have is the rate Roostro's, being so rare, age.  It takes about two days for them to turn into Elder Roostros, while siring a dozen Hen Hens.  Then, it's a race to HOPE to find another Roostro to breed for meat, beating back every Pink slime and Tabbie that goes near it in hopes of being able to cultivate more.  It would help if they didn't become Elders unless another Roostro is born, or have a higher Roostro drop the day after yours turns into an Elder.  Otherwise, it's find and hope, and I can't tell you the amount of times I was entirely crestfallen, finding one that gets devoured by a Tabbie just hopping by.

The Steam store is oversaturated with low effort 2D retro platformers.   So when launching this game, I expected just another forgettable entry.
Tales From Space: Mutant Blobs Attack shares almostnone of the low effort, weak attributes of so much indy shovelware that we see today.  Instead, we get an admirable and fun game.
Support for 4K! Keyboard support!  Non-janky controls! But most importantly, instead of another Mario clone, we get what Spores first stage blended with a 2D puzzle platformer.
Controlling the blob is a lot of fun as you hoover up various objects, which in turn makes you grow big enough to surpass various obstacles.    The look and feel of the game is very well polished - most low effort indy games lack this polish and janky controls ruin the experience.  No so here.
Only two real criticisms for this - the TV screen overlay is distracting, while it adds to the aesthetic, after a while it's just in the way of a clear sceen.   Secondly the choice of controls is a bit off - the apostrophe key for the attack?  Doesn't work well.   Customisable controls would go a long way, but the quality of the game experience overall lets us gloss over this.
If you have to play a 2D platformer, this is one of the better examples.

The amount of fun to be had in No More Room in Hell is purely based on who you play with.
Yes, this may also be true for the majority of online multiplayer games, but it is especially true when it comes to cooperative games. No More Room in Hell is less a game, and much more a social experience. If the social mechanics are removed, or non-existent, there is zero to no enjoyment to be found here. Unfortunately, many times you join a server, no one is communicating by voice. Not even via the text chat. This limits the overall gaming experience of No More Room in Hell to a valueless venture into a boring and uneventful zombie apocalypse scenario. Other times, you will join a server and be in the presence of voice chatters who are playing very loud music or TV in the background, or people who are only interested in communicating and playing with their friend, in their common language that no one else understands, while ignoring everything and everyone else. Then there are the people you will find that aren't actually playing the game for its purpose at all. Luckily, there are the rare times that you join a server and most, if not all people involved are communicating well, attempting to succeed in the game's objectives, and being helpful in the survival of all participants. People from all over the world, working together. Sadly, these perfect moments in No More Room in Hell are few and far between.
The Source Engine server browser has its many known faults, and blacklisting servers often does not work. There are many servers out there that ignore the game's purpose in every way possible. These servers have taken No More Room in Hell and spoiled every objective, every gameplay mechanic, and have made it their own worthless variation of it. If you join them, you will find that the standard game's survival and cooperative mechanics have been replaced with unlimited ammo, a free and unlimited guns menu, and other server-side changes, such as automatic respawns and other options that are there to simply ruin the standard game. Those servers are not playing the game created by the developers.
No More Room in Hell has a surprising amount of content for being a completely free game, and the developers seem to be devoted to its continued success with frequent and sizable patches and updates. They are often responding to posts in the Steam forums, and sometimes can even be found playing the game and answering questions using the voice chat. The game may be quite unpolished in certain areas and low budget, but for it being 100% free, it's still impressive at some level. Hit detection when it comes to melee combat is definitely an area that takes some getting used to, but once you learn how to handle the various melee weapons, it does become satisfying to down zombies with one hit. The firearms also feel agreeable, and collecting then exchanging ammo with the other survivors can be very fun. At the moment, there are two game modes. One is objective based, while the other is centered on defense of designated areas and wave survival. Both are extremely enjoyable if played with the right group of people.
Playing the server lottery in a cooperative game can be disappointing, but if you are lucky enough to be able to find a server with people playing the game to its full potential, No More Room in Hell can be a lot of fun. It's just a shame that most people aren't playing the game that No More Room in Hell is intended to be.

Dishonored 2 is a strange beast. Let me get this out of the way first... this is a great game and if you liked dishonored then you will love this one. However there are a couple of points worth mentioning for those considering buying this. First and foremost is that this game, while potentially stunning, well designed and fun to play feels more like a large expansion pack than a sequel. To be fair that is because the first game was so good it would have been foolish to mess with the formula too much. Those going into this shouldn't expect an entirely fresh experience if you have played the first game and while the levels are often thrilling to play none of them quite recapture the magic of the series' best (masquerade ball).
I'll also mention here that the story also feels little derivative of the first one with characters that don't feel quite as deep this time (despite the fact that most of them return from the first game). The start to the story in particular just happens so quickly and feels so forced that it can come off as a little ridiculous. In any case once Dishonored 2 gets settled in the story is engaging enough to keep you playing and the gameplay itself, as mentioned before is pure gold.
Perhaps the story gets significantly better when you play as Emily. However this brings me on to my main problem with the game. As of 11/14/2016 this game is buggy as hell with frequest CTD's and odd bugs. The devs switched from UE3 and somehow managed to carry over the aliasing issues the first game had into the new Void engine (based on ID tech 5 apparently). This combined with the aforementioend CTD's and corrupt save files became a huge irratation. The game every crashed for me during the end credits!
So would I recommend this game? Yes it's an amazing first person stealth action game which is as good as the original, without being better. However in it's current state you better be damn patient to get through it.
8.5/10 (if the bugs were fixed I might even give it a 9).

I recently finished my first playthrough of the game on very hard going for low chaos with Corvo. I have to say that this game is phoenomanal. I was a huge fan of the first, and I love stealth games, so I was excited for this game. I was hoping that they wouldn't mess this one up, and thankfully they didn't. The game isn't perfect, but I definately recommend it.
The game's story is gripping and deep. It plays off of the first game and its DLC, so fans of the game will know what's going on. The start of the story is very abrupt, (even more so than the first game) but it tells you everything you need to know. This is the bad guy, she's really bad, find a way to take her down. There is a twist (sort of) that had me staring at the decision screen for a good ten minutes because I was genuinly torn on what to do. The ending is...meh.
Now the gameplay is really hit or miss. Unlike other stealth games, you can easily recover once you've been spotted, or not even sneak around at all. Sneaking around can be tedious and boring if you don't like stealth, and the combat is so simple that you shouldn't have any difficulties parrying and inta killing most enemies. The only real consequence for beeing spotted is....well being spotted. If you are going for a ghost run you will absolutely have to plan your way through a level...at first. Near the end of the game I felt like a god. You can get crazy overpowered if you collect all the bonecharms and runes. At about level 6 I had to stop myself from collecting any more because the game was getting too easy. It actually wasn't until the last level that I figured out the upgrade system had more than one page, and after that it was all over. The beaty of the game is that you can play it however you want. I simply stopped stopping time and seeing through walls, but if you use those all the way through the game will be a cakewalk. The only complaint that I personally have with the stealth system is how it tracks your detections. I like that it shows you at the end of the level how many times you were detected, but there was one time where I set off no alarms, didn't get into combat, and no enemy gaurds were alerted to my presence whatsoever, but somehow I was spotted thirteen times. I trust that I was spotted, I just wished I knew when. Unless I missed thirteen gaurds chasing after me, it's possible that you can be spotted without alerting anyone, and that's annoying.
All in all it was a good game, probably my favorite at this time. I'm excited to play through as Emily who has a whole new set of powers!

It does feel like Tamriel, but there is a bit of disconnect that I think they can and will improve over time.
The thieving just came out, so I'm hoping for a full blown thieves guild quest line in the future, but who knows.
tl;dr, at least try the game out. Expect good quests, expect a good mmo, don't hold it up to your normal TES standards, though. Take it at face value and you'll not be disappointed.

Sometimes you have less than $5 in your Steam wallet and decide to roll the dice on an Indie title and it pays off. Survivalist is one of those diamonds in the rough that delivers a satisfying zombie survival/RPG suitable for the nostalgic gamer like myself-meaning you've got to have hard-core gaming chops and a strong stomach for retro visuals. The environment responsive face-cam window on the UI was an interesting choice but ill-concieved considering that the portrait models look like♥♥♥♥♥♥overall the art of this game-is pretty terrible quality on the close-up components-especially on the conversation exchanges and the title screen despite having "good enough" graphics to accomplish its gameplay goals plus nice aesthetics and environmental set design in the overworld. It harkens back to the old Fallout games in a lot of ways visually and in terms of deep narrative but with a less advanced and comprehensive dialogue system and using a real-time combat system rather than the turn-based tactical systems of those pre-Bethesda games. There is a more acute survival component and a community building element that while somewhat clunky provides something similar to a low-fidelity Fallout 4.
My first 2 hours with the game almost caused me to return it because even with the tutorial it is hard to get in to at first-in fact-I would say the tutorial is to blame. The main character of the tutorial should have been the girl with diabeetus-then "you" as the player would have to value her as a non-expendable character and be thereby compelled to follow the linear sequence to the point of obtaining and maintaining your supply of insulin. The plot around this is somewhat nonsensicle with Joe as the main character having to begrudingly accept her and it is unclear in the beginning how linear the game intends to be on account of the forced dialogue and character scripting around these events. You can deviate from the linear story but you will suffer for it in multiple ways...but it also has its advantages if you survive. The key is understanding that the reload option push from a failed mission is a courtesy and not a command-you can continue on after failing an objective-such as not responding to a certain SOS signal before thirst and diabeetus takes it toll but you will not able to access a few features until you recruit some additional members nor will you have the necessary construction training or tutorials available for base building with Isham.  The combat will be too fast paced for many I fear and harassment from random roaving mobs (especially if they are looters) from even the first two towns will discourage a lot of folks from going forward with the game given the time differential between building a fence versus time it takes to burn by molotov cocktail.
You've got to be willing to give this ugly duckling a lot time to develop into the totally awesome but slightly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ plaid & polka-dotted flamingo that it will become...and you've got to love grinding and have lots of time and patience for  running around the desert, reading conversation text including asking everybody their name and "what's up?' then beating the ♥♥♥♥ out of them for money as the most legit job available. I have been considering using this game for some videos on my channel but it would need to be heavily edited because the time it takes to do things on this game are ungodly. That said, it is pretty brilliant in a lot of ways and the only reason I am so hard on it is because I see the massive potential for the game (or the announced sequel-since Bob indicated that after MP was added the game was done and he was shifting focus to that) Here's hoping that you will be able to roll a character with military/police, athelte, bartering/social-skills, farmer/construction worker, stealth/thief skills, and medicial archetypes and customizable secondary skills to help organize community roles better than just having stackable skill books that anyone can use which although easy is kind of lame. Having no stealth, melee weapons, vehicles, nor a robust skill and item crafting system seems criminally negligent and the addition of these critcal elements along with more adequate dialogue options and less detracting visuals to a sequel would go along ways to making it truly outrageous...I'd buy that for a dollar ;)

Oh Astroneer...Why don't I love you? You are the right genre, the right aesthetic even, but something's missing. It's not you, maybe it's me!
I will start by saying the game is not very intuitive, not many tooltips on how things work or what goes where. I understand that experimentation is at the forefront of gaming sometimes, but the issue is more so a source of frustration when dealing with high-tech doodads. Somehow I'm on this planet, an astronaut recently departed from an orbiting space-ring, but there's not even a hyerogliphic explaining what the hell a machine does with what and the result. I understand there's wiki's everywhere, but having to tab out to know what to do with the particular material I'm holding doesnt really fit my style.
The second issue is more akin to one I have frequently with other games. This game is fun in multiplayer. Lots of fun. Perhaps enough fun that it may override the above criticism. At least that's what I keep hearing. And if true then at least be warned: it's not in single player. It's lonely to a fault. Many of the tasks and bigger features like rovers and such are more appealing when there's not empty seats and your friends are along for the ride.
The last bit of a complaint is that there's some of the original vision missing from the product *thus far*. Things that excited me from the original concept pre-launch trailer. Bases with rails and so on. Go watch that trailer to know what I mean.
Would I recommend? No. Would I wait? Yes, at this time the game is changing with patches and maybe it will be worth a try again in the future.

So, this is the game that I was waiting for a long time, and overall wasn't disappointed.
Pros:
+Good controls and smooth camera movement, huge improvement over port of first part. Controller is recommended, but keyboard+mouse work great too, especially if you have multi-button mouse.
+Graphics. It has its own graphical style, not a "skyrim_ultra_tons_of_mods", but my eyes were happy.
+Atmosphere and lore. While the story isn't told much here, lore part compensates this absolutely. Every item description, every NPC dialog, even little moments of pre-fight videos can tell you something about history of the world. I recommend to read forums after completing the game to read theoris of how all the things are connected.
+Thoughtful fights. You can't just cookie cut every enemy here like you are demigod or something. You are not god, you are actually almost nothing, many enemies can 2-shot you. You will die, but with every death you will think "Oh, so that's how these guys move before slicing me to dust. I shall do something." Then, of course, you will die again, because that's how you learn everything. But with every death you get, you will get better at this game.
+Online features. Bloodstains showing places where other people died, messages from those who survived, signs from people who want to go coop with you to help you slay some enemies. And of course, invasions. At almost every time you can be attacked not only by mobs, but also by other players willing to get rewards or fun from your death, and this adds to the whole atmosphere of fear.
Cons:
-Bosses. If you haven't played first part, you will probably like them, but if you're familiar with bosses of DS1, most of these bosses will likely be not-so-awesome for you. Luckily, there are some exceptions to this rule, for example, a Chariot boss running circles and killing both you and its own allies or Looking Glass, who is able to summon other players to fight against you right in the middle of the fight.
-Disbalance. Many people right now complain about certain builds being too overpowered, and in some things I agree with them, but if you don't go pvp often, that is not much of a problem.
-Frustration. If you don't like games that make you die over and over, this is not for you. Funny to compare these, but here it is close to games like Super Meat Boy. Matter of taste, anyway, but I had to say it to warn everyone.

Remember the time, where we all can't wait for the new Call of Duty? It was fresh! The day Activision released Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare was like Christmas. It was new and fresh. Modern combat with Call of Duty gameplay? Yeah!
Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare tries to fit that boots. And it can manage that in my opinion. My last Call of Duty was Modern Warfare 2.
The campaign is good and is long. I played ~8 hours on veteran without much trial and error. There are plot twists and a world, which can happen. It's authentic. Even a little bit USA critic is in the game. But the glorious US marines still save the world... again. So enough patriotism for the people who like that.
The game itself is classic COD. Fire, run and there is the new part with the suite. You can jump higher. The game goes vertical. And it works very well. I have fun with the game.
The graphics are okay. No competition for a Battlefield 4, but the performance isn't that good.
The multiplayer is classic. A few guns, a few modes and little maps. If you like that, enjoy.
You also have "loot". You can loot different equipment like outfits or even clothes with status points like handling +1. Your soldier is fully customizable and your equipment is basing on the “pick” system of the previous titles. You can pick here 13 perks.
The kill streaks are not overwhelming good, and they’re not spam able. They’re point streaks and can be customized. Better perks for the streaks result in more points to call them. Which is a good deal.

!!DISCLAIMER!!= NOT A TRADITIONAL ELDER SCROLLS EXPERIENCE!
Firstly I have to say since the release last year this game has made some improvements. And it is a fun game if you're playing with your friends. And its about to drop it's subscription requirement so that is why this game is "recommended" in my case. But it is a typical MMORPG and it does not really capture all the things we loved about Skyrim and Oblivion. Enjoyable yes. Dissapointing, yes as well. I'll list the games highs and lows and you can decide for yourself.
I am a huge fan of the past elder scrolls games. I've played them all and fell completely in love. This game holds the elder scrolls name, but that is where the similarities end. Don't get me wrong. I'm not dissing the game. Its a good game. I'm just being honest. So many reviewers on other websites and youtube channels (ESPECIALLY AT RELEASE) danced around the differences, not really telling you what they are. If you want a elder scrolls experience, this is not the game for you. However, it's not your typical MMO either, and is a little more fun than most.
Lets talk about some of the differences between elder scrolls and this game:
The combat UI: The health, Mana, and Stamina bars are the same as they were in Skyrim; however the rest of the combat UI just doesn't feel quite right, it doesn't feel as smooth when hacking and slashing as it did in Skyrim, and it holds a little more of a typical MMO type combat, similar to the KOTOR online combat. This is especially true with the archery, where as in Skyrim and Oblivion archery was realistic and a little challenging to master, In ESO you basically just draw back, point it in the enemies general direction, let loose and the arrow will simply find its mark.
The graphics: The graphics differ alot from Skyrim, but they are not bad. The character graphics are good, you can tell little things and aspects of your character, very clear and crisp coloring. However I feel like the graphics slipped a little from the realism of Skyrim into the un-realism of some other MMO's. It is only slightly though, they luckily don't even come close to the cheesy WoW graphics. This also depends on what graphical setting you run your PC on.
The questing system: The questing system itsef is actually really impressive. The entire game is fully voiced, by wonderful voice actors. And the conversation with NPC's has a similiar look to Skyrim (just to give you an example). That being said, some of the quests are pretty boring, typical MMO "go for" missions. But there are several fun quests, and the game leans moe towards exploring than questing anyway.
The weapons: I have to touch on this because a part of me was super dissapointed. I really dislike the way most of the weapons look, especially the one handed swords and bows. They just look cheesy and un-realistic. Now that being said, some of the weapons are alot easier to use than in past games, take a two handed sword or axe for example, in skyrim you were limited because they were so incredibly slow. They move alot quicker and alot more fluidly, which gives you the power of a two hander without a huge speed reduction.
The PvP: Now this feature I like, I wish there was more of it. When you reach a certain level, you and your friends can besiege a castle controlled by other players, if you win, you keep the castle and get rewards. You can also gain and use siege weapons (like catapults and ballistae) If you control all the castles around the imperial city, you control imperial city and the highest scoring player on your team becomes emperor. There can be hundreds of players in PvP which makes it daunting, but fun at the same time.
I hope you can see that this game is its own type of beast, if you want a elder scrolls experience, you're out of luck; if you want a typical MMO experience, you won't really find it here. This game is enjoyable but after playing it, I have to say I wish I would have waited for full "free-to-play" instead of paying 60 dollars for it. But if you've got the money, and can't wait to try this out for yourself instead of reading about it, go ahead. The subscription fee is about to be dropped anyway, but who knows how big a role in-game purchases will become. It may end up that we were better off subscribing. Just remember all the things I told you in this review, know what to expect so you're not dissapointed, and enjoy. I hope you found this review helpful.

So this is my first review, so I'll try not to be boring and over-word things please dun't hate me iz trying to help.
First, I'd divide the game into two categories: Art/Ambience and Gameplay
The art is spectacular - it's fun, simplistic indie-style texture makes the game awe-inspiring, and almost peaceful. The music when the sun comes up, sets the mood of wonder and exploration, and really peaks my interest. Then, when the game gets serious, the atmosphere seems to work in reverse. Sand storms happening at any time, making the world impossible to see, with a volley of objects streaking towards you. When exploring the caves, the air gets gloomier, the colors cooler, making it scream danger. Oh, and then theres the dead astronauts that you may just happen upon on your way. Overall, the studio knows what they're doing, and created a new and interesting look on space survival.
Gameplay for me is a bit more complicated. For one, I think the backbacks are great. Gone are the Minecraft days where a single person could carry trees that are larger than life, and still have enough room in their pockets for a few stacks of stone - replaced by a simplistic inventory style, with a reasonable amount of space for items. Going off of that, when you carry something(not inventory), your character slows and can no longer jump, adding to the realistic feeling. The gathering system is a bit wonky(I mean, why should I mine several colossal compound structures for one little item?), but all survival games have a foraging portion to them. However, the biggest thing is research. It is a GRIND like you wouldn't believe. You have to make this clunky machine that takes up a whopping amount of energy, sit there with fuel for EVER just to keep it going. The machines themselves can't be moved once added to your habitat (but they are currently fixing that :]  ).
Overall, for ambience I would say yes, but for sheer survival gaming I would say no. As great as the whole ambience is, that still doesn't make me want to grind for research points (called bytes) for hours, or go dig a gargantuant hole for all of three foraging items.
HOWEVER
I recommend this game because it's in alpha. It's cheap, it has great potential, and the devs LISTEN. Bruh, golden opportunity to put your two cents in on a kick@## indie space game. Buy the game, try it for yourself, then yell at devs to fix research grind. Seriously. That s#@$@ annoying.

A simpler life is what I long for. A life of entrapping cute slimes in digital fortresses, and then force feeding the adorable critters so I can sell their poop for profit, ah… the good life of a Slime Rancher. Developer, Monomi Park, has done an incredible job managing their first project. Despite being an early release title that was only in version 0.4.1 when I tried it, the content that was available felt polished and even in its early version the game provided nearly 18 hours of game play. While I normally criticize the pay for early release model, Monomi Park has provided a wonderful experience in Slime Rancher at a fair price with more content coming soon! Now let’s get into the details!
Basic Premise!
You are a Slime Rancher in a colorful new world with a few empty farm plots and a Luigi’s Mansion style vacuum pack on your back. You’ll soon wonder off your farm into the wild, untamed Dry Reef area surrounding your farm where Pink Slimes bounce around joyously eating wild carrots and pogo fruit. These pink profit producers are your first vacuum victims, with few other options you’ll find yourself sucking up Pink Slimes, their poop, and probably some fruits and veggies as well….. WAIT, DID YOU SAY POOP?!... yes I said poop…. Well it’s really called a “plort” in the world of Slime Rancher. This is a good time to mention that the main means of making money in Slime Rancher is selling poops or plorts in the plort market! Corral up your Pink Slimes and feed them to make them produce plorts. Suck up the plorts and shoot them into the Slime market to make a sale, its easy, fun, and addicting! The cash earned from your plots will allow you to build more corrals for slimes, unlock new areas on your ranch, and upgrade your gear!
After selling your first batch of pink plorts you’ll notice that the market has prices for many different kinds of plorts with pink being one of the least valuable. Want to make more cash? Get exploring because there are 10 unique slimes to collect, corral, and cash in on (more are expected in future versions)!
The World!
The vibrant and colorful world demands your attention and rewards exploration with new slimes and items. Certain fruits, vegetables, and chicken breeds are unique to specific areas. If you plan on maximizing your plort profits exploring to find a new slime and its favorite food are a must. You will not have immediate access to the entire map at first. Locked doors that require slime keys will impede your progress and vacuum pack upgrades are nessesary to hover over gaps in bridges or valleys.
The Dry Reef
The Ranch itself shares a theme with the area immediately surrounding it known as the Dry Reef. A coastal, desert themed region that is teeming with everything a new Slime Rancher needs! Basic fruits, veggies, and some of the more common slimes hop around in abundance. This area provides multiple opportunities to find slime keys and includes doorways to the other regions.
Indigo Quarry
Some of the more valuable, yet dangerous slimes inhabit Indigo Quarry. A rocky, mountainous region with caves and seemingly inaccessible plateaus provides peril and fortune for the entrpenural rancher. You’ll need to purchase a few vacuum pack upgrades to fully appreciate the area so wrangle up some slimes and harvest those plorts!
The Moss Blanket
The tropical rainforest themed Moss Blanket hides one of the most elusive slimes in addition to sharing a few common inhabitants also found in Indigo Quarry. You’ll find a relatively large amount of freshwater here which comes in handy as this area lends itself to a lot of unwanted Tarr slimes forming.
In addition to finding unique slimes and foods in each of the available areas they also produce unique resources needed for Slime Science which is unlocked later during game play.
The Slimes
There are 10 slimes available in the current version with more expected in later releases. All of the slimes can be found here but ill describe a few of my favorites!
Crystal Slimes
Metallic crystal spikes stick out of a smiling purple blob. These slimes are as valuable as they are dangerous! They regularly generate crystal spikes on the ground that explode on contact. Crystal Slimes also have one of the most difficult favorite foods to find. A smart Rancher will combine these spikey specimens with a Slime that favors an easier food to find.
Rad Slimes
Bright green slimes that emit a radioactive field. The slimes small size means you can pack many of them into a corral without fear of an escape attempt. Their plorts sell for one of the higher prices in the market and these slimes have an easily obtained favorite food. They are great for boosting your profits early in the game but be careful, spending too much time in their radioactive field is bad for your health!
Boom Slimes
Balls of molten lava complete with adorable eyes and a happy smile. They produce a valuable plort but can be difficult to contain. Boom slimes will randomly explode, flinging items in all directions and damaging careless ranchers who wonder too close. Their favorite food is a specific breed of hen found in The Moss Blanket so have this area unlocked before collecting Boom Slimes in mass.
Overall Recomendation
I strongly recommend giving Slime Rancher a try! For a fair price of $19.99 you’ll get a game with overwhelmingly positive reviews on steam. Despite the game being less than half way to version 1.0.0 you’ll still get near 20 hours of game play from the current version 0.4.2 and access to all future updates. Given that this is Monomi Park’s first project I am confident they will bring the game to completion. If you are a streamer this is a great game to go live with. Its adorable, fun to play, well-paced, and has calm periods making chat interaction easy. It is also not saturated by thousands of streamers meaning small streamers can expect decent audience exposure.

I used to be a sucker for this game. I just came back to gaming, and this will be the first game that I'll come back to.
This game has the deepest customization system that I've seen in any games so far. When it comes to terms of vehicles and clothing, it outranks Sims.
On vehicles, you can change your antennas, bumpers, wheels, tires, side-skirts, hoods, you can add custom registration plates, you can add custom decals, and paint your vehicle in a thousand different ways.
Police vehicles have a variety of siren models, colors, and audio.
Not to mention that there is a plenty of vehicles.
On your characters, you can add tattoos, makeup, pubic hair, skin scars, birthmarks, your body build, your weight, your age, lots of face details, dozens of hair, facial hair, and body hair to choose from.
There is lots of different clothing items; badges, necklaces, earings, piercings, t-shirts, shirts, cargo pants, jeans, skinny pants, sweatpants... Not to mention that you can add custom decals to your clothes, and paint♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ suspenders, arm patches, emblems, buttons, nametags, etc.
You even have an in-game music editor, in which you can make your short "signature" song.
It also has a really big collection of nice songs in the in-game radio, and you can also add your own music to your music player.
I haven't played in a while, so I can't think of more at the moment, but I know that there are a LOT more customization features than what I've mentioned.

This would be awesome, imagine all the Sims fans coming to the game, haha.
Since I started playing I kept hearing new/unskilled players moaning about "pay 2 win". There is no pay to win in the game. You can pay, yes. But paying only gives you less customization limits, and it gives you some weapons that
player can obtain through a bit of grinding, except that you get some paintjobs, too.
Missions usually don't take more than 20-30 minutes, and can sometimes be as short as 5 minutes, which is great if you just want a game to play after a long day.
Again, if you just want a game to play after a long day, then this is for you. You can spent hundreds of hours grinding the game to get the finest weaponry in all of
San Paro, but you can perform just fine in the tracksuit, SCAR and that small electric-looking car that you get during the training once you learn how to use it.
Investing any money (real or not) is not essential.
Getting new weapons won't make you stronger, it only gives you the opportunity to use what suits you best.
Yes, there are prepubescent players screaming that you are a hacker, but luckily, there is no global chat, so you won't have to buy a new headset every week.
There is plenty of people that you can just chill with in the social district, play hide and seek, ♥♥♥♥ around with animations (there are plenty of animations!), race, drive around...
If you're not really a battle-born type of a person, you can just stick to the social district and make uniforms, cars, designer shoes, songs, or whatever for people, and get paid well for it.
You can also be a smuggler, unlock higher-level items, and then sell them for more to lower-lever players.
Keep in mind that if you wish to be a designer it will require some initial grinding to unlock clothing parts, decals, etc.

One-hitting other players in invasions that they cannot avoid without playing offline: 10/10 GotY.
After playing through Demon's Souls, Dark Souls, and Dark Souls 2, I cannot recommend this game. PvE mechanics, Storytelling, and Single Player in general are notably worse, even in ways that they should  not. It seems everything was sacrificed for a better online experience, but online isn't much better. Matchmaking is easier, but you are constantly invadable. Netcode has been praised, but I have not seen much if any improvements (20 MB/s connection, still getting ghost hits, and backstabs). Balance is centered around NG+ now, and many of the spells used in PvP result in one-hit kills even against players who push health and resistances to its upper limits.
Singleplayer needs specific mentioning because of how painful it is. The story is heavy-handed, transparent, and unusually self-aware. Many bosses are copied in part or whole from Dark Souls almoast shamelessly and without innovation. Enemies in general have less attack variety, and rely more heavily on "record player tracking" and hitboxes that extend well away from their weapons. Rolling has been crippled, along with player weapon damage, but rolling is faster for most weight levels. The end result is the game forcing you to use a heavy shield and a reach weapon. Furthermore dexterity-based weapons have less durability now, with most weapons having durablility comparable to Crystal weapons from Dark Souls 1. Dexterity weapons typically have 20-60% the durability of their strength-based counterparts. You must have multiple backup weapons to fight enemies to the next area, or run past many of the encounters to prevent breakage.
Maybe the game will recieve a patch to make the singleplayer more enjoyable, and perhaps multiplayer will recieve significant rebalancing, but I can not enjoy the game as it is right now.

Tales From Space: Mutant Blobs Attack is a physics-based platformer, with a bit of Katamari Damacy thrown in for good measure, about a space-blob that escapes from a lab, goes on a journey to rescue its friends, and consume the entire planet in the process.
Through a series of a couple dozen levels and a smattering of dialog-free cutscenes, Mutant Blobs Attack tells the story of a blob out for revenge against, well, everything for imprisoning it and all its blob friends and conducting horrible experiments on them. The military tries to stop or destroy the blob, but what fun would the game be if they pulled that off?
While the story is rudimentary at best, Mutant Blobs Attack manages to create a fun, light-hearted, but still slightly dark-comedic atmosphere. The backgrounds of levels are full of references to other games, movies, and internet memes. Some work better than others, but they’re trying to create a humorous tone in a game where a silent, gelatinous protagonist attempts to devour every living thing on earth. The fact that they did it without being too morbid is something of a success in and of itself.
Like any good platformer, it features a couple of collectible types: blue dots that really only affect the end of level score, and the afore-mentioned blob friends. The other blobs, two per level, are often hidden away or behind some nasty trap, making them a bit tougher to collect.
You are never held back for not collecting enough dots, or missing any of the blobs, but they bring a nice little challenge and some replayability to the game.
The two main mechanics besides basic platforming in the game are size and magnets.
Your blob will absorb office supplies, garbage, food or whatever else it comes across, increasing its size and allowing it to get over or through larger and larger obstacles. It’s very similar to the early part of Katamari Damacy stages, where you really aren’t worried about the final size of the ball, but more about how to get big enough to absorb whatever obstacle is keeping you holed up.
It works well for Mutant Blobs Attack, and while your starting size adjusts from level to level for… story reasons, it does a good job of matching the feel of the level. Not that realism is the primary goal here, but it would feel a little weird sneaking around a lab, trying to escape unnoticed as a four-foot tall, spike-covered blob. The later levels featuring the blob taking on the military and townsfolk running in terror are a real treat, and a fun way to wrap up the game.
There are also zero gravity segments where the blob can shoot a jet of fire out of… wherever blobs shoot jets of fire, in order to maneuver around. These sections still revolve around absorbing junk and avoiding lasers and other platformer-standard traps, but break up the pace a bit. A nice touch.
The other big mechanic I mentioned earlier centers around the blob’s magnetic abilities. Fairly early in the game it gains the abilities of an electromagnet of sorts, either drawing itself toward or repelling itself from certain metallic objects, which are always conveniently glowing purple. It works well and has you looking at all four edges of the level for how to get where you need to go, as opposed to simply jumping from ledge to ledge.
This game started life as a launch title for the Vita, but it doesn't suffer for it. Many launch titles feel rushed and awkward, but Tales From Space: Mutant Blobs Attack manages to feel comfortable in its own skin. Everything just… works. The developers knew exactly the game they wanted to make, and executed that plan exceptionally well.

Very nice casual platformer!
It's more old-school, collect-a-ton, like Super Mario, rather than the more modern precision platformers like Super Meat Boy. So, even if you don't really like how tough most platformers are, this one you can certainly enjoy.
I've never played Katamari Damacy, but the idea is clearly similar. More recently, perhaps Agar.io. Also, Gish!
The physics were absolutely nailed, as the character you control really feels like a blob. Very fun to just play around, trying to collect everything.
The level variety is fairly high, with different sections, some timed, some more puzzle oriented (although there is very light puzzling only), etc. The levels are replete with references to other games through alien-related puns.
The graphic style reminds me a lot of old cartoons, and the music fits the silly, old sci-fi vibe very well too.
If you're into leaderboard climbing, each level counts pretty much everything you do, from collectibles to time spent to count your score, so that may be up your alley. I'm not sure how much better the levels would seem with a 100% speedrun mindset, but many of the orbs' arrangements do seem to have an optimal path. So yeah, if mastering physics is your thing, I'd doubly recommend this!
A very fun diversion, if nothing else! If you enjoy more casual platformers, give it a go. It's fairly short, though, as I've finished (with about 90-95% of the collectibles and medals, etc.?) in 3.7 hours.

text: I was praying that this game wouldn't be like Colonial Marines. I was hoping that this game was going to be spectacular. Needless to say, I was blown away. Three hours in on the hardest difficulty and I can definitely say that the immersion never is broken, I can sit all day and play this game and still feel the tension and the anxiety. You can hear the Alien stalking you all throughout the beginning, little hisses and metallic clanks and he crawls above you. You hide in a locker but if you make the slightest noise, be it from your motion tracker or your breath, the Alien will rip off the door. The Androids seem invincible, you shoot them over and over again, they catch your melee attacks. This game is probably one of the most atmospheric and terrifying game I've ever played, it rivals Outlast and Amneisa: TDD, and even some of the older Silent Hill games. I can definatly say that this was my most anticipated game of 2014 and I am beyond happy. If you're a fan of the Alien series and want to truly feel terrifyied, pick this game up, you won't regret it.

If I wanted another Aliens: Colonial Marines I'd have pandered to Gearbox or EA or another company with too much invested in other IP's to devote enough credible attention to something like this. Alien : Isolation is just outright pretty with nice rich environments and highly detailed characters and that wonderfully intense score I'm smitten, die a thousand times and struggle to accept that I'm being often hunted by something that tracks you by your goddamned phereomones, has acid for blood, a tough as hell chitinous exterior and can survive in SPACE... but I'll still love it.
This is a great continuation of the Alien franchise in the 1st person survival horror style - highly recommend !

I used to be a sucker for this game. I just came back to gaming, and this will be the first game that I'll come back to.
This game has the deepest customization system that I've seen in any games so far. When it comes to terms of vehicles and clothing, it outranks Sims.
On vehicles, you can change your antennas, bumpers, wheels, tires, side-skirts, hoods, you can add custom registration plates, you can add custom decals, and paint your vehicle in a thousand different ways.
Police vehicles have a variety of siren models, colors, and audio.
Not to mention that there is a plenty of vehicles.
On your characters, you can add tattoos, makeup, pubic hair, skin scars, birthmarks, your body build, your weight, your age, lots of face details, dozens of hair, facial hair, and body hair to choose from.
There is lots of different clothing items; badges, necklaces, earings, piercings, t-shirts, shirts, cargo pants, jeans, skinny pants, sweatpants... Not to mention that you can add custom decals to your clothes, and paint♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ suspenders, arm patches, emblems, buttons, nametags, etc.
You even have an in-game music editor, in which you can make your short "signature" song.
It also has a really big collection of nice songs in the in-game radio, and you can also add your own music to your music player.
I haven't played in a while, so I can't think of more at the moment, but I know that there are a LOT more customization features than what I've mentioned.

This would be awesome, imagine all the Sims fans coming to the game, haha.
Since I started playing I kept hearing new/unskilled players moaning about "pay 2 win". There is no pay to win in the game. You can pay, yes. But paying only gives you less customization limits, and it gives you some weapons that
player can obtain through a bit of grinding, except that you get some paintjobs, too.
Missions usually don't take more than 20-30 minutes, and can sometimes be as short as 5 minutes, which is great if you just want a game to play after a long day.
Again, if you just want a game to play after a long day, then this is for you. You can spent hundreds of hours grinding the game to get the finest weaponry in all of
San Paro, but you can perform just fine in the tracksuit, SCAR and that small electric-looking car that you get during the training once you learn how to use it.
Investing any money (real or not) is not essential.
Getting new weapons won't make you stronger, it only gives you the opportunity to use what suits you best.
Yes, there are prepubescent players screaming that you are a hacker, but luckily, there is no global chat, so you won't have to buy a new headset every week.
There is plenty of people that you can just chill with in the social district, play hide and seek, ♥♥♥♥ around with animations (there are plenty of animations!), race, drive around...
If you're not really a battle-born type of a person, you can just stick to the social district and make uniforms, cars, designer shoes, songs, or whatever for people, and get paid well for it.
You can also be a smuggler, unlock higher-level items, and then sell them for more to lower-lever players.
Keep in mind that if you wish to be a designer it will require some initial grinding to unlock clothing parts, decals, etc.

There are a number of bad reviews on this game and honestly I don't know why because I love this game but I think it comes down to a number of considerations to take before purchasing. Number one and most important is that this is an early access game and that holds implications. Firstly it means it's an incomplete game and thus will not have all the components you may expect. But it also means that the game will improve over time and in my opinion that's extremely cool and part of why I like buying early access games. You get to not only support the developers but also get to watch the game become something more right before you eyes which allows you to constantly come back to a new and fresh experience and in the case the devs update it pretty regularly. Now to gameplay itself. This isn't a game that creates the fun itself. It's up to you to go out exploring and getting yourself into the inevitable hijinks that await you. If you play this game safe and don't take risks then it really won't be too much fun. Furthermore, most of the fun I've had in the game is just exploring, maybe finding a mountain and being like "ya know I think I just want to drill through this mountain and see what comes of it". So if you're looking for an extremely exciting and constantly fast moving environment this isn't for you. But if you want a nice relaxing non stressful and fun game then Astroneer is worth every dime.
