A simpler life is what I long for. A life of entrapping cute slimes in digital fortresses, and then force feeding the adorable critters so I can sell their poop for profit, ah… the good life of a Slime Rancher. Developer, Monomi Park, has done an incredible job managing their first project. Despite being an early release title that was only in version 0.4.1 when I tried it, the content that was available felt polished and even in its early version the game provided nearly 18 hours of game play. While I normally criticize the pay for early release model, Monomi Park has provided a wonderful experience in Slime Rancher at a fair price with more content coming soon! Now let’s get into the details!
Basic Premise!
You are a Slime Rancher in a colorful new world with a few empty farm plots and a Luigi’s Mansion style vacuum pack on your back. You’ll soon wonder off your farm into the wild, untamed Dry Reef area surrounding your farm where Pink Slimes bounce around joyously eating wild carrots and pogo fruit. These pink profit producers are your first vacuum victims, with few other options you’ll find yourself sucking up Pink Slimes, their poop, and probably some fruits and veggies as well….. WAIT, DID YOU SAY POOP?!... yes I said poop…. Well it’s really called a “plort” in the world of Slime Rancher. This is a good time to mention that the main means of making money in Slime Rancher is selling poops or plorts in the plort market! Corral up your Pink Slimes and feed them to make them produce plorts. Suck up the plorts and shoot them into the Slime market to make a sale, its easy, fun, and addicting! The cash earned from your plots will allow you to build more corrals for slimes, unlock new areas on your ranch, and upgrade your gear!
After selling your first batch of pink plorts you’ll notice that the market has prices for many different kinds of plorts with pink being one of the least valuable. Want to make more cash? Get exploring because there are 10 unique slimes to collect, corral, and cash in on (more are expected in future versions)!
The World!
The vibrant and colorful world demands your attention and rewards exploration with new slimes and items. Certain fruits, vegetables, and chicken breeds are unique to specific areas. If you plan on maximizing your plort profits exploring to find a new slime and its favorite food are a must. You will not have immediate access to the entire map at first. Locked doors that require slime keys will impede your progress and vacuum pack upgrades are nessesary to hover over gaps in bridges or valleys.
The Dry Reef
The Ranch itself shares a theme with the area immediately surrounding it known as the Dry Reef. A coastal, desert themed region that is teeming with everything a new Slime Rancher needs! Basic fruits, veggies, and some of the more common slimes hop around in abundance. This area provides multiple opportunities to find slime keys and includes doorways to the other regions.
Indigo Quarry
Some of the more valuable, yet dangerous slimes inhabit Indigo Quarry. A rocky, mountainous region with caves and seemingly inaccessible plateaus provides peril and fortune for the entrpenural rancher. You’ll need to purchase a few vacuum pack upgrades to fully appreciate the area so wrangle up some slimes and harvest those plorts!
The Moss Blanket
The tropical rainforest themed Moss Blanket hides one of the most elusive slimes in addition to sharing a few common inhabitants also found in Indigo Quarry. You’ll find a relatively large amount of freshwater here which comes in handy as this area lends itself to a lot of unwanted Tarr slimes forming.
In addition to finding unique slimes and foods in each of the available areas they also produce unique resources needed for Slime Science which is unlocked later during game play.
The Slimes
There are 10 slimes available in the current version with more expected in later releases. All of the slimes can be found here but ill describe a few of my favorites!
Crystal Slimes
Metallic crystal spikes stick out of a smiling purple blob. These slimes are as valuable as they are dangerous! They regularly generate crystal spikes on the ground that explode on contact. Crystal Slimes also have one of the most difficult favorite foods to find. A smart Rancher will combine these spikey specimens with a Slime that favors an easier food to find.
Rad Slimes
Bright green slimes that emit a radioactive field. The slimes small size means you can pack many of them into a corral without fear of an escape attempt. Their plorts sell for one of the higher prices in the market and these slimes have an easily obtained favorite food. They are great for boosting your profits early in the game but be careful, spending too much time in their radioactive field is bad for your health!
Boom Slimes
Balls of molten lava complete with adorable eyes and a happy smile. They produce a valuable plort but can be difficult to contain. Boom slimes will randomly explode, flinging items in all directions and damaging careless ranchers who wonder too close. Their favorite food is a specific breed of hen found in The Moss Blanket so have this area unlocked before collecting Boom Slimes in mass.
Overall Recomendation
I strongly recommend giving Slime Rancher a try! For a fair price of $19.99 you’ll get a game with overwhelmingly positive reviews on steam. Despite the game being less than half way to version 1.0.0 you’ll still get near 20 hours of game play from the current version 0.4.2 and access to all future updates. Given that this is Monomi Park’s first project I am confident they will bring the game to completion. If you are a streamer this is a great game to go live with. Its adorable, fun to play, well-paced, and has calm periods making chat interaction easy. It is also not saturated by thousands of streamers meaning small streamers can expect decent audience exposure.
Since the last time I played (in version 0.4.1) developer Monomi Park has released version 0.4.2 with small additional features and fixes. patch notes below!

*Edit*
I feel like I should update this review, and i'll start by saying that prehaps I jumped the gun when I agrilly ripped this game to pieces initially, as almost immediately after,, I started to enjoy myself more and more, to the point where I now believe this could quite possibly be one of the best stealth action games I've ever played.
Now that dosen't mean any of my initial critisisms don't still exist. This game  plays VERY similarily to Dishonored 1, so if you didn't like that game, you probably  won't like this either, and I still don't like that the chaos system is the only determining factor on the ending you get, but aside from that, this game gets a lot very right.
The one thing that sets this title apart from the original, is the fact that this one gives you far more options, lethal and non-lethal, to help you deal with enemies. It also has some incredibly detailed environments, and the gameplay animations are excellent. They also refined many of the core gameplay elements from the first that makes the game feel smoother and more polished.
The best thing though are the 4th and 7th level. They are easily  some of the coolest gameplay mechanics I've ever seen in a video game. They are worth the purchase price all by themselves and the innovation that they offer makes up for the familiarity of the rest of the game.
If you're a fan of first person action / stealth games, this is one you don't want to miss.

Before reading my review, please understand that this game wasn't made for me and that it might be for you. I strongly recommend actually watching gameplay. The reason I was upset with this game is because I was expecting a game like Contra: an actual campaign, actual storyline, etc.
In most games I don't like, I appreciate the theory of the game they are trying to make, but have problems with the execution... However, Broforce suffers from the opposite. I actually do think this game fulfilled what it was attempting to make, but I don't like even the idea. I bought it to play with a friend, and I will update this review if playing with him has changed anything.
I don't like the short 2-minute levels. That is the entire campaign. Everything is 1-hit, you and enemies. Like Super Crate Box, if you collect the Bros (boxes) you will change Bros (weapons) and eventually unlock new Bros (weapons). There is no health bar, no struggle to stay alive. All death feels accidental. There's no real teamwork because you can't protect people from 1-hit kills. It's a free-for-all.
Pros:
-Some nice little details: Sound in headphones follows character on screen, good particle effects
-Includes many famous characters from famous American movies which does embody the American opinion of power and patriotism
-I really enjoy the feel of the characters, especially Snake Plisskin, J from MiB, and Ash Williams
-I like the friendly AI, I didn't expect it and it does allow some strategy
-Movement is very smooth and I like swinging from underneath rocks
-Playing as the big robot is a nice change-up
-The rocket-launcher guy is my favorite boss fight, please do more of this, and earlier in the campaign. Each different area is too long. The 2-minute battles ruins it for me.
-Each different area is in the place of a typical action movie and is nice-looking, but gets old sometimes.
-Character diversity can be good, but also can be bad. Usually good, though. Most characters aren't too similar to one another, except for the generic action heroes.
Cons:
-Getting to the end of a level to find you destroyed too much of the environment to continue is unpleasant
-Killing enemies is unrewarded - only the demon/devil/red man is required to be killed to win
-Game punishes you for getting bros - increases time (albeit time is not that important)
-Game punishes you for not getting bros - do not unlock new bros to play as
-Friendly AI is pretty bad, though I appreciate the mechanic
-few characters require strategy but McGuyver
-Same background and each level is indistinguishable from the next - gets boring for me, maybe not others. Areas are too far between from the next. 30 2 minute jungle missions until the urban area felt like a chore.
-This game doesn't actually have any jokes aside from "Free, two, one" and the humor of the actual gameplay, and the humor is appreciable but doesn't make me laugh
-Because this game wasn't enjoyable for me and I released a negative review, I will probably get a 3% helpful rating
-Doing anything crazy is discouraged because you only have 1 HP

This is a great game for any Survival Horror fan. No More Room in Hell is a dark, "realistic" twist on most of the zombie games we have all played and loved. You start out with nothing in your inventory, and have to scavenge the map for things like ammo, first aid kits, guns, melee weapons, and the occasional key to a locked room or pathway. If you have played games like Left 4 Dead or Call of Duty: Zombies, you may find yourself running headfirst into the hordes of zombies. DON'T! This game treats zombies like their movie counterparts: They can only efficiently be killed with a blow to the head, and if they bite you, you will become infected and slowly die, without the constant use of pills. Whenever a player dies on the map their body will come back and attack other players. All of this makes this game very hard, but with time and skill it beccomes more  seemless. I recommend playing with a party of friends, and microphones, because the more people playing, the more co-operation there needs to be,
+ This game is 100% Free. No pay to win crap.
+ Challenging
+ Online Co-Op
+ A Ton of Maps (Developer and Mods)
+ A Very Walking Dead Feeling Game
- Occasional Lag
- Lack of Playable Characters

I have to say,this is one of my favourite zombie games.And,it's free! So,this is probbably going to be a longer review,so if you don't want to read it all,just know that this is really awesome game.
First thing first,there are objective and survival maps.I find survival maps easier,but I enjoy playing on both.There are servers with unlimited ammo,and a few maps that are made for mostly just killing zombies,so if you just want to kill zombies,you can do that too,but of course,I recommend trying survival and objective.
Next thing:weapons.There are a lot of weapons.From meeles to guns.Crowbars,axes,baseball bats,hammers,pistols(Berreta,Colt,Smith and Wesson...) and guns(Mossberg 500,Winchester,Remington,Berreta Perennia,Sako...) You are going to have a hard time finding a weapon that you like,and then you are probbably going to need to search the whole map for ammo.You are probbably going to need to learn for what guns is what ammo,but I learned the most pretty quick.There are servers where you just need to type !guns and you will have a menu where you choose it,but I found it more fun to struggle with finding all that stuff.It is more realistic.Teamwork is very important thing if you want to survive in this game.Communication especially.You can share weapons and ammo,and health stuff.
So,health stuff.Yes,you can get infected.If you get infected from the first waves,it's better to die,now there is a option where you can kill yourself,so killing yourself shouldn't be a problem :) Keep in mind that you have to take pills every few minutes,and if you die out of infection you are going to turn into a runner.You can say to your teammates that you are infected and that they should shoot you in the head,so you won't turn into the runner.But on some servers there is not frendly fire on,so they better prepare for you becoming a zombie.(There's aid kit-for health,and bandages-for bleeding.
Zombies are pretty well made,the can walk really slowly,a little faster,and they can run(runners).There are children zombies.Yes.Many people were saying to remove children zombies,because it is kinda disturbing.Yes it is kind of sad,but children aren't immune,ya know?Oh,and they run :3
And now graphics:they are awesome,the game is very detailed,so if you care about graphics so much,YES it IS  good.
Now,there's a thing I don't like in this game.It usually happens when you use meele weapons.You kick a zombie and even if you really damaged him,somethimes he won't respond and just continue walking like nothing happened,(it removes health but zombies aren't responding to that,they usually do,and they take a few steps back).And if you are close to them,they are going to get you.Luckily there's shove zombie buttont(V),so you can kick him away from you,BUT you can still get infected.You won't going to like that where zombie doesn't respond on a kick,especially if it's alot of runners there :P For me that is only con,if I found another one,of course I will write it.
In this game you really feel like you are the one surviving because it is VERY realistic,atleast for me.
And there's a tutorials in the game,so if you are new,it is going to help.ALOT.I had to learn it all by myself,because there wasn't a guide to whole game.And one thing I really like:you can barricade the door,and it is really good when it comes to survival,and it can be a good thing in objective maps too :D.I just had to point that out :)
SO I  REAAAAAALLLLLYYYYY recommend this game,and it's totally free,so it won't hurt to try it :D I hope you read the whole thing,and if you did,thank you.Sorry if it was long,but I wanted to tell mostly all about this game,because when I read a review about a game I always need to read a lot of them to know all stuff.

I recommend this on most counts, but there's one problem that REALLY hurts it. The Alien is basically "tethered" to you. Meaning, it will always be within a few rooms of you in the areas where you're supposed to be avoiding it. (At this point I've only done the Nostromo DLC, but friends have told me this is the same in the main game.)
Let's say you complete an objective and the Alien shows up. You hide! If you stay there and make no noise, it will keep patrolling the area around you. Forever. If you sneak past it, and go to the other end of the level? It will climb up into a vent and go to that area so quickly it may as well be teleporting, and then resume patrolling the area around you.
It's really easy to pick up on, especially once you get the motion detector. It feels cheap and transparent, and it hurts the game immensely.
**Revised after playing the whole game: This is most noticeable on Hard; the problem largely goes away on Normal, which I recommend as having a really good balance between the Alien being present and the Alien being tied to you with an invisible rope. I don't know who decided to have the difficulty selection screen describe Hard as the intended experience, but they have bad ideas.

+More character interaction. Much of the lore is fleshed out via NPCs as you journey through the game, with characters having more to say (and more to sell).
+Better networking and better co-op. A new ring essentially makes your summon sign only visible to your friends.
+More accessible covenants. While most covenants in DaS you had to jump through hoops just to find, overall DaS2's covenants are easy to join and more enjoyable to level.
+Dual wielding is greatly improved. Power stancing lets you swing both your weapons in new combos.
+Magic is greatly expanded and includes a new catagory for Hexes.
+Greatly improved NG+ experience. Bosses drop new items, new enemies spawn in special areas, and some bosses gain new mechanics.
(huge problems that will [probably] never change):
-Terrible map design. Most levels are very simplistic, with some even being a straight corridor from beginning to the token boss.
-Heavily unbalanced covenant rank-up requirements. Heirs of the Sun's 30 sunlight medals can be achieved in a few hours for max rank, while BoB & Blue Sentinel's 500 kills requires NG+ or nonstop victories in the arena (losses count as -1 rank points... why?).
-Overabundance of forgettable, humanoid bosses. Some are recycled later in the game (or later playthroughs) as normal mobs or bosses. Many bosses have similar attack patterns and fall apart when you circle strafe and roll.
-Swarms of enemies everywhere. While DaS focused on intense 1v1 fights, there were occasional cannon fodder slaughterfests. DaS 2 will regularly throw multiple heavily armored & long-reaching (polearms, ultra greatswords) enemies at you.
-Parrying and riposting are harder to perform and less rewarding. Even if you manage to riposte, you can now be damaged while riposting by the swarms of enemies in DaS 2.
-Overabundance of healing items and consumables. There's no reason to start as a Cleric because of 3 different purchasable lifegems (HoT consumable), 12 Estus Flask+5s (easily attained on first playthrough), and 8 other consumables that restore spells or cure statuses on top of healing you.
-Terrible plot and story telling. The last few levels (and especially the ending cutscene) make no sense and it feels like the devs just wanted to add "cool" stuff to pad the game.
(nitpicking and balance problems):
*Iframes have been removed from backstabs, ripostes, using fog gates, doors, and other environmental actions.
*Roll iframes & estus flask drinking speed are tied to a stat.
*No pyromancer starting class. You have to get roughly through one-quarter of the game to find your first flame and pyromancy and its very easy to miss.
*Tons of balance issues with both PvE & PvP. Near the end of the first playthrough magic becomes very powerful, even in PvE. In PvP most spells worth using in PvP will kill you in 1 or 2 hits even with strong magic defense.
*No un-cracked Red/Blue Eye Orbs and cracked orbs aren't sold by NPCs until NG+.
*Changes to equip load mean everyone is some kind of hybrid class, doing normal rolls while wearing full Havels with a cloud of
Affinity over them while waving a flaming katana around.
*Cheaters are currently a huge issue on the PC version. You can now be invaded while Hollow and not being human is a big HP handicap, meaning you will run into cheaters much more often than in DaS.

Hopefully FromSoft's next Souls game has some actual soul to it... Otherwise we might just end up with another Armored Core situation with a new half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥sequel being pooped out every few years.

I'm now a PC gamer for the first time since the early 2000s. Being new to modern PC gaming and even Steam, Wick has prompted me to make my first review since setting up my gaming build a few months ago.
Wow, what a great little game! I didn't like everything about it. The cartoonish style diminished the fear factor a little. And overly long death animations in horror games, where you get a really good look at your antagonist, also removes fear and mystery. But other than that the jump scares came thick and fast but were not too repetitive. There are enough spooky characters with their own unique ways of messing with you that this cheap, short little game never overstays its welcome.
More specifically, I really like the way that the different ghosts mess with you in a way that punishes staying put and forces you (sometimes literally) to move about and explore the environment. And this leaves you feeling as vulnerable as all hell.
At this price I really couldn't recommend it enough. Even if you're new to the survival horror/jump scare genre. Thank you Hellbent games. I'd love to see a much bigger, more slow burning horror game from you guys but maybe with more realistic and graphic visuals.

A game that has few peers, the closest that most people interested in this genre of gaming could compare it to would be a Total War game - you manage armies and resources to take cities and project your power.
To stop at this point is a disservice to how unique Hegemony is as a game. A major component this game tries to focus on is the complexity of waging war beyond simply marching a larger army to where your enemy is and beating them around the head a few times. You need to think about your supplies, the seasons, the number of recruits you have waiting to be called up, and the time it will take to defeat the enemy. You'll be frustrated as a planned lightning assault gets bogged down by a stubborn city resisting you, and then gobsmacked when a relief force arrives and you realise you need to pull back or lose your army because you ran out of food.
At this point there are many players who would be turned off by the complexity of this. "Why is the game punishing me for such small mistakes?". For me the most satisfying moment was learning from those mistakes and realising that the AI is as much at the mercy of these factors as I was. Starve out that impregnable mountain fortress, or build your own fortress on the route the relief force has to take to bide you the time you need. Along with the immense care taken by the developers in making the map the challenges you face each time are unique and interesting.
With that said I want to recommend this first game against the latter two; Hegemony Rome and Hegemony III. The former is a transition between the two, and the latter is a great game in it's own right that however doesn't capture the immense care and individuality of this first game.
It is well worth the price.

I recommend this on most counts, but there's one problem that REALLY hurts it. The Alien is basically "tethered" to you. Meaning, it will always be within a few rooms of you in the areas where you're supposed to be avoiding it. (At this point I've only done the Nostromo DLC, but friends have told me this is the same in the main game.)
Let's say you complete an objective and the Alien shows up. You hide! If you stay there and make no noise, it will keep patrolling the area around you. Forever. If you sneak past it, and go to the other end of the level? It will climb up into a vent and go to that area so quickly it may as well be teleporting, and then resume patrolling the area around you.
It's really easy to pick up on, especially once you get the motion detector. It feels cheap and transparent, and it hurts the game immensely.
**Revised after playing the whole game: This is most noticeable on Hard; the problem largely goes away on Normal, which I recommend as having a really good balance between the Alien being present and the Alien being tied to you with an invisible rope. I don't know who decided to have the difficulty selection screen describe Hard as the intended experience, but they have bad ideas.

I have to say,this is one of my favourite zombie games.And,it's free! So,this is probbably going to be a longer review,so if you don't want to read it all,just know that this is really awesome game.
First thing first,there are objective and survival maps.I find survival maps easier,but I enjoy playing on both.There are servers with unlimited ammo,and a few maps that are made for mostly just killing zombies,so if you just want to kill zombies,you can do that too,but of course,I recommend trying survival and objective.
Next thing:weapons.There are a lot of weapons.From meeles to guns.Crowbars,axes,baseball bats,hammers,pistols(Berreta,Colt,Smith and Wesson...) and guns(Mossberg 500,Winchester,Remington,Berreta Perennia,Sako...) You are going to have a hard time finding a weapon that you like,and then you are probbably going to need to search the whole map for ammo.You are probbably going to need to learn for what guns is what ammo,but I learned the most pretty quick.There are servers where you just need to type !guns and you will have a menu where you choose it,but I found it more fun to struggle with finding all that stuff.It is more realistic.Teamwork is very important thing if you want to survive in this game.Communication especially.You can share weapons and ammo,and health stuff.
So,health stuff.Yes,you can get infected.If you get infected from the first waves,it's better to die,now there is a option where you can kill yourself,so killing yourself shouldn't be a problem :) Keep in mind that you have to take pills every few minutes,and if you die out of infection you are going to turn into a runner.You can say to your teammates that you are infected and that they should shoot you in the head,so you won't turn into the runner.But on some servers there is not frendly fire on,so they better prepare for you becoming a zombie.(There's aid kit-for health,and bandages-for bleeding.
Zombies are pretty well made,the can walk really slowly,a little faster,and they can run(runners).There are children zombies.Yes.Many people were saying to remove children zombies,because it is kinda disturbing.Yes it is kind of sad,but children aren't immune,ya know?Oh,and they run :3
And now graphics:they are awesome,the game is very detailed,so if you care about graphics so much,YES it IS  good.
Now,there's a thing I don't like in this game.It usually happens when you use meele weapons.You kick a zombie and even if you really damaged him,somethimes he won't respond and just continue walking like nothing happened,(it removes health but zombies aren't responding to that,they usually do,and they take a few steps back).And if you are close to them,they are going to get you.Luckily there's shove zombie buttont(V),so you can kick him away from you,BUT you can still get infected.You won't going to like that where zombie doesn't respond on a kick,especially if it's alot of runners there :P For me that is only con,if I found another one,of course I will write it.
In this game you really feel like you are the one surviving because it is VERY realistic,atleast for me.
And there's a tutorials in the game,so if you are new,it is going to help.ALOT.I had to learn it all by myself,because there wasn't a guide to whole game.And one thing I really like:you can barricade the door,and it is really good when it comes to survival,and it can be a good thing in objective maps too :D.I just had to point that out :)
SO I  REAAAAAALLLLLYYYYY recommend this game,and it's totally free,so it won't hurt to try it :D I hope you read the whole thing,and if you did,thank you.Sorry if it was long,but I wanted to tell mostly all about this game,because when I read a review about a game I always need to read a lot of them to know all stuff.
And sorry,I'm not English,so they are probbably going to be some mistakes,well mostly because this is so long :P

Revenge is a dish best served cold and gelatinous which is why it's so satisfying to roll over everything that has mistreated the titular mutant blob, growing with each new acquisition like a sentient snowball. Conquering an area is followed by a little newscast vignette, showing those yet to be consumed in increasing stages of panic. Tales from Space: Mutant Blobs Attack creates the feeling of playing an old horror movie complete with dust-cracked edges (just like the CRTV you'd have to watch it on). The bonus levels delve further into this 'blast from the past' aesthetic by mimicking older game experiences. The change of play style that the bonus levels offer is also a welcome change of pace from the series of similar set pieces positioned around the very basic goal of growing larger and moving to the right.
The game has a keyboard and mouse control scheme that is more than functional, but clearly it was designed around a console as a controller offers greater precision. Oddly enough, there is still one mechanic that the mouse served better for which makes the ability to switch between the two control schemes on a whim an absolute boon. The point system is similarly flexible as it presents an incentive to be meticulous and thus makes things more difficult without punishing players that choose to take an easier way out. The 'beat my high score' mentality this creates gives the short game some much needed replayability.

Hegemony is truly a game about building an Empire. Once you begin expanding your Empire you will soon notice that you need more food, Supply nodes, Gold, troops and suitable defensive locations in order to just exist.
You can never be satisfied because just outside your borders lies the mines and or fertile lands that may fuel your next campaign across Thessaly, The Danube River, Asia Minor or many, many other provinces that, once within your grasp, will enable you to recruit allied/Mercenary troops to complement your native army, land and sea supply lines to feed your cities and army, gold to fuel your diplomatic and military needs and more territory to call your own.

Speaking as someone who has a degree in History and knows a lot about antiquity and Mesoamerican civs, the game does a amazing job of presenting Ancient Greece, it's warring states, cities, people, and events. If you have any interest Greek History, Military tactics and Geography, this game and it's successors are exelent as a introduction on the matter.
To Quote Phillip II, the great: " My son, ask for thyself another kingdom, for that wich I leave is too small for thee".

This game is about Macedon. But not yet another game about Alexander the Great !
It's even better, it's about his father, Philip II of Macedon, whose achievement was even more incredible than conquering Persia and India : he unified Greece.
Yes, he is the Guy who beat Athens, Thebes (The Dragon of Beotia) and even Sparta !
The game is about tactical battles, some simplistic diplomacy, strategy, but more important, logistics.
Troops need moral. And moral needs food. And food doesn't magically move itself from fields to warriors. You need supply routes.
The main campaign is driven by a lot (and I mean a lot) of Objectives. Some of them, historical, being mandatory for your progress towards victory. All of them having their own rewards.
Battles are tactical, with use of charging and flanking being very important.
The game is not perfect (far from it). Graphics are mediocre. It can sometimes be teadious.
But the journey of Philip II to become the Hegemon of Greece is just amazing.

Hegemony is a grand strategy game from indie developer Longbow Games. It's pretty similar to Total War in a lot of ways, except that everything happens on the world map. All the action is in real time, but the player can pause the game and issue orders at will. This becomes very important as your empire expands, because the map is very large and past a certain point you'll likely be fighting multiple battles at any given time. Overall, it's a much slower-paced and deliberate kind of game than AoE or Starcraft that depends more on careful planning than actions-per-minute, but still much faster than turn-based strategy. It's also a rather low-stakes game, since no particular battle field defeat is likely to be fatal to your empire, and you can pretty much always recover with some time and effort. Outright losing a campaign would essentially require intentional self-sabotage.
In terms of production values, the game clearly shows its creators' lack of resources. The unit models lack fidelity, the map is somewhat plain (aesthetically, that is, in mechanical terms there are a wide variety of environments), the sound effects are functional but get repetitive quickly, and the less said about the (thankfully rare) voice acting, the better. Still, none of these issues impact the gameplay itself.
Like Total War, units are created as groups rather than as individual guys, and fight in formation. There are only a few broad unit categories, and most of the factions (especially in Greece proper) are pretty much the same, but most factions have at least one unique unit, and some of these really do alter strategies quite a bit. Basic tactics revolve around a battle line of heavy infantry, and an unskilled player could probably get through the game eventually just by swamping the enemy under as many hoplites as possible, but a mixed army with ranged support, light infantry for flanking, and cavalry for fighting the enemy light units will perform much better if used properly. Units have a morale stat, and the goal of most battles is to break the enemy's will rather than fight to the death. Broken units drop their weapons and attempt to flee at top speed to the nearest friendly city, at which point they return to their home town and join the reassembling unit there. If they are captured, they can either be executed or enslaved, without moral judgement. Units recruited from the player's native faction gain experience with each victory, which the player can invest in a few different stats (speed, morale, rate of food consumption, and siege skill).
There is also naval combat, though the trireme (with Athenian and Persian variants) is the only ship available. it's a little bit finicky, to be honest, since how much damage you do is determined largely by the angle and speed at which the ships collide and they maneuver like, well, ships. It's usually just about who brought a larger fleet, or being lucky. Fortunately it isn't very important unless you're conducting amphibious invasions or raiding naval trade routes.
A lot of the strategy in the game revolves around supply lines. Trade routes are constructed by the player, but in most cases it's pretty clear where they're supposed to go and it's mainly just a matter of connecting the dots. These routes produce a bit of gold, but their main purpose is transfering food. All land combat units consume food, and if they run out their morale will quickly drop to zero. Since demoralized units are pretty much useless, keeping an eye on your food supplies and ensuring that the far-reaches of your empire don't starve is in many ways more important to victory than the actual fighting. Harrassing an enemy's trade routes and pillaging their farms to starve a city's defenders can be a very effective strategy that the AI practices routinely. Since food production varies by season throughout the in-game year, the timing of a campaign can be very important. Do you want to move during harvest time so your armies can forage off the land while they slowly overcome the well-fed defenders, or in the middle of winter to more easily starve the enemy but at the risk of your units collapsing from hunger? There's no one "correct" strategy, but your tactics will have to reflect the specific conditions you're marching into.
There's no base building in Hegemony, which ordinarily I would be disappointed by, but here it works for me. All structures have fixed, pre-placed positions on the map to reflect the actual geography of Ancient Greece. In addition to cities, there are forts, mines, watchtowers, farms, and shrines. The first three can be deconstructed, and are often found ruined, but the site can always be rebuilt. Forts and watchtowers are pretty self-explanatory, mines can be filled with either paid workers or slaves to provide gold, which acts as a population limit, and different types of shrines (heroic, logistics, and healing) provide different benefits to the units of the faction that controls them.
There are three campaigns in the game and a sandbox mode. The campaigns are a bit more structured than Total War since the player is given specific objectives throughout, and the rewards for completing them are often substantial, but there aren't any time limits and once you complete the tutorial section of the beginner's campaign the map is completely open. I spent about 60 hours conquering the entire map in my first playthrough of the Macedonian campaign, even though I had technically finished all the objectives much earlier than that. As a history student, I personally really appreciate the Civilopedia-style background information on pretty much everything in the game, and the developers make it clear that they've done their homework.
There are a number of different factions in the game, and a diplomacy system, but it's very simplistic. Other factions have a fixed hostility level to yours, based on the historical relations between them, and a variable intimidation statistic that depends on your relative strength and how close they are. These factors affect the frequency of attacks, and how much it costs the player to establish a truce or an alliance. The most important effects of the faction system are on the main gameplay. A faction's hostility determines the size of the garrison required to supress the inevitable rebellions, while allies fall under the player's control immediately and don't require a garrsion at all. Allied units are also slightly superior to the mercenaries recruited from most conquered cities, though they still have weaker morale than the player's native units, and don't gain experience. As I mentioned earlier, each faction also has unique units which can only be produced from their native cities. I often choose my targets specifically to gain access to a particular unit I like.
In conclusion, Hegemony is an extremely innovative game which makes up for low production values with simple but deep mechanics. Highly recommended to all strategy fans.

Broforce: Essentially Super Crate Box with short 2-minute levels instead of endless survival.
Can be fun, but I wouldn't buy it again. I do enjoy it, though. I will continue to play it; I would just have rather spent my money on another game.
[Post-Scriptum: This game is reminding me more and more of Super Crate Box, another Devolver game. (or Vlambeer at least). The menu, the small character, weapons, changing of weapons like the crates.]
[Post-Post-Scriptum: I played Expendabros. It is free-to-play, and is a seperate game, so I cannot include its review here. I can say, though, that it is a sell-out game, and an advertisement.]
Before reading my review, please understand that this game wasn't made for me and that it might be for you. I strongly recommend actually watching gameplay. The reason I was upset with this game is because I was expecting a game like Contra: an actual campaign, actual storyline, etc.
In most games I don't like, I appreciate the theory of the game they are trying to make, but have problems with the execution... However, Broforce suffers from the opposite. I actually do think this game fulfilled what it was attempting to make, but I don't like even the idea. I bought it to play with a friend, and I will update this review if playing with him has changed anything.
I don't like the short 2-minute levels. That is the entire campaign. Everything is 1-hit, you and enemies. Like Super Crate Box, if you collect the Bros (boxes) you will change Bros (weapons) and eventually unlock new Bros (weapons). There is no health bar, no struggle to stay alive. All death feels accidental. There's no real teamwork because you can't protect people from 1-hit kills. It's a free-for-all.
Pros:
-Some nice little details: Sound in headphones follows character on screen, good particle effects
-Includes many famous characters from famous American movies which does embody the American opinion of power and patriotism
-I really enjoy the feel of the characters, especially Snake Plisskin, J from MiB, and Ash Williams
-I like the friendly AI, I didn't expect it and it does allow some strategy
-Movement is very smooth and I like swinging from underneath rocks
-Playing as the big robot is a nice change-up
-The rocket-launcher guy is my favorite boss fight, please do more of this, and earlier in the campaign. Each different area is too long. The 2-minute battles ruins it for me.
-Each different area is in the place of a typical action movie and is nice-looking, but gets old sometimes.
-Character diversity can be good, but also can be bad. Usually good, though. Most characters aren't too similar to one another, except for the generic action heroes.
Cons:
-Getting to the end of a level to find you destroyed too much of the environment to continue is unpleasant
-Killing enemies is unrewarded - only the demon/devil/red man is required to be killed to win
-Game punishes you for getting bros - increases time (albeit time is not that important)
-Game punishes you for not getting bros - do not unlock new bros to play as
-Friendly AI is pretty bad, though I appreciate the mechanic
-few characters require strategy but McGuyver
-Same background and each level is indistinguishable from the next - gets boring for me, maybe not others. Areas are too far between from the next. 30 2 minute jungle missions until the urban area felt like a chore.
-This game doesn't actually have any jokes aside from "Free, two, one" and the humor of the actual gameplay, and the humor is appreciable but doesn't make me laugh
-Because this game wasn't enjoyable for me and I released a negative review, I will probably get a 3% helpful rating
-Doing anything crazy is discouraged because you only have 1 HP

This game gets a tentative "not recommended" after my having played this game since 2011 for a variety of reasons.
The reason it is tentative is due to the game being still fun if you play with friends and can forgive it's massively glaring faults.
First, is the publisher / developer Gamersfirst promising and failing to deliver time and time again. Second is all of the stuff outlined below.
The game is however immensely customizable, moreso than basically any other game on the market right now except maybe Forza... and that only matches the level of car customization, not clothes, symbols, and songs.
As for why I'm not recommending it, we move on to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t on offer. Let's keep this simple.
1.) If you are good, you will be accused of hacking constantly
1.5.) This game has a decent amount of actual hackers, this is why you will be accused of it.
2.) If you are average, chances are you'll be a Gold threat and be forced to play against people much better than you (or hackers).
3.) If you are bad, people will♥♥♥♥♥♥all over you constantly... try sticking to Bronze Districts.
4.) This community has more drama and toxcicity than YouTube and Twitter combined.
5.) For a new player, it is extremely difficult to start out since most of the community is either tryhards or hackers, and if they notice that you're not good they (especially the only average players) will go out of their way to make you miserable and chase you down for kills.
6.) G1 or GamersFirst, the company that currently develops APB, kind of has their heads up their asses. Their development cycle runs on Valve Time, partly due to the frankenstein code this game has and partly due to G1's laziness.
6.5.) GG1 has promised to update the engine to make the game look better for running on 4 years now, and has stopped giving updates to that regard almost half a year ago. There is no release date in sight.
7.) I hope you like it when 60-70% of all in-game events involve spending money in the real money shop!
8.) Very small community. Likely only 500-600 players strong MAX, with only 100-200 online at one time.
8.5.) The exception to the rule is if you're Russian. Even if not, you will see Russians and Brazilians a LOT.
9.) Can't upload your own pictures or music, it has to be made in one of the in-game creators, symbol-based and synth-based respectively (though the music editor is actually pretty good)
(and lastly) 10.) G1 support seems to prioritize people who pay more, so if you never intend to pay a cent into this game you may never hear from them if you have a serious issue... but if you pay thousands, you'll hear back within a few hours. Don't criticize this customer support in front of mods, or you may get banned (My friend got banned for a few hours for jokingly calling a GM a "Peanut"!)
If you have friends to play with however, and you can put up with the above issues, the game is very fun and there is nothing quite like it on the market today. Just keep in mind that anyone starting out fresh should stay in the Bronze districts until they're forced to move up to Silver when they hit Gold threat... I myself bounced between the two many times in my 600 hours on steam + a few hundred pre-steam! Only recently have I been basically permanently gold, and I'm still not good enough for it.

Ah, this game, one of my first games on steam, but, nostalgia won't interfere with an honest review.
Tales From Space...yeah, I'm not gonna say the whole title, I'll just use TFS, is a platformer game made by DrinkBoxStudios, in it you control a Blob, who, after seeing the other blobs experimented on, escapes and decides to absorb everything.
One of the interesting mechanics of this game is your size, to progress, you need to be large enough to eat corks blocking your path, you do this by absorbing objects that you CAN absorb at your current size, and this may let you become large enough to absorb bigger objects. This setup sometimes encourages you to explore, and sometimes you may have to solve a small puzzle to get stuff to absorb.
This game does have challenges though, you may have to avoid being hit by Army helicopters or tanks, or you may have to precariously avoid spikes, or you may sometimes have to outrun lasers, while performing other tasks, such as collecting objects to absorb or rotating something to pass.
Another mechanic are the powers, you can have Rocket Boosts, which offer air mobility, sometimes to collect out of reach items or escape a laser. You also have magnetism, which helps you attach to surfaces and avoid obstacles. Then you have telekenesis, which let's you open up paths, move objects, or launch yourself.
The music in this game kinda gave me a Rayman Origins feel at times, I have no idea why, but it was enjoyable to listen to. The graphics vary in style, one minute, you can go from an 80's/90's style to a pixellated style.
The game overall is kinda short, even if you try to get all the achievements and 100% the game. This game overall gets a 9/10, the only part that could be improved is making the game a bit longer.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is one of, if not the best, truck simulator game out there right now. It focuses on the very core of Europe; allowing you to create and grow your own trucking business to your own liking across the motorways and roads that spread across the land, with your own customised vehicle with many upgrades and additions that make the game dynamic and gripping.
- Huge map to a decent scale of Europe, including many of its key cities and locations that allow you to discover new places, stores, recruitment centres etc. encouraging you to explore - giving you an aim.
- Levelling system of unlocking new parts of the game, upgrades for your truck, and a business is brilliant - you are constantly striving to grow bigger and better.
- Ability to create, manage & expand your own business which operates all around Europe with your own staff, trucks, and money.
- Weather is although decent and realistic, only offers minimal options - features like snow would be a brilliant addition.
- Roads are repetitive and plain; however updates are routinely being brought out to help tackle this (as well as DLCs available to open more diverse locations).
- For the average gamer it may be seen that to set up a business and to customise your truck to a satisfactory level may take more time than would be preferred.
The game is a must if you are a truck fanatic or generally wanting the simulated experience, it offers a realistic approach to trucking in the modern day world. You even have the option of playing multiplayer with thousands of other truckers (an unofficial mod, but trusted by all) which makes the game more diverse and interesting than it already is. Buy it, and you definitely won't regret it.

Preordered it and yet no regrets about this - poor pc optimization won't break the greatness of this piece of art.
Few weeks of patience and it will become a GOTY 2016.
Pros:
- Storyline, oh god it is so detailed! Have you ever imagined to read a book, watch a movie and listen to stories at the same time? Here you will get it. Going straight forward is not a good deal with this game. Read all the notes you can find on tables, listen to all the talks nearby - they all will sink you into the game atmosphere.
- Arts are gorgeous. Victorian steampunk style is one of my favorites in this game.
- It's an old-good Dishonored stealth. Having a great fun by running silently in No-kills and No-detection challenge. The best thing about that is that game encourages you to play stealthy in lot of ways and this one is the most enjoyable.
Cons:
- Yeah, poor optimization. It runs 50-60 fps on my 4570+1060 3Gb rig on medium-highs but that 60 fps aren't smooth at all. However, get a patience - this game deserves to be played and not to be refunded. Just give it some time for polishing.
- Skills/runes/amulets - some new skills added but I was waiting for more major improvements. Yet not a big issue.
Great game anyway, I recommend it for those who liked a previous part and for all who prefers and has enough patience for a stealth-way of game walkthroughs. Rushing with sword through the enemies wastes all the passion the art part of Bethesda had put in this game. Be safe and watch your back: enemies around!

What a waste.
There are some promising aspects of Wick from the opening levels. As a veteran player of first person horror titles, and as someone who first got into horror games during the craze of microbudget Unity horror games ignited by Slender, it felt pretty nostalgic returning to a similar environment - a haunting dark forest full of genuinely creepy ambience and a wide variety of NPCs to run away from - and at first, I thought this would be a game that built upon the Slender-esque mechanics and atmosphere with refined gameplay and story. I was wrong.
Wick is marred by annoyingly tedious gameplay and an abundance of cheap deaths that ultimately ruin an otherwise passable indie horror game. The "survival" horror comes from outlasting groups of enemies in the same map every level. Sure, player and item spawns are randomized, but it gets old pretty quick. What killed Wick for me was pretty much the second half of the game. The sheer volume of enemies encountered is ridiculous. Take a similar but far superior horror game - Slender: The Arrival. It switches up the environments with great setpieces, and different enemies to match. Not in Wick - they just throw the same goddamn monsters at you in different groups and greater numbers. This results in spending hours on one level that's roughly 15 minutes - the repetition is truly a chore.
Are there some good scares in Wick? Yes. The earlier levels boast some inventive qualities, I particularly enjoyed one enemy which floats and tampers with the player's vision. Otherwise, the enemies are pretty cookie cutter - there is one (Caleb I think) which bizarrely feels like the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ son of Bugs Bunny and the miner zombie from Plants vs Zombies.

I'm already six hours into Alien: Isolation and I am terrified in the best way. These days most entries in the survival-horror genre barely phase me yet this one has sunk it's teeth deep into my psyche. In short, I'm loving every minute of it (although I do find myself taking semi-frequent breaks to let my heart rate go back to normal).
Performance: The game performs much better than I expected it to on my computer. I was very surprised to see it running at a solid 60 FPS at ultra settings on my $700 gaming rig. I was sure I'd have to turn down a few settings to get optimal performance but that wasn't the case. The game seems very well optimized and runs nicely. I have only encountered one minor bug at this point so it seems pretty stable as well.
Gameplay: Like I said above, the game is a wonderful mix of terror and fun. I've spent almost the entirety of my time sneaking and hiding, collecting and crafting, rather than being aggressive with the survivors or androids and it's served me well. The few times I've tested the waters with combat it did work fairly well but that definitely isn't the focus of the game and I wouldn't rely on it unless necessary. Too much noise will lead the alien right to you. Encounters with it are a varying mixture of trial and error at first. You will likely die a lot. Once you get a feel for things it gets a bit easier but the alien makes for a quick, intelligent, and unpredictable enemy-one which learns how you play and adapts.
Graphics: The visuals are awesome so far. The designers really captured the spirit of Alien with the low-tech sci-fi aesthetics. Environments are gorgeously detailed and nicely laid out. The lighting is also fantastic. My only gripe is that the human NPCs do move a bit stiffly but there aren't that many of them so I've hardly noticed. The alien moves fluidly and looks great though.
Sound: The soundtrack is phenomenal, finding that perfect balance between suspense and action while simultaneously taking many cues from the original movie. The sound design is excellent as well, especially if you've got a surround sound setup. I've found myself wincing constantly as you can hear every scuff of your own shoes on the floor and countless other tiny sounds as you move through the environment. Making too much noise will alert the alien and in a lot of cases you'll hear it before you see it too. A thump in a vent, a quiet hiss, or the dull thud of feet on the floor and you know it's there, somwhere. Time to hide! Waiting and listening from a hiding spot can be tortuous too as you strain your ears to hear the alien moving through the room over the sound of your own heartbeat.
Overall, I'd give the game a solid 9/10 so far and don't expect my rating to change anytime soon.

Hegemony Gold: Wars of Ancient Greece is a very intelligent game, both immediate and deep. I would define it as an "operational grand strategy game".
The emphasis is obviously on logistics: the real trick to success is keeping your troops well supplied and in good shape, and that can be hard, especially during sieges and winters. Sieges in particular are rather well represented in a fun way, as you'll need to block enemy supply routes, both on land and on sea, while keeping your own open.
Strategical maneuvering is also very important, and delaying the movement of an army might mean the collapse of your empire. Your state is almost like a house of cards: lose a key region for your supply network and your income, and you'll find yourself in big trouble. The AI itself is very skilled at exploiting those weaknesses in your grand strategy, and you'll find yourself often at war on multiple fronts. Unlike many strategy games, as you grow there won't be any kind of avalanche effect: you will have more resources and more troops but your borders will also be longer, and you'll find out that you can't deploy that many troops in a specific campaign anyway: small and mid-sized kingdom still pose a very tangible threat even when  you're the biggest empire on the map.
The tactical part is simplistic: it's an RTS at that, but the mechanics are a bit lacking. Also, proper tactical maneuvering is still very important but most of the time you'll find that there isn't a lot of room for maneuvering.
Other than that, this game has a huge plus: the immersion value. It recreates the era pretty well, and to this day I've never seen a more detailed recreation of Ancient Greece in a videogame, with many historical kingdoms and city-states making their appearance in Hegemony and so many missions you have to complete to establish your dominion over Greece. You'll never get bored as you'll always have things to do, and the historical grand campaign lasts many, many hours.
In short, I highly recommend the game. It's a very original and innovative title, and if you like historical immersion and strategy go for it: you won't be disappointed.

Features include:
*Building a community, pretty much werhever you want really, but the game recommends you stay in a huge, defendable canyon
*Scavenging food, water, bandages and luxuries to help improve you rrelations with your fellow survivors
*Ability to recruit tons of survivors in the game, though recruiting means you have to do a lot of work or give gifts to them first
*You can command survivors to do things, like scavenge certain resources from a building, defending from towers or pillboxes, or farming, which lasts untill you tell them to stop
*Fun, exciting, but difficult quests that give some much needed color to this barren apocalypse
*No loading screens except for loading, launching and jumping into your last save takes less then half a minute
* You can beat bandits or other camps and force survivors to join you
I really love playing this game and would recommend this to anyone, so they can get obsessed like me, however, there are some things that I'm not crazy about and hope they fix or add in the future, I'd play it all the time if they did already.
Features I don't really like:
*The main character is pretty bland and uncustomizable,  you play as Joe Wheeler, a wealthy man who hid away for a year from the zombie apocalypse in his own private bunker but now has to leave to find more food and resources
*The entire map is pretty much a gigantic desert, though the locations are very interesting, being able to find a nice bit of green or a lake to settle near would be nice
*Zombies are very powerful for some reason and some, even thought they're just individual zombies, will soak up dozens of your survivor's bullets, even with headshots
*Leveling up skills takes forever, and some ou'll need to go out and find books that give you a bonus to that so you can actually use that skill, and then level up while using the book,
*There actually aren't that many items in the game. There's canned food, chips, corn, bottled water, wood and chicken wire and cement, which makes up 80% of the items you need to gather in the game
*No way to carry more stuff without backpacks, with the second largest backpack in the game, and just a pistol, you'll only be able to carry about 2 planks of wood; the survivors will only walk when you tell them to go gather resources, and you'll eventually have to go further and further away from camp, which is dangerous and can take about a half hour in real time to get maybe a dozen planks
*Most of the time survivors will just stand around not really doing anything but complain, it'd be nice if there were more jobs to give, like cook, repairman, lumberer, doctor, rancher or miner
*No customization at all
*No animals at all
*Corn is the only thing you can farm, but there's never enough of it
*Survivors can't last longer then a real life hour going out questing as they need rest and eat and drink
*Your community can grow up to the dozens, but there's only one way to switch characters, by cycling through them one by one
*You can swap characters, but if your main character, Joe dies, game over,
*The main characters starts out pretty much useless and you'll even have to swap characters because people will naturally not like Joe's personality or because Joe doesn't know how to hammer a fence
*Equipping your survivors with a gun, bullets and a bulletproof vest takes up most of their inventory, leaving no room for loot
*Bulletproof vests are the only protection you can wear
*Switching, between your building's inventories and the survivors in it can be confusing
*No categories to make searching inventories easier, like "Food and Water" "Weapons and Ammo" "Construction Materials"
*There will be times that you get stuck, you'll have the people; not the food, you'll have the weapons; not the survivors, or you'll feel  like you have everything you need but your useeless diabetic friend needs more insulin which is expensive as hell and currency is really hard to find
*You can only build two types of fences and gates and towers, and one pillbox, one type of house, and outhouses
*It's implied you should keep everything in your bunker but that makes it very difficult to find what you're looking for, the only real option would be storing things in different houses
*You can't negotiate peace in some cases, and some achievements want you to recruit some peoeple, which will either die or end up hating you for finishing quests you need to do.

Survivalist is an open world RPG best played with friends, to enjoy the Zombie apocalypse together in a cozy bunker and provide to your little community. Without other players it is possible to give tasks to the different characters that can be recruited, and I was surprised to see that the AI did a good job managing them.
The different systems for survival are logical and work well, without being too hardcore to be a hassle. Survival is definitely not a constant chore as in Don't Starve.
Killing a Zombie is easy... Except when there starts to be more of them. Shooting is not too fast, it's not a shoot'em'up, but it still works well enough to balance fun and tension, especially when it becomes possible to aim specific body parts.
Just don't expect too deep. Not much is said about each characters, they just all have enough to be different,  Overall it's a light take on The Walking Dead, free for you to express your own story.
The graphics seem a bit poor at first, but once again this is very functional as the zoomed-in/portrait camera allows to give more personality than a top-down view would do alone, and ends up being quite endearing.
To conclude, Survivalist managed to be enjoyable to me despite not liking survivals and RPGs. I found that it is because all its systems are very functional. Everything is well done, a perfect balance between easy and difficult. Enough complexity without being unforgiving and annoying.

I never wrote a review here before, but this game is truly a hidden gem! The gameplay is a very satisfying blend of rpg and strategy (I found it somewhat reminiscent to the Jagged Alliance series). But in this game, the world is much more open-ended and realistic. For example, it seems as though it is theoretically possible to recruit almost any NPC to join you by making certain decisions and using certain items. After the initial, classic-rpg small-group portion of the game, you also start to build your own town, complete with shacks, outhouses, defenses, and corn. The balance of finding items to survive early on and eventually having to make your own is very well done. As you start to manage a larger group of survivors you can also make use of automated commands such as "collect materials", "farm" or "guard" that give portions of the game a sort of apocalyptic Sims feel. In terms of gameplay, I found fighting zombies annoyingly hard, but using auto-combat mode basically turns it into more of a pure strategy game. Fighting other people, though, the computer interestingly does not do so well, so I manually control my survivors then. There are a few weaknesses I'll list below, but overall this is the best $3 I've ever spent and I hope the developers will produce many more games in the future!
Pros: Great blend of rpg/strategy, gritty and realistic post-apocalyptic environment, recruit many survivors, build you own town, multiple endings, nice survival balance
Cons: Graphics are a bit simplistic, some NPCs look the same, zombies bite too much unless you use auto-combat, no way to fast-forward through sleeping or resource collecting, music is just alright
Overall: Great indie game, one of the best I've ever played, highly recommend!

I usually tend to stay away from Early Access games on Steam, but Broforce has been calling to me.  I haven't heard anybody that's played it that didn't like it, so I gave it a shot and man...I love it!  With my limited experience with E.A., this has to be one of the best 'non-complete' games I've played yet.
The game play is straight forward and simple; rescue bros, shoot bad guys, blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up!  And man, it is so fun.  The terrain is highly destructible, so your sense of causing utter destruction is really grand.
While the game play itself is simple, the games difficulty is quite tough.  You will die, frequently.  You're going to swear a lot too. But with the game's restart feature, it's painless to just keep coming back and trying over and over until you can get through to the end.  Different unlocked bros have different skills as well. Some are shot guns, some are machine guns, some have grenades, some have knives.  They each add a great little spin on the game to keep it fresh and exciting. And on top of all that?  This game's pretty funny too!
Now again, this is Early Access.   So the game's incomplete.  Which blows my mind, because in its current state, Broforce is a blast.  (Pun intended.) The developers, Free Lives, are adding content to this regularly, so there's also no fear of this becoming abandoned.  Just last week they added two new bros and some game play tweaks to go with them.  It's a really solid outfit and if this isn't on your wish list yet, I'd add it a.s.a.p!

By far the best representation of Ancient Greek warfare I've come across in a video game. A great complement to the History of the Peloponnesian War.
Cons:
- Clunky interface
- The campaign is very long, and as such gets quite repetitive by the end.

If you're me, you'll immediately pick this game up without looking at the reviews because you're a Greek History nerd.  If you're me again, you are deeply satisfied with the results.
Hegemony Gold is a game set during the wars of Ancient Greece, specifically around Philip II and the Peloponessian war.  Instead of a game like Total War, all battles are set on the same map and provide a difficult challenge.  You have to make sure your troops have sufficient morale and food or else they'll rout and either be captured and executed, or have to reform at the nearest city.  It basically focuses more on the logisitics of war than the battles.  Very interesting and highly recommended.

Listen. I understand if some of you like this game, but it just didn't click with me.
Let's get this over with.
+ open world zombie game
+ has a lot of RTS elements - you collect resources, build your own base, recruit survivors and protect it from raiders
+ multiple endings and many choices
+ quests can be completed in all kinds of ways
+ generally very open-ended - do the main quests or just wander around the desert and expand your base.
Now I get mean.
- HORRIBLE MUSIC. I mean, seriously! When I play a zombie game I expect something dark and heavy, some rock, maybe metal. Heck, western tunes would fit with the setting of the game. But instead you get some music made by teenage boys that would fit more for Unturned (no offense for Unturned btw, it's a great game). But yeah, you're walking around the desert killing zombies, and then... ugh. I have no words.
- the graphics. I understand that this is a low budget indie that started as a small game for consoles. If you have a weak laptop, then you may like it. But for me? I'm not a "graphics are everything" guy, but... nah.
- the animations. Check out how the character walks. This is a placeholder from a prototype, not a fully relased game you pay money for.
- the combat. This is pretty much a twin-stick shooter, but there's something very important. You don't aim manually, intead when you draw the gun the game just locks on to whatever is in front of you. And this is really annoying when your ally is getting eaten and you just lock on to all the zombies swarming around you but not the one you need to shoot.
- the infection. If you get bit, you get infected. When that happens, you need a cure. But there are different kinds of zombies, and each one requires a different cure. Remember the previous part? Yeah. You know what happens. What's worse is that cures are pretty hard to find, and they are used automaticaly. Now for example a green infection takes a few days to kill you. It doesn't really weaken you in any way, but instead of saving it when you will really need it, you will just jam it right away and then probably get bit again.
-t    h    e     f   r  a   m  e   r   a   t  e. Now that's the worst part about the game. In 60 FPS the game runs in slow motion. Now there's a reason for that: enemies move pretty fast, so you need some time to react. I would understand if this slo-mo activated in combat, but it will be on even when there's no enemies around you and you're just walking to the nearest town. And with slow motion, it will take ages. Meanwhile when you turn on 30 fps, slow motion disappears, and you now move much faster. This is better, right?
Right?
NO! Zombies are not slow like the old-school ones, they run at the speed of light at you, then they leap at you draining a lot of stanima forcing you to knock them off. If you're in 60 fps, you can actually dodge the leap and watche the zombie gracefully fly right past you in slow motion and slowly ragdoll on the ground. But if you're in 30 fps, you get no time to react and get grabbed and molested repeatably untill you get bit and probably killed. It's worse when you're fighting enemies with guns, because then you will be literally showered with bullets and killed befoe you even think about getting to cover.

Okay so I've had this game since it's original release with RealTime Worlds and I was here when it was
and then I quit, for a long time. Partly because friends stopped playing, or because of other things I was interested in. The hours I have logged on Steam are by no means representative of the total amount of time I've spent in this game, since there were multiple clients before APB was ever tied to Steam.
With that out of the way...
Contrary to popular belief and reactionary players with 3 hours of gameplay on record, this game isn't so bad. The customization, although dated, is almost the deepest customization I've ever seen in a game, coming in a close second to Black Desert Online (another game I play). There's music to listen to, a wide array of weapons, mods, clothing and so on to choose from, plenty of things to do and if you've got a sort of GTA itch but don't exactly want GTA, then this game works.
I'm blown away that even after all this time, the game is still being supported and worked on, and honestly, I do hope the future for APB is only improvements.
Also, you've probably read a lot of reviews of people crying about "p2w," but here's a hint: This game isn't actually p2w. What they think p2w is, is bypassing some of the game's grind and getting right to later content. But that's not at all what p2w actually is, and that's the only advantage you can buy in APB's cash shop (and getting straight to endgame absolutely does not mean you're going to win).
Pay to win is when you can buy gear from a cash shop that doesn't exist in the game already, gear that is overpowered and able to easily kill other players in a PVP setting, i.e. winning. There is none of that in APB. The cash shop weapons here aren't even better than the top tier weapons you can get in the game without paying. APB absolutely isn't pay to win, but it
pay for convenience. Which isn't even a bad thing to have.
I actually only have a few cons here, and these are it:
Aimbotters
Optimization issues
Toxic community
Are there aimbotters and should you be aware of that? Yes. Granted, 90% of the time when someone is screaming about hacks, there is actually no instance of hacking happening, but every so often you
unfortunately see that edgy player with the snap-autoaim taking you down in 2 seconds flat—And they're only wearing trainee pants. The best thing to do is /report them and move on, but if you're coming into this game you should know that, like other online shooters, this one has its fair share of people who can't play without automated assistance.
The optimization issues are a pain, in that even on a midrange system that can play GTA5 at nearly max settings, if I have just a web browser and some chat program open, APB will stutter like crazy. Close all of that out and the game is fine, but it's annoying, and I hope the upcoming new engine fixes that problem.
Then there's the community. It's about what you'd expect from a multiplayer PVP game. You have the edgy 13 year olds who think "triggered" is a funny meme, or that SJW is somehow an insult. You have the grown adult men who think voting for Donald Trump is somehow a reasonable and intelligent thing to do, and more often than not, these are the same players with Nazi symbols on their cars and clothing.
And then you have the regular people who at least sort of seem to be able to use their whole brains in social situations. It's a mix, and if you pay too much attention to it instead of just playing the game, it'll get frustrating. Also, I'm
sure G1 bans the neo-nazis.
Would I recommend this game? This is a tough decision to make here, because right now I feel like there is an iffy balance between pros and cons. I feel like if the devs actualy work to improve the game in the coming months, then the recommended I'm giving it will be justified. If not, maybe I'll just have to change this later.

If you haven't already got the game, you're probably wondering, like I did, what all the fuss is about with Euro Truck Simulator. At its core it's exactly what you'd imagine: Drive a truck from point A to B and deliver cargo. Doesn't sound very exciting?
Well it isn't, not really. ETS2 is more about relaxing, sitting back and enjoying the scenery. That's not to say it isn't challenging. Driving a truck through cities of various sizes and winding roads does sometimes require a lot of concentration, not to mention parking the trailers. It doesn't sound like a lot but there's something immensly satisfying about playing this game.
After you've done a few jobs you can upgrade your truck or buy a new one. There are many different, licensed trucks you can buy and the upgrading adds a sense of progression to the game.
There is a business management side to this game too. You can buy garages, upgrade them, hire drivers and watch them gain experience and earn you more and more money. This side of the game is very basic though and once you hire the driver and buy them a truck you pretty much just let them get on with it.
So what's the catch? In my opinion the base game has far too much motorway driving. This might be realistic (or not- I'm not a truck driver) but it still gets boring after a while and until I got the Scandinavia DLC it was that aspect that really put me off after a while.
So while we're on the subject of DLC... There is lots of it. I've heard criticsm about the amount of it but I personally think it is worth it. Particuarly Scandinavia and France add a huge ammount to the game and I'm looking forward to the upcoming Italy. They're much cheaper and higher quality than the DLC for Train Simulator (rant at Dovetail but thats for another place).
But even without the DLC, the base game holds its own and more than worth the money. It's perfect if you're looking for a game to help you chill and unwind.

This is an extremely well-made game, considering the fact that it still is in early access (though it feels like a complete game already). The devs (originally a team of two) did a wonderful job with everything - the soundtrack, artwork, and gameplay. The soundtrack never gets old after hours of gameplay, the music really sets the mood in the different biomes right, and the slime sound effects are perfect. The artwork is exactly what you see in the screenshots - cute (the tarrs are slightly more terrifying though..). The game play is pretty amazing; there's just two standard actions vaccing and shooting and this game utilizes them remarkably well and the controls feel natural and fluid just like in other FPSs. Moreover, the achievements felt like just the right amount - very rarely do some of the games I play have a good balance between attainable v. hard to attain achievements - it took be about ~20 hours to get 41/43 achievements (The "Glass, smoke, mirrors" achievement at the time of this review is unattainable b/c the area has not been included yet). A huge plus of this game is the small team of very dedicated devs - the patches come frequently and they listen to the community, unlike some other early access games. With each patch, more and more of my minor complaints are fixed - and some of these complaints I hardly recognized I had until I read the patch notes and thought, "huh, yeah, that was annoying but now it's fixed!" One of the major last improvements that could be made would be the ability to have some form of multiplayer mode, whether it be local or online. Other than that, I have to give the devs huge props to creating a game that can hold the attention span of someone like me :)
