Wick short review (Don't worry I will play more of no way out)
What I think: I really loved the game. It was better then most horror games out there and it needs more attention. Wick had me on my toes figuring out and trying to avoid the enemies. Let me explain more here!
Story: The game had a good background story once you attempt to dig deep enough. The story at the moment is you play as a young teenager (Sam) who is taken to the woods by his friends and left there until he has survived the game Wick. You must avoid the enemies as much as possible and not get caught. The "ending" to the game will shock you to the core! It has an amazing background story and the evidence you find in the game really helps you figure out a lot of details. The events are also helpful to figure out the game. And the new DLC got us way deeper into figuring it all out.
Gameplay: In this game it is styled to be a normal first person horror survival. You must walk around the entire map in order to avoid the enemies and collect items. Once the enemy has found you, you have no choice but to run away. Every enemy has its own special abilities that you must firgure out how to avoid. The game is smooth and nice and I thought the gameplay wasn't original but it was made much better then any other horror game.
Art: The art is really good (except for me I had to lower the graphics). The enviroment was creepy and dull and that was one of the reasons why I really loved the game. The enemies are really well designed and they don't look bad at all. However if you brighten up the gamma the game doesn't look good. Keep the gamma low for the best gameplay!
Music and sounds: OMG the atmosphere has to be one of the best things in the game. The sudden footsteps behind you. The noises of the background and the sudden tense music that can really give you goosebumps. Every noise you heard was unsettling and unwelcome. The music for the game was great. The Chase themes are well made and it suited the enemy. The music itself was nicely made but there is only one theme... Hope they release the free soundtrack.
Pros and cons
Pros
- Enemies were fair and balanced
- Ambience and music
- Artstyle

- The hour are not to long compared to FnaF
- Unsettling game events
- Wonderful lore
- Free DLC
Cons
- Game is to short
- OMG WHERE THE HELL ARE THE CANDLES!
- Cheap jumpscares when exploring (Troll)
Either way the game was worth the money so if you are a huge horror fan then play this now! You won't regret it!

This is a fun little game and will chew up your free time if you let it.  Supposedly relaxing but can be quite hectic on some levels.
There is one major flaw in this game - one of the achievements is impossible.  The "Hero" achievement is broken.  Level 12 is supposed to have 100 seedlings you can find/rescue on the map (on top of your starting 100).  There are only 60.  The devs acknowledged this issue and promised a fix several years ago.  It has not eventuated.
As I am an achievement hunter, this ruins the game for me completely.
Game is 9.5 out of 10 for me for just the game but, due to the broken achievement which makes it impossible to get a perfect completion in Steam, I cannot recommend this game to anybody with any level of achievement OCD.
EDIT:  I found that there are LUA files for each level.  I modified the LUA file for level 12 so that it no longer has only 60 seedlings to rescue.  This allowed me to complete the "Hero" achievement for the game.  Note that, even with that adjustment, there are actually too few seedlings to rescue to make the achievement possible (adding the extra 40 was not enough) so adjust the numbers accordingly and the achievement will unlock.  I am amending my recommendation based on my discovery and completion of the game.

If the title didn't really tell you, this game radiates charm in everything it does. Playing like a 2D Katamari, you journey as an adorably grim blob out to have revenge for its tortured blob comrades, and you do so in some gloriously well paced and charming ways. While there are puzzles to be found in this physics platformer, none pose more than a few minutes of challenge to figure them out, as the main draw is simple catharsis of consuming the planet. There is a bit of challenge to be found in the secondary task to find your friends (and eat them), but most can be found fairly easy and only occassionally serve any real challenge. Making this sound like a bad thing is rather foolish of me, as this game is meant to be enjoyed for what it is. Given how this is pre-Guacamelee Drinkbox, I loved seeing their roots and their love of reference-filled billboards clearly has been an ongoing gag of theirs. This game's main draw for the hardcore is speed and time attacks, but I was never really compelled to do so, as I had far too much fun seeing what weird things I got to eat next. Play this game for the experience and the charming cutscenes, but don't expect much else outside of the main storyline. It's worth the short playtime, I assure you.
(Note: I played this game while my power was out, so my play time is a bit inaccurate. I finished it in about 5 hours overall to give you an idea of how long it is.)

In space, no one can hear you scream...
In fear and frustration.
So far Alien Isolation has proved to me that the game does tension, atmosphere, sound, and aesthetic perfectly. If you're a fan of the original film you'll find yourself in love with the way the game looks and feels. They got it right. No, they got it perfect. Lighting, steam and sounds that echo back to the 1979 classic and you get to live it. For me I was excited, we've seen enough games in the universe that follow the action side of Aliens but nothing quite like the horror and dread of the first film. You have it here. So far the best part for me was the pre-order Nostromo DLC; I was like a kid on Christmas when I played as Ripley on the Nostromo running through all of the steam-filled halls as the ship was about to explode. The nostalgia got me something fierce.
As for the main game, I've put about 4+ hours into it so far and I'm liking it. Everything feels like Alien, 1970's sci-fi with tube TVs which need to be tuned, bulky objects and tools turned weapons. Sevastopol feels warn out and lived in, and you're stuck in the aftermath of the events that took place prior to your arrival. It feels believable and it's interesting to explore and wonder how everything went to hell. There's also a certain beauty to it, colorful lights keep things interesting for the eyes but it's still bleak, objects are strewn about and some will rattle your nerves as you accidently kick physics enabled cans which rattle down hallways leaving you wondering "Did anything hear that?"
Sevastopol feels a lot like Dead Space 2's Sprawl station, if you've happened to play it you'll feel it's a bit familiar. The inhabitants of Sevastopol come in three flavors: humans, androids and the Alien. Encounters with humans tend to be Mexican stand-offs, allowing you to leave them be or having you try and take them out though several times I tried getting around a group and they opened fire on me regardless. The androids are properly creepy but are slow, only coming after you with a power-walk like pace and you can outrun and hide from them with ease but they take a beating to go down. As for the Alien, well, you're screwed. You can't outrun it and you'll have to use your tools and they environment to sneak by, only later will you get a flamethrower that will temporarily ward it off. You can build med-kits, pipebombs and noisemakers and there's also lockpicking mini-games, power panels and computer terminals to interact with. Don't worry, the mini-game isn't annoying a you'd probably think. One point in the game, which was a highlight for me, I was trapped in a room at the end of a hallway, the Alien was on patrol right outside coming to the room. I hit the emergency override on the door to keep it closed and used the Rewire panel in the room to trigger an alarm at the end of the hall to grab the Alien's attention. He ran to the end of the hall and I made my escape. It's really rewarding when you come out of encounters unscathed but when you don't, there's the biggest flaw the game has.
That same encounter didn't go so well the first time and cost me 20 minutes of gameplay. The saves weren't that far apart but they took place during an Alien encounter, so you have to be slow and methodical least you want to reload your game. The game uses save stations, there's no quick-save or checkpoints (unless it's the beginning of a mission), so from my initial save I spent 20 minutes creeping around, looting boxes and corpses for materials only to have it wiped away by an omnipotent Alien. That's one thing I hate about the Alien encounters, because there's only one and it's the star of the show they've made it so it's always a threat when it's around. That's good, but it's feels almost scripted and not natural. That encounter I talked about was essentially two large areas with halls and rooms to explore, you had to go from area A to area B and back through area A. How it went down was the Alien showed up in area A, I made it through to area B without making a sound but as soon as I made it there the Alien showed up and patrolled area B and never went back until I did. Because of this this small section took up a lot of time and at the very end, without making my presence known the Alien B-lined it for me and killed me, at this point I didn't have the flamethrower so I was as good as dead. Good show. Load save.
Technically I haven't had any issues, my GTX 780 is pushing 120 frames easy and has never dipped though if you turn off V-Sync you'll notice a lot of screen tearing during the prerendered cutscenes which there's a decent amount of. It's pretty annoying.
Ultimately it's hard to not recommend the game but I'm a total fan of the film, if you are too you probably already have it. Currently I'm 5 hours in and apparently that's a quarter of the way there, so there's a lot of value here. The DLC is great as well but if you've missed the boat for it you'll have to get the season pass and there's no release date for the Nostromo stuff yet. If you're on the edge and enjoy horror titles with a sci-fi flavor you'll enjoy Alien Isolation.

Simple Review?
You might like this game if you enjoy:
1: Destructable environments.
2: Pixel Art.
3: Making fun of America's stereotypes.
4: Action Movies.
5: Run'n'gun combat.
6: Explosions.
7: Explosions!
Things you might not like:
1: You constantly change characters, even when you don't die.
2: You never get to choose what character you play as.
3: Your character is not as durable as action characters in action movies.
3a. You will die.
3b. A lot.
3c. Henceforth, if you get a character you like, you will swiftly be replaced with one you don't.
I like this game. A lot. However the entire concept of this game revolves around running and gunning, killing everything, but when you die with one hit it feels like I'm being punished for playing the game the way I'm supposed too. One minute I'm on a killing streak as Rambro, only to be hit by an exploding canister that fell on me from off screen. Now I am Brochete, who is still awesome, but not who I wanted to play as. Now I have to save a hostage, and instead of being Brobo Cop, the character I was lucky to get at the start of the missiob, I am someone completely different, who I don't like.
The entire playthrough of this game I enjoyed MOST of it. When I was going on a crazy rampage as the character I wanted, I was extremely happy. When I spawned as my favorite character, only to save one hostage and be replaced with my least favorite? Not as much.
Take all this as you will. It's an AMAZING game, full of great moments, and crazy ammounts of gung-ho action, and you will get your money's worth (and more considering it's still being updated), but it has a few small drawbacks.
All in all, recommend!

As of now I have about 20-30 hours logged into the game and am level 13 currently, so I think it's time to finally base my opinions of this game. First of all, I am not comparing this to previous Elder Scrolls games. I am viewing it as it should be viewed, as an MMO.
First off, combat: The combat so far has proven to be very demanding of attention. It's also very fluid and is diverse as well.
Second, crafting: As far as crafting goes, I have no complaints. It's not too difficult to a frustrating point but it's not easy enough for a beginner to get going right off the bat. Your crafting levels don't take forever to level up either like other MMOs and don't require extreme amounts of materials. It's fair.
Third, quests: Questing in this game is generally the same as most MMOs, but feels very different. Everything is voice acted and the quests are fairly easy to follow along. They actually provide a story to the quest and make it feel meaningful, like what you're doing will actually mean something and isn't just a means for you to level up.
Fourth, customization: Cosmetic wise, the game is great. You can get disguises through quests and use those as costumes if you wish. You can also unlock dye colors for your armor and dye them whenever you want for no charge. (But they get bound to your character)
Fifth and final, skills & leveling: The skills are similar to previous Elder Scrolls games, where the more you use something the more you level it up and unlock more for that skill. Leveling up your main level takes a bit of time, but it's not too difficult.
How would I rate this game? If I had to be honest, I'd give it a clear 9.5/10. With this much exploration, heart pounding fights, and deep questing all in one game and with the removal of the monthly subscription, I would say this game is a must buy for MMO lovers. Even if you're not a fan of Elder Scrolls, if you like MMOs I would deffinetly give this game a chance.
[Edit]
About 150 hours in and I finally see some issues with this game, although very minor. The most annoying being that with the class system, ALL class abilities use magicka, regardless of which one you choose. So it's very difficulty to make a stamina based class that doesn't use magicka at all.
Secondly, there are some tech issues that can be very annoying, such as the "0.01" error that happens when trying to sign in(Not sure if this happens often to anyone else). Although that's usually fixed with repairing the game.
Thirdly, this is more opinionated but I dislike the racial system, where each race has a certian skill tree of their own. It takes away the freedom of customization.
On a side note, this game still is not boring. With 150 hours in and still going strong, I feel this game is very well worth $60. If you're tired of looking for an online game you can quest, adventure, and level up with friends then I would highly suggest this game.

i got well into black ops back in the day, on the sony play station platform. on black ops 1 i was pretty much a pro tbh not blowing my own trumpet or anything, but this one time i did get chopper gunner twice in the same match with sniper rifles (in care packages). and that time i skewered this dude in the head with the spring loaded knife was pretty cool too, especially as the screen was flash banged but i pulled it off anyway, probably because i had a special perk ability activated.
combined BO 1 and 2 i played a lot. hours, days, weeks certainly. surely not months? i cannot say for sure.
anyway i got sucked away by less vital things (girlfriend and job) and had to move out of the house i was staying in and alas had to leave behind the xbox and playstation we shared.
anyway cut a long story short i decided to give COD AW a go. it had good initial independent reviews and i had a new rig (expensive gaming pc put together as a hobby) to test out. also a month off from work. also no girlfriend (we broke up she's not dead or anything).
anyway the reviewy bit;
artistic license has clearly been taken with 'AW' and largely it works, i think. if your into the single player campaign then especially this works, as the exo suits make for an interesting new dynamic to the generic mix. im not into single player at all generally anymore and i played just the first few levels just so to give it a try and also see and hear what kelvin spacey looks like in 2057 or something (he looks pretty good). i did have some fun but got bored after about 3 'levels'. i think i heard it referred to as 'a glorified shooting gallery' and i don't think i could put it better myself. it was pretty to look at first, fun too, but got bored so quickly.
with games like cod it's all about MP and that's what the rest of this review will focus on.
the exo movement takes some getting used to and kudos for making a change like this. always a balance has to be struck and i think the exo movement was a savvy maneuver the games developers knew cod gamers would embrace one way or another. to be sure if you don't then you will die even more than you think is already possible and will keep doing so until you get used to it or just quit.
the exo movement clearly extends to map design as well, and clearly a lot of time has been put into creating some interesting spaces for jumping around in army grasshopper style.
personally, having very fond memories of BO1 this change in design is difficult to get used to. i've played 40 hours so far and have prestige'd once. while the graphic dimensions of the maps are in places brilliant (that map with the tsunami warning / tsunami is stunning) in others they feel bored and samey.
the weaponry is similar with a few new takes on some. they've done well by keeping the '13 points' load-out structure too, which seems to work very well. my biggest gripe here is with the sniper guns, which they've played around with in a way which is not to my liking. there's only 4 of them (standard), but one of them has a '2 fire system' and so far i don't see anybody bothering with it.
as you may have already guessed i was a bad♥♥♥♥♥camping sniper boss in bo1, and i feel a little bit lost so far not knowing how to use even the semi - auto or the 'MORS' effectively. perhaps if i get to know the maps better that will change.
Regardless of my own expectations of the game in bo1/2 there was definitely more 'space' to sneak around in and perhaps dig yourself in, especially with effective teamwork. with the new player movements it does feel like the same tried and tested run and gun formula has been jacked up that few more notches. at it's worst it's jittery spray and pray, and this aspect is relentlessly unforgiving if you've not got the patience to die over and over and over and over and over again until momentarily things slot into place a little bit. then it's good. that bit comes right before getting dumped on the head by your own 'orbital' care package.
it's the same run and gun, arcade style ffs on legal performance enhancing steroids, and can be really good fun.
this is not a comprehensive / serious review, but well done for reading the last sentenceses. based on my own first impressions and feelings im giving this game 3.5 stars out of 5.

Hegemony is a top tier real time strategy game. In it you must expand your starting kingdom through war and diplomacy. There is also historical campains which start in certain senarios, however I have not played these and therefore will not comment on them.
Pros:
- In this game you have to plan your campains wisely, each season will directly impact food production, which is central to gameplay. The impact of feeding your troops (logistics) really deepens the campain over other strategy games such as total war.
- The camera can be scrolled in and out to see the larger picture or into great detail. It reminds me of the supreme commander camera.
- Aestheticly this game has an interesting "board gamey" style, with units lookng like peices on the board. I enjoy this art style as it is unique from other games.
- The map is huge, and gives players vast areas to conquer.
- There are small histroy notes scattered throughout the map which help immerse you (and are interesting to history buffs like me).
- The music is simple but also helps immersion into the ancient greek world.
Cons:
- The diplomacy in this game is very shallow, and boils down to paying your enemies enough so they will stop invading you so you can focus on eating another nation.
- You will constantly be raided by Athens throughout the entire game, as Athens has naval island bases scattered throughout the greek world. This is not really a con as it gives a difficulty boost to the game, but it can be annoying.
- The unit diversity is not very high. All the greeks have the same hopilites, barbarians have the same medium cav, thrace has the same peltasts. However, some of the greek factions have hopilites which are stronger in combat, some are stronger at seiges. Thracian petalst are vastly different to greek peltast. Persians have elite heavy cav. You will find the unit diversity to be simple, yet effective.

This game isn't worth $5... it's worth at least $15.
The game is very immersive presenting you with ethical dilemmas such as, stealing to keep yourself alive, saving the many by damning the few, hell - there's even a literal gay couple dilemma in here. While not listed this game IS a sandbox game as you have the option of building anywhere which makes the game even more immersive as you'll probably spend many hours simply deciding the layout of your base.
There are a ton of quests. Most of these quests, if not all, have diverging paths you can decide from similar to Fallout or Skyrim.

Coop is fun. You and your friends share the community members which works great as one person can handle the construction or farming and another person can finish up quests and scavange. During the difficult quests you can bring a friend or have your followers back you up. (Peer 2 Peer style coop - someone hosts, others join. No servers req.)
The developer(s) has been pretty transparent with this game often replying to community questions in the forums. I believe a sequel is due and I look forward to playing it. If you're looking for a cheap game that you can easily spend 30+ hours on this is the one.

In space, no one can hear you scream...
In fear and frustration.
So far Alien Isolation has proved to me that the game does tension, atmosphere, sound, and aesthetic perfectly. If you're a fan of the original film you'll find yourself in love with the way the game looks and feels. They got it right. No, they got it perfect. Lighting, steam and sounds that echo back to the 1979 classic and you get to live it. For me I was excited, we've seen enough games in the universe that follow the action side of Aliens but nothing quite like the horror and dread of the first film. You have it here. So far the best part for me was the pre-order Nostromo DLC; I was like a kid on Christmas when I played as Ripley on the Nostromo running through all of the steam-filled halls as the ship was about to explode. The nostalgia got me something fierce.
As for the main game, I've put about 4+ hours into it so far and I'm liking it. Everything feels like Alien, 1970's sci-fi with tube TVs which need to be tuned, bulky objects and tools turned weapons. Sevastopol feels warn out and lived in, and you're stuck in the aftermath of the events that took place prior to your arrival. It feels believable and it's interesting to explore and wonder how everything went to hell. There's also a certain beauty to it, colorful lights keep things interesting for the eyes but it's still bleak, objects are strewn about and some will rattle your nerves as you accidently kick physics enabled cans which rattle down hallways leaving you wondering "Did anything hear that?"
Sevastopol feels a lot like Dead Space 2's Sprawl station, if you've happened to play it you'll feel it's a bit familiar. The inhabitants of Sevastopol come in three flavors: humans, androids and the Alien. Encounters with humans tend to be Mexican stand-offs, allowing you to leave them be or having you try and take them out though several times I tried getting around a group and they opened fire on me regardless. The androids are properly creepy but are slow, only coming after you with a power-walk like pace and you can outrun and hide from them with ease but they take a beating to go down. As for the Alien, well, you're screwed. You can't outrun it and you'll have to use your tools and they environment to sneak by, only later will you get a flamethrower that will temporarily ward it off. You can build med-kits, pipebombs and noisemakers and there's also lockpicking mini-games, power panels and computer terminals to interact with. Don't worry, the mini-game isn't annoying a you'd probably think. One point in the game, which was a highlight for me, I was trapped in a room at the end of a hallway, the Alien was on patrol right outside coming to the room. I hit the emergency override on the door to keep it closed and used the Rewire panel in the room to trigger an alarm at the end of the hall to grab the Alien's attention. He ran to the end of the hall and I made my escape. It's really rewarding when you come out of encounters unscathed but when you don't, there's the biggest flaw the game has.
That same encounter didn't go so well the first time and cost me 20 minutes of gameplay. The saves weren't that far apart but they took place during an Alien encounter, so you have to be slow and methodical least you want to reload your game. The game uses save stations, there's no quick-save or checkpoints (unless it's the beginning of a mission), so from my initial save I spent 20 minutes creeping around, looting boxes and corpses for materials only to have it wiped away by an omnipotent Alien. That's one thing I hate about the Alien encounters, because there's only one and it's the star of the show they've made it so it's always a threat when it's around. That's good, but it's feels almost scripted and not natural. That encounter I talked about was essentially two large areas with halls and rooms to explore, you had to go from area A to area B and back through area A. How it went down was the Alien showed up in area A, I made it through to area B without making a sound but as soon as I made it there the Alien showed up and patrolled area B and never went back until I did. Because of this this small section took up a lot of time and at the very end, without making my presence known the Alien B-lined it for me and killed me, at this point I didn't have the flamethrower so I was as good as dead. Good show. Load save.
Technically I haven't had any issues, my GTX 780 is pushing 120 frames easy and has never dipped though if you turn off V-Sync you'll notice a lot of screen tearing during the prerendered cutscenes which there's a decent amount of. It's pretty annoying.
Ultimately it's hard to not recommend the game but I'm a total fan of the film, if you are too you probably already have it. Currently I'm 5 hours in and apparently that's a quarter of the way there, so there's a lot of value here. The DLC is great as well but if you've missed the boat for it you'll have to get the season pass and there's no release date for the Nostromo stuff yet. If you're on the edge and enjoy horror titles with a sci-fi flavor you'll enjoy Alien Isolation.

You walk around a dark forest while enemies randomly pop out of you in a rather hilarious way, you survive the night, onto the next night, and so forth. Imagine combining Slender: The Eight Pages and Five Nights at Freddy's into a game. Wick is literally that. Walk-through-a-forest-and-always-look-away simulator with some pretty cheap jumpscares that are only scary the first three times. I'm a MASSIVE horror junkie and I've played just about every horror game out there, so I can tell what's a quality horror game from one that's not. Wick gets boring rather fast without improving much to any of the gameplay. It does add a new enemy type to each night you survive, however, I rarely enccountered these enemies. The only characters to really pose a threat are the main enemy type; the ghost children. With bad design and dumb jumpscares, they lose their sense of being a scary threat too. The candle mechanic was done very well. You have a limited number of matches, which you use to light candles to keep the ghosts away while providing a light source. The candle starts to melt, so you have to be very careful with how you use your matches. If the enemy types were more scary and agressive, this would've made for a great game. If you enjoyed Slender and FNAF and are looking for games like them, Wick is worth the $10. However, if you're looking for a horror game that's different and doesn't misuse jumpscares, look further. A good horror game with great atmosphere and scares and around the same price range as Wick, try The Cursed Forest. I'm going to give Wick a 5/10.

A very pretty, polished arcade platform puzzler available for Windows, Mac & Linux, of the "absorb random stuff so you grow large enough to absorb yet more random stuff and escape to the next part of the level" genre.  Sounds simple enough, huh?  :)
Pros:
+ Graphics (looks and feels as beautiful as you might hope it could from the screen shots, even on a modest machine!)
+ The mechanics and physics (comfortable, intuitive and well behaved)
+ Gameplay (enough differences between the levels to keep you interested, stimulated and challenged.)
+ Difficulty (progresses in a friendly and carefully linear way: not too hard to upset a casual player, but a gamer who wants to get 100% will scratch their head until they hit that "Doh" moment when it all suddenly becomes obvious!)
+ Sound (great soundtrack, but see below.)
+ Multiplatform (Windows, Mac AND SteamOS/Linux comatible - I've mainly been playing under Linux.)
Cons:
- Very hard to find anything bad about it, but perhaps there's not quite enough variation in the soundtrack sometimes if you're playing a bit of an addicted marathon - however, it's such a minor point it's not worth fixating on.
In summary:  I have nearly a 100 games in my steam library, but I just can't stop playing this one; hence I felt compelled to write my first steam review.  I can often measure the amount by which I enjoy a game by whether or not I just want to get to the next level OR whether I'm enjoying this level so much that I'm determined to clear it to 100% -- a rarity for me (as I don't often trying to fully complete games) Mutant Blobs definitely fits into the later category.  :)  Although I bought this game in a bundle, I would actually have been happy to pay full price.
Definitely recommended! :)

This is a very interesting arithmetic-based roguelike with an unique concept! I actually played Zeno Rogues other roguelike, "Hyperrogue" first and the completly different, yet just as unique concept of that game intrigued me to get this one as well and I was not dissappointed!

The description of this game does not do it justice. Roguelike based on mathematical puzzles sounds like an arithmetic quiz program or someone packaging puzzles in a mediocre framework. One of the reviews even said it would be ok without the math. I envisioned puzzles where there was a correct solution every time.
This is first a roguelike (oldschool roguelike), and the 'puzzles' are, like a game play in awell designed roguelike, emergent - naturally arising from the procedurally generated world. There are often many good solutions to the puzzles, and the game play revolves around finding good enough solutions, and using your resources wisely.
This also sounded like it would be novelty alone. It isn't - at least for me. The weird way the weapons work makes it so every level there are interesting decisions about which to keep - there aren't any that stand alone, you are judging the effectiveness of your weapons by the combinations you choose. This contrasts with most role playing games where you find a good weapon, use it for a while, then replace it with a better one - one which is obviously better.
The arithmatic in it won't be for everyone, but if you don't mind it, and like old school roguelikes, then I would bet you will like this game. Make sure to use the potions of knowledge - they will teach you how to think about the puzzles. Also make sure to use the auto explore ('o'), it speeds the boring bits along.
Definitely worth 3 euros. Where else can you meet a 33565-headed hydra and have to decide with which sword you need to strike first?

I picked up Hydra Slayer during the 2016 Summer Sale, because I really dig roguelikes. Due to its mathematical nature, I wasn't 100% sure that I would gel with it, but I gave it a shot. I'm very glad I did.
Hydra Slayer is one of the strangest roguelikes I've played -- and I mean that in the best way possible. At the core, it's a mathematics-orientated game, where you have to use basic maths functions in order to defeat hydras. Your weapons come with a power rating, which dictates how many heads it chops off a hydra in one attack. When a hydra loses all of its heads, it dies. The downside is, you can't make an attack with a weapon with a stronger power rating than the heads on a specific hydra. If you had a sword that did 8 damage, you can't use it to kill off a hydra with, say, 6 heads.
The idea is that you equip yourself in a way that you can cleanly kill the hydras you come across. If there's a 14-headed hydra and you had two swords, one doing 8 damage and the other doing 3, you can attack once with the 8 (14-8=6) and then twice with the 3 (6-(3*2)=0) to kill it. It seems simple enough, until you learn that both hydras and weapons carry an element to them, and they react with each other in set ways. A flame dagger (power rating 1) against a 2-headed ice hydra will take off one of its heads without any regrowing; a bone dagger, however, will cut off one but regrow two more!
More heads means more attacks and more wounds, but sometimes allowing a hydra to populate heads puts it 'in range' of a bigger weapon, allowing it to perform a clean kill. There's even an item in game that makes a hydra grow more heads and become more powerful, with the benefit that the amount of heads that grow makes the hydra more optimal to slay than before the item was used. Other items include a potion that tells you the optimal weapon usage for killing a specific hydra, a potion that gives you another weapons slot to play with, and even a scroll that turns a hydra into mushrooms (should they prove to be totally unhandleable).
It's important to note that newcomers shouldn't stick with the Human player race, assuming it's the easiest to play. While its the easiest to start learning the game with, it's not the easiest to
with -- even the game tells you that. Once you get a grasp of the game and want to progress big time, try Echidnas. They have the permanent power to attack with any number of weapons they like, so their strategy is all about one-shotting hydras. When playing Echidnas, you want to set yourself up so you can insta-kill
hydra you come across with the weapons you have. When you begin, you'll have a strength 1 and 2 weapon, which means that any hydra with 1-3 heads can be removed instantly. When you get a third weapon, you can raise the 'ceiling' on the hydras you can one-shot. Equipping a second strength 2 weapon will allow you to murder 4 (2+2) and 5 (2+2+1) headed hydras. Keep raising the 'ceiling' without losing the ability to slay
hydra below said ceiling, and you should get pretty far. There's an optimal loadout in the Guides section that you can use -- see if you can work it out for yourself, though!
And if you're not very mathematically minded and a little intimidated by the nature of this game, realise that I'm terrible at maths and, at time of writing, currently
. If I can get that far, so can you!
To finalise, Hydra Slayer is the perfect addition to a roguelike enthusiast's library. If you love maths, a good puzzle, or just sick of mashing your numpad keys to repeatedly bump into enemies until they die, give this little gem a shot.

Hydra Slayer is a rogue like game which tasks the player with.... Killing Hydras.  Hydras are large snake like creatures, killing them requires cutting off their heads..  The game has various weapons and magics, each weapon can remove a certain number of hydra heads, the task is to eventually widdle the head number down to zero, using math to figure out the correct weapon or magic to use.  It qualifies as a rogue like game but onw in your typical go into dungeon, slash up enemies, and collect up items.  This game has enemies, and items but the math aspect makes the game unique.
This game won't be for everyone, the math and different weapons aspect seems to be both cliche and unique.  I personally found the game to be rather exciting to play, it came across as a roguelike, but had some puzzle elements, and the added math problems made it challenging enough to last for numerous hours.
The graphics are kind of minimal, but they really aren't needed to enjoy the game.

is a fun little puzzle-platformer that’s very light in both the puzzle and platforming departments.  It boils down to a short-but-sweet casual experience that will entertain, slightly challenge, and not frustrate.
The game is extremely light-hearted and is very casual.  The levels are pretty short and simple.  That being said, I really enjoyed the level design in this game: you have to pay attention but you don’t really have to
.  It’s a nice experience: it mildly challenges (mostly only if you’re going for the gold medals), has plenty of checkpoints, and there are no overly frustrating parts.  As someone who prefers casual games to frustrating ones; I can say I really enjoyed this.   If you are someone who enjoys punishment from their games, you may want to look elsewhere.
There is no real story or anything, but it doesn’t need a story.  There are a few catoon-esque cutscenes.  The cartoonish art style and the music are a perfect match to the gameplay.  The platforming was smooth for me; I used a controller and was never frustrated with controls/response.  It is a short game, and is pretty easy to 100%.  As you progress, there are a handful of platforming mechanics that are mixed around to keep thinks interesting.
To surmise:
is a casual platformer with mild puzzle aspects and a cartoon finish.  A short-medium length game that is pretty easy, yet very entertaining.

Tales From Space: Mutant Blobs Attack is a puzzle-action platformer. You are a "blob", an alien that has only one goal : eat everything through 24 levels (6 worlds) + 5 mini-games.
You can jump, fall onto the ground with strength to break things, use special power to get close or away to metal objects + move some specific objects. That is simple, but enough to give you tough challenges through some levels.
For each level, you can get a medal (silver or gold, depending on your score : the higher, the better) and you have to look for 2 Blob Friends (1 for the mini-games). Tip for level 16 : in order to get a gold medal, your score has to be at least 29000, which means that you have to eat almost everything available, pretty difficult !
There is a leaderboard, so, if you want to be the best among your friends or even around the world, it adds some replay value !
Overall, this game is pretty fun and 5-6 hours should be enough to get all of the achievements.

I am a die-hard fan for Ridley Scott's original Alien movie.  The games that previously came out before this, however, did not give the reason why we loved the face-hugging, chest-bursting, and the "alien interspecies♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; (yes this term is used by some of the creators of the original Alien film) that came from one of cinema's most iconic monsters.  However, Alien: Isolation redeems that idea of that terrifying, scary, and 80's feeling from the first film.  Sega has given us back a piece of cinema gold that gave fans the chills of seeing that monster come down the hallway, or, more appropriately, crashing through the vents of your spaceship.  If Kane were to be alive, I'm sure he would've loved to play this game before having his chest being ruptured again.

This is how survival horror should be done.
If you're familiar with the Alien franchise, you'll feel right at home. Every inch of space is filled with advertisements and notes, and all are easily legible, which I found myself spending more time reading at the start of the game than looking for supplies. There is so much detail and affection given to this game that it surprises me, after seeing so many 'AAA' titles using pixelated jpegs for backdrops or posters. This just adds more to the immersion, and it does it well.
There seems to be a number of tools you can collect along the way that will allow you access to different rooms, giving me a sense of a Metroidvania game, but blended well with elements of horror and suspense.
The ambiance is stellar, tensing you up and putting you on alert at all times, reminding you to be cautious. The game slowly eases you in, letting you get accustomed to the controls and how the rules work, introducing a new element one at a time as you progress.
One of the biggest things I noticed was the lack of a waymarker - and I actually like that. It makes exploring the ship feel more like an adventure to survive, instead of following a big glowing arrow to the next story piece. You can always bring up your map to check where to go if you get lost, so it's not leaving you totally in the dark.
You are given tools to defend yourself, but only as a last-ditch effort to survive, as ammo is scarce, and some enemies won't fall to a single melee swing. Thankfully, you can craft numerous gadgets to get you out of any situation, and there are plenty of hiding places to wait out. The other thing I noticed is the detection range on enemies seems to be a bit more realistic, instead of extremely wide. I've walked by the side of someone while crouched, and they didn't notice me right away until I made some sort of noise.
The Alien in the game is absolutely amazing - equal parts fascinating and terrifying. I actually found myself receeding deeper into my chair every time it appeared, gripped with a need to escape and survive, as though it was actually me on the ship, staring the Alien in the face.
I cannot think of a single thing bad to say about the game. This is a game that I would recommend to anyone, especially fans of horror games and the Alien movie franchise.

This game is fantastic. I prefer this old Making History game over any of the new ones.
I imagine I'll reach up to 1000 hours of play time on this game, by just how entertaining it can be.
PROS
The game looks great first of all, just simple unit model designs, alongside a simple map design. But it's quite pleasant to look at. This game was originally made for classrooms, so even the worst toaster-pc could run it.
You can mod a ton in this game, and that's where the most enjoyment comes from. There's a lot you can mod, but most the time it comes down to creating new nations.
If you have other friends who own this game, then you can setup matches with hamachi, and play multiplayer. (If you need help with this, comment). Having friends with you in the game makes everything much more interesting, since the AI often becomes boring, and predictable.
Simple game mechanics make this game relatively easy to get the hang of. Learning how to build up your production, research, and population, is all quite simple.
CONS
The simple gameplay may be a bit too simple at times. Population especially is a bit weird. Each region has its own population count, and it takes ages to go up (WIthout modding). Sadly you dont get to see how fast your population grows in a particular region, but only how much is growing in the nation as a whole.
Diplomacy seems too simple. If you give a nation an alliance offer, they'll only accept if they're at war, which is a bit annoying. Peace deals are really linear as well. You can only demand 4 things, or concede 4 things.
Its a bit of a dead game as well, sadly. There's a small discord server community running, but the alive community really is small.
TLDR: Fun game, simple game mechanics, not so great diplomacy, decent modding capabilities. 8/10

I did not receive a review key and this review is my own opinion.
While Hydra Slayer easily qualifies as a "proper"/"traditional" roguelike, having turn-based, grid-based combat, dungeons, levels, weapons, potions and monsters,  the combat is non-traditional as it involves calculating how to kill hydras based on how many heads they have, how many they will regrow and how many each of your different weapons will slice off, while also adding game mechanic-changing items into the mix.
This was originally a 7DRL (7 day roguelike) and is a perfect example of one as it has one central bizarre twist on top of traditional roguelike elements.
There are currently some rough edges: music on the game over screen glitches, isometric mode has way lower fps than it should have (30ish using opengl and 10-12 on my machine using sdl2 (which could be using dx or opengl)) and there are some grammar errors (mainly the "fewer" / "less" thing which comes up a lot becuase of the heads mechanic).
Graphics are not very good but functional and there's the option for ASCII which is great. Different race options provide new interesting ways to play and there's a daily challenge mode. All in all there seems to be enough longevity here and the price is good.

---
With that being said, it isn't nearly as frustrating or pure-coffee-break game as
.
A great majority of the enemies are hydras with varying number of heads. The weapons you wield can kill or stun a certain number of heads, therefore making it a bit of a math puzzle in how you go about taking down the hydras on every level. Once you kill all the hydras on a level, you progress. There are no shops. Items are found scattered throughout the levels in a mostly pre-determined fashion.
Once you learn the system and know where to look, the game does alot of the math for you. If you absolutely hate adding a few numbers in your head, I'd probably stay away, but otherwise don't let the 'math' portion of this scare you away.
+Brilliantly fresh new mechanic for a roguelike. It all works so well.
+I love games (specifically roguelikes) that truly reward learning the system. The kind of thing where a newbie has < 5% chance to succeed, while a veteran who understands the nuances has >90%.
As time goes on, I can easily get to higher/deeper levels. There are no meta-game unlocks either.
+The playable classes are all brilliantly thought out, and vastly different. I could go on and on about this point, but simply explore that for yourself!
+I play
of roguelikes, and the items in this game are far more functional and really fun to use compared with most other roguelikes. Nothing feels redundant or wasteful with the item functionality.
+Keyboard controls are super smooth, as should be for any classic rougelike.
+There is like three or so majorly different layouts you can choose from. Ranging from a hex-grid to isometric, and more.
+The Steam achievements are very appropriate, and will have you coming back for dozens of hours, if not more.
-Music and sound could be better. I mean they are ok, but really what you are getting here is a hugely addictive gaming mechanic.
-Artwork is ok as well, but I would
to see some wicked pixel art tiles!
-As with
, the engine can give some slowdown, but it is fairly manageable. There are alot of settings on NotEye, so maybe I just haven't found the sweet spot yet.
-I'm hoping a community-backed Wiki pops up! Or at least some detailed Steam guides woud be great. Its not a 'con' of the game, but something I'm putting out there! I will try to make a guide after I have more hours under my belt (I am at about 15 total so far).
Y'know if you are on the fence you can try the game for free by downloading it from the developer's website, but I assure you it has earned its asking price. This is a no-brainer for any lover of the classic roguelike.

Survivalist is a great game. The thing I like about it most is the fact that you can control an entire community of people. The trailor didn't necessarily do a good job of showing community so I will talk about that and then tell you some Pros and Cons of the game(there are way more Pros).
In the community you have to provide for each and every need that all your survivors have. You need to provide them with water, food, ammo, sleep,insulin (for Alice a person with type 1 Diabetes) and protection. You can farm crops or scavenge nearby towns for food. For water you can make wells or scavenge. For ammo you have to scavenge gun shops. And for sleep you need to make sure you have enough buildings constructed or taken over that provide your members with sleep. Each member has a certain amount of respect and approval for you and if you fail to provide them with these necesseties they will lose approval and respect. There are two ways to recruit people to join you. You can help them and make them like you and they might join, or you can force them to join you by having fun with a bullet and rifle. You can tell your people to be guards, farmers, build things, follow you and help you, medics, scavengers you can even set up a team to explore. These are just the first parts of owning a community but I hope it helped.
Here are the Pros and Cons
Pros
You can control your characters directly or in a control mode
You can control each character
There is a huge variety in skills and a really cool skill system
The game slowly gets harder and harder as you progress
The game has a cool zombie system with different strains that are harder
The game periodically sends hordes or groups of zombies and looters to attack your base
I love the missions in the game
Good online gameplay except for one thing(see Cons)
Cons
Graphics aren't the best
Sometimes glitches will happen when forcing someone to join your community
In multiplayer if you get in a big fight against zombies the game will sometimes lag
overall I believe survivalist is a very clever and cool game and I really hope this review helped.

I am not going to spoil the game story line.
The game has so much to do even just an hour in and you feel like there is a lot of pressure on you. You have to make sure that your female companion has insulin regularly and also you have to make sure all three have enough sleep, water, food and so on. The game truly does give you a feeling of survival, one mistake could mean the death of your player. However the game isn't unforgiving, if you fail you should just go back to your last save (from what I know.)
I believe there is a few issues that I had that I will state in order:
1) The interface.
The interface makes it annoying to work with and this problem links directly to number two.
2) The quest menu layout.
To me, as a noob, it's a pretty confusing layout sometimes that just doesn't need to be. They could have easily segregated the most important parts to the side quests.
3)The Ctrl mode
Although this mode is ingenious for someone who really doesn't want to have to cater for all three individuals one at a time. The buttom theme/controls could have been layed out better and at the beginning has really confused me.
My absoloute favourite parts about this game are:
1) The dialouge and story line so far.
The story line and dialogue is extremely believable and does really make you feel like these are real people in real situations.
2) The survival aspect.
The starvation, dehydration and sleep deprivation aspect really gives the game an extra boost of realism, sure the graphics do not however the game does give you some realistic aspects.
3) The other settlements
I love that there are other settlements all around the place, it does help when you really need more insulin or you are in need of medical or food and water supplies.
Overall the game is well worth the price it holds and has really portrayed the zombie apocalypse well. The developers of this game should be proud of this one.

While it cannot be said that I have played this game "extensively," I feel as if I have played it long enough to have a good view of what this game is. I will be disregarding the campaign because, honestly, who still plays CoD for the story? All that needs to be known is that it's slightly less generic than the previous installments. Now, onto the multiplayer. (There is a TL;DR at the bottom.)
Advanced Warfare's multiplayer is one of the best CoD multiplayers that I have played since Black Ops II thanks to the new and fleshed out movement system. Players will frequently utilize what is called an "Exo-Suit," which is used to quickly make your way around the battlefield. In Advanced Warfare, players have access to double jumps, dodges, mid-air strafes, and special "Exo-Abilities," such as temporary speed boosts, camouflage, hovering, and much more. Because of these changes, Advanced Warfare is much more "versatile," so to speak. Originally, in every previous CoD, the MVP would usually be the person with the fastest reaction time and best aim. However, in Advanced Warfare, the extra movement granted by the Exo-Suit allows players to quickly move themselves out of harm's way, and maybe even allow them to turn the tide on the person who ambushed them. For example, I found myself in a wide-open plaza and was surrounded by three other players. I double jumped into the air, mid-air strafed towards one of them for the punch kill (yes, you punch instead of knife), then took cover behind a car to shoot another at range, then charged the last enemy with a sliding shot (when you slide and shoot at the same time). For those of you who just want the original, and, in my opinion, stupid, CoD formula, there is always a classic mode where the exo-movements have been removed.
Now, onto talk about the weapons and progression system: most of the high-tier weapons are given to you right off the bat. As a matter of fact, I got from rank 1 to rank 40 almost exclusively using the KF5 with a red dot, foregrip, and laser sight. The fact that players are given extremely good guns from the get-go removes the "satisfaction" of grinding to a certain rank to unlock that new, shiny, badass gun everyone wants. There are also different "versions" of guns that can be given to you randomly through a mechanic called "Supply Drops," which are seemingly given to you randomly as you play. The awards from these supply drops can range from customization options, such as a new shirt, helmet, etc., or another version of a gun. For example, the KF5 has a version of it that has significantly more range than the base KF5, but has a reduced amount of rate of fire. To unlock attachments for guns, you have to complete certain challenges, much like how it was in the previous installments (i.e. Get X amount of headshots, get X amount of kills while hip-firing, etc.).
A little side note of the supply drops, I have heard that they are given every 30 minutes or so of in-game time. However, I get very little supply drops in the time that I play. I play exceptionally well in this game, yet there is no reward for it. I believe that players who play well should receive supply drops as rewards. I am a stickler for fashion, being VERY big about "Fashion Souls" in Dark Souls, and it bugs me that I see non-prestiged level 20's with more badass looking gear than mine.
Now, you may be thinking to yourself why I don't recommend this game, right? The simple answer is this: there are no dedicated servers. Matchmaking is done peer-to-peer. This results in extremely laggy gameplay, and if you aren't the host, expect to be waiting a long time for a map to load up just to play with stutters, teleporters, and droppers. I haven't run into this issue too often, but I keep running into the problem where hits don't register on someone when I actually hit them, which results in me having to empty an entire clip into them before they drop dead. I have played games with worst lag before, so this is something that I am able to compensate for, hence why I will still keep playing this game. However, if severe lag puts you off, do NOT buy this game; at least not for it's $60 price-tag. If it goes on sale for maybe $35 or less, then yeah, go ahead and buy it; I guarantee that you will have an awesome time if you manage to look past the lag.
TL;DR: New innovations to the game and its mechanics allow for a more interesting gameplay. However, the lack of dedicated servers results in heavy lag and may give way to hackers.

First things first - this is a very fun and engaging little budget platformer, but I can't recommend it at it's base price. $8 for essentially a 3ish hour game simply isn't worth it unless it's a clear step above its competition and in a world where Super Meat Boy and Rayman Legends exist, this game doesn't cut it.
However, if you can grab this game on sale for about $4 or less, I fully recommend getting it.
+/- Graphics are standard 2D fare with nothing that will push even the lowliest of toasters. That said, the art design is great, creating a fun and interesting visual look that takes what could easily be a bland looking game and pushes it above other budget titles. The developers found the look that worked for them and took full advantage of it.
+/- Controls are fairly basic but control well. Rarely did I ever feel that I failed because the game didn't respond to my inputs correctly. Basic platforming is fun and responsive, but while the game adds some variety to basic gameplay, never really grows beyond its basic premise.
+/- Puzzles and minigames give you some breaks from traditional platforming. The minigames are well done, if way too easy, as they re-imagine the game as an 8 bit top down arcade game. Despite the great twist on visuals and gameplay, there literally is zero challege to them other than "how fast can you complete it" with no fail states. Puzzles are likewise fairly easy and quite repetitive, basically moving some platforms about to block/avoid lasers. While they are fun the first time, they quickly get tiresome.
TL:DR - a fun, if short platformer that isn't worth full price, but grab it when on sale if you like indie platformers with alot of charm.

is a charming combination of side-scroller and platformer that balances out its lack in difficulty and very short length with its humor, appealing story and fluid gameplay.
In
, the player controls a single blob, escaped from a flask, bent upon conquest by consuming all in its wake. The blob utilizes all that it is capable of, including its platforming skills and low viscosity in order to maneuver through various areas of different shapes and sizes. It even later uses magnetism and telekinesis to manipulate terrain. The game provides over twenty-five levels spread through six areas to play through. (This level count includes a number of minigame levels, which are notably shorter than main levels.)
The game is satisfying to play. Despite the fact that the blob never talks or expresses thought, players will still connect to the amorphous creature - its progressive growth, guided by the player, makes the player feel somewhat like a parent to the creature. Further satisfaction comes from being able to easily devour objects which were insurmountable in earlier worlds. Bright colors and a bouncy soundtrack layer the game into being a cartoon-like experience. This shouldn't be conveyed as a turn-off to older or more mature gamers; rather, it should simply mean that the game is lighthearted.
Gameplay functionality varies between game modes. The majority of levels, the side-scrolling platformer sections, are effective. Controls are tight and responsive, leaving the majority of blame for damage on the player. Wall-jump mechanics are a noted exception, though this does not hinder core gameplay much. Airborne sections of the game are less effective. The propulsion systems on the character are too imprecise for slight movement, which when combined with obstacles that require finesse to maneuver around leads to frustrating experiences in this mode. The third game mode, the top-down mode, functions well, and its visual differentiation from the rest of the game just makes these sections even more pleasing than they already are.
For how much fun this game is, it will not last. The whole game can be completed in around three hours. Additionally, the game is quite easy throughout. For the few sections which provide ample difficulty, players will receive a notification from the game with a tip - even further simplifying the game, despite being a useful mechanic. The single-player campaign is the only mode in the game - having some sort of multiplayer mode, whether that be in the form of competitive races, a vs. mode, or co-op levels, would have increased the longetivity of the game significantly. Some replayability comes from retrying the levels to earn gold medals or find the two blob friends that are hidden in each area, but with only 24 levels the experience could become monotonous for some players. With such an easy difficulty and a cartoony interface, younger players may find the best experience with this game.

This is how survival horror should be done.
If you're familiar with the Alien franchise, you'll feel right at home. Every inch of space is filled with advertisements and notes, and all are easily legible, which I found myself spending more time reading at the start of the game than looking for supplies. There is so much detail and affection given to this game that it surprises me, after seeing so many 'AAA' titles using pixelated jpegs for backdrops or posters. This just adds more to the immersion, and it does it well.
There seems to be a number of tools you can collect along the way that will allow you access to different rooms, giving me a sense of a Metroidvania game, but blended well with elements of horror and suspense.
The ambiance is stellar, tensing you up and putting you on alert at all times, reminding you to be cautious. The game slowly eases you in, letting you get accustomed to the controls and how the rules work, introducing a new element one at a time as you progress.
One of the biggest things I noticed was the lack of a waymarker - and I actually like that. It makes exploring the ship feel more like an adventure to survive, instead of following a big glowing arrow to the next story piece. You can always bring up your map to check where to go if you get lost, so it's not leaving you totally in the dark.
You are given tools to defend yourself, but only as a last-ditch effort to survive, as ammo is scarce, and some enemies won't fall to a single melee swing. Thankfully, you can craft numerous gadgets to get you out of any situation, and there are plenty of hiding places to wait out. The other thing I noticed is the detection range on enemies seems to be a bit more realistic, instead of extremely wide. I've walked by the side of someone while crouched, and they didn't notice me right away until I made some sort of noise.
The Alien in the game is absolutely amazing - equal parts fascinating and terrifying. I actually found myself receeding deeper into my chair every time it appeared, gripped with a need to escape and survive, as though it was actually me on the ship, staring the Alien in the face.
I cannot think of a single thing bad to say about the game. This is a game that I would recommend to anyone, especially fans of horror games and the Alien movie franchise.

It's difficult to appreciate this if you come into playing this with the mindset that this is a "game".  You will get a lot more enjoyment out of this if you consider it a "creepy interactive experience".
As a game it fails.  The only thing you do is walk around a forest avoiding random "enemies" you can't fight while trying to keep candles lit which isn't even necessary for survival.  That's it.  Yeah, you can find certain objects in each hour you're in (there are six), but I never felt particularly compelled to go looking for them. I just ran across them.
As a "creepy interactive experience" this is very well done.  The atmosphere does a wonderful job making your skin crawl.  It's always dark except for the candle in your hand.  The trees sway in the wind.  Fog is always rolling about making it hard to see in the distance.  Weird things can happen to you randomly, like your candle gets suddenly blown out, creepy disembodied kid voices talk into your ear.  The music adds a lot to the tension of walking around waiting for something to pop out, which something will multiple times.  If you like jump scares, this experience will satisfy you immensely.
I do not consider this a game.  If I did, I would hate it.  But as an creepy interactive experience, I really enjoy it.  I enjoy how tense I feel when walking around a dark, creepy woods waiting to avoid whatever is out there.  I enjoy the sound of the wind blowing through the forest.  I enjoy all the weird things that happen to me.  I especially enjoy the tension-adding music.  If you can buy this on sale, it's worth it.  If you're into creepy atmosphere and jump scares, you might just enjoy yourself with this.

This game blew me away.
I was several months late discovering this. I saw quite a few YouTubers playing it, and finished a whole gameplay in one day. I was estatic, especially at the end. I was legit freaking out, and excited. I wanted to know more, and I defintely wanted the game for myself.
PROS-
-Amazing story. It's still confusing, with not all the pieces put together, but it's unique. I love games that leave you with so many questions at the end. I'm excited to contribute my theories and ideas to this community, and I hope this community thrives.
-Graphics! My my, one of my favorite things about this game. I studied how the trees moved, the fog moved, the hand motions the player made. They're all amazing! The fog can be a bit buggy, and the trees can look funny, but there is NOTHING that makes it unenjoyable. Everything looks real, and clean, and fantastic. There are a few things out there, such as vines that aren't 3D, but they still have shadow to them, which makes it almost unnoticable. My favorite part, however, is how your hand moves in front of the candle to shield it from wind, how the candle flame flickers and moves, and how smooth the animations are. Everything is fantastic, like I said before. Good job. I hope you people keep making games!
-Game in general! Now, I love a good scare. This game really did deliver; I knew the popups were coming but they got me every time! Talk about embarrassing. Wandering around in the forest at night has always been a fear of mine, and the fog topped it off. The forest idea wasn't very original, there are lots of horror games taking place in the forest. But that's no big deal, I personally love forest-based games. The candle idea was very interesting, too. I love how you move around and pick up candles, and they run out as time goes on. I know some people think of Wick as a Slender and FNAF mix, with the pages, and the "survive each hour/night" mechanic. But really, this game is so unique and beautiful that I don't mind at all. It's not exactly like any other game, and that's perfect.
Really, though... The scare factor isn't everything. To me, what makes a good game is story, especially a horror game. This game has a great story, hard to piece together, but still fun nonetheless. So really, GREAT job!
CONS
-Do I dare put something as silly as this here? THE FENCE. What are you talking about, what fence? The one you are dropped off at in the beginning. Looking at it, you could climb over it if you were desperate enough. But look! Barbed wire, and there's also the possiblity of electrical, shocking wire. I know a lot of people are picky with their games, and something like a short fence would really set someone off. Not me! That fence barely bothers me, and I put this in the CONS just to alert anyone about such a factor. But something as simple as a climbable fence will NOT take away the thrill of the game.
-Few bugs. I've encountered several, from Tim doing some funky little dance-run in front of me, to Lillian teleporting me on the wrong hours. I'm not sure if the teleportation thing is a glitch, or if it's meant to happen, going back on the first hour, but it doesn't bother me. What happened was only me getting up to the 3rd hour, and then going back to find Tim's blade in the first. I was teleported and heard Lillian's giggles, but it wasn't that much of a problem. And actually, Tim doing that little dance was just plain funny! I'd pay to see that again.
Alright, I could waste your time and think of more PROS and CONS to put, but I won't. You can decide if this game is for you. It was for me; I watched an entire gameplay and still bought it to play it for myself! Definetly recommended, although this game may not be for some.

What can I really say about this game that hasn't been said before? Dark Souls 2 (and the whole Souls series in general) is one of the finest RPG's to ever grace gaming. Its challenging but not unfair. Has some very vague but gripping lore. Dark Souls 2 also manages to introduce some much welcome changes to its  well established formula. Enemies are now more aggresive and can't be so easily backstabbed. The more complex stats system means that builds are no longer so uniform (in Dark Souls 1 it was pretty much the standard precedure to dump 21 points in Vitality and 40 in Endurance no matter what type of character you wanted to make). Oh and it has the sword of Guts from Berserk. GOTY 2014 confirmed!
Yeah the game has some issues such as the fact that the level design is not quite up to the level of the first game (though it's still pretty damn good and never gets as bad as the worst seen in DkS 1 (Lost Izalith **shudders*)). Furthermore the game takes a quantity over quality approach to its bosses. Out of 30 or so bosses only a handful are truely challenging and fun to fight.
Despite its minor shortcomings though Dark Souls 2 is a terrific game that I would highly suggest checking out. Though, if you are reading this, chances are you already have. But if you are one of those who hasn't bough this game: go give From your monies now and start praising that sun!

Overall, it's a solid sequel to Dark Souls 1.  Unlike Dark Souls 1, however, it's actually a decent PC port.  It supports multiple resolutions and the keyboard and mouse support is a lot better.  However, you'll still probably end up using a controller, because that's just how the game is designed.
The story is acceptable ("Something something souls something something Drangleic"), the covenants are a lot more prominent and accessible, and the game does manage to feel like an improvement over its predecessor instead of a bland rehashing.
However, the one thing preventing this game from being perfect is the nigh-unplayable PvP.  People will say "I don't encounter any lag in PvP whatsoever.  You just need a better connection." and those people are full to the brim with♥♥♥♥♥♥  My connetion is fine.  You'll get hit by sword stabs that aren't anywhere near you, people will roll out of attacks that should have hit them, and you'll get stunlocked by phantom hits all day erry day.  You'll feel like you're fighting the lag more than you are fighting your opponent.
It's huge bummer because I consider PvP the ultimate end-game and the source of replayability, so this game's replay value has been greatly diminished.  However, every other aspect of the game's awesome, and it's definitely worth picking up.
If I had to give Dark Souls 2 a score, I'd give it a 8/10.

Survivalist is a game akin to State of Decay that gives you control of a group of survivors during the Zombie apocalypse. You start out with one guy exploring the world by doing quests and picking up other survivors on the way to form your own little community. There is a rudimentary source gathering mechanism to nourish your community, provide them with shelter and protection. There are quests, often quite elaborate, that keep you going.
There are notable differences with State of Decay. In Survivalist the most dangerous opponents are other humans and not the zombies. Also in Survivalist characters do have personalities that impact their behavior towards you and rubbing people the wrong way can make them leave and even hostile enough to refuse to help or join you during quests. Also while State of Decay stressed the importance of silent weaponry, with melee weapons and silenced guns, Survivalist has no melee weapons and allows the wanton use of guns. There is a certain irony in that State of Decay offers a wide set of different fire-arms, while Survivalist has just five types. A last but not unimportant feature is that Survivalist allows you to control your survivors at the same time and create your own groups and send them off in different directions to do different tasks.
For me the main weakness of the game became glaringly noticeable on the second run through. Discovering the world took a backseat and I was aiming for doing things better and more quickly. And then Survivalist becomes a plodding game.
For the most part you are trudging from point a to point b and back again as part of quests and to gather resources. Early into the game you can't take much with you thus your characters have to go back and forth a lot. Some of this activity can be automated, but not everything. Especially some quests seems to consist of going to one side of the map and then to the other side of the map several times over and it feels a bit like that that chipmunk Ratatoskr from the Norse mythology that runs up and down the world tree to carry insults between an eagle in the crown and the dragon at the root.
Moving your base requires a herculean effort if don't do it early in the game, but even then it is boring work, especially as your community is constantly beset by roaming bands of zombies and looters.
The game becomes also wearisome because your survivors require a lot of looking after. If you don't they might get themselves or you killed, especially during battles. But even more, they will put on hold their assigned tasks to go in search for food and water if you don't supply them with it, which in itself is a tedious task, or go and sleep, even when you want them to finish that final gate before the next zombie horde arrives. The only way to do that is by controlling that character yourself and wait around until it has finished the job.
Survivalist is a nice game I would recommend for the first time around, especially for the price, but when the thrill of the first time experience is gone it becomes a dull game with too much walking about and waiting around for your characters to finish their assigned jobs. To go through it a second time requires from you to be a determined person. But then, maybe you are that person.

The watered down Hearts of Iron model that emulates Axis and Allies is admirable, but the broken diplomacy and logistics mechanics ruin the game. Communist China can be liberated by Japan to become fascist. Countries will declare war on you even if buffer states are in the way. You can't test factories to see how long they'll take to produce something else without actually resetting the original production process in case you don't like how long your option would take. This is especially awful with gearing. If you produce the same item back to back, you get a production discount, but that discount disappears from testing.
If you want to ally with someone, but another member of your alliance disapproves, you're screwed. Alliances only come in the way of coalitions. You can't end up with complicated situations like what happened with Finland or Poland in real life between the Western allies and the Soviets. You also can't end up with complicated situations like how Germany and Japan signed alternating neutrality pacts with the Soviets while the other one was fighting it. Latin America often screws things up because of this too. Don't be surprised if Argentina or Brazil get you into trouble.
This is especially awful when trying to liberate countries too. If you and another country like America and Britain invade someone like France, you can't liberate your territories on your own if you don't capture the capital. Transferring becomes possible only after you annex territories instead of simply occupying them, and you can't annex until a war is over. Some countries like Germany won't surrender until completely conquered, so you're stuck until the very end of the war. Furthermore, you have to feed and supply them based on penalized farming and factories that can't produce 100% food or goods like if they were liberated. This can be a serious drain on your economy.
The opposite situation also applies in case you and someone like Germany and Italy invade France. The computer is very reluctant to transfer territories even if you're in a strongarm position. If Italy grabs some wealthy or connecting territories you want while allied, then you can't tell him to give them to you because the AI's so stubborn. This is especially important when fortifying the Atlantic Wall to prevent the D-Day counterattack. Italy can leave major gaps in your line. Also, you can technically sign peace treaties that force countries to change ideology (like how Vichy France became fascist, or how post-war West Germany became democratic), but this rarely ever works. The computer forces other computer countries to change ideology all the time, but it will never listen to you.
Oh... and don't get me started on transport capacity either when trying to ferry troops across oceans and seas. There's no way at all to tell if you have not enough or too much transport capacity. It's a guessing game the whole way through. The same thing goes for figuring out how strong your relationship needs to be with another country to directly buy or sell resources so you don't have to gamble with free trade over time. Aid never works either. The United States won't help Britain defend against the blitz... not that Germany will even try it. It hardly ever tries to take Africa, and Italy always fails miserably. Britain never retakes the Middle East either. Iraq and Iran always remain independent. Heck, it usually takes South Africa to liberate Ethiopia...
...and don't even try to invade China as Japan. The computer always does it, but it knows how much TC it needs.
There are just major issues with this game. It doesn't really work unless you want to play as the Germans or Russians to conquer the world, and don't want to ally the Japanese in the process since they'll make issues for you with overlapping British, French, Dutch, and American Pacific colonies. Just buy HoI when it's on sale. You can get HoI2 or 3, Arsenal of Democracy, or Darkest Hour for a couple bucks when it is. This game tries to simplify things, but it makes a mess in the process.
