A very excellent turn-based, global-scale, war-game, with tons of freedom and options.
"Making History" as the title is perfect, because you basically pick out your nation and then engage in World War II. Everything plays out independently. No scripted historical events.
You can play starting in different time-frames, but at its heart, the game is a giant "WW2 sandbox" game. **NOTE: Although game "scenarios" have an "end-date", GAME IS ENDLESS. You can keep playing. You can adjust Scenario setttings to customize.
Some aspects remind me of:
Superpower 2 (RTS game) you can wage war on any nation, make treaties, do whatever you want on a 3D Google-Earth like map.
Supreme Ruler 2020 (RTS game) is like that but on flat 3D map, and more complicated, in that you can build unique, individual structures on each territory you control.
Making History is sort of like a fusion of both, you don't quite have "buildings" on each territory, rather just cities and oil wells mostly on some, but you have all the tools needed to manage each individual territory. Boost production of Goods in Alaska, upgrade farms in Florida, improve infrastructure in New York. Etc.
Biggest downside to this is that it's USELESS, and the interface/menu system is cumbersome and confusing. BUT THAT'S OK. The game is actually WAY more simple than you think.
The biggest problem most people will have with this game is simply "overthinking" the game
WHY?
I played as the USA starting around 1935 or 1936, and spent 10 years of game time, actually BALANCING my budget, selling resources to warring alliances, and making a profit; trying to balance trade, etc. HOWEVER, I couldn't figure out how the computer was producing massive amounts of tanks, ships, troops, etc. Not only were the computer players producing them fast, the computer was producing them in large numbers.
There was no way I could product as fast without destroying my economy.
How could the computer balance it's economy and do this?
The answer: IT DIDN'T!
YES, the computer nations all went into MAJOR debt.
Like a few other strategy games, you can go "into debt". If you reach zero, you then go into the red.
And NO, your assets don't start getting magically "sold off" like in certain other games.
No, you still have everything, you just owe a lot of money......to SOMEONE. Who?
WHO CARES!
SO, when you get this game, FORGET about managing the economy, it's all a waste of time.
In this game, when you go into "debt", it only lowers the effectiveness of your units and a few things, but I found it rather unnoticeable.
ALL YOU HAVE TO DO:
Set all of your areas to maximize production.
As for what to produce: set about 90% of them to upgrade industry. A city's industry is rated by a simple point system. A city worth 20 industry points, is usually "Light Industry". If you set production to whatever "Industry" option it has, after X number of turns, it will gain a point. Turns can go fast, so before you know it, it might become "Heavy Industry" and later to "Advanced" (Advanced can build units others can't, like Advanced tanks, nuke bombers, super-carriers, etc).
WHY DO THIS?
Because the higher it's industry point rating, the FASTER you can produce units.
You'll need to set the rest to produce Research and Transport Capacity (if not enough Transport Capacity points, you won't be able to move all your units overseas at once, they'll have to 'wait for the next ride').
That's about it. You'll be spamming out units in no time, and sending them into the grinder of an endless World War.
You will go into massive debt, but it doesn't affect gameplay all that much at all.
I was like $149 billion or trillion in debt by the end of my game. NO BIG DEAL.
That's too bad, but I guess maybe the developers found the economic system too restricting on enjoying the game.
That was the problem Supreme Ruler 2020 had, the economy system was made by people who didn't know how economies work. They tried to make it the way they "envisioned" only to have it cripple the game (not to mention all the ridiculous click-fest with logistics) that detracted from enjoying the game. Yikes. Making History keeps it simple and let's you focus on gameplay.
DIPLOMACY:
Very, very limited. It's basically you can join an alliance, leave an alliance, or try to get another country to join in an alliance with you. The computer players will leave/join alliances all the time. Like "1984", you'll be at war with mortal enemy "Eurasia" for a long time, only until one day, to now be at peace with them, and at war with new mortal enemy "East Asia", the next day.
This aspect of the game can actually turn out to be pretty fun at times, watching nations for "super alliances" and then stab each other in the back. I wish there were more diplomacy options, but this is a war game after all. HAHAHAH.
Territories/provinces can also break off and become part of a new nation.
You can even grant independence to conquered areas and make them an alliance, you'll see new nations formed frequently. You'll see Nazi Germany maybe take over Ireland and form a Nazi Ireland. Or Soviets take over India and form Communist India.
There are competing ideologies in the game that are visible and those with similar ideologies will favor relations with each other over others.
CONTROL:
Controlling armies is EASY. You just click on a unit, and tell it where to go. Sort of like the Europa Universalis games. Only thing, sometimes, seems like units not moving but it's really they need time to cross out of large territory and enter next one. In those EU games, you'll see a meter or bar that shows progress but no in this one. Not a big deal, just a cosmetic thing.
You can also stack and split units, so no problem there.
NO NEED to load units on ships or anything. When you tell them to go overseas, they are automatically converted into a "ship" fleet unit. Of course, they are weak. Best to clear the way or have ships patrolling the zones they must go through to stop enemy raiders.
EDITOR:
The game comes with an editor so you can make your own mod/world, edit unit stats, edit countries, anything. Can be a bit cumbersome to put together. People have made some online you can download through developer's site. I haven't tried any though.
CONS:
-The economic system, while totally useless, the menus/navigating suck. You won't use it much anyways, but finding out it's useless after wasting so much time, was frustrating "You mean I don't have to manage any of this, I can go into trillions of dollar in debt and still fight on just fine?!" I hear the "Gold" version of this game, makes the menus easier.
-Nukes! You can build ICBM and mobile-nuke units, HOWEVER, they fight like regular units, that only do major damage; but they are weak and get destroyed easily. STRATEGIC NUKE BOMBERS are the only "real" nuke units. You can direct them to nuke a city. If it succeeds, the city is permanently destroyed. It will just be ruins without any production ability.
-Subs can't be set to auto-defend an area. If an enemy surface ship enters water area you have a surface ship in, they automatically fight. If you have a sub, they don't fight. You have to manually order them, which enables enemies to sail right by. FAIL!
-Loading game, you have to remember to reselect your nation. You can load your saved game, play as other nation. By default, the nation you saved game playing as should already be selected.
If you're looking for some "historically accurate" WW2 game, you can forget about it.
It's MAKING HISTORY: you make your own history---ITS FUN TO DO!
The game goes on for however long it takes for you to reach your goal.
I conquered the entire world around 1957. I had modern supercarriers and jet fighters by that time, 638 warships, like 1300 armored divisions.
Very rewarding game.

TL;DR: A surprisingly deep, yet inexpensive, game that covers a lot of ground left undisturbed by many titles in the survival genre. I highly recommend it!
Survivalist has a lot of things going against it, to be honest. It's one of a plethora of titles in the survival genre, it employs a very basic graphics package, and it's developed by a relatively small shop, just to name a few. That said, in my opinion it far surpasses so many of its peers in so many ways. Here's my short list of exactly how it does it:
- Choices matter. Virtually everything you do has consequences, including your interactions with the environment, your community (i.e. the survivors who join you) and NPCs. These consequences do have some remedies, but they take work to get around.
- There's a lot of quests/missions. In my playthrough, almost nothing has to be done in a particular sequence, in that you can put things on hold if you like and do your own sandbox thing for a while.
- Strategy AND tactics. You can choose the RTS controls for some overarching activity, and then take control of a particular character to make sure something is done the way you want it. Perfect for your micromanaging streak while allowing you accomplish a lot of the mundane stuff without pulling your hair out.
- Scavenging. The map is full of useful stuff, and you get to choose how to use it, particularly when it comes to building your base.
- Replay value. This relates strongly to the first point dealing with choices, but because almost everything can pivot the game in at least a small way, things can be very different depending on what you choose.
- Performance. My machine is definitely middle-of-the-pack, but it has no issue running this game with several different background apps.
- Active development. The developers just released a major patch today that implements online co-op, and they've been regular about updates and bug fixes since launch.
There are some things to be aware of that some people won't find that attractive.
- The graphics are very basic, but it's by design.
- The crafting system is rudimentary, but you also don't have to pull your hair out putting things together.
- Music gets a bit repetitive.
Seriously, for the money, it's going to be very difficult to get a game that rivals all you can enjoy here. Really well done!

The original did feel more balanced, as I feel like a few of the HD levels weren't intended for some of the new features. For example, one of the maps, Hide and Seek, intended for you to abandon your previous planets and move onto the enemy's stronger planets. In HD, they added a feature to strengthen your planets by sacrificing soldiers, so you can simply farm seedlings on a throwaway planet and bolster a crappy planet's stats until it can take on a giant, taking away from the level's original goals.
The fast forward feature is a blessing in HD, and it'll be hard to go back to the original for this reason alone. The only thing it's missing is a multiplayer feature!

A fantastic game. I was slow to playing and finishing it, I never had much time to play games these days.
I finally got around to it now, 50 hours in 2 weeks or so, and I feel positive about the ending that I followed.
-The game allows you to build a new thriving society however and where ever you want in the game world, but you're limited to the supplies you have and can find.
-Zombies. It is a zombie survival game but it's not boring. It has an interesting and depressing story behind it where there are no right answers.
-Karma. A Karma like system exist in which NPCs will either like you or hate you to a certain degree. Some will like you so much that the price of items go down while those who hate you will leave your community or outright attack you.
-Scavenge. It wouldn't be a survival game without some scavenging involved. Set up supply routes with your survivors to keep your flow of wood, wire, and cement going strong. Be wary of Looter Gangs and Infected Hordes that emerge from the small towns.
-Control or command. Control each survivor in your community individually or command them as a group as you would an RTS. Issue orders such as Guard, Farm, or Supply run to keep them busy. Don't worry about their needs. If they need food, water or sleep, they can do so themselves and return to their assigned duties. I found it useful to have a larger community with good fighters to cover the Watch Towers. So say 10 Watch Towers, with 20 Guards on shifts. One guard goes to sleep the others take their place. Giving the community 24/7 protection from anyone or anything sneaking in, and the buggers do manage to sneak in if you're not careful.
-Story. There is a story involved and it's good. You meet your main character Joe Wheeler, likely of Captain Planet fame which explains why he's so despicable. He survived in a Bunker for a year but now needs to venture out. He meets a damsel in distress. Ok cool, what does she need? Oh that's easy. Kill her sister... well she's infected so good news. Bad news is telling her she's infected. I am joking. Now Alice Ivers plays as your secondary main. Her Chat options are much kinder than Wheelers and will achieve more friendships than Wheeler will who is better off as an imposing figure to intimidate people to his will. Finally we meet the third character who players only use to build the base. Isham Seely, the sole survivor of his community who joins up to assist in helping Alice with her problem. She needs Insulin and there isn't a lot to go around.
So now with Wheeler as a fighter, Alice as a healer, and Isham as a builder, you're off to a great start to playing this game the best to your ability to swindle, convince, fight, and manipulate others, or, are you being manipulated yourself by those you trust the most? Honestly, I trust the Antagonists of this game more than I do any one else. At least they're honest about what they do.
After 85 hours now, I feel accomplished. What an experience and for a very low price. This is a survival game that doesn't get boring so easily. The map isn't too big, there are over 400+ characters with their own stories and needs, and you can choose to help them or kill them outright. You can build your home where you need it to be or build multiple homes. Burn homes down, take over territories, whatever. It was a blast and I cannot recommend it anymore than I can right now.

I have played 3 moba games so far and I wasn't really into trying another one but recently I wanted to give it a shot since I heard about it a lot and got released on steam. I now play mainly hots and I love it but I will play Smite as an off-moba sometimes cause it has some features that don't require me to invest time to learn from the beggining a new moba and set it part a bit from the classic "strategy" focused lol and dota. So if you too are heavily invested in a main moba, here are the reasons why you should play Smite to blow off some steam every now and then. 1) It has 2 game modes that require no jungling or warding and it is just mindless massacre: arena and assault, mainly arena is the pure massacre with no real towers, just plainly kill each other. 2)It has the option to auto lvl up and auto purchase items, so if you can't bother like me to learn about new items and skills or whatever this contributes tremendously in just going in and kill gods, eventually though you will start wanting to purchase your own items since you will play enough to have the urge to change your build a bit. 3) It gives away for free some starting gods that are relatively easy and fun to play so no need to farm asap for your first god. Generally it is a unique gameplay wise moba and the action based camera and combat have an amusing feeling. At first it will be hard to get used to the gameplay specially if you come from another moba game but eventually you get used to it and it is quite fun. If you are a starter on moba genre, I wouldn't suggest Smite as your first moba as it is not a pure representative of genre nor as easy as the other isometric camera view moba games. It retains the "fed" concept from lol and dota but not in a terrible scale but the 50% of your hp-one ability concept exists. Also the concept of fighting gods is really great and if you love mythology you grow a special feeling when you play your favorite mythological god no matter what his/her abilities are. Smite's referal program is quite rewarding and by simply logging in every day in 4 weeks you get a free skin with the amount of gems they give. In-game currency progression is faster than lol's and hots's but not by far and the graphics are quite decent although they could use some improvement in some models, the environments are pretty great though. Final verdict: try it if you have played another moba, come back if you are rookie after you have played another moba.

Alien: Isolation is a very atmospheric game, with all the dim lights, steam, and busted pipes that should be expected. The gameplay could be described as a first person version of The Last of Us. You collect all these little pieces of junk used to craft items such as flares/flashbangs/medkits. You'll sneak around, killing unsuspecting looters, then you'll try and avoid the Alien, who reacts to sounds and is very much like a Clicker. You can throw flares just like bottles to create a distraction. One of my favorite ways to deal with hostiles is to throw a noisemaker so that the alien comes running, and takes them out for me. Things get very tense when you realize that you haven't save for almost 20 minutes and you're trying your hardest to stay alive. Running is a great way to get yourself killed because running is as loud as gunshots for whatever reason, I guess Ripley is wearing some squeaking clown boots. This is why I cannot compare it to Outlast, because in Outlast, you can ALWAYS run, you can outrun enemies and speed through the game. Here, in Alien: Isolation, that will not work. Running will attract the Alien and he is MUCH faster than you, so you have to think before you run in this game. Death is really frustrating, considering that the Alien could come from anywhere, sometimes he will grab you from a vent above, so it takes determination to get through the game, because you will die! A lot! Sometimes you can go through vents or floor panels that have blinky lights on them, some of which is required to go through in order to progress. And hallelujah! There is absolutely no annoying jump scares!
Lots of graphic options to select, but the game is very optimized and really should just be cranked all the way up. There is also a FOV slider!
There's no jump button, so you gotta walk around a pile of rubble instead of jumping over it.
I'd say this is worthy of an 8.5/10

Visually stunning, gripping immersion, terrifying audible atmosphere and a great dive into the vision and master minds of Ridley Scott and H. R. Giger's world of Alien!
(No excuses for TLDR, this is an indepth and well worded review of the game)
(With only a few hours of gametime, I personally was scepticle to review this game, however I would like to upon the great enjoyment I'm having so far.)
Firstly, it's clear to say this is definitely a more thrilling and money-worthy game than Aliens: Colonial Marines. The game promises the real fear and intensity of facing the incredible and ferocious Xenomorph and portrays the alien in a much more darkening light. Most previous games that feature the Xeno's are all about killing masses of them whilst not really being that scary. Alien: Isolation turns this around and instead of gunning these creatures down - you're really wanting to stay as far away from them as possible.
The gameplay evens out nicely, whilst it's not too challenging, it's also not a walk in the park. There are different routes around specific areas, a plethora or opportunities and items to accumilate or interact with along your way. You can make items such as the Smoke Bomb, or Noise Maker to use as a distraction - but make haste - for your decisions will surely need to be quick, careful and precise. There are weapons in this game too, however, they way you want to use them is entirely upon you - just be catious, guns make noise... and noise attracts unwanted attention...
The atmosphere is well done. Whilst arguably it may not be 100% perfect, it's definitley as good as the orginal Alien movie and suits well to the game. You'll find a lot of dark areas that will make you reluctant to traverse through as well as noises, such as engines or the humming and odd beeping of machines that may make you stop and listen. The atmosphere can often trick you into thinking there's something around, sometimes it's not the case but... be cautious!
Other than just the game itself, there's some great and nifty little features. The map and menu systems are nicely done, with the poor quality of 80's styled computers, paying real homage to the original Alien film. There are collectables too which gives you more reason to have a good explore around and keep an eye out for items you can use as well as these collectibles. There are many interactable objects that can be rather fascinating and you can even use to your ability to aid you in the environment you're in.
None the less, this is definitely a game that most fans of the Alien saga should check out and even try. There's an amazing amount of detail and it's clear that a lot of thought and effort was put into this game, especially so with the help and insight of the original movie cast. There are plenty of ways to make a short game work, and Blameless takes one of my favorite routes. It’s a game centered around a single payoff, and everything within it serves only to make that payoff even sweeter. Games of such limited scope usually don’t work on larger scales, and many fail to make the buildup or payoff all that they can be. Blameless threads that needle though, giving you a dark and moody house to creep through before up-ending everything on you.
You play a freelance architect, summoned to a remote house in the dead of night. The fellow showing you around wallops you one over the head, and you wake up in an unfinished section of the property. Using tools and construction materials lying around, you must escape your makeshift prison and escape the house before… well, before things get any worse. In your search you’re sure to turn up just how much worse things can (and will) get for you, giving you all the more reason to puzzle your way out.
There’s not a lot to do in Blameless besides wander the incomplete halls of the construction site and piece together tools and clues, but these interactions provide more variety and immersion than a lot of indie horror joints manage. Right from the initial room you’re dropped in, you’ll find a wide assortment of items laying around with all the construction accouterments. There’s a vice you can open and close, pliers in a nearby drawer, a hammer, a pipe, and other makeshift tools that will help facilitate escape. Throughout the house there will be more items secreted away just by their natural placement, and used to further your escape and explain just what the hell is going on.
Blameless is a short game but can prove pretty challenging simply because of how detailed it is, and how well the key items blend in with those details. The graphics are remarkable for a free title, with just about every room filled with unique bits of brick, rebar, piping, and mud. Immersion plays a big part here, and I couldn’t help remembering that feeling of wandering around the construction sites of new houses in my neighborhood when I was a kid. Poking through those incomplete shells was always thrilling and unsettling, since you didn’t know how much was complete or safe.
Here, that sense of insecurity helps build the atmosphere of horror from mundane foundations. The house in Blameless is spookier than many crypts or ruins I’ve played through because of how expertly the lighting and sound design give it sinister overtones. Lights will flicker and go out right when you think you’re about to find something. Creaks and door clicks will happen when you feel most exposed. And the climax of the game will make all of those little mounting fears explode into full-blown terror. It seems odd that such a short, grounded title could evoke a powerful reaction but perhaps it helps that the pacing is tight and the tale feels like something that could be happening in the world right now.
It’s not a perfect package by any means, of course. As detailed as the items and interactions are, it’s not always clear what solution is intended by the developers. There are a few non-intuitive ones as well, like having to physically retrieve a key from a lock to be used a second time on an unrelated lock. And then there’s the voice acting, which treads dangerously close to being worse than no voice acting at all. In contrast to how effective the scares are and how immersive the rest of the game is, these are but minor quibbles. Blameless nails that key feature of horror, the threatening environment, and builds a tight and engaging tale atop this solid foundation.

Ok this is a true story!
I came home from my boring day job on release, I sit down in my comfy chair and turn on my pc.
It took 13.7 seconds to boot, then display the windows 10 login screen.
I then open steam to find Dishonored 2 has been released. Great I had this pre-installed.
After waiting 20 minutes for steam to unpack the files In which time,
I cooked and ate a full roast dinner and shampooed the dog.
Sitting back in my comfy chair I hit play, then to be greeted by a picture with a load bar.
I thought to myself, "that's a loading screen, yep that's what that is."
Then I hit the menu and turning it all to Ultra settings @ 3440 x 1440 I hit play!
My whole world when down hill from here, things get rather... graphic. You have been warned! (See what I did there?)
I then hit play, My anxiety was overwhelming! I'd waited my whole life for the moment.
Then I hit another load screen, then a cutscene thats when it hit me.
30 fps came swing at my face like a mule kicking me in the teeth!
I fell to the floor, crawling in anger I lashed back almost snapped the monitor in half.
I knew my hand was broken but I couldn't stop myself swing wildly at the screen.
all I saw was red...                                                                   pixels.
After 30 seconds had past it had felt like a hour I was exhausted!
while I sat there panting I knew my fps shouldn't have that low my Titan X (Pascal) should have destroyed that game.
Thats when I remembered my dog Buster that I was shampooing was still in the bath, I rushed back to find him floating above the water, "Uh Damn" I said to myself.
It was at this moment my wife walked in.
Me in a bathroom, a bath full of water. and a dead dog.
She left me that night.
I felt so Dishonored I had to write this review.
10/10 would shampoo again.

A 3X strategy game sporting a minimalistic art direction is given fresh life in Eufloria HD. Eschewing complex space combat, which is the dominating genre for the 4X game, in Eufloria you take on the guise of a organic army that has set out to plant itself around the game space. Eufloria sports a couple of "super units" each with their own special abilities, two types of "base structures" and a simple upgrade system which adds depth to an deceptively complex strategy game. Not many hours of first-play-through time, but at its standard low price its quite enjoyable. Once you have defeated the campaign it garners replayability through "arena" modes and a second play through of the campaign at higher difficulty, entitled "Dark Mode." I recommend this.

I'd actually say that this game reminds me the most of Pikmin in feel and my emotional connection - the little seedlings and their trees can get really compelling but still I sacrifice hundreds to the cause.
If you're not particularly good at games but you like to play them, you're looking for a visual experience that doesn't prioritize realism, don't mind being challenged in surprising ways, and want satisfying strategy gameplay without the bloodshed, try Eufloria out. The HD version is worth the increased prettiness and control specificity, but the original has all the elements that make this game great.

No More Room in Hell (NMRiH) is an extremely difficult cooperative zombie survival game that's heavily inspired by the classic Romero zombie films. The vast majority of zombies are slow in the game, but there are a couple exceptions (runners and children). Despite this, their numbers do add up over time becoming a major threat.
The game itself features two modes of play: objective and survival. Objective mode forces the team to complete several tasks before heading out to an extraction point. Survival mode pits the team against wave after wave of zombies until an extraction is possible.
The game requires extreme cooperation due to the following features
As much as I want to say that this is a must have game that's perfect for playing out your ultimate zombie survival fantasy, I really can't recommend it at this time. While the game definitely has potential, the game just falls short in several areas at this point in time.
A typical objective map will go along the lines of
After awhile, objective maps feel a lot like a virtual "Where's Waldo" with zombies.
The Survival maps are even more repetitive since it's essentially the same game except your more or less stay in one spot and have no objectives other than survive by fighting off wave after wave of the same three types of zombies.
Other great zombie games (such as the Left 4 Dead series) get around redundancy by having several different enemy types and by creating different scenarios to engage the zombies. Remember storming the bridge at the end of Left 4 Dead 2? Or Holding out at the Midnight Riders concert while the madness ensued? Do you remember getting hit by that sneaky boomer while trying to avoid the tank? Now that's good game design. On the other hand, I highly doubt anyone is going to remember looking for [insert random item] while a bunch slow zombies pursued (like they do the entire game).
If you are anything like me, you try to unlock the achivements in the games you play. It's always satisfying to me to unlock a particularly difficult achivement that requires some measure of skill. With that being said, I despise "time waster" achivements which NMRiH is full of. Imagine if Left 4 Dead had the following achivements and you'll get a feel for what to expect with this game.
Unfortunately, the game does have developmental bugs at this time. There's nothing more frustrating then finding out you can't complete a map because an item you need spawned off the map (i.e. a door key spawns on the other side of the locked door). This kind of stuff gets extremely frustrating fast as you can imagine.
Also, I've come across an issue where the game freezes/crashes if you minimize (or alt tab) out of it. While this technically could be a issue on my end, I've experienced this problem on more than one computer on both Windows and Mac OS operating systems (not to mention that none of my other games does this) leading me to believe it's a problem with the game. In both cases, I'm required to forcibly close the app.
While this is really not an issue with the game itself, it's something that's worth mentioning. This game is really designed for a group of friends with good communication and teamwork to play. In fact, I would go as far as saying this would be a really fun game for a LAN party; however, everything goes out the window when considering that most people will play with random players online. Here's a few unfortunately common scenarios you will most likely deal with while playing this game with random players.
It's really annoying having a gun with no bullets because your teammate took the all the ammo (especially if they don't even have a gun to use the ammo in). Worse than this is if your team snatches everything up leaving you to fight bare handed while they carry numerous "backup weapons".
While most of the maps aren't too large, some of them can be very confusing at time and it's entirely possible to get split off from your team. If this happens, you don't have a way to notify your team that you're lost (unless your teammates are carrying walkie talkies-- which in my experience is rarer than unicorn farts).
While every game has its trolls, it's exponentially worse in this game due to the high dependency on teamwork. Imagine the teamwork problems I mentioned before except now you have some online jerk intentionally doing them. Also, don't forget that friendly fire is on... It's really annoying having someone join your game only to randomly kill half your team.
Objective mode is even worse. Need [insert item] to proceed? Well guess who has it... Nothing more frustrating than needing to open a door at the end of a map only to find out that one of your clown teammates who's trying to kill your team has the key...
While I definitely do think this game has potential, I really wouldn't recommend it to anyone right now unless you have unbelieveable patience and are willing to deal with all the issues I mentioned above. Hopefully, the development team will address some of these issues down the road. With a few changes here and there, NMRiH could become an amazingly awesome game. Until then, play this game at your own risk and don't say I didn't warn you.

Alien: Isolation is a very atmospheric game, with all the dim lights, steam, and busted pipes that should be expected. The gameplay could be described as a first person version of The Last of Us. You collect all these little pieces of junk used to craft items such as flares/flashbangs/medkits. You'll sneak around, killing unsuspecting looters, then you'll try and avoid the Alien, who reacts to sounds and is very much like a Clicker. You can throw flares just like bottles to create a distraction. One of my favorite ways to deal with hostiles is to throw a noisemaker so that the alien comes running, and takes them out for me. Things get very tense when you realize that you haven't save for almost 20 minutes and you're trying your hardest to stay alive. Running is a great way to get yourself killed because running is as loud as gunshots for whatever reason, I guess Ripley is wearing some squeaking clown boots. This is why I cannot compare it to Outlast, because in Outlast, you can ALWAYS run, you can outrun enemies and speed through the game. Here, in Alien: Isolation, that will not work. Running will attract the Alien and he is MUCH faster than you, so you have to think before you run in this game. Death is really frustrating, considering that the Alien could come from anywhere, sometimes he will grab you from a vent above, so it takes determination to get through the game, because you will die! A lot! Sometimes you can go through vents or floor panels that have blinky lights on them, some of which is required to go through in order to progress. And hallelujah! There is absolutely no annoying jump scares!
Lots of graphic options to select, but the game is very optimized and really should just be cranked all the way up. There is also a FOV slider!
There's no jump button, so you gotta walk around a pile of rubble instead of jumping over it.

The game promises the real fear and intensity of facing the incredible and ferocious Xenomorph and portrays the alien in a much more darkening light. Most previous games that feature the Xeno's are all about killing masses of them whilst not really being that scary. Alien: Isolation turns this around and instead of gunning these creatures down - you're really wanting to stay as far away from them as possible.
The gameplay evens out nicely, whilst it's not too challenging, it's also not a walk in the park. There are different routes around specific areas, a plethora or opportunities and items to accumilate or interact with along your way. You can make items such as the Smoke Bomb, or Noise Maker to use as a distraction - but make haste - for your decisions will surely need to be quick, careful and precise. There are weapons in this game too, however, they way you want to use them is entirely upon you - just be catious, guns make noise... and noise attracts unwanted attention...
The atmosphere is well done. Whilst arguably it may not be 100% perfect, it's definitley as good as the orginal Alien movie and suits well to the game. You'll find a lot of dark areas that will make you reluctant to traverse through as well as noises, such as engines or the humming and odd beeping of machines that may make you stop and listen. The atmosphere can often trick you into thinking there's something around, sometimes it's not the case but... be cautious!
Other than just the game itself, there's some great and nifty little features. The map and menu systems are nicely done, with the poor quality of 80's styled computers, paying real homage to the original Alien film. There are collectables too which gives you more reason to have a good explore around and keep an eye out for items you can use as well as these collectibles. There are many interactable objects that can be rather fascinating and you can even use to your ability to aid you in the environment you're in.
None the less, this is definitely a game that most fans of the Alien saga should check out and even try. There's an amazing amount of detail and it's clear that a lot of thought and effort was put into this game, especially so with the help and insight of the original movie cast. Fans will be immersed into this incredible and gripping game and it's fantastic ways and familiarities to the classic film back in the day.
I recommend this game to fans alike as well as people who enjoy a good immersive horror survival! - 8/10

If you're into free roam, open world, sandbox style games with no strutured missions/objectives then you will probably enjoy this game.
The game starts a lot like Minecraft does. You're dropped off into the world with little to no guidance. It isn't hard to figure out though. The problem with this game is the lack of enemies. I hate to keep referencing Minecraft, but if you've played it on peaceful (without enemies) you know how boring the game gets. The only thing that can kill you in Astroneer are plants that emit toxins, falls from heights, suffocating, and storms which throw debris. These can all be EASILY avoided. So without any enemies there isn't any real difficulty. And after some time the game starts to get boring. Now if you're looking for a relaxing game this is perfect. I enjoy playing it while watching Netflix.
The game runs well. It's straight forward and easy to jump right into, which makes it a good game for a younger gamer.
I do recommend the game, but before you buy it understand it is still in its early stages. With the lack of enemies the replayability isn't too great. However if you're into the free roam sandbox style you will get your money's worth out of this game.

Survivalist is one of those games that you play that you can't wait for a sequel. There are a lot of great things about the game and there are some things that could have been done much better.
First the pros:
The storyline and content of the game are impressive. With a variety of win conditions that allow players to decide what type of person Joe Wheeler wants to become in the post apocalyptic nightmare that is his new life. It also has a plethora of recruitable NPC's which have their own backstories and personalities.
The combat system is straight forward and as you increase your abilities you get more ways to ensure that in a fight you're the last one standing. The fact that your characters can be infected makes fights with the horde all that more dangerous since one bite and you better start running for some anti-gen otherwise get ready to lose one of your companions and be in danger of losing even more when they finally turn.
Of course with a large cast of characters you're going to need more than just a small bunker in order to keep them all together. This leads into the construction system which is similar to combat in that the higher your level the more things you can do. Sure you can craft yourself a wooden gate but, if you want a watchtower you got to have the skills before you can actually build it.
The game gives you a small tutorial though you have to complete it in a certain time limit if you want one of the characters to stay alive. It introduces you to all of the basic skills in the game but, does allow for some trial an error (no complete hand holding but, enough of a hand to know what you're doing.)
One of the more unique takes on it has to do with the female lead. Since she's a type 1 diabetic she'll need insulin for the entire game if you want to keep her alive throguh it. This  allows for insight on exactly how difficult a post-apocalyptic world would be on those with poor health conditions. It also gives a sense of urgency to you depending on if you want to keep her alive or not.
As far as the graphics go it's not excellent but, when you take into account the game was developed by one person it's much higher quality then certain games done by teams.
For the con's there are quite a few but, mostly things that just required more work rather then actual demerits.
First the Ally AI is fairly shoddy even if those characters are profecient in weapons they don't usually use the tactical skills that they have acquired (IE: no head shots or knee capping) in command mode they will either run full speed until their fatigue bar is full or they will walk at a normal pace. Unlike a player who would mix running with letting the fatigue bar lower after a while.
Both of these can be reworked by messing with the AI however the important one (for survival sake in roming) so that a character will be told to "run" until the fatigue gauge is  at a certain level before going back to a walking pace.
For consturction there is a far too little selection in the amount  of things you can build. A few different style of shaes would be nice or being able to set up automated defenses.
Next, Farming. The farming system is fairly convoluted. First it takes several days before what you plant actually grows. Also it doesn't tell you when there is food ready at your camp so the farmer ends up hording it. The fact that the plants tend to blend into the ground doesn't help much either.
Raising your skills- Even though you can get a character that doesn't mean their stats are perfect. However raising the skill of a single character takes a long of time and the game doesn't really give directions on how skill gain experience (other than the obvious of "using them increases skills)
Finally the last major issue is in combat or rather "ranged combat" If you're in a fight with a set of ranged enemies it's most likely not going to end well. Even with a bulletproof vest all it will do is protect from some of the damage as you get turned into swiss cheese. Fights can be won or lost on a dime when it comes to facing human eponents
All in all I highly recommend this game in spite of it's faults because the game is very fun and gives a realistic view of what would happen if the "zombies" infested the planet. The only big problems are less about the actual game and more about the gameplay itself an how it could have done something better.
Final score 8/10

Survivalist is an open world, survival RPG where you play as Joe Wheeler, a self-centered businessman who has built a bunker just before the apocalypse with resources sufficient for one year, lived in his bunker during the apocalypse without any connection with the outer world, and finally decided to go out into the wasteland when he got out of resources. He doesn't have the slightest idea about the events happened after the apocalypse, unfamiliar with the surroundings, people and of course zombies.
I will start with pointing the best thing about this game: the atmosphere. The feeling of isolation, chaos and depression, which are the outcomes of apocalypse are perfectly reflected. There will be times when you will have tough chocies, times you have to decide between two parties and you can't simply pick the 'evil' out of the sides, as moral values/ethics are simply not valid anymore; in a world where looting is the only way to survive, killing a person is justified by a simple conflict of interest and overall, being strong is the ultimate goal of everyone.
As humanity has taken a step back from the civilization, there are no laws and no enforcers. People have done what they had to do, in order to increase their chances to survive, they have gathered and started forming groups. There are small civilized settlements which started raising their own crops, outlanders, bandits, looters and all sorts of groups in game.  Now with such a case, a logical human being would find a decent community that shares his/her interests and join them. But Joe Wheeler happens to have a better idea; without knowing absolutely no one in this world and having nothing to offer, he will start building his own settlement.
This is the goal of this game. To make Joe Wheeler lead the biggest/strongest settlement in the area (i.e. feed his ego). Other than the first two characters who join you within the progress of storyline, people are not willing to leave their current, steady systems and join your newly-founded formation. And neither they are going to do it for the sake of your baby face and well-tailored businessman suit. You have to convince them. People have flexible opinions about you and to make them join your group, you have to act accordingly.  You can either complete their quests, protect them from raids and deal with someone they dislike to make them respect you, or pick the correct approach with your dialogues and bribe them with rare trinkets (e.g. chocolates, wine, books etc.) to make them like you. Only then, you can have enough influence on them to make them join your group.
Map is huge. And it is not empty at all. I need to say that I am really surprised with finding so much content here, as there are various events/characters/loot all around the map and this encourages discovering. Even when it gets really hard with lots zombies around, you know that you'll find something significant in that area and it definitely makes up to your effort.
Story progression is in a way that teaches you the mechanics of the game, which is appropriate as the game has so many things to do and you need to get to the end step-by-step. You also get to recruit people, explore the world and have better equipment with side quests, alongside with getting in the middle of conflicts between the factions and overall the intriguing plot.
According to your play style, game almost always allows you to choose between a diplomatic and a violent approach. Every choice you make show it's unique consequence in story progression. While you may find it more beneficial to rock the boat and loot loads of corpses for items, recruiting people instead of killing them makes your group bigger and thus, increases your chance to survive.
The game has a simple, strategy-game style of base building system. You need to have tools, materials and builders for building. You build houses, barns and wells for the needs of your group; and walls, watchtowers and pillboxes for the protection of your settlement. Protection around the settlement has to be set strategically, as there will be numerous zombie/rebel raids against your settlement and they get more frequent with the increasing population. The game sets a great balance for protection issues. If you assume that you will be perfectly safe after building wooden walls around your settlement, I am afraid you will soon find out how long it takes for a molotov coctail to burn down wood.
Protection is not the only issue. You need resources for your group. While you can usually find plenty of water around, food is not that easy to come by and you will quickly run out at some point. The game introduces another asset here: farming. This is also well implemented; you manage to feed your group with the food you scavenge around until the time you have access to crops/farming and after that, all you need to do is tasking some members of your group with farming and wait.  With more population, the amount of crops you have to plant also increases.
I believe these are enough for convincing people this game is amazing in terms of its RPG and sandbox factors.
Shooting mechanics are not hard if you follow some simple rules: stand still, aim and wait for the crosshair, shoot. Spraying is only a waste of bullets. The more you use weapons, you earn experience and get your firearms level up, this allows you to use more weapons and makes you shoot more effectively.
Sound effects and graphics are quite good for an indie game; I haven't had any staggers or graphical glitches despite the huge map with various interactive elements.

The only negative I could think of would be the controls. They are kind of way-out and this may make the game seem tedious first, however I got used to them in my first two hours and understood the way things work, so it's not really a big issue if you are interested in playing the game.
I am simply amazed by the content I got from this game. Really well-made and fascinating in many aspects. Brilliant as a RPG, a survival, a sandbox and in the end, for this price, this game is a steal. Kudos to the developers for getting it right with their first game. I can't recommend this enough.
Edit: Nominated for the “No Apologies” award.

I wanted to like this game, I really did. But the short version is, everything about it was disappointing.
To me, this game's cardinal sin was that it was too short. Not as in "I PAID $XX FOR THIS SO IT SHOULD BE THIS LONG!" or as in "Man it ended but I just wanted to keep playing!" I mean that for this game, the story they were telling and the mechanics they were trying to develop, there was simply not enough game time to flesh it all out decently. You're strung from one plot point to the next, never really being given a chance to process or even care about what's happening in the story. Mechanics introduced early in the game are never given adequate time to be developed, and your existing mechanics never feel like they grow or transform over the course of the game. With a few additional missions in the middle, the game wouldn't seem like it was so rushed.
The second big disappointment was the mechanics in the game. Very early on you're given a "gravity glove" which allows you to interact with the environment. This glove is used almost entirely to stack boxes and throw things. There are only 2, maybe 3 instances in which a player character with moderate strength wouldn't be able to get by without the glove at all. I feel like there was a real opportunity to find innovative uses for this tool which was completely missed. Plus there are a variety of other mechanics introduced early on which are rarely ever seen - there are maybe 6 flip plates in the entire game, and 2 barrels to hide in.
A huge third disappointment was the story itself. You take one look at the head of the corporation and think "okay he's totally evil". Then "misfortunes" happen related to him and you think "yeah, evil." I kept waiting and waiting for the twist, for the moment when the game said "no, he's just bad at not looking evil," but I think you can all guess where that's going. The tiniest bit of subtlety could have really been a positive here.
So at the end of my playthough, the only thing really going through my mind was, "wait, that's it?" It was an experience in waiting for a breakthrough, in story or mechanics, that never came.

Pros:
-Game's pretty, models are fairly well-animated.
-Premise is interesting.
-Music's fairly decent, both in ambience and otherwise.
Cons:
-Too short. Game can be finished in three hours, even if you take your time and search for secrets. Sure, you can replay it, but there's not much reason to.
-Too easy. No enemy in the game is very threatening - guards can be stunned from a distance and are terrible at pathing around obstacles.
-Boss fights are outrageously simple. Wait for specific timing, pick up projectile, hurl at boss, repeat. Only time I died was when I fell into a pit after a fight had ended, and that was because of wonky platform hitboxing.
-Puzzles aren't difficult or complex or even interesting - hope you like the ol' switch-puzzle sewer-pipe-puzzle light-mirror-puzzle cliches, because that's all you'll get.
-The physics-manipulation-mechanic is a gimmick. I wish I'd just been given a stun gun and the ability to pick items up and carry them above my head, because they'd have the same utility - and be a lot easier to use.
-Story is cliched and uninteresting. Try to guess what's going to happen next in the plot, and ninety percent of the time you'll be right. "No, vaguely-threatening mustached-man, I'm VERY convinced that that was an accident and you're distraught about my near-death."
-Voice acting ranges from ok to awful. And somebody's always yammering in your ear.
All in all, this might be worth it if it were on sale for $5. At $15 it just isn't, unless you really are so starved for interesting graphics that you can muddle through the mediocrity of... everything else.

City-state empires, impractically large machinery, Victorian bird masks, and villains with twirling mustaches. Gatling Goats’ Traverser isn’t being shy with its steampunk aesthetic. But it’s also doing more with the genre than adopting a pastiche of visual tropes, diving into its thematic waters to attempt to tap into something more resonate than copper spider robots.
Steampunk, insofar as it can be succinctly generalized, effectively serves to allow its audience to have their cake and eat it too. It recognizes the impracticality of early 20th-century industrial optimism, while simultaneously reveling in that same dream of a finite, knowable universe, at which center humanity resides and dictates. Steampunk is perhaps among the most self-indulgent of genres, but at its core, it seeks to display the ignorance and danger of unregulated industry and nostalgic refusals to modernize. With Traverser, Gatling Goats have attempted to inverse steampunk’s tradition of romanticized empire within an Orwellian dystopia, while also weaving in elements of environmentalism and socialist sentiment.
Within this melting pot of political disorder, Traverser emerges only half formed. The foundation is built, pieces are put in motion, but with nothing to hold them together Traverser is left to scramble from one plot point to the next, as if exposition for exposition’s sake is enough to guide the game toward a state of cohesion.
Traverser’s world is one constructed in the aftermath of a global freeze. The sun has died, chilling the earth’s outer layer and forcing humanity to take refuge underground. With the surface now inhospitable, clean air becomes the most valuable currency in the city of Brimstone, humanity’s last bastion of civilization. Controlling the city’s air supply, and by extension, the city itself, is the Raven Corporation, a comically evil industrial empire whose spy birds and art deco propaganda posters do little to hide its nefarious intent. Entering into the center of an underground civil war, largely by happenstance, is Valerie Bennett, a recently appointed traverser who, on account of her position, is able to travel to both the upper and lower city in order to “keep the peace” between the two socioeconomically dissonant locals.
World building is among the few areas that Traverser handles quite well. The concept of a dualistic city personified by both their inverse political and physical positions is a rather blunt analogy to the contemporary gap between the upper and lower class, but it functions as a clever hook that serves both narrative and mechanical goals. Theoretically.
While Traverser displays confidence in crafting its setup, like much of steampunk, it doesn’t know where to take it after the introduction. One of steampunk’s most persistent issues is in fixating on the setting to a degree that partially, if not entirely overshadows the actual happenings of the place that has been so meticulously created. To its credit, Traverser goes to great lengths to flesh out the narrative threads utilized to craft its environments and characters, but it remains so married to what has become an almost fetishistic obsession with steampunk’s look that it is unable to carry them through to completion.
The best it can do is to borrow Bioshock’s now ubiquitous form of environmental storytelling, but even then, the stories left behind by the residents of Brimstone are but disorderly snapshots of a world which feels constructed out of cardboard and glue; a city which appears vibrant and sprawling until you catch a glimpse of the empty stage immediately behind its unconvincing front. Traverser’s narrative is quickly bogged down by more characters and goals than it can support, leaving it to introduce plot points only when they are immediately needed, before immediately transporting you to the next.
It is easy to characterize Raven Corp. as evil, in fact, contemporary sentiment on capitalism effectively does the work for you, but explaining how they view themselves and why they operate as they do (both of which Traverser attempts) in a way that extends beyond cartoonish villainy is a lot harder. So is creating a rebellion movement with a more nuanced plan than giving air equally to everyone, as if the only stopping block in the path to true economic equality is corporate greed. Nevermind detailing why the rebellion is also convinced the surface has become habitable again, and how they have determined that it is worth risking the whole of humanity to see for themselves if it’s true. Traverser may be altruistic in its fictional worldview, but it tries more than its narrative can hope to adequately address, and the game as a whole suffers for it.
Filling the gaps between Traverser’s verbose voiceovers, are, predominately, a lot of rocks (and enough boxes to spare). Traverser plays as something halfway between a physics puzzler, and a 3D platformer. After becoming a traverser Valerie is equipped with a gravity glove, allowing her to move objects far too heavy to lift by hand in order to progress through increasingly cluttered environments. Naturally, in a world full of retro-futuristic technology, this entails a lot of heavy objects being put on presser plates, opening doors to more objects to be placed on more pressure plates. These puzzles are relatively inoffensive, but they’re also tremendously dull, requiring less in the way of logical thinking than they do patience on account of Traverser’s many obtrusive design decisions.
Most disruptive of these is having the camera locked at an isometric perspective. 3D platformers already have a history of camera related struggles, and all of them – environmental clipping, obscured platforms, inexplicable control anomalies – become exaggerated when the player is forced to view everything from a fixed angle. The lack of gamepad support also causes the platforming to be finicky, due to the lack of analog control, and the tradeoff of using the mouse to control objects with the gravity glove is minimal at best. Objects frequently misbehave and move at speeds and angles which are difficult to gauge, and even harder to control. This isn’t hugely problematic, as Traverser rarely presents you with puzzles requiring a great amount of precision, but during boss fights, every control issue becomes a monumental hurdle to overcome. The troublesome checkpoint system is just melted icing on the half-baked cake.
Traverser tries to differentiate itself from the swathes of steampunk media being released, but ultimately its problems lie mostly in an inability to do so. Gatling Goats built a world I was ready to get lost in, but as the through-line began to bloat and exposition-laden characters continued to be introduced, the Brimstone’s layers of intrigue fell away, leaving its streets filled with nothing but familiar box puzzles and Victorian fashion trends in its wake.

I've spent well over 100 hours playing this on console back in the day. I'm a little rusty at it now, but I have to say that this is one of, if not THE best, strategy game I've ever played.
It's not particularly complex; you are in control of seedlings looking to colonise asteroids in some distant future. You use seedlings to fight enemy seedlings, scout out out unknown asteroids and grow trees that allow you to populate your seedling army, or protect your own asteroid. Each asteroid has 3 traits that determine what attributes your seedlings will have when they grow; energy, strength, and speed.
That's essentially it, but with these basics rules the game becomes heart pounding. The first few sections are basic tutorials, but after a couple of hours you are waging wars against hundreds and hundreds of enemies, wars of attrition and patience. Holding key asteroids on the front lines, and managing which asteroids will become seedling producers and for what traits, becomes crucial in large battles. I've had games last for hours because of the attrition warfare, and because of how relaxed the game is. Timing is also key; do you rush an enemy asteroid in an instant to secure a quick victory, all the while leaving another asteroid unguarded? Or do you slowly build your force, moving from asteroid to asteroid, claiming each for your own in a slow but secure campaign?
The art style is a huge draw for this game. It's something I can't quite describe. With simplistic but vibrant colours, and a beautiful soundtrack by Milieu, the game lies somewhere between a surreal nature documentary and some kind of 1970's late-night cartoon fever-dream. I spent many gloomy days being absorbed into a kind of trance because of the visuals and sounds.
Overall I'd very much recommend this title if you are even a passing fan of RTS or somewhat relaxing games. One thing I will say is that I personally prefer using a controller for this, but it's equally as playable with a mouse

If DayZ and L4D had a child, this would be it.  The game is using the HL2 engine, the physics, the movement mechanics, and the object interactions are all the same.  This game is not for the faint of heart and it is ESPECIALLY not for people looking for a L4D alternative.  The game is challenging and more realistic that most zombie survival games (though not as randomly specifically realistic as DayZ).  If you are willing to work at the game, you will have a blast.
First things first, the game is gritty and buggy.  The controls are solid and consistent.  There aren't a ton of keybinds to memorize, so the basic movement/fighting/shooting/interaction isn't hard to pick up.  That being said, there is no hand holding in this game.  You can do things like board up a window or door, but to do so, you have to have the right materials and tools (which they don't tell you).  However, they did try to make things intuitive.  For example, to board up a door, you need a hammer (which is both a tool and weapon) and boards (SURPRISE!).
This leads to the UI.  I feel like the UI needs a bunch of work.  It's not bad, just difficult and unforgiving in terms of use.  For example, in one of the game modes, you hold a location and try to keep zombies out in a wave style format.  However, my team mates died and I was the only one left.  Upon being overrun, I respawned in 5 seconds and my team mates did not.  There were no indications of why or how they were to respawn.  Upon looking through the keybinds (while hiding behind a door so the zombies couldn't get me), I found that there's a suicide button (how morbid).  Upon using it, the entire round ended and everyone was respawned (but why?).  Without knowing that, most people will just leave because spectating some guy getting ripped to shreds by zombies and respawning over and over gets boring.
Things like boarding up doors is also unintuitive.  You may be looking at the spot you want to board up, but it won't actually nail the board in unless you look at a different spot, leaving you frantically waving your mouse around until your hands decide that the time is right to settle down and board up your base.
The guns and explosives are varied and interesting.  I really like the attention to detail they put into the varying ammo requirements and how the guns reload (for example, reloading a six shooter takes longer than a magazine fed M1911).  They also varied how the weapons handle (the six shooter is single action, so you must pull back the hammer each time), which only adds to the realism and becomes a serious consideration when choosing weapons.  The explosives are actually explosives (obvious statement is obvious?), I killed myself by accident expecting the explosions to be (as per usual) flashy but with a small radius.  Instead I got tossed across the room and died.  Nice!
The game feels more like a true survival game.  You have a limited amount of inventory space (you can't even hold unlimited amounts of ammo, each bullet takes up a certain amount of weight), so you MUST choose what you take and what you leave behind.  Want to load up on guns?  Too bad!  They take up a realistic amount of weight, so you cannot carry 9 shotguns, 5 LMGs, 2 pistols, and 10 grenades.
Now for the hard part, multiplayer.  The multiplayer aspect isn't bad.  It was designed to be co-op, which is both a great and terrible aspect.  Because of the realistic nature of the game, the CO-OP part is key.  If you find yourself playing with pugs, you are likely to not get far.  However, if you have a group of friends working together, the game because a new and challenging obstacle filled with close calls and frantic shouting for reinforcement.
The game is solid enough to be playable and with the gigantic FREE sign on it, it actually becomes a very good game (you get AAA titles that have the same problems, but you pay $60 for them?).  The game definitely needs some refinement, but it is definitely playable.  If you enjoy a challenge (and aren't looking for the feel good jaunt through a field of zombies), this is definitely a game for you!  And at the low low price of ZERO dollars, order now and get it for all of your friends!

Been playing this game on the original launcher for 1 1/2 years. This is the best free to play game I've ever played.

A refreshing twist on the MOBA genre, if games like League of Legends and Dota 2 were to slow or boring for you then Smite might be just what you're looking for.
Gameplay
Has the usual MOBA setup of 4 abilities, passive and items, but puts you into a 3rd person view point and focuses much more on skillshots and action gameplay. It has a variety of gamemodes and is a lot quicker than your usual MOBA game. The game is balanced really well and you'll be able to get your feet wet straight away.
F2P
One of the best F2P models out there. Daily login bonuses allow you to gain premium currency by just logging in and leveling bonuses allow your to work out what kind of god you'd like to buy. You can also pick up every current and future god for $30 USD, a crazy good deal and you'll even get refunded from the gods you've already bought it you decide to pick the bundle up down the line. The only negative I could say is that it has a small rotation roster (5 gods), but due to how easily you gain currency through login bonuses and daily games it's something that's not going to leave a sour taste in your mouth.
Servers

Building an MMO is a grand undertaking, so I wanted to give this game some leeway to catch up to certain other MMOs in quality before judging it, but the more I think about it the more I feel its entire design is irredeemably flawed.
The main problem I have with the game is the simplicity of the game mechanics.  Specifically the lack of any sophisticated mechanics that add any element of strategy to the selection of skills or abilities.  Ostensibly, there are only three relevant stats: Health, Magicka, and Stamina.  Your combat abilities scale entirely based on Magicka or Stamina, depending on which resource they use.  There is no further optimization of stats or choice of specialization, which would be acceptable if even those two stats mattered at all.  As far as I can tell, your character recieves 20 points of each stat per level and a choice of where to add an additonal 10, up to a soft cap depending on your level which all but prevents you from specializing at all.  So every character is going to have almost identical stats reguardless of desired specialization.
Moving on from stats to abilities, most abilities do nothing except various kinds of damage.  Some do area damage, some have longer range, some have extremely minor debuffs that don't work on any enemies that actually matter.  A small handful of abilities provide some variation, such as defense or moving yourself or enemies around.  Since you only have 5 ability slots, each of these abilities cuts into your offensive ability.
The aesthetics of the game are acceptable, but nothing to write home about.  They seem to have opted for a hybrid of the realistic style of TES games, mixed with the cartoony style of most fantasy MMOs.  I think they would have been better served by one or the other, most likely the former so as to appeal to TES fans who seem to have largely rejected the game already.

From Software has managed to outdo themselves again with Dark Souls 2. Most every problem I had with the original Dark Souls has been fixed. Input buffering has been reduced, you're now allowed to redestribute stat points via use of an item, ability to summon people after killing an area boss, being able to reset the boss in an area via the use of a Bonfire Ascetic, and best of all the game now runs on dedicated servers!
This is all in addition to countless other small changes to the overall experience. And don't think that just because this game is a sequel it's easier than the first Dark Souls. Quite the contrary. With the addition of a 'Health Reduction' mechanic for each time you die (up to 50%), inspired by Demon's Souls, failure in battle now carries a lot more weight than it did in the first game. I've never looked at the Souls games as being fair, but rather a representation of how patience can overcome even the most lopsided of situations. Dark Souls 2 capitalizes on this aspect, possibly even more than its predescessor.
While the diminished graphical fidelity compared to the E3 showing is indeed unfortunate, this is still a game that RPGS and hardcore gamers alike should not miss! Though, be warned. Do not play this game without a 360 controller until the M&KB issues are fixed!

For the most part I found Survivalist to be a very solid and enjoyable game.  On first appearances it may seem like a casual version of Dead State-lite but its not even turn-based. If you are a fan of State of Decay then you will be pleased to find a number of similarities with that game.
Its a zombie survival RPG played in real-time with exploration, combat, character fatigue/hunger/ thirst, community recruitment, base building, tied together with some complex quests.  Unfortunately there are a few really frustrating things such as overly complex quest-arcs, somewhat frenetic combat and some very gamey aspects to recruiting and achievement hunting that bring it slightly down from being great.
Overall the game possesses some really well designed and implemented features which together add up to surpass the sum of its parts.  However it can be difficult to get into if you dont enjoy the feeling of not being in complete control.  If you are not great at multi-tasking or you dislike the pace and frantic nature of real-time combat then I would give this a miss or dont expect too much!
Those things almost put me off during my first aborted playthrough.  Yet if you can overlook them or possess a methodical approach to gameplay there's a very good game to discover.   One that surprised me but only if you have the patience and persistence to try.
Story-driven, zombie survival isometric RPG.  Played in real-time.
A post-apocalypic scenario full of rival communities in a fictional desert region around mid-west United States.
Take control of Joe Wheeler a successful hedge fund manager (i.e. tosser) who built his own bunker before the zombie apocalypse started.  After a year of surviving alone and with dwindling resources, its time to take your first steps into a harsh new world, recruit characters, form a community, build a base, gather resources and complete quests, while fighting bands of looters and avoiding infection from zombies.
The story is fairly deep, with a complex main quest.  One that demands your full attention otherwise you can lose your bearings and get bored.  This is further complicated with the time sensitive nature of the insulin quest and your need to find more of it to keep a certain NPC alive.  Unfortunately there is also at least one convoluted quest where you have to wait, wait and wait for someone to die (if you dont want bad karma) to get an item you may desparately need [for more insulin].  These plain suck and take away from the satisfying quests.
A multiple story driven campaign played out on a single map with around two dozen quest arcs of varying length, complication and effort.  The main story arc has about 20 sub-quests to complete.  The core gameplay will take in excess of 50hours easily.  My playthrough took 90hours and it was far from comprehensive.  If you fail a quest you are given the chance to reload automatically.
The whole game takes place on one explorable map populated by survivor communities, zombies, deserted towns and looters.  The map is not fully open-world restricting exploration through the the nature of the insulin quest and the need to keep an eye on your community members.  The game can be continued after the main quest is finished.  If you are lucky you can attempt to complete the other two alternatives to the central quest.
An almost perfect blend of features for the genre. Contains a good number of well conceived multi-option quests, well-rounded and flawed characters and a clever dialogue system even though sometimes gamey recruitment requirements for key characters - such as luring zombies near to them to increase respect.
There is also excellent base building and community management, substantial item inventory, and a good RPG-lite stats for each character that determine key actions such as fitness, combat, construction, healing and farming.  Combat is frenetic in real-time which was hit and miss and, a fairly robust A.I. that allows you delegate tasks to community members even if it was not perfect.  Resource collection was a tad too slow, making the game last too long.
Zombies are unfortunately not the main threat in the game.  They exist alone or in small groups in unexplored areas.  They will try to run and bite your characters either alone or in groups until despatched.   Once the fog of war is exposed those areas are clear. Humans come in two forms: survivors and looters.  Combat doesnt necessarily need to occur with humans but once you start they will remain hostile until they are dead.  These attack with numerous weapons and in groups so are much more dangerous.  However periodically the groups of roving zombies and looters will target your base to keep you on your toes.
The game possess some solid A.I.  It allows you to manage what tasks individuals are assigned, while having them seek; food, water and rest when they require it.  They will even hunt down ammo if they are low.  The A.I. was so well-made that the paltry issues I had were that farmers did not collect and store corn and if water wasnt available, they did not seek it from nearby wells.   Combat is straightforward enough, as they will shoot any perceived threat or attempt to kick them off if overwhelmed.
Fine but not completely initutive for a PC user.

These are wide ranging.  Only a few are simple.  Some are overly complex.  If you are expecting easy and fast achievements this is not the game for you.  There are a couple that are insanely difficult to get and very time consuming!  On the other hand when you do trigger one its very satisfying.  Some of the achievements will need at least one replay.  Likely more.
None but a sequel is planned by the developer.  Yes I said developer.  It was made [mostly] by one person!  So kudos to him for a sterling effort!
Did not try co-op but I would imagine if its stable the game would be twice as engrossing to play with two of you in the same group.
For a real-time RPG and indie game this really surprised me.  It has alot of great content even if only the main quest is replayable.  I think fans of games with the story and questing of Baldurs Gate and Icewind Dale, and the zombie survival and party/base management of State of Decay, Dead State wil definitely enjoy Survivalist.  Even if it appears to be the poor relation graphically.
The game is built for at least one playthrough but given the complicated nature of the quest arcs and the all to real possibility of messing up something you could be playing this twice or three times as there are three possible player sanctioned goals that require the best part of the game to slowly achieve.  These are: Love, Money and Power.  Each has its own set of sub-quests you will really need to make and to some extent grinding goals to chip away at as you play.
One of the few titles I would recommend at full price.  Getting it on a sale would just be a bonus.
