Before I get into the actual review I just want to preface this by stating that I had absolutely zero issues with the game.  Because of the number of reported problems I think it's safe to say that I'm fortunate, so I can give a full review of the game without taking performance issues into consideration.  Keep this in mind because those who have had issues have every right to be upset so hopefully I can provide some insight into how the game actually plays once the patch rolls out.
First things first, if you played and enjoyed the first Dishonored then you are going to absolutely love the sequel.  In so many ways Dishonored 2 is what a sequel should be.  It takes a tried and true formula, keeps it mostly intact while adding some new shine and elements and ends up being an amazing experience.  The gameplay is pretty identical to the original but feels so much smoother.  I played the first game on Xbox 360 with a controller and I can honestly say keyboard and mouse make the precision of power usage much more enjoyable.  One of the common complaints I've seen is that the mouse sensitivity was extremely low by default (15) but once you find your personal sweet spot you're good to go.
Enemy AI is pretty intelligent for the most part.  If you so much as peek around a door at the wrong time and they look at you, their state of alert changes and they will actively search for you.  They don't hear things go bump in the night and then continue meandering about.  Depending on your actions (and any potential upgrades you've made that can alter your sound) they'll either flat-out attack you if you were careless or begin patrolling in hopes of seeking you out.  They barrel through doors and will sound alarms and call for help.  Even civillian AI doesn't mess around.  If you're in an area you're not supposed to be in they will typically pause and tell you to leave.  If you don't listen they'll begin screaming and shouting for help and this can cause some epic bottlenecking of enemy guards dispatching to your position.
My first playthrough was a High Chaos Emily run and I can easily say her powers are geared towards such a thing.  She can still be played full-stealth, of course, but her myriad of powers are just way too much fun in combination to sneak around.  Far Reaching to a suitable sniping position, Domino-linking multiple enemies and then ripping a Crossbow Bolt into one person's skull only for all of them to vanish thanks to Shadow Kill turning killed enemies to ash.  There's a lot...A LOT of replayability in this game.  Not just because of the endless combinations of powers relative to a playstyle, but you play as either Corvo (Dishonored's protagonist) or Emily and you remain as that person for the entire game.  So you can play a High Chaos Emily like I did and then immediately start a Low Chaos Corvo run and effectively have a whole different experience.
Visually the game is stunning.  Truly unique; an oil painting come to life.  The distinct visuals are even more impressive here on PC because the level of detail is breathtaking.  Arkane's world-building is phenomenal and their ability to create a living, breathing world for you to run around stabbing people in is top-notch.  I was able to play the entire game, almost 20 hours, with everything set to High and I had zero issues as I stated.  Again, this seems like a rare occurence but believe me when I tell you it'll be worth the wait.  I found myself stopping and staring into the distance and absorbing the world so many times that I probably tacked on a good 30 minutes just from sight-seeing.  If you had problems with the game running you couldn't appreciate the game's look but when everything gets sorted out you're going to be impressed.  Sound design is also pretty solid with nothing too exciting to write home about.  Just be careful sneaking around because if you're concentrating on stealth and being quiet and then end up kicking a bucket you're probably going to scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of yourself.
Story wise, Dishonored 2 seems to follow many of the same beats as the first game.  It's not a complete rehashing but many elements were familiar.  Each mission starts off with you riding a boat into a dock attached to the area.  Guards and other various enemies and obstacles are littered around for you to take care of how you see fit.  There are Runes and Bonecharms strewn across the map for you to find and upgrade your powers.  Black Market shops to refill ammo and acquire other goods.  Bloodflies replace Rats from the first game as the current "infestation" that directly correlates to the number of people you kill.  After navigating the area you find a key target that you either kill or incapacitate by other means.  Very, very similar to the first game and very simple.  The subplot involving the Overseers and Howlers doesn't really add much to the game while various books and notes will add detail to the overall game lore.  These notes, books, letters, etc. add so much backstory to the game and are more interesting than the actual main story that you should go out of your way to read them.  It really adds strength to the gameplay and how the main story unfolds to read various accounts on Emily as an Empress and the health of Karnaca and Dunwall.
The story is definitely the weakest part of the game but Dishonored 2 is a visual and gameplay goldmine that can be experience multiple times in multiple ways and it's a golden experience for it.  If you enjoyed the first game you will LOVE this one.  If you're even remotely interested in the game I recommend getting it and I think you'll have a great experience.  Even if you aren't keen on stealth games there's still something here for you.  I hate stealth and I'm just not very good at being sneaky.  But you can play the game geared more towards direct combat and you don't get punished for it.  You still have to be smart and pick your spots, but that's what I loved about it.  It went from being a stealth game to a cerebral combat game and it was an absolute blast.
But I do want to touch on the widespread issues again.  As I've said, I had no problems whatsoever.  That doesn't mean you won't have problems.  If you're reading all these reviews and seeing the negative remarks due to performance issues that should tell you something:  it is a legitimate problem.  I'd advise reading up on all the latest news relative to the situation if you don't think your PC can handle the game smoothly.  If you're on the fence with this game AT ALL then I highly recommend waiting until the patch gets released and scope out the feedback and see if it helped those with issues.  I can't stress enough how good Dishonored 2 is and it's a shame that it's marred with such serious issues.  Every single person that bought the game and found it unplayable has every right to be upset.  I would be too and I was nervous because I've had the game pre-ordered for months and even invested extra money in the Collector's Edition.  I'm happy to say I had a flawless experience but keep an open mind and open eyes towards the game.  And if you're someone that bought the game, couldn't play it and you're currently cursing Bethesda:  I feel you.  I really do.  But once everything gets sorted out there's an incredible experience waiting for you and I hope you give it a shot.

I'm not going to pretend to know anything about autism, but I do know a little about Twine, the interactive fiction software which was used to realise this product. Therefore I'm only going to review this game as an interactive novel, and as a sci-fi/fantasy story (which it very much is, even if I suspect there's also a fair deal of analogy I simply didn't "get"). In essence, I'm going to aim to be as "objective" as I possibly can be (wish me luck)!
Firstly, it's quite well written, though not spectacularly so. It's short, but definitely replayable given the wide range of endings and Achievements (it's certainly not an unreasonable price, all things considered). The story is quite trippy and inter-dimensional: The Twilight Zone, with a slightly modernised Y.A. twist. Nothing terribly original, but not bad for all that.
The one notably negative criticism I could perhaps make is its level of agency, which is very low for a piece of interactive fiction. While your choices definitely have consequences, and can lead you on some very different paths, decisions in a single playthrough are few and far between. I'll leave it up to the individual to decide how important this particular factor is for them.
There are, interestingly enough, two versions of the story being offered here, and they're very different. The "remake" is definitely a more adventurous and creative exploration of Twine's technical and creative possibilities, and on the whole I'd say it's the more enjoyable and "accomplished" of the versions on offer. But they're different enough to justify playing through both of them, should you be interested enough. My curiosity, if nothing else, was enough to take me through a couple of quick playthroughs of each, before I simply went back and spammed for any remaining Achievements (since they were easy enough to nab).
I'm not going to lie: this simply wasn't "my thing". I can only assume that it might mean more to those with experience of autism, and I also suspect that it may be of more appeal, overall, to females than to males. (Or, to put it a bit more crudely: it was all a bit "girly" for me). There's certainly no denying that quite a bit of love and personal perspective was put into this project, so it's earnest if nothing else. Beyond that, it's really just a matter of personal taste (like almost everything in this world, really).
Verdict: 6.5/10.

Long story short: I love it
I've clocked in... too many hours playing this game in it's original form. I enjoy this sort of game though I'm sure it's not for everyone - try the demo first if you're concerned. The updated HD version is a little bit different in the mechanics but I've already gotten used to it and I think it's for the best.
My work requires that I be rather creative and that can be a big mental drain sometimes. This game has been a great way for me to wind down after a long day. There's still plenty of thinking involved but the ambient sounds/music makes a relaxing atmostphere even when my minions are getting slaughtered. I also appreciate the fact that the game doesn't really force me to be something I'm not - there are some levels where speed or sneakiness wins the day but typically, you play the strategy you like best and as long as you play well, you'll win.
The storyline is fairly simple, just enough to carry you from mission to mission, teaching you different strategies. I kind of wish more games taught this way in their campaign modes. Maybe to some it seems like hand-holding, though. Regardless, I appreciate not having to think so hard in a game while still feeling engaged.
The downsides: not much. It is what it is - an 'ambient strategy game'. Sometimes the really big missions get a bit boring when you have to wait for enough seedlings to accumulate in order to make a key move. The new speed change option in the HD version pretty much fixes that issue for me, however. But still no co-op. I think they're could be great potential there... maybe in Eufloria 2 or something?

The HD remix has revived my obsession with this game. For those of you who have played before: The tutorial has been greatly improved, both in pacing and in clarity. The UI is much easier to read at a glance, and much more intuitive to boot. I also greatly appreciate some of the features they've added - beacons, terraforming, etc. It's definitely worthwhile to revisit.
If you haven't played before, Eufloria is a unique RTS through and through. It's amazing how this game pairs a relaxing setting with challenging goals.  I get so absorbed I often don't realize how much time has passed. There is a time element, but it's not strict. You can pace yourself however you wish. The game increases in difficulty somewhat slowly, but the hardest levels kept me entertained long after I finished story mode. There's a surprising amount of complexity arising from simple mechanics. The fact of the matter is - I played 50+ hours of the original, and here I am years later, and the mechanics are still feel fresh and challenging. That, my friends, is the mark of a good game.

I loved the original (back when it was called Dyson) and this version is only better. It's a very simple game with minimalist art and music to back it up.
It's mostly a swarm management real-time strategy where you spend your attack units to grow more attack units. Each node has different strengths for the units that grow there. So you must decide when to defend/attack and when/where to spend your resources. There's 25 story missions that don't vary too much, but usually create tricky start positions that you need to build from.
Recommended if you like to amass large armies and crush your enemies... (evil laugh echoes around the halls).  Seriously, more fun then playing with actual trees and seeds.

Tales from Space: Mutant Blobs Attack is a side-scrolling puzzle platformer about a mutant blob that can consume anything that is smaller than itself, yet grows every time it consumes something. I think you know where this is headed...
For starters, Mutant Blobs Attack is very well designed. The art style is truly awesome, a cartoony world in a 1950's horror movie setting, most likely with a wink to Steve McQueen's (hilarious) The Blob. Combined with small cutscenes in a similar style, this side of the game is genuinely funny. The soundtrack is catchy and fits well with the chosen aesthetics.
The level design is excellent, its never too hard to figure out where to go next. With 24 levels in 6 zones the game provides plenty of variation, with an enjoyable mini game in each of these zones. The puzzles are no brain teasers but do provide a nice shift from otherwise continuous platforming. The gameplay in general is fairly straightforward, but every level has another approach or gimmick that took away every sense of repetitiveness.
While in general Mutant Blobs Attack is not very challenging, once you go for the gold medals and finding every secret there's a whole new level of difficulty for those seeking a challenge. The checkpoint system is rather brilliant, avoiding that even the harder parts of the game become frustrating. The controls are decent, with the exception to wall-jumping, which is a little dodgy.
Concluding, Mutant Blobs Attack is a truly funny game that excels to great heights if/when you also decide to challenge yourself. It's not perfect, but its definitely one of the best platformers I've ever played. And for its price, you really should not ignore it.
+ Hilarious visual presentation
+ Fitting soundtrack
+ Challenging if you let it be
+ Smart checkpoint system
+ Never becomes too repetitive
- Dodgy walljumping mechanics
- A wee bit on the short side
8.5/10

Blameless is a succinct and somewhat suspenseful puzzle game. Curiosity and ingenuity are rewarded as most puzzles are cleverly designed to have a secondary solution. However, the ending doesn't seem to follow suit. Though the closing narration appears to give you hints on how to avoid that outcome the next time around, I couldn't seem to change it whatever I did.
The environment has a similar issue with interactivity. Some objects can be manipulated in surprising ways allowing for outlandish but still logical puzzle solutions. Other objects which seem to be obviously useful can't be picked up and still others are red herrings that can be picked up but are useless.
All dialogue is fully voiced, even the notes you'll come across. Unfortunately the voice-overs themselves sound like they've been put through a text-to-speech which raises the question as to why they bothered. The textures on all of the objects, however, look great. Not top of the line, but better than I would expect from a free game.
Blameless does a few things quite well and the rest is certainly not unforgivable. It's both free and very short, so you won't be wasting anything. But I can't say you're going to find anything new or memorable here either.

Pros:
*GREAT learning experience, easy to get into, very user friendly.
*Easy moving system, nice controls.
*Easy economy system.
*Easy region control and production control.
*Not all full of reports and pop up's about battles and the economy like in Hearts of Iron III or similar games.
*Cheap and fun.
*Never really gets boring. Has different campaign starts incase you don't want to spend a lot of time playing.
- First campaign starts from 1936 and is mostly economic based up until 1939 when the war starts and then ends in 1945. It also involves a lot about the Spanish Civil War and lets you ask, or change/repeat history, whether Republican Spain would win or if Nationalist Spain wins and whether Nationalist Spain joins the Axis beyond political support or if Republican Spain joins the Allies, or vice versa.
- Second campaign starts shortly before the war, in 1938, showing the rise of Germany and their moves in Czechoslovakia and the Rhineland. Ends in 1945.
- Third campaign starts at the brink of the war, 1939, with the invasion of Poland and sorrounding countries. Ends in 1945.
- Fourth campaign starts in 1941 with the entry of America into the war after Pearl Harbor. Ends in 1945. Also involves the invasion of the Soviet Union(Eastern Front). Ends in 1945. Also has the battle in Africa.
- Last campaign starts in 1944 and involves the invasion of France by the hands America, Britian and Canada(Operation Overlord/D-Day). Also involves the final stages of the Pacific War and the end of the war. Ends in 1945.
*Has other historically correct events(unless you are the country that would've caused that event, in that case it is your choice if you follow history), such as the civil war in China with Communist China and Nationalist China, economic problems in America, Japan's crazy expansion, etc.
*Easy way to make your own scenarios.
*Lets you do what you always wondered and see what happens. Play as Germany and avoid a war with the Soviet's and see if you can conquer all of non-Soviet Europe. See what happens as Japan if you had not declared war on America. See what happens if, as the Soviet's, you make a move against Germany first. SEE WHAT HAPPENS!
*Area that was formally Allied is given back to the former country when conquered by an Allied army. Ie. Normandy is given back to France after America wins the battle in Normandy.
*Countries are never defeated until the whole alliance is destroyed.
*Turn based instead of real time(might be a con for some, but it makes it easier for planning purposes and reviewing mistakes quickly.)
*Almost no lag.
*Great mod support/custom scenario sharing support.
Cons:
*Area that is occupied is given to the country that fought first, not the country that contributed to the battle the most.
*Hard to recover from major losses in an area.
*No way to have production to reinforce in areas that you conquered back for a country you are Allied. Ie. America can't build stuff in a French factory in a region that they conquered for France.

Before I get into the actual review I just want to preface this by stating that I had absolutely zero issues with the game.  Because of the number of reported problems I think it's safe to say that I'm fortunate, so I can give a full review of the game without taking performance issues into consideration.  Keep this in mind because those who have had issues have every right to be upset so hopefully I can provide some insight into how the game actually plays once the patch rolls out.
First things first, if you played and enjoyed the first Dishonored then you are going to absolutely love the sequel.  In so many ways Dishonored 2 is what a sequel should be.  It takes a tried and true formula, keeps it mostly intact while adding some new shine and elements and ends up being an amazing experience.  The gameplay is pretty identical to the original but feels so much smoother.  I played the first game on Xbox 360 with a controller and I can honestly say keyboard and mouse make the precision of power usage much more enjoyable.  One of the common complaints I've seen is that the mouse sensitivity was extremely low by default (15) but once you find your personal sweet spot you're good to go.
Enemy AI is pretty intelligent for the most part.  If you so much as peek around a door at the wrong time and they look at you, their state of alert changes and they will actively search for you.  They don't hear things go bump in the night and then continue meandering about.  Depending on your actions (and any potential upgrades you've made that can alter your sound) they'll either flat-out attack you if you were careless or begin patrolling in hopes of seeking you out.  They barrel through doors and will sound alarms and call for help.  Even civillian AI doesn't mess around.  If you're in an area you're not supposed to be in they will typically pause and tell you to leave.  If you don't listen they'll begin screaming and shouting for help and this can cause some epic bottlenecking of enemy guards dispatching to your position.
My first playthrough was a High Chaos Emily run and I can easily say her powers are geared towards such a thing.  She can still be played full-stealth, of course, but her myriad of powers are just way too much fun in combination to sneak around.  Far Reaching to a suitable sniping position, Domino-linking multiple enemies and then ripping a Crossbow Bolt into one person's skull only for all of them to vanish thanks to Shadow Kill turning killed enemies to ash.  There's a lot...A LOT of replayability in this game.  Not just because of the endless combinations of powers relative to a playstyle, but you play as either Corvo (Dishonored's protagonist) or Emily and you remain as that person for the entire game.  So you can play a High Chaos Emily like I did and then immediately start a Low Chaos Corvo run and effectively have a whole different experience.
Visually the game is stunning.  Truly unique; an oil painting come to life.  The distinct visuals are even more impressive here on PC because the level of detail is breathtaking.  Arkane's world-building is phenomenal and their ability to create a living, breathing world for you to run around stabbing people in is top-notch.  I was able to play the entire game, almost 20 hours, with everything set to High and I had zero issues as I stated.  Again, this seems like a rare occurence but believe me when I tell you it'll be worth the wait.  I found myself stopping and staring into the distance and absorbing the world so many times that I probably tacked on a good 30 minutes just from sight-seeing.  If you had problems with the game running you couldn't appreciate the game's look but when everything gets sorted out you're going to be impressed.  Sound design is also pretty solid with nothing too exciting to write home about.  Just be careful sneaking around because if you're concentrating on stealth and being quiet and then end up kicking a bucket you're probably going to scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of yourself.
Story wise, Dishonored 2 seems to follow many of the same beats as the first game.  It's not a complete rehashing but many elements were familiar.  Each mission starts off with you riding a boat into a dock attached to the area.  Guards and other various enemies and obstacles are littered around for you to take care of how you see fit.  There are Runes and Bonecharms strewn across the map for you to find and upgrade your powers.  Black Market shops to refill ammo and acquire other goods.  Bloodflies replace Rats from the first game as the current "infestation" that directly correlates to the number of people you kill.  After navigating the area you find a key target that you either kill or incapacitate by other means.  Very, very similar to the first game and very simple.  The subplot involving the Overseers and Howlers doesn't really add much to the game while various books and notes will add detail to the overall game lore.  These notes, books, letters, etc. add so much backstory to the game and are more interesting than the actual main story that you should go out of your way to read them.  It really adds strength to the gameplay and how the main story unfolds to read various accounts on Emily as an Empress and the health of Karnaca and Dunwall.
The story is definitely the weakest part of the game but Dishonored 2 is a visual and gameplay goldmine that can be experience multiple times in multiple ways and it's a golden experience for it.  If you enjoyed the first game you will LOVE this one.  If you're even remotely interested in the game I recommend getting it and I think you'll have a great experience.  Even if you aren't keen on stealth games there's still something here for you.  I hate stealth and I'm just not very good at being sneaky.  But you can play the game geared more towards direct combat and you don't get punished for it.  You still have to be smart and pick your spots, but that's what I loved about it.  It went from being a stealth game to a cerebral combat game and it was an absolute blast.
But I do want to touch on the widespread issues again.  As I've said, I had no problems whatsoever.  That doesn't mean you won't have problems.  If you're reading all these reviews and seeing the negative remarks due to performance issues that should tell you something:  it is a legitimate problem.  I'd advise reading up on all the latest news relative to the situation if you don't think your PC can handle the game smoothly.  If you're on the fence with this game AT ALL then I highly recommend waiting until the patch gets released and scope out the feedback and see if it helped those with issues.  I can't stress enough how good Dishonored 2 is and it's a shame that it's marred with such serious issues.  Every single person that bought the game and found it unplayable has every right to be upset.  I would be too and I was nervous because I've had the game pre-ordered for months and even invested extra money in the Collector's Edition.  I'm happy to say I had a flawless experience but keep an open mind and open eyes towards the game.  And if you're someone that bought the game, couldn't play it and you're currently cursing Bethesda:  I feel you.  I really do.  But once everything gets sorted out there's an incredible experience waiting for you and I hope you give it a shot.

I cannot stop Euro truck simulating.  I've been known to screech home in a real vehicle in order to drive a fake vehicle to Hungary in order to deliver plums.  The game itself I can definitely recommend assuming you have some self-control with regards to time spent on virtual trucks.
You start off with no truck of your own, and are forced to work for the man driving other people's trucks short distances to a limited selection of destinations.  As you progress and earn money you can buy your own truck, drive to wherever you want, accept whatever jobs you please, and as you gain experience (and assign skill points) open up a vast array of job types that were closed to you before (e.g. fragile cargo, dangerous cargo, express deliveries, long distance hauls etc.).  You can also buy garages in many of the towns and cities you come across, and hire other drivers to base themselves at your garages and truck for your profit.  This leads to empire building and truck-based megalomania in my case.  Another useful feature of owning garages is that you can quick travel between them, making travel between some distant backwater and a lucrative job-rich city a snap.
The driving itself can be very relaxing.  The drone of the engine, the miles of road being swallowed up, your favourite songs playing on the radio.  Then you'll get an AI driver slam their brakes on in front of you and all your relaxation will go up in smoke as you lock up and screech into the central reservation in an attempt to not wipe out three generations of an entire family.  Them's the breaks I suppose.

Plot normally helps people go toward a goal,but if there is no goal,there isn't that much to aim for. We don't even know why Beatrix decided to sign up for the range exchange. At least some backstory gives us insight to the characters goal.
Most games that the population flocks towards have a goal. Beat this monster,go back home,save the world ect.  Human beings are driven towards completion. If there's no plot,there's no end. If there's no end,there's no sense of completion,which means people will start to lose interest. The recent addition of the lab made it last a bit longer,but how many people do you expect to stick around to put decorations in every nook and cranny? The answer should be less than 100.
To summarize the giant block of text I made,this game has no end or plot to keep us going,so it'll wind up sitting on our computer,dead. If there has some plot or backstory added in the future,then I may change my review,given the quality of said plot or backstory,but until then my review will remain negative.

In my opinion the best Borderlands game to date. Fun gameplay, interesting loot and amazing story / narrative. My massive love of this game comes from the art style and the overall feel of the game. The art is beautiful and very detailed which complements the setting of Pandora. The narrative is funny but is sometimes contrasted by deep and dark events. Handsome Jack is probably my favourite villain, constantly giving witty comments and insults while you attempt to save the world from destruction. The loot systems is fun yet simple and keeps the gameplay changing so it is never boring. The main thing that separates it from the other Borderlands titles is the late game. The late game is so good and the difficulty scales well so the player is challenged but never completely helpless which makes the games replayability rather high.
Sadly, I feel some of the best elements of the game are from DLC which will cost you some cash. If you want to truly experience the late game 'The Ultimate Vault Hunter Upgrade Pack' and 'Ultimate Vault Hunter Upgrade Pack 2' are required. Furthermore, although the looting system is great sometimes it becomes tedious to clear your inventory and keep track of all the weapons you wish to keep (I have sold many a great gun by mistake). Some of the characters have less impact on the late game than others, for example Axton is that great when you start getting to the higher levels despite having a fun kit. Overall, these are minor complaints about a fantastic game but need to be mentioned.
To conclude: shooting bandits has never been so fun.

A worthy sequel to Dark Souls in terms of game mechanics, Dark Souls II is an improvement on its predecessor in many ways. Unfortunately, it ultimately feels like a sequel in both the best and the worst ways. What I mean by this is that it really feels like the goal from the outset was "Dark Souls, only moreso- bigger world, more and more varied levels, more bosses, more covenants, more EVERYTHING." And from a gameplay perspective, this is a great thing. However, in the process, the feel of a single contiguous world is lost, and with it some of the "soul" of its predecessor. That said, what I said about Dark Souls still applies to this game.

As most space games, I'm a sucker for them. Astroneer is one of the many that I can't help but play and play again. While my hours might not say much at the moment, there's a good reason that I've seen stated by a few others: there's not much to do.

You have to gather materials from caves, sometimes other crash sites that have been buried over time, and it's all very fun. After a while, you'll have yourself a rover, a large base and possibly a way of transportation to get to the next planet [I haven't, as of writing this] and once you do, there's not much else other than to just keep on going from planet to planet.
So, if you'd like a game to just come back to every now and then, as I do, just to relax and gather, then this is a good game. I'm sure the devs will add something in the future story-wise/end-goal-wise once the game is 'finished' but as for now it's more of a game just for relaxing.

Ditching the recent mindset that platformers for some reason need to be mercilessly difficult, Drinkbox Studios instead pours their heart and soul into the area I feel matters most in a game, that unquantifiable "fun factor", and it shows in every inch of Mutant Blobs Attack.
The comical and cartoony presentation is no doubt its biggest asset, creating a game that is both delightful to hear and behold, as well as one that somehow turns the act of mass murder into a lighthearted affair. It also packs in more indie game references than possibly any before it, which had me grinning the whole way through as I saw my favorites reimagined in very amusing ways. What's more, none of this comes at the cost of great levels or mechanics. Although it shows obvious influence from games such as The Maw and Katamari, Mutant Blobs carves out its own niche in the platforming genre with consistently clever design that feels wholly unique. Again and again it defied my expectations which is by no means something I say often.
Other than a handful of times I had to wrestle with the controls, there is virtually nothing I dislike about Mutant Blobs Attack. It's hilarious, polished, and most of all a ton of fun. Some might find the 3-4 hour length a little unfulfilling, but to me this is something of a compliment in and of itself, as the only reason I want more is because what is here is just that good!

I've clocked in over 500 hours since the game launched in April, I've only one VR14 toon and a handful of lower level alts. I've recently bought the game on Steam to add it to my Steam collection.
The game isn't without it's flaws, from launch it was beset with issues such as bugged quests, gold selling spam - all the usual fare for an mmo. Add to that the fact that the product (rightly or wrongly) didn't meet the inflated expectation of rabid Elder Scrolls fans, missing key aspects like crime, justice, open exploration and even sitting in chairs, and a lot of people were disappointed.
However, this is not Skyrim 2. It's an mmo.
I've been playing mmos for many years now, I've experience in subscription, B2P and F2P models. I've played sandbox, theme park, action mmo and a few other more obscure ones too. In my opinion, this ranks as one of the best mmos on the market today, period.
Why? It's gorgeous for a start. The quests and story are engaging (more so if you turn off the NPC chat text using an addon I have installed - really helps you focus). Crafting is intricate and actually means something - some of the best gear in game is crafted, it goes toe-to-toe with world drops. Trading is a lot of fun, the absence of a global auction house, favouring instead a segmented guild store system means you have to think about the best markets open to you, it's a mini-game all of its own. The combat is okay, I like the action style and the minimal hotbar. They're also bringing in combat updates with the next patch to improve combat animations and a lot of the skills.
The most important thing for me however, is how accessible the dev team are. I recently spent time playing Archeage, one of the most poorly managed western releases I've ever had the displeasure of playing. Devs were unreachable, community managers were silent or hateful - it was a complete mess. Here though, ZOS do everything they can to manage expectations, respond to concerns and are refreshingly open about the future of the game. Add to this that they've responded excellently to fan suggestions and it's a great mmo to play in.
A lot of the updates over the past eight months have brought the game a long way - added guild kiosks to make items publicly available for purchase, a dye system, dungeon scaling, and the upcoming crime/justice system are just a few of the additions which make this mmo far superior to any of it's themepark peers.
Yes there are still issues, but an mmo is always a work in progress. This game has come a long way since release, and the road ahead will bring further improvements and a lot of exciting new mechanics to the world of Tamriel.
Looking forward to 2015 - can't wait to see what comes next!

An enjoyable, relaxing RTS game with great atmosphere.  Don't be fooled by my playtime, I played the original Eufloria years ago, and it's still in my Steam top-20 with nearly 50 hours played.  Impressive for a small indie game, especially if you consider I don't generally like RTS games.  And now these wonderful developers decided to gift the new improved HD version to everyone who bought the original game.
The game isn't complicated at all, the tutorial levels do a great job to teach you all you need to know.  You start with seedlings around an asteroid under your control.  You can move them to other asteroids within your influence sphere, possibly attacking enemy seedlings in the process, or plant them to grow a tree.  Trees produce seedlings, with increasing output overtime when they become fully grown.  Seedlings come with 3 characteristics, based on the quality of the asteroid they were grown on : energy, strength and speed.  Strength and speed are obvious, higher energy means you will need less seedlings to conquer an enemy asteroid.  Some more complexity later on, but those are the basics in a nutshell.
What makes this game great is the atmosphere, sound & graphics.   It really looks gorgeous, with a high attention to detail (e.g. seedlings stats also change the way they look).  You notice how the developers really made this with a passion.  The levels are partially procedurally generated, the level will never be identical, but some parameters stay the same.  The music is nice and relaxing.  You also have a lot of control over the speed of the game, allowing for both rushed gameplay or a relaxing experience.
If I have to mention something negative, the only thing I can think of is the lack of complexity.  Levels start to feel too similar after awhile, because you are growing seedlings and invading asteroids over and over again.  There is some variation in each level's initial strategy, but usually it's pretty obvious if you have to grow, attack or flee to beat the level.

When I first saw the game,my thoughts went more towards "Is there some kind of plot?". The answer,like with a large amount of farming simulators,was no. The game is fun and cute and all,but once you find all the slimes,pop every gordo,and have a stable farm,there's nothing else to do. Plot normally helps people go toward a goal,but if there is no goal,there isn't that much to aim for. We don't even know why Beatrix decided to sign up for the range exchange. At least some backstory gives us insight to the characters goal.
Most games that the population flocks towards have a goal. Beat this monster,go back home,save the world ect.  Human beings are driven towards completion. If there's no plot,there's no end. If there's no end,there's no sense of completion,which means people will start to lose interest. The recent addition of the lab made it last a bit longer,but how many people do you expect to stick around to put decorations in every nook and cranny? The answer should be less than 100.
To summarize the giant block of text I made,this game has no end or plot to keep us going,so it'll wind up sitting on our computer,dead. If there has some plot or backstory added in the future,then I may change my review,given the quality of said plot or backstory,but until then my review will remain negative.

I really want to like this game, I really do. The multiplayer is great when it's actually working and the base game is good. Didn't enjoy single-player that much no one plays COD for single-player anyway.
So lets look at multiplayer, no dedicated servers which really blows, lag compensation can be pretty bad, sledgehammer default lobby join status can be up to 800 ping. FPS is unplayable online at anything above 200 (and that's pushing it). Also everytime I start up the game it'll ask me if I want to cripple myself with an xbox controller I have plugged in, really not necessary to ask me everytime but that's a minor gripe. (you can turn this off by editing the config files btw)
As far as game modes go you can only really get into TDM, DOM or FFA on PC. It's a shame because the uplink game mode looks awesome but the player base just isn't there. Skill based matchmaking isn't helping either, making an already small playerbase even smaller.
Another thing to note is that this game does not give reliable performance, many people reported stuttering and freezing throughout their games. This was somehow caused by an unusually large page file and also using a ton of RAM. I experienced this myself too and quit playing for a week. When I came back it has somehow fixed itself with no game patches or GPU driver updates. So your mileage may vary.
Outside of these glaring issues it really is a fun game, it's just a gamble if it will actually work for you.

The game itself is a unique strategy game with ambient soundtrack and an original idea : conquering huge systems of planet with your army of flower-like spaceships.
Learn to defend your outpost planets, scout with high-speed breed of seedlings, gather a gigantic swarm of flowers, control the space with mines, enhance your babys by terraforming their native stars, and bring death, doom, destruction, and despair to your ennemies in a raging tempest of lasers at a cosmic scale.

Okay, I bought this game when it was on sale.
I expected some half-baked game worth a few hours of fun.
I. Was. Wrong.
Typically, I am the type of person who isn't interested in games with zombies, and I thought I would give this game a shot.
Granted, I initially played the game up until Alice gets her first five insulin and I stopped playing the game for 5 months.
Eventually, I did return. I was bored, scrolling through my Steam Library when I saw this game.
"What the hell" I thought "might as well give it a shot".
I played it for 30 minutes, which turned into an hour, which turned into 6 hours.
I loved it. The game was amazing, and when I finished my first play through (I chose Love over Power and Money), I was hungry for more. I am now starting my second play through, choosing Power, which is no easy task.
So far, I have not run into any bad bugs or glitches. The physics do sometimes do weird things, for instance, if you shoot a zombie as it is jumping at you, the body can end up going several feet behind you. A similar instance is when you kick a zombie in front of you, it can end up flying in the direction you pushed it, several feet away. Regardless, it's not a "bad" thing, just funny.
My point is: give this game a shot. I initially hated it, but I grew to enjoy it a lot.
Also, I realize that my review says that I have only played 0.8 hours of the game, but I played it offline on a separate harddrive.
9.5 out of 10.
A little tip: if you're going to threaten looters to get them to join you, use a character other than Joe. That way, there is less of a chance of people leaving your group (people often leave if they dislike Joe). People with the Sociopath trait are great at intimidation.

When I first saw the game,my thoughts went more towards "Is there some kind of plot?". The answer,like with a large amount of farming simulators,was no. The game is fun and cute and all,but once you find all the slimes,pop every gordo,and have a stable farm,there's nothing else to do. Plot normally helps people go toward a goal,but if there is no goal,there isn't that much to aim for. We don't even know why Beatrix decided to sign up for the range exchange. At least some backstory gives us insight to the characters goal.
Most games that the population flocks towards have a goal. Beat this monster,go back home,save the world ect.  Human beings are driven towards completion. If there's no plot,there's no end. If there's no end,there's no sense of completion,which means people will start to lose interest. The recent addition of the lab made it last a bit longer,but how many people do you expect to stick around to put decorations in every nook and cranny? The answer should be less than 100.
To summarize the giant block of text I made,this game has no end or plot to keep us going,so it'll wind up sitting on our computer,dead. While I should say that Borderlands 2 should be lauded for its hilarious dialogue, diverse skill sets, and detailed cell-shaded environments, it is simply not a game you can play alone. The story offers no incentive to invest yourself in the characters, there is no real conflict, and dialogue is just often said because it sounds cool. If there ever has been a balance between bizarre humour and quality story, Borderlands 2 just hasn’t met it.
But co-operatively? It just makes sense. Because you face so many enemies earlier on with slightly higher levels, the game looks to be designed for co-operative sessions with divergent skill sets to make it more fun. Alone, the game will take much longer and appear meticulous. Even the weapon looting and trade-up system will seem tedious after the first hour. However, this is not to say that the weapon and core gameplay is necessarily faulty - it’s just fundamentally grind-y, no matter if you’re lathering bullets, acid, or god-knows-what-else on your foes. Not only that, but it punishes people who just want to see the game’s story through by making you partake in tedious sidequests - otherwise you can find yourself massively underleveled by just doing the story quests.
The DLC adds more of the same, with a zaney couple of quest lines. Great with buddies, I’m sure. Otherwise, the cool environments and funny dialogue does not make up for the game’s repetitive nature.

Where to begin...This game is f**king fantastic, the game is so good that i decided to 100% complete it on every character on 360, 100% it on PC with only halve of my characters and buy it on xbox one cause the game is so good.
The game takes place after Borderlands 1 and doesn't give much exposition on what has happned, that is why we now have Borderlands: Pre-Sequal (Which is sh*t btw). the game much like the first one follows your character who you can chose to be, the gunzerker who can dual weild any two guns, the siren who can phaselock enimeis in the air for teamwork, the commando who can use his turret to kill many enimeis and the assasin who can turn invisable and silently take out his enimeis. Two more where added through DLC's the psyco who can rush his enimeis with his buzz axe and the Necromancer who can summon a robot to fight at her side.
The story follows your chosen character and 3 others if you chose to play with friends either way the game is still awsome with or without friends but you may feel boared after a while without them. The game is about your character being requested by the head of Hyperion, which has risen to power through eridium wehich started to appear after the opening of the vault in borderlands 1. After being approched by Hyperion you get stabbed in the back by their leader and you spend the very well voice acted and awsome 50+ hour campaign, there are also many side missions to explore and a lot of guns and loot to collect along the way.
The main story, without any doing any side missions, is very short and is easily done in about 30+ hours if you speed run it but because of the way the games leveling system works and how you need to be a certain level for a certain area youll have to spend more time leveling up to continue with the story. also, youll feel enticed to do the side missions because certain missions give you high end rewards which are normaly not found within the game world.
There are 3 playthroughs of the game to do, essentialy they are just the same but they get harder each playthrough. the first playthrough caps at about 35, the second caps at about 50 and the finale can be repalyed and links all the enimeis to the highest leveled player and the cap for this is 72. There are OP levels which where added to make your character 80 but you are still seen as 72, the OP levels are just there for a challenge. The OP levels and the third playthough was added through DLC's, the same DLC's also incresed the level cap from 50 to 72.
The four Story DLC's are a must have, these add to the games already expansive games loot and gives the player more content to play around with. The other DLC's known as headhunter packs are less needed because these where just festival DLC's (In my eyes they where just money grabbing with these DLC's but im trying to be none biased), never the less they are still very good and can normaly be done in about 45 mins but the story DLC's can take anywhere between 10-15 hours.
to conclude this game is f**king awsome and they need to make a third. if you ever see this on sale and are struggling between Borderlands: Pre-Sequal, get this one. I give this an 9/10 and a must buy.

The clockwork soldiers are much harder to kill and the bloodflies are much easier to get rid of by just shooting the nest once.

Due to me putting 130+ hours into the game, I feel like I have a right to review it.
Compared to other games such as Europa Universalis or any other Grand Strategy game, The Calm & the Storm is pretty simplistic when it comes to gameplay. Diplomacy is simple and combat is relatively easy to learn.
One thing I will mention though, is that the world market is your best friend. if you play as anyone but the U.S USSR or Germany (I'm not sure about the U.K or China) then you will become dependent to the world market. Surprisingly, the same goes to self-sufficient countries if you want to keep a fairly steady income.
That's all I'm going to mention about the game because if you download custom scenarios (which I HIGHLY recommend) then the gameplay, research, resource consumption, world market, etc will change depending on the scenario.
For an example, I downloaded a scenario that let me played as the Holy Roman Empire in 1936, I fought the Nazis, conquered Europe, and fought the USSR and the U.K as a pro-Fascist SuperPower. Yes, Hitler was beaten by Julius Caesar.
I definitely recommend this to anyone who wants to get into Grand Strategy games. This is a good place to start with it's cheap price and its simple gameplay mechanics.

So this game has really impressed me with it's great visuals and overall feel, a must for any alien fan. I bought the deluxe edition of this game on steam, which includes the season pass. From what I can see it gives you the other pre order DLC for this game, so that's Crew Expendable and Last Survivor.
Right now that's get down to the actual game here shall we.
This game has done exactly what it was supposed to do, bring honor back to the Alien franchise. So during my playtime I had been taking in that epic atmosphere that this game creates. It feels like a real Alien experience, closely resembling the first film in how it creates that intense environment. The way it uses the music, lighting and atmosphere to create that suspense, a feeling of anxiety.
The story is so-so, I mean don't get me wrong..it's a great story with a great setting and background, however it just doesn't keep me glued to it, it also went on longer than you would expect and no, that's not always a good thing. The characters are also so-so, of course Amanda is probably the strongest out of the lot however Samuels and Nina seem to come across as rather..blank, but don't get me wrong, they are still great to have around. Now the most interesting thing about this game is..of course..the Alien, I well designed A.I that is just brilliant at creating that anxiety, I mean it's movements and how it reacts is so erratic, they really did create the perfect organism.
Right well the game itself runs very well on PC, now I don't really have much experience with PC games at release but I can say that this game runs as smooth as butter.
Settings wise it does give the user a range of choices to suit your liking, for instance film grain. For my experience I decided to turn off film grain as I wanted my experience to be more immersive. Now there are many other options to fiddle around with for instance Motion Blur, Particles, Depth of field, Chromatic Aberration, Planar Reflections and all the usual things you'd expect on a PC game. Now I've had no trouble playing this game so far, everything is maxed out, mostly.
I'm going to be honest and say I am very impressed with this game, it fulfilled all my expectations. I was totally immersed in what was going on, and next to Shadow Of Mordor this is one of the more suprising games of the year. Overall I recommend this game to anyone who's a fan of thr Alien series, in fact it's a must have, even if you're not an Alien fan or have no experience with the series I would still recommend buying it, it's a great and fun game full suspense that will keep you on the edge of your seat.
So don't be afraid to purchase this game because trust me, it's nothing like Alien Colonial Marines.

Although this game is suffering from poor optimization, it is fun and great.
They really expanded on the lore from Dishonored 1 and quite a few of the characters return from the original game.
The gameplay has been improved: adding different augmentations to abilities, adding bonecharm crafting (and rune crafting but it's not worth it), and adding many new blueprints for gear.
They have replaced and added a few enemies in the game. The tallboys are replaced with clockwork soldiers and are much fewer to come by. The rats are replaced with bloodflies and very few people will effectively become zombies protecting the nests. The clockwork soldiers are much harder to kill and the bloodflies are much easier to get rid of by just shooting the nest once.
Having only played Corvo so far, his powers are essentially the same but with room for improvements such as having the stop time while holding blink and not moving ability that Daud had, being able to possess corpses to hide from enemies, and so on.
One thing I'll say about the beginning is that they almost try to shove playing as Emily down your throat and they even show Corvo killing people before you decide who to play as.
Playing the Low Chaos so far, it seems that whatever chaos playthrough you are playing in the moment will reflect the decisions made in Dishonored 1. Example: I'm playing on low chaos and they mentioned keeping Daud alive.
This game is worth it if you can run it or deal with low frames/quality. I'm getting 40-60 fps on very high with some settings turned off (god rays, volumetric lighting, bloom) and turning adaptive resolution down to about 70.
The graphics look great maxed out but is unplayable. Btw, I have an FX-8350 and a GTX 970 with 16GB of RAM.
UPDATE: I finished the game on my first playthrough. The story was okay until the end. The final mission felt like it was a bit at the very end. The overall story was decent enough but felt very short. I will playthrough a second time and I'll try to explore more. I felt limited at the end and I wasn't able to get both the "no killing" and "no alerting" achievements at the same time.

The game is a valiant first attempt at a World War 2 grand strategy game, but it falls apart on a number of levels.  Its diplomatic model is obtuse, and unable to actually reflect events of the period (when one person in an alliance is at war, it's all in, so you can't have Italy's late entry or Japan being part of the Axis but not at war), the combat model is reasonable enough - simple but effective - but production is a mess (it's hard to tell, but it looks like you need the same amount of consumer goods whether you're at war or not), and the UI gets pretty fiddly.  On top that, the starting force set-ups are incredibly ahistorical (Germany starts with a larger army than UK and France combined, in 1936!).  It's too complicated to be accessible, and too simple (and ahistorical) to draw in enthusiasts of the period.
It's confusing at first. But it becomes amazing.

Had no idea such a simple game on the surface could be so darn addicting in execution. Think State of Decay meets Project Zomboid mixed with 28 Days later zeds  and you got the gist. Building up a community is fun and engaging. Even the..ahem...complications with one of the starting chracters I found made the game more compelling when it could easily have been bloody irritating. So kudos devs for taking a creative chance there.
What really makes this game for me however is command mode. Basically, you can go into a Sims style overworld view to tell chracters your not directly controlling what to do. Gather resources, build, or whatever. And the best part is you don't have to micro-manage every little thing! They need food or water? They find it! They need more materials for that build? They head to the nearest cache and grab materials. And mostly they intelligently defend themselves (wouldn't suggest letting them auto into looters though. That never seems to end well).
All in all, a fantastic game especailly given the price. And the recently added multi-player serves only to give it more replayability. I would highly suggest this one to anyone more interested in community interactions with their zombie survival instead of just scavaging and waiting to die.
Oh, and last note. The combat I find to be extremely engrossing. The fast paced zeds and erratic nature of shoot-outs with looters will keep you entertained!

I am a fairly new Dark Souls player, but the hype got to me, I pulled my pants up, finished DS1 and got into the sequel. This game obviously isn't for everyone, but I get the impression that the difficulty has become the key selling point here, which is a bit of a shame for me.
Dark Souls 2 will murder you without mercy, but if you can take it and overcome it, you'll feel like the ultimate badass. The game is more polished, bettel looking, has better mechanics and overall is na improvement over DS1 in those terms, but is a bit lacking in terms of story and lore. If you liked theprevious Souls games, this is a must have.
However, there are some things that make DS2 fall short. First of all, it seem like they went to extremes when it comes to crancking up the difficulty. If you play this just becasue it's hard, you will love it. For me it feels a bit disappointing. Contrary to Dark Souls 1, this game is less fair - enemies attack in groups, bonfires are not always safe, there are some f*** you style traps that you cannot avoid and enemies in general hit you in situation where in DS1 they wouldn't. I get the impression that the first Dark Souls was hard, but wanted you to overcome it and that made is satysfying, while the second one is just kicking you butt to live up to the hype.
The location are also more linear and less impressive and the open world is not as brilliantly interconnected as in DS1 if at all. It seem like FromSoft focused more on gameplay and difficulty, rather than the genral design and lore here and for someone whole loved DS1 for those aspects, it will be disappointing.
The lore and story is inferior to DS1 IMHO. Dark Souls was an epic yet sad story about a dyning fantasy world, while DS2 seems to be more focused on the protagonist, and being Dark Souls, there isn't really a consistent plot. This makes it feel bland and the whole story/lore thing seems like something  not on par with the first part. A lot of stuff is just taken straight out of the previous game and one cannot help but feel the devs went all lazy in some parts. Linear levels, a less gripping story and a lot of reused concepts might discourage the people who loved DS1 for the atmopshere.
All in all a great game, but if you have never played Dark Souls, you'd be better off starting with the first one, than watch some opinions on YT and decide for yourself, if part two is something you want. If you're a hardcore Souls fan, you'll get it anyway. This is one of those sequels that take a step forward in some aspects and a step backwards in other.

A half-decent truck simulator with reasonable graphics and enough variety to keep you driving for a while.  There is also a huge modding community to be found with new maps, physics, trucks and accessories.
The game isn't very well optimised, needs the graphics to be lowered to run at a steady framerate.  There is also a huge lag when you enter certain cities, so to avoid this settings need to be set even lower, or just struggle through it with spikes and slowdown.
There are lots of options to play with to make your game more fun or realistic, although some of the precision mechanics are either broken or I'm totally useless at it.
It is a great game to find a truck, accessorise it how you like and then hit the road listening to one of the radio feeds in the game, or just chuck on a podcast or music from an external source.
The modding community has lots to choose from however from version to version these will crash your game or put massive demands on your CPU or GPU.  This is almost a necessary evil as the game only comes with a handful of trucks.
Sadly all the trucks are modelled after real world modern trucks, with little visual or performance differences between them.  All the trucks have a ton of power, GPS and cruise-control so there is little skill involved, compared to having an underpowered truck needing constant gear changes and extreme vigilence to ensure you have time to slow down for speed traps or obstacles.  You can acheive this through mods and creative use of money and upgrades, but its not included at all as standard.
As a game I'd give this a 5/10 but as a truck simulator I'd give it an 8/10.

I understand a lot of people are having performance issues with this game. I'm one of the lucky ones, in that my rig (OC'ed i5-6600K, 980 Ti Strix, 8 GB RAM) is running this game like a champ at 1080p. My review is going to be on the gameplay, story, and game world. I hope you guys get a patch soon!
The gameplay is excellent. The core mechanics and game world will be very familar to Dishonored 1 fans. This is definitely a Dishonored game. But almost everything about the game has been improved. Levels are more complex, more vertical, and offer more options on how to progress through each mission. Guards are a little more difficult (slightly easy to alarm, they swarm you quickly when you screw up), but the difficulty curve seems fair. The new enemy type is a good addition to the game and introduces some freshness to the standard gameplay. The game is visually appealing - I never get tried of looking at the scenery as I'm exploring a level. I'm having a lot of fun playing this game.
As far as negatives, there aren't a lot non-technical ones. The story isn't as good as the first. It could be that I'm missing the "newness" of the I felt the first time I played through Dishonored 1, but I liked the first game's story better. The voice acting was uneven at times as well. Neither the story or voice acting are bad, mind you, but I do think the "averageness" of these parts of the game stand out a little because the rest of the game is so well done.
I'm playing as Emily and trying a non-lethal, non-ghost run as my first playthrough. I like Emily's powers overall. Far Reach is a little finicky, but most of the powers are fun and useful.
Long story short, this is a great game that I don't regret buying at full price. It has my highest recommendation. I can understand anyone not wanting to risk buying this game right now, but if you decide to wait, definitely keep it on your radar for later when the issues get ironed out. It's worth platying.

This game is excellent. The story is captivating, the music suiting and clever, the graphics are unique and great in their own right, and the levels are varied and complex. On top of that, the game has excellent combat and the powers mesh nicely with your more traditional weapons. The difficulty curve is slightly odd, with a spike and plateau about halfway through. At that point, the game starts to rely upon mechanical differences to increase difficulty instead of giving you different or tougher enemies. I enjoyed this immensely, as it kept the game fresh much longer than the original, which is good, because this game is also a fair bit longer than the original.
However, the enemy AI is inconsistent with it's intelligence. I played on Normal, which may explain it somewhat, but enemies almost always have the same reaction to any detection, be it seeing the player or a body or even hearing a noise. often they won't call help when seeing a body, which just leaves me with yet another body on to trap another guard with..
Overall, a 9/10.

Note: This is a review from an Elder Scrolls fan, not an MMO player.
Pros:
1) Lore is very good; there are interesting NPC's
2) the combat was waaaaaay more better than the typical Elder scrolls combat
3) the maps do seem big and wide open, just as we want it (more on this in cons though)
4) community actually seemed, well, like a community when I played. Not infested with obnoxious people every where like you might fear (although I'm sure there are Disciples of Sheogorath out there somewhere on the server)
Cons:
1) People running around CAN improve the experience, but it is utterly annoying/distracting 85% of the time. I know, its an MMO, but when you get stuff like: "you are the chosen one, sent to a hidden cave that only you know about to defeat an evil only you can stop....'cept, you know, those 20 other dudes strutting around in the same cave"
2) First person view is not good; puts you at a signifcant disadvantage compared to 3rd person view during combat
3) *The sense of adventure is not quite there* This is a big one. The main gripe here is because of MMO's zoning, you cant go wherever you want, whenever you want. This was a crucial part of what made Skryim seem so big. Also, exploring isn't quite the same--you either find nothing, or you find a start of a big quest. There's no inbetween, small little caves filled with Trolls or small huts where a fisherman was just killed by a bear.
4) **Never connected w my character** This one is hard to explain, and it might just be a personal problem, but I figured I might as well list it.
I know, I know, those are abstract cons, but hey.
If you are on the fence, I HIGHLY recommend waiting until it is $20 on sale. It's not a bad pickup for that, even if you don't end up playing too much of it. Also I've heard that the updates since I've last played are darn good. I hope to get back into this game eventually, maybe before ES6 comes out

The story of
is pretty simple: You play as a blob breaking out of a blob torture research center and getting his revenge. On his way to do so the blob automatically absorbs everything that is smaller than him and so he is getting larger and larger and is able to absorb even more.
Over the course of the game you gain new abilities like smashing, telekinesis, magnetism and sometimes you can even fly around. Combined with the six different themed world stages and the never stopping growth of your blob the game never gets to repetitive besides it simple basic gameplay idea. The puzzles in the game are fairly easy what I did not really mind. The platformer part on the other hand is a bit tougher mainly for one reason. Besides the blob being a blob, and therefore precise movement can be a bit tricky, the controls are unusual. I have read some complains about them, because the game contains parts where you have to use the mouse. People playing the game solely on keyboard or gamepad have to shift over what can be annoying (Edit: This has been changed since the initial released and the game is playable with gamepad only by now). Personally I played the game one hand on the keyboard and the other one on the mouse. This combinations works pretty well. And even if you die you will start by one of the nearby checkpoints. Normally you should pass each passage with less than five times dying except you are trying to get the gold medals or you are collecting your blob friends.
Those unusual controls are a left over from the porting because the game was made initially for the PS Vita. Another leftover are the mini-levels which are a lot easier in the PC version but still fun. The graphic is cartoon-like and colourful and fits the theme of the game. The music is nothing special. It does not really stand out but it does not annoy you as well. The game took me eight hours for completion of all achievements and replaying some of the levels for getting better times in the leaderboards. And for that the price tag is really fair.
All in all
is a really, really fun and colourful game if you can forgive some sometimes clunky controls and you do not mind the repetitiveness of the basic gameplay idea. Obliteration of mankind can be so enjoyable.

If you want a real war, go "hardest". But if you just want to have fun and conquer the world, choose "easiest" difficulty and choose Germany.
Overall, this is an enjoyable game, save for two things: the aforementioned monotonous clicking and a very, very annoying bug that makes it impossible to play the game due to an error concerning the game's apparent inability to find its own engine. When this happens, the only thing that will help is to restart Steam in Administrator mode and launch it from there. It should work then.

Caveat: This review is about a multiplayer experience only, as its probably the ONLY way I'd play this game.
The gist: Might* be fun some day, pretty bad in its current state.
Problems TL;DR:
1. Looks like a terrible console port, despite being a PC game
2. Online coop (no more than 1 player per computer) still forces a coop bound camera
3. No way to choose a preferred character (that I could discern,) you're handed them at random
4. Saving "hostages" or whatever auto swaps your character (see point 3)
5.  Melee characters are garbage (see point 3)
6. " 'MURICA" novelty gets old, fast.
First off, the general UI is just bad as it stands. It all seems so heavily keyboard/controller driven. I understand that the control scheme of the game suits that style; but things like server select for multiplayer can still use the mouse. What you're left with is scrolling through a list of a hundred or so servers, one at a time, until you find the game you want to join. The devs REALLY need to relook at how you navigate the game outside of play. Having a mouse-driven server browser at the very least would boost usability a lot. The game has no volume slider. What? The only way to change the volume is via your OS's volume mixer, enjoy.
When playing online, you are forced to suffer the terrible camera despite being the only player on your machine. Similar to Nintendo's Super Smash Bros. franchise, the game really, REALLY wants to keep each player confined to one screen. And it does this by constantly shifting in all directions to best fit everyone onto the screen. This also means that if you split up too much, you will eventually get bounded by the camera. This can be extremely problematic if there are enemies just offscreen, or if one of the boondock twins gets stuck behind a pebble and drags your camera a screen back so you cant progress. Frankly, this is just plain unacceptable and bad design.
Not only is it awkward, but the camera rather detrimental to the readability of the game. The game is already rather chaotic, having no clear frame of reference for the player just makes it even more opaque and confusing. The devs should really consider looking at games like Metal Slug (which I assume they're working from) or Risk of Rain for how they handle their cameras. Metal Slug likes to only pan forward, and otherwise sticks to static venues when mobs appear (this may be bad since terrain is destructable.) Risk of Rain did the surprisingly simple yet effective solution of just centering the screen on your character. I understand that the current camera is for local coop players so they can always see their characters; but I would imagine that an option or replacement to split-screen would be farm more enjoyable for people who actually want to see where the hell their character is. During my play session with friends, each level basically ended up being a bunch of unintelligible confusion until there was only one person left. Then, the last survivor could actually proceed through the level and beat it. Chaos might be a novelty for some; but, I consider the camera to simply be a detriment entirely. It is literally a deal breaker for me.
Hero selection is non existent, you get what the game gives you as far as I can tell. You had better like all the heros' weapons, or just suffer through the ones you don't. Not only that, but rescuing prisoners, or "hostages" in order to get an extra life, ALSO happens to swap your hero to another random one. Hope you hate consistency, because it doesn't exist here.
Limited hero range can also be a problem, since most enemies bullets travel forever while some of yours may actually not. Until you learn the ranges of each hero, you may run into circumstances where an enemy will kill you because his bullet can reach you, while yours cannot reach him. Why does the rocket guy have fullscreen range AND a splash attack, when rambo can barely shoot 10 feet away?
Melee heroes are especially boned given the AI. Any enemy that is in an "spotted" or aggroed state is basically a russian roulette as you close the gap to punch them. You may die, you may not. Dogs are just horribly designed, as they just eminate a hit aura that kills you as soon as they touch you.
* - Early Access famous last words.

If you haven't played a MOBA (like DOTA, League of Legends, Heroes of the Storm), this is a great place to start. And if you have, I think it will be a welcome change. After a year of playing League, this game is an example of how to do it right. Rather than chucking you in the deep end, they have good systems for beginners like the tutorials and auto skill increases and item purchases. Their currency and unlocking schemes are also a lot friendlier, and the launcher is much more robust.
Also, it's a heck of a lot of fun to play - the 3rd person perspective and having to aim really changes the feeling, and using WASD to move instead of the other games' RTS style mouse movement is both more familiar and easier on the wrist.

Note: This is a review from an Elder Scrolls fan, not an MMO player.
Pros:
1) Lore is very good; there are interesting NPC's
2) the combat was waaaaaay more better than the typical Elder scrolls combat
3) the maps do seem big and wide open, just as we want it (more on this in cons though)
4) community actually seemed, well, like a community when I played. Not infested with obnoxious people every where like you might fear (although I'm sure there are Disciples of Sheogorath out there somewhere on the server)
Cons:
1) People running around CAN improve the experience, but it is utterly annoying/distracting 85% of the time. I know, its an MMO, but when you get stuff like: "you are the chosen one, sent to a hidden cave that only you know about to defeat an evil only you can stop....'cept, you know, those 20 other dudes strutting around in the same cave"
2) First person view is not good; puts you at a signifcant disadvantage compared to 3rd person view during combat
3) *The sense of adventure is not quite there* This is a big one. The main gripe here is because of MMO's zoning, you cant go wherever you want, whenever you want. This was a crucial part of what made Skryim seem so big. Also, exploring isn't quite the same--you either find nothing, or you find a start of a big quest. There's no inbetween, small little caves filled with Trolls or small huts where a fisherman was just killed by a bear.
4) **Never connected w my character** This one is hard to explain, and it might just be a personal problem, but I figured I might as well list it.
I know, I know, those are abstract cons, but hey.
If you are on the fence, I HIGHLY recommend waiting until it is $20 on sale. It's not a bad pickup for that, even if you don't end up playing too much of it. Also I've heard that the updates since I've last played are darn good. I hope to get back into this game eventually, maybe before ES6 comes out

Pros:

-The exo suits allow quick manoeuvres such as dodging, and double jumping.

A half-decent truck simulator with reasonable graphics and enough variety to keep you driving for a while.  There is also a huge modding community to be found with new maps, physics, trucks and accessories.
The game isn't very well optimised, needs the graphics to be lowered to run at a steady framerate.  There is also a huge lag when you enter certain cities, so to avoid this settings need to be set even lower, or just struggle through it with spikes and slowdown.
There are lots of options to play with to make your game more fun or realistic, although some of the precision mechanics are either broken or I'm totally useless at it.
It is a great game to find a truck, accessorise it how you like and then hit the road listening to one of the radio feeds in the game, or just chuck on a podcast or music from an external source.
The modding community has lots to choose from however from version to version these will crash your game or put massive demands on your CPU or GPU.  This is almost a necessary evil as the game only comes with a handful of trucks.
Sadly all the trucks are modelled after real world modern trucks, with little visual or performance differences between them.  All the trucks have a ton of power, GPS and cruise-control so there is little skill involved, compared to having an underpowered truck needing constant gear changes and extreme vigilence to ensure you have time to slow down for speed traps or obstacles.  You can acheive this through mods and creative use of money and upgrades, but its not included at all as standard.
As a game I'd give this a 5/10 but as a truck simulator I'd give it an 8/10.
