I am a fairly new Dark Souls player, but the hype got to me, I pulled my pants up, finished DS1 and got into the sequel. This game obviously isn't for everyone, but I get the impression that the difficulty has become the key selling point here, which is a bit of a shame for me.
Dark Souls 2 will murder you without mercy, but if you can take it and overcome it, you'll feel like the ultimate badass. The game is more polished, bettel looking, has better mechanics and overall is na improvement over DS1 in those terms, but is a bit lacking in terms of story and lore. If you liked theprevious Souls games, this is a must have.
However, there are some things that make DS2 fall short. First of all, it seem like they went to extremes when it comes to crancking up the difficulty. If you play this just becasue it's hard, you will love it. For me it feels a bit disappointing. Contrary to Dark Souls 1, this game is less fair - enemies attack in groups, bonfires are not always safe, there are some f*** you style traps that you cannot avoid and enemies in general hit you in situation where in DS1 they wouldn't. I get the impression that the first Dark Souls was hard, but wanted you to overcome it and that made is satysfying, while the second one is just kicking you butt to live up to the hype.
The location are also more linear and less impressive and the open world is not as brilliantly interconnected as in DS1 if at all. It seem like FromSoft focused more on gameplay and difficulty, rather than the genral design and lore here and for someone whole loved DS1 for those aspects, it will be disappointing.
The lore and story is inferior to DS1 IMHO. Dark Souls was an epic yet sad story about a dyning fantasy world, while DS2 seems to be more focused on the protagonist, and being Dark Souls, there isn't really a consistent plot. This makes it feel bland and the whole story/lore thing seems like something  not on par with the first part. A lot of stuff is just taken straight out of the previous game and one cannot help but feel the devs went all lazy in some parts. Linear levels, a less gripping story and a lot of reused concepts might discourage the people who loved DS1 for the atmopshere.
All in all a great game, but if you have never played Dark Souls, you'd be better off starting with the first one, than watch some opinions on YT and decide for yourself, if part two is something you want. If you're a hardcore Souls fan, you'll get it anyway. This is one of those sequels that take a step forward in some aspects and a step backwards in other.

Before I get started, I want to openly state that Serious Sam itself is not a bad series, nor is this a bad game, but it's neglect shows and this is a scenario of the cons outweighing the pros.
Serious Sam: Revolutions, is supposed to be a fusion of TFE Classic and TSE Classic with a whole new twist. It's really supposed to bring the classics back to life with new multiplayer servers (since gamespy is long dead), new weapons, , enemies, resources and a updated graphics engine to support modern systems. However, the inconsistant update schedule has punished this game severely and has left many angry with alligator pit.
Lets start with the pro's, shall we?
Pros:
+New Weapons (Ghost Buster from SS:Test 1. PlasmaThrower and Minelayer from Warped DM)
+New Enemies (Alpha Enemies have been restored, Unique new enemies, such as Biomechanoid Artillery, Biomechanoid Spawner, Beheaded Commando, Beheaded Vaporwave and more.)
+New resources for mappers and modders alike.
+Updated to get along better with modern graphics cards.
+Classic mods are backwards compatible for the most part.
+Merged TFE and TSE so you don't have to switch between.
Cons:
-Workshop is heavily glitchy, unstable and tends to not function properly for the slightest mishaps. The game can get hung up on one wrong addon and refuse to update workshop until you flush the cache, delete the workshop folder and then reinstall SSR
-Development is unreliable, not abandoned but they do take a long time between updates. (last update was Christmas 2016)
-Most workshop content is pretty much reuploaded from various sites or just horridly/lazily made.
-Game is clearly unfinished, multiple crashes happen when using certain mutators (randomized enemy spawn is a huge one) or just in general some massive rendering error occurs.
-Changing certain settings breaks certain parts of the game, especially with the Xbox HUD and some levels.
-Bug Reporting site is pretty much full of bugs but none of the have been tended or answered to in quite some time.
-Modding community is pretty dead, no one has really taken advantage of the new content revolutions brought in. Almost no workshop levels have the new weapons or enemies in them. Most of the workshop levels are russian ports where enemies are thrown right in your face and you get swarmed in a room the size of a studio apartment.
-Community in general is really dead, outside of the forums you'll only see around 7-8 players on at once. That's on weekends.
-Netcode is horribly bugged and unstable, hasn't been patched since release.
-Bright Island has pretty much became the HL3 of the Serious Sam Community.
It's sad to see this game in such a hurt locker. I know alligator pit is busy with other projects, so I can't get too mad at them for how the game is. I just wish it got more love and attention.  It's not bad but it's clearly unfinished and buggy, and given it's in beta, it was bound to happen.
The classic versions of Serious Sam are available in the Serious Sam Gold Pack or the Serious Sam Complete bundle, which drops to 10 bucks on all sales and is on sale frequently. So if you really want the classics, I suggest getting the originals instead, even though the multiplayer is dead on them.
Serious Sam Fusion is much more updated and shows quite a bit of promise, it comes with the bundle and if you want it, you need to buy Serious Sam 3:BFE, TFE HD and the TSE HD. I also recommend adding TSE and BFE's DLC bundles for more mayhem and potential workshop content.
All in all, the game means well, it just doesn't do well. I hope they come back to it someday and fix it up. Because in it's current state, it's nowhere near ready.

The game is really well done, despite not being fully optimized for PC. For the sake of this review, I'll be ignoring that and will mostly be focusing on what I noticed while playing through the game.
Arkane did a really good job creating the world of Dishonored 2. The maps are huge, easily twice as large as the maps in the original game, including area and heighth wise. There is much more detail too, as they've stated in previous showings. For each mission, you'll go into a different district of Karnaca with its own mood, music, and npcs. However, I do have to point out that the "random dust/sandstorm" that can happen at any time is only during one mission. I myself was under the impression that it could have happened at any point in the game, and was slightly dissapointed when I realized this wasn't the case.
Another complaint of mine is the smaller number of essential npcs. In the previous game, you had the whole Loyalist Conspiracy that had your back (then stabbed you in the back), the Whalers, and Slackjaw and Granny Rags (which was part of a subplot that was probably one of my favorite parts of the first game). In comparison, Dishonored 2 is much more shallow. The small amount of npcs left me less inclined to ask around and feel included in the world like i felt in Dishonored 1. In a way, it almost felt like the game was shorter because i wasn't spending half an hour running around the Dreadful Whale constantly spamming F before and after every mission. However, for some this may be seen as an approvement.
Speaking of feeling shorter, Dishonored 2 definitley is shorter than the first game. Which in my opinion was a really short game as is, excluding the DLC. The story felt rushed, too quick and not very fleshed out. It felt like Arkane was hoping that the game would rather have great replay value, making the player look forward to their next playthought, than making the story and characters as intriguing as the first one. Despite this, I still can't wait to see what kind of DLC Arkane has in mind for this game.
I feel like I've been pretty negative about this game, but there are definitely some great things happening. Emily's powers, while i was first hesitant when they started announcing them, are super fun to use. Honestly there's not one power i hadn't used, or just stopped using as i progressed through the game. Far Reach is a bit more sensitive than Blink, but it's still easy to use.  I've only played one run as Emily, but I am looking forward to doing another as her. Another thing i thoroughly enjoyed was the voice acting. While i loved silent Corvo, the addition of voiced playable characters improved the game in my opinion. Where the lack of npcs almost broke the world for me, hearing my character's opinion on their situation brought me back in.
tl;dr  Great maps, less interactive npcs, shorter gameplay, Emily's powers are cool, and voiced player characters improved the story. 8/10, would be 9/10 if not for buggy launch.

This game is worth a buy and is a legitimately good experience. It retains the difficulty, atmosphere, and cryptic ambiguous nature of the original. However, it is laiden with problems that cause it to serve as a massive dissappointment compared to the original.
Without giving too much away, many of the core gameplay mechanics have been tweaked to be more balanced in PvP. This includes basic movement functionality from the original (dodging, parying, backstabs, and overall movement). Much of the actual control of the character has been locked behind a new stat, to force a feeling of balance when chosing how to build your characters. The problem is that this causes a huge decrease in skilled enjoyment and rewarding combat in PVE. PVE and PVP are also both currently plagued by unfortunate issues of bad hit boxes, latency, strange clipping, and occasionally unresponsive controls. Most of this was either not much of a problem, or completely absent from the original. This makes a lot of deaths feel more like a problem with the game cheating you than as if it was actually your mistake that caused your death. This is a huge problem for a game whose very foundation is built on the idea of "tough but fair".
This problem is coupled with the fact that overall, the game is much easier. With simpler bosses and easier enemies and less interesting level design. Although certain areas have beautiful level design and atmosphere, much of the game is plagued with nonsensical or simply lazy level design. The dev team was obviously thinking "how do we make this part of the game difficult" when they should have been trying to figure out how to make the area INTERESTING. Dark Souls was difficult, not because it was specifically designed to be, but because the difficulty happened to be a side effect of it being interesting. It is true, that even in Dark Souls 2, every area and encounter is one that requires thought as you adapt to a new situation. It still inspires a sense of tension and tactics that are lost in the majority of games out today, excluding strategy games and the like.  The problem, however, is that most of the time in Dark Souls 2, they decided to make the area challenging by adding in tons of powerful enemies thrown lazilly in. Whereas in Dark Souls 2, they decided to make an area interesting by combining a difficult enemy with an advantageous postition in the level design, causing you to figure out a way to deal with the particular strange situation. This allowed each scenereo in Dark Souls to leave an impact as they presented a challenging idea and moved on. Dark souls 2, however, keeps bashing the idea of "HOARDS OF DIFFICULT ENEMIES" over and over again, which becomes tedious and fairly uninteresting, forcing the player to usually come up with cheep tricks to just cheese the enemies instead of coming up with unique ways to deal with them. This being said, Dark Souls 2 still does have it's fair share of really excellent level design and bizarrely compelling encounters, it's just lessened by the great number of encounters that AREN'T interesting.
Finally the plot, presentation, and aesthetic of the game simply missed the point and soul of the original game. This particular point is difficult to discuss without giving away any spoilers. I will say this. Where the first game was minimilistic, cryptic, tragic, poetic, and ambiguous, Dark Souls 2 is a convoluted retread with nothing of value to present.
Dark Souls 2 IS a great game. It's just not the masterpiece we come to expect from a Souls game. It is as much a dissappointment as it is an enjoyable experience. I recomend this game, however I recommend you play Dark Souls 1 if you haven't done so.

Mostly positive experience with this game.
+ Quality graphics that run well even on slightly older machines (like mine)
+ Very good tutorial systems to get you into the game quickly
+ Crafting missions (certifications) easily introduce you to each trade
+ Highly immersive story based missions that can change the game as you play
+ Weapon and ability skill system reminiscient of the single player ES games and well executed in the MMO environment
- Ran afoul of the crashing bug requiring the use of OpenGL drivers over D3D11, this caused a slight framerate drop
- UI add-ons are almost required to get the most out of the game*
-> *Examples include no built in mini-map, no built in spam (gold-seller) filtering, experience and resource (health, mana, stamina, ability) bars are not persistant and can often fail to appear when they would be useful.
To be fair the crashing bug, while persistant over several patches, seems to affect a minority of players and there has been some indication that the develpoment team is trying to find solutions. Unfortunately the solutions over the last couple of patches seem to help some players while creating problems for others.
While UI add-ons make the game easier they are by no means required and you can make your way through the game quite well without them.
Overall I would say this is an excellant game that has the potential for a reasonably long life as far as MMO's go provided the dev team can get it stabilised/optimised a little better.

Great game, and well worth it's asking price. The Calm & the Storm is somewhat of a mix between total war and risk. Of course there are no real time battles to speak of but that does make the game more calculating in the fact that you don't really control the outcomes of battles.
Positives:
Many times you will fight your own world war II fighting for power and struggling for dominance! The A.I. is great with unrelenting force they will plow through an opening in your defenses and quickly consolodate their forces if you attak.
On a player VS COMP map you will quickly realize how aggresive the A.I is. You can no longer declare war on all the weaker nations and exspect the world powers to not respond. You then will have to face down pretty much anyone who is not allied with you for the desperate resource grabbing to keep your war machine up.
In this way the game makes it's greatest sucess at a slower paced game with a good amount of tension.
Negatives: There is a ♥♥♥♥ing lot of them
The game of course has it's flaws and should not be overlooked. Me being the man I am could not handle mainstreaming WWII as germany or the U.S. so I liked to play as smaller nations who can barely hold their own. All to quickly you will realize this is impossible as the major players like Germany and the U.S. have WAY too much under their belt from the get go and will trample you if you dare attack anyone they like.
The game also gets repetitive. Fast. If you like WWII games than you will find this game able to last you a long time but that does not change the fact that A.I. have limitations and will work together to fight the player being as superior as you are rather than the German Facists who are right at their doorstep.
The diplomacy as with pretty much any stratagy game is underdeveloped and lacks any real options.
The trade seems unfair, almost designed so you have to give up on something to get anything (which is realistic, but does not help the gameplay) you almost can never have enough goods or especially arms to get you anywhere. AND GOD FORBID you have a large army and try to produce arms for it. Your resources (most notably your oil) will go down so damn fast that you can't hold it up for more that 10 turns.
Games are over relatively quickly in this game(we are talking 2-3 hours max) and don't even have a "turn limit off" or a "Conquest" game mode. Though the game does help itself by allowing you to keep playing indefinately even after the game has ended. So a "kinda" conquest mode
You are gonna wan't to play with other players. Preferably people you know so you can set up rules and have an actually fun time. (randoms don't bring the thrill of fighting your friends.)
Also while you do struggle sometimes. Once you get a hold of this game it can be pretty easy to play so I would recommend turning that default difficulty up a notch.
Final Verdict:
This game is worth buying for five dollars but no more. I would actually recommend you buy one of the newer Making Historys as I have heard/read that they have adressed many of these issues.
Still when I picked up this game it was less than a dollar. (like 78 cents) and that was a steal for this game so if you a money grubber like me. Wait for the sale to happen again or just pay the damn five dollars I mean I payed over 9 dollars in copies for my friends to play with me because they are struggling hard right now.
But I repeat For FIVE DOLLARS this game is well worth it. So pick it up now and relive WWII while you still got the motivation in you.

I've been playing Smite since early summer 2013. It was (and remains) the only MOBA I've ever really enjoyed playing, largely due to it's third person PoV making the game feel much more like an action game than a RTS like other games such as LoL and DotA can do at times.
While easy to pick up and play, with simple controls and and easy to navigate UI, the depth of stratergy and item builds in Smite means I would not personally recomend it to anyone who doesn't want to spend time learning the meta. Like any MOBA Smite requires a reasonaly large knowledge of the game to play effectively and get the most enjoyment. For people willing to take the time needed, there is a wealth of content on Twitch and You Tube to help you get started.
I won't pretend the game is perfect. It has struggled often with matchmaking and server issues, though both are becoming less of a problem as time goes on, and the inevitble trolls that come with all online gaming. That being said, I have found the community of Smite to be better than most, willing to guide new players and not get too angry when things go wrong.
Smite is a strong 9/10 for anyone who wants a competative online experience with a wealth of strategy to experiment with.
Simply the best Moba you can find, and the best part is that Smite isn't one of the pay 2 win games.

This game is excellent and free to play! I have played NMRIH since before the original Steam release and it has seen many improvements for both playability and stability. NMRIH is an otherwise straight-forward FPS zombie survival theme with both objective maps and wave survival. The game is a mix of Left For Dead 2 and the zombie mode in Call of Duty. Unlike Left For Dead 2 the challenge remains in co-op survival without dependence on a player controlled enemy. Deceased team members will become a more powerful AI controlled opponent if they pass while infected. You can board up windows and wander the maps at your own leisure which removes the area restriction you will find in the Call of Duty Zombie mode. If you like wave survival there are maps for this and if you want to progress through a map seeking extraction there are maps designed for that also.
NMRIH to me is more fun and less linear/arcadish with a good amount of depth for casual play. Many new maps have been added since the original release and some user made maps are fun also. There's a small learning curve getting used to the game mechanics (ie. FEMA bags/Zone Percentage/Respawn Tokens/controls/menus/binding & using "shove" etc.) and while that can be frustrating to new players it increases game depth and the survival challenge for more experienced players.
NMRIH is an underrated game and is slightly underpopulated as a result but you can often find servers to play in and the game can be just as fun with 2-3 players as it can be with 7+. Maps can be played solo. Some servers host unlimited ammo and menus to ease achievement progression but the classic mode is by far more challenging and rewarding as you learn the maps and interface.
I would highly recommend this game as one of my favorite zombie survival games next to Left For Dead 2 and Resident Evil, however it is entirely fun in its own way. A good game that is FREE and an excellent addition your game list.

Caveat: This review is about a multiplayer experience only, as its probably the ONLY way I'd play this game.
The gist: Might* be fun some day, pretty bad in its current state.
Problems TL;DR:
1. Looks like a terrible console port, despite being a PC game
2. Online coop (no more than 1 player per computer) still forces a coop bound camera
3. No way to choose a preferred character (that I could discern,) you're handed them at random
4. Saving "hostages" or whatever auto swaps your character (see point 3)
5.  Melee characters are garbage (see point 3)
6. " 'MURICA" novelty gets old, fast.
First off, the general UI is just bad as it stands. It all seems so heavily keyboard/controller driven. I understand that the control scheme of the game suits that style; but things like server select for multiplayer can still use the mouse. What you're left with is scrolling through a list of a hundred or so servers, one at a time, until you find the game you want to join. The devs REALLY need to relook at how you navigate the game outside of play. Having a mouse-driven server browser at the very least would boost usability a lot. The game has no volume slider. What? The only way to change the volume is via your OS's volume mixer, enjoy.
When playing online, you are forced to suffer the terrible camera despite being the only player on your machine. Similar to Nintendo's Super Smash Bros. franchise, the game really, REALLY wants to keep each player confined to one screen. And it does this by constantly shifting in all directions to best fit everyone onto the screen. This also means that if you split up too much, you will eventually get bounded by the camera. This can be extremely problematic if there are enemies just offscreen, or if one of the boondock twins gets stuck behind a pebble and drags your camera a screen back so you cant progress. Frankly, this is just plain unacceptable and bad design.
Not only is it awkward, but the camera rather detrimental to the readability of the game. The game is already rather chaotic, having no clear frame of reference for the player just makes it even more opaque and confusing. The devs should really consider looking at games like Metal Slug (which I assume they're working from) or Risk of Rain for how they handle their cameras. Metal Slug likes to only pan forward, and otherwise sticks to static venues when mobs appear (this may be bad since terrain is destructable.) Risk of Rain did the surprisingly simple yet effective solution of just centering the screen on your character. I understand that the current camera is for local coop players so they can always see their characters; but I would imagine that an option or replacement to split-screen would be farm more enjoyable for people who actually want to see where the hell their character is. During my play session with friends, each level basically ended up being a bunch of unintelligible confusion until there was only one person left. Then, the last survivor could actually proceed through the level and beat it. Chaos might be a novelty for some; but, I consider the camera to simply be a detriment entirely. It is literally a deal breaker for me.
Hero selection is non existent, you get what the game gives you as far as I can tell. You had better like all the heros' weapons, or just suffer through the ones you don't. Not only that, but rescuing prisoners, or "hostages" in order to get an extra life, ALSO happens to swap your hero to another random one. Hope you hate consistency, because it doesn't exist here.
Limited hero range can also be a problem, since most enemies bullets travel forever while some of yours may actually not. Until you learn the ranges of each hero, you may run into circumstances where an enemy will kill you because his bullet can reach you, while yours cannot reach him. Why does the rocket guy have fullscreen range AND a splash attack, when rambo can barely shoot 10 feet away?
Melee heroes are especially boned given the AI. Any enemy that is in an "spotted" or aggroed state is basically a russian roulette as you close the gap to punch them. You may die, you may not. Dogs are just horribly designed, as they just eminate a hit aura that kills you as soon as they touch you.
* - Early Access famous last words.

I have a bit mixed feelings about this game. Overall I would say my opinion is positive with slight mix of mild dissapointpent in later game. I did get about 30h out of this game which is pretty good number before I felt that I'm kind of losing interest. Thing is I was expecting more - the first impression of the game was very positive. There seemed to be enough wheels and buttons and complexity to keep one going for at least few hundred hours - first impression was that its even more complex than hearts of iron III with a better supply model.
And it is good and challening game at the start. I started as Germany in '36 aiming to grab as much as I can without triggering the world war and then were looking forward to keep what I gain until about '66 while securing my borders and working on getting as self sufficient resources wise as I can. And it was all nice until about '39 when the first cracks of the AI started showing in the event and diplo system. Some of the events felt a bit forced, I opted to not fire the events for throwing an ultimatum to Poland. That in turn seemed to freeze the diplomatic AI of the allies who just got seemingly frozen up in some indecisive state ignoring me taking out balkan, greece, egypt and saudi arabia in short sucession until in the end Japan triggered some kind of scripted event at the end of '41 making US to get inolved in coflict. Gremany refusing to get involved with US and accepting a bunch of southern american puppets as valid war targets when defence packt with Japan triggered them made AI to go totally haywire with wars. At this point the game lost good bulk of its charm as things were no longer plausible anymore. There is no challenge to be able to declare war on Sweden and Norway without allies batting an eye and Poland sitting right nect to you doing its best to look the other way.
Resrouce system and economic side is also interesting at first but the model breaks down relatively fast if you are increasing your GDP in a rapid manner by funneling majority of your resrouces into industrial expansion. There is no option to conserve manpower by using higher levels of automation or something so the demand for goods will increase faster than what the natural growth of your manpower pool (even with all the medical research you can do) is capable of coping with.
I would say it is a bit simpler game than hearts of iron 3 its just that at first glance it manages to look more formidabble with higher learning curve than it actually is. I have not tried mods for this - perhaps I will return to it at a bit later date and give this thing another round if I stuble upon a promising mod. At this point it seems I'll be heading back to hearts of iron iii with historical plausibility mod to give another round of trying to get away what I described above.
The combat AI - its a bit mixed bag. It's pretty competent with land units and can sort of work ok with air but it totally melts down as far as naval units go. Ships hang around solo, there is no merchant shipping to intercept so subs are sort of pointless in their traditional role. The commbat AI is capable of doing naval landings at least but unfortunately seems to be rather dumb in the way it handles it when there is opposition and it's losing transports at sea - it just ignores these losses and is happy to send your entire army against single enemy destroyer picking its nose somewhere enroute until you get involved and direct some combat ships to deal with it manually. Also - there is no naval bombers in the air section. So you cant just ignore the naval fleet side by opting instead to focus on keeping the enemy few hundred km away from your shores by building up large force of airplanes intended to attack ships. Naval balance wise - AI tends to focus on just building as many battleships as it can pretty much ignoring most other ships - cant really blame it as it stands as that seems to be the most effective tackic in this game for naval.

I would rather recommend to buy Hearts of Iron, or at least Supreme Ruler Ultimate, because this game gets updates.(neither Supreme Ruler 1936 nor Cold War does)

(TL;DR can be found at the end of the review)
I've been a huge fan of the Call of Duty franchise when Modern Warfare hit the stores. For years I've been playing pretty much nothing else and dumped hundreds, if not thousands of hours into it. I also played Modern Warfare 2 & 3 but it wasn't the same for obvious reasons. Since then I wanted to buy another CoD that could bring back the nostalgia. Then Advanced Warfare comes along and actually gets a lot of good reviews and I get curios: Another studio, a longer delevopement time and fast dropping prices.
I bought this game for 20 euros and pity the fool who preordered it for 60 euros and thought that he would get a good game. I lowered my expectations as far as possible and still I got disappointed. I really can't see why so many people like this game and where all the good reviews come from. Okay, better than Call of Duty: Ghosts. But being better than something really bad doesn't make it good. You can polish a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥as much as you want, you can gold-plate it and wrap it in present paper but it still stays a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ On to the actual review:
I enjoyed the campaign far more than I would have thought. The story is alright, yet very predictible, the characters ain't great (except Kevin Spacey for the sake of being Kevin Spacey) and the AI is still far away from being "intelligent". But all the new gagdets they could introduce with the futuristic setting make up for it easily. On top of that they added a ton of vehicles stages. It's the kind of singleplayer you would expect from a CoD game.
You won't miss anything if you don't play the campaign as it is very forgettable but it's a fun non-brainer if you want to pass 6-7 hours. Sadly it has absolutely no replay value. Less cutscenes, quicktimes events, press f to do action x, following or waiting for npc's to do one specific action and a certain minimum of freedom could have done the trick there.
But let's be honest. We all want the game for the multiplayer ;) And this is where♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan.
Singleplayer is alright, but you won't miss anything. Multiplayer feels like a very bad fusion  of the generic CoD gameplay and Quake, Unreal Tournament, Crisis or Titanfall with massive lags making it an unenjoyable gaming experience. I wouldn't pay more than 10 euros for this game, maybe 15 with a season pass.
Some big patches could get the game into the right direction but I highly doubt it as they probably focus on getting the DLCs out.
__________________________________________
Update #1 (15/01/12): So here they are. The costumization DLCs. For at least 2€ each you get nothing but a few cosmetic items that add nothing to the gameplay. I wanna play a shooter and don't dress up a doll or paint my weapon. Way to go...
Update #2 (04/02/15): Nearly 3 months have passed since release and now a 1,6 gb patch comes around, adressing a few things I mentioned: Several weapons get buffed, while the ones that are really broken stay overpowered, matchmaking and connectivity were improved a bit, a security and anti-cheat programme is added and several maps got improved for different game modes. I'll have a look into it but I don't think this patch will turn me around. Also it is overdue and should have been released a long time ago.
Update #3 (24/02/15): Connectivity really has improved but is still far beyond every other shooter using dedicated servers. The lag is horrible. I also met quite a lot of aimbotters on the double xp weekend. Only way to get rid of them is leaving the game and hoping not the be matched again with them. You can report them ingame but I am not sure if this results in a ban for them. I think there is a fun game hidden in this mess but as for now the devs don't seem to be interested in reveiling it and I can't recommend it.

This game is one of the most complex strategy games I've ever played. I mean, I needed 12 hrs. of playtime only for the Tutorial. *lol*
Supreme Ruler 1936 is a global political-warfare simulation that begins in early 1936 and can be played into the 2070s. Yes, the 2070s. That is when the tech tree runs out. You can literally start the game with biplanes, and end up fighting with Mechs. You have the ability to play as any major or minor power, with thousands of possible unit designs to select from. Complex economic system and technology tree. You can choose between 54 different countries in the sandbox modus. World Ruler with Liberia? No problem in this game. xD
Gameplay is fairly simple; it is basically a RTS (Real Time Strategy) game. Controls are standard for most RTS games—the ability to select large numbers of units at once, and other basic RTS controls. Furthermore, selections can be screened for specific unit types (air, naval or land) allowing for mass movement of forces. Land units are further divided in general categories—artillery, infantry, transport, armor, etc. Technology is fairly straightforward. Some can be traded or bought from other countries, while some have to be researched by each country individually and are non-tradable. Diplomacy is fairly detailed, with a wide variety of agreements possible, but given the scope of the game can be somewhat odd at times.
The combat system in SR36 is really the shining achievement of the game. “Chaos” perhaps describes it best—explosions, units advancing and retreating, the roar of naval gunfire, strafing aircraft, often at the same time. Dishonored 2 is as good, if not better than Dishonored.
Positive aspects :
+The gameplay is still as good as the first one. The choice of playing Corvo or Emily isn't only esthetic, but also changes in the powers given to you (i.e Possession for Corvo, Creeping Shadow for Emily).
+Corvo's mask revisited. The mask looks much more threatening and intimidating than the first one, who was "meh"

+The world adapting to your choices. Not only talking about Chaos, but I'm also talking about changes you make in the past (level 6 or 7, in Stilton's Mansion) who gave a really interesting twist to the game mechanics.
+The game is doable even if you chose not to take any powers (but Jindosh's Mansion is still a pain in the a*s)
+The level design is really good.
+The game is challenging, with new enemies. Clockwork soldiers, who are tallboys on steroids, or even one assassination target, "The Crown Killer", is very interesting to face.
Negative aspects :
-Performance issues at the launch kept me from playing such a masterpiece from the get-go
-Jindosh's Mansion / Clockwork Soldiers ; it's a pain, no matter how you look at it. They're challenging and interesting, but they are equal to demigods when playing on harder difficulties.
For those points, I strongly recommend the game. 10/10

* * * OLD REVIEW (previously not recommended):
I just want to review the game without any inclination towards "I recommend it" and "I don't". This game is in early access so I expect to change my review if this is addressed.
I went into the game expecting a casual, laid-back exploration game with farm-management. I got a micromanaging grind-fest designed to get you so overwhelmed with balancing resources that you don't realize you aren't accomplishing anything.
Past a certain point, I believe it was the time I realized I didn't have to feed slimes, I realize that while the slimes are cute, the gameplay is solid, the world is fun to explore... I had one nagging question in the back of my head: "Why am I doing any of this?"
Certainly, the idea of running a farm could appeal to a lot of people, but once I got into the swing of things, I realized all of my efforts weren't working towards any other goal than sustainability. From what I can tell, there is no story or endgame to speak of; leaving the player to their own devices. I had fun exploring everywhere! I had fun building my farm! I bought all the plots of land, gathered as many diverse slimes as I could, built crops and hen fences... But after I did all that, all that was left was to simply feed the slimes. All of it felt like a build-up with no release or satisfaction of gathering such a collection of slimes. I guess all I wanted was a story... Something to string me along and tell me at the end: "Good job! You done it!"

This review is a bit outdated, since it's based on before 1.6 patch.
1.6. patch removed sub fees, added crown store and added justice system and champion system into the game. It also made many tiny areas of the game a lot better, such as animations and provisioning has now better named items, and yes you can fish yourself a meal now.

I honestly don't understand why people hate on it so much. As an Elder Scrolls fan who loves the crap out of Morrowind, this seems like a fair MMO in TES world. I like it, the exploration is fun and no restrictions when it comes to building a character, apart of the class skillset. For example, you can make a heavy armor sorcerer who uses bows. Silly and cool combinations can be made. You can also play as a brawler, but they don't have weapon skills. You just gotta rely on your fists with that one.
Combat is tons of fun, I see myself doing it a lot instead of trying to avoid it like in some MMO's. Justice system is great fun and adds thievery in ESO. I suggest reading more about it from the ESO website. This game is also a lot more immersive than other MMO's I've played.
What I could complain about is the default interface is a bit clunky, but luckily community has made some mods that solve the problem really well (thank you UI mod support!)
Then there's also the blatant "shortcuts" and other lore-breaking stuff in the game, that come up at some points, but I'm enjoying the gameplay a lot so they don't bother me that much. (The three pacts thing is a bit silly but considering it was made because of PvP I understand it.)
Cyrodiil PvP can be a bit laggy sometimes, or thats what I've heard from North American players. As an EU player I haven't really seen any lag in Cyrodiil at all, but this is something no-one can predict.

Summary: New features not presented in any COD before. But definitely missing key aspects of earlier COD, such as balance, survivability, slaying, and functional scorestreaks. That aside, there are many bugs for PC users, and noticable lag in kill cams.
In my opinion, this is the worst COD I have played, and I have played all since COD4.
That being said. This game's main feature is exo movements, but it is argueable whether or not the movements contribute to fun gameplay. The increased mobility adds a new element and quicker game pace, but I often find there is seldom tactical use of dashing and much more dash and jump spamming. Even if you do use the dash as a way to dodge bullets, it is rare that it will work due to the heavy amount of lag comp in the game. Dashing quickly behind a corner as you are being shot it will often result in you dying anyway. Then as you watch the kill cam, everything will be a second behind what you saw on your screen. This is a major problem in this game and often ruins any fun I am having.
Guns and perks have little balance, and this COD has less balance than any other COD I have played. Even earlier games with stopping power had worse balance than this COD. Blast suppressor removes the exo movement ping on the mini map, This makes Blast suppressor necessary, which essentially removes any stretegic gameplay aspect. You will die from behind countless times wondering how the enemy even flanked you without any warning. On top of this, footsteps are nearly silent. Enemy callouts were supposed to make up for this but they do little. On top of this they made it so you can have a stealth perk in every tier. Low profile is overused making UAV essentially worthless.
All of these things combined with map design make choke points non existent. One of the major advertising points for AW was that they had 3 lane maps, but with the exo movements, terrible spawns, and abundance of stealth perks, the choke points have been almost eliminated. Spawn trapping has been almost removed from the game, except in a few levels where you can basically kill them as soon as they spawn. Spawn trapping has been a viable and effective method in many CODs and always added a way to control their spawn point and yours meaning you would not have enemies sneaking up behind you ruining your streak. Without that in this game, getting streaks is very difficult.
Speaking of streaks, they essentially nerfed streaks hard. They decreased how easy it is to gain streaks, and decreased how effective streaks are. In domination (known for having sturdy spawn points in previous cods), you only get 50 points towards a streak per kill, 150 per point capture, and 125 for each defense kill (kill enemy capturing point) and attack kill (kill while you capture point). This means playing the slayer role is worthless.
Don't believe the hype in this game. I think it is even worse than ghosts was aside from increased mobility. The time to kill is brutal and feels horrible when you add the lag comp. I see this game as being a favorite of kids, but if you like any amount of stretegic, planed game play, then don't play this. It is at best a mosh pit of chaos with little order.

Advanced Warfare is the first Call of Duty that I've purchased in quite a few years, the last one being Black Ops. I was cautious about this ever since seeing it at E3 back in June but decided to pre-order it anyway. I told myself if it was bad, then I'd never pay for a CoD game again. Sledgehammer has done a great job however, I was completely surprised by how much fun I was having in the campaign despite it being utterly stupid.
Some of the set peices in the campaign are embarrassingly bad, such as an objective as crossing the road. However, there are some phenomenal ones as well. Ziplining down a mountain just to find out a forest is actually an illusion hiding a military complex, dropping into Seoul and gunning your way through the streets, dropping a sniper on a Greek island, and fighting in crevices in Antartica are just a few that come to my head. It's superb.
The graphics are pretty for a Call of Duty game as well, you can tell it's using a dated engine yet I'm still impressed how well they made it look. The gameplay is pretty standard for CoD, if you've played one you've played them all, except there are some exciting new weapons to use. EM1 is a laser beam gun which is always fun to use, and punching people with your EXO-suit and watching them fly is always a joy to behold.
EXO-suits are probably the reason why I like this game as much as I do. They breathe new life into a stale IP I feel, and I hope they bring them back in the next iteration. Not doing so would be a step backwards in my opinion.
In conclusion, if you like playing Call of Duty then you should definitely get this, if you're not too interested in the multiplayer portion of the game then I suggest wait for the price to drop (which may take ages knowing activision). If you've been wondering whether to get this or not but you're not a fan of Call of Duty, wait for it to go on sale then get it. That way you haven't spent £40 on a game you didn't like in the end.

Before you read: Keep in mind I'm still playing, and I've only played about 25 minutes so far, and died once.
So, I think my experience with this game is... odd, so far.
You're dropped into nowhere, with very little explanation of what's going on. You have no tutorial, no helpboxes short of just the occasional "E to interact" "Space to pick up", etc. You're not actually taught how to use the items, you need to kinda figure it out.
The graphics are a bit weird, they kinda remind me of DayZ's early days and I think it's a little bit rough. The lighting is very peculiar, and the flashlight doesn't really help all that much - especially after you've taken damage.
That's another thing: Damage. When you step into the fog, or get hit by any of the creatures, you sustain damage which shows itself as blood on your screen. The blood fogs your vision (pun intended), and while I understand the sort of "realism" you were going for with the tunnel vision idea, it's a little grating considering how you're set up with very little to help you and you have almost no clue of what to do.
The stamina isn't really that great either considering how little there is and how you have virtually no weapons to help right away from what I've seen - but then again, I haven't found any so far, so I'll provide an update as soon as I happen upon anything.
I think it's a bit odd too that you keep putting in "this needs a key to be opened" when for a couple of them you can just climb over a wall or go through a hole. I'm just nitpicking by this point, but I suppose the OCD side of me is like: "Well, is there actually a key?" Once I got into the school, I was wondering how to get back out again, so I suppose the key part would probably make sense there.
One other thing - what's with the music? It's not atmospheric or anything, it's just kind of there. It feels like you just chose something from the playlist at your local halloween carnival or something. Not meaning to be harsh, it does put you off a tad, though. At least in my case.
Anyway, will keep playing and update as I go. Gonna be a thumbs down for now - but I will change my mind if I see anything significant, though this game has left a lot to be desired in such a short space of time I couldn't help but want to do a review right away.
Update: I tried combat. The enemies kill you in two hits, but take an infinite amount of bullets to the head, to the body, and the only indication that I had that I did anything to it was that when I had pumped a great deal of handgun bullets into it, it noclipped through a fence and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off right back to freaking Narnia or wherever its home was.
I don't know what's going on, there. As far as I'm aware, you can't avoid combat, because the enemies spot you within a fraction of a second of actually being in their line of sight - even dozens of feet away.
You get your first handgun while narrowly avoiding one zombie, and are given a key to a farm house where another zombie is basically just waiting to jump you. You can open the door, but unless you hide in the nearby corn, I don't think it comes out of the house unless it sees you're there outside. Dying is exceptionally easy because of the two-hit K.O. and once an enemy sees you, you can't run away from them as they easily outpace you.
If you die, you get sent straight back to the beginning of the game. My best guess here is that this was supposed to be an early access title that wasn't supposed to be released as complete - my biggest hint here is the fact that when you go to options/controls, you see where it says save?
In the area next to it, it doesn't have a button or anything for that, it just says "Soon".
I wanted to like this game, and I wanted to give it more of a chance, but quite frankly, it's disappointed me at every turn with its nonsensical gameplay, odd graphics, lack of any kind of user-friendliness or guidance, and OP AI/enemies.
I might come back to it to try and complete it - but I wouldn't count on it. 2/10 - the only saving grace is the Stephen King reference... though this is a very poor tribute to a good piece of literature.

I've played Smite for the longest time before it came to Steam, back in the Beta in fact. For those who are familiar with anthor Steam favorite, Dota 2, Smite is fairly similar while holding a few differences, that being the camera and the multiple game types. For those either coming from Dota or who are new to the MOBA games in gerneral, Smite is a much more casual style MOBA which is fun for both beginners and experts to the genre. What else is there to say but pick it up and give it a go. :)

A different take on a MOBA this game delivers well with its different take on characters. Rather than have fake or imaginary creatures of some world, this game focuses on Religious gods and godess. With a third person view and a new form of movement (wasd as oppose to an point and click) this game has made combat fun and interactive. Heros have four main abilities which affect your certain play style, and different characters to accommodate them as well.  While items are on the less side, they still determine the way you can approach the late game. Multiple game modes are presented such as arean, assualt and other traditional game types. But with every game comes its goods and bads, they game runs great and is fun to play, but getting used to can take some time. Some gods are frustrating to play against(Loki Koff koff) constantly getting the upper hand on your team no matter what the circumstances are. And every week 5-6 gods are free to play (along with your other previously unlocked ones) which only really effect new players or player who dont want to spend 30 dollars on teh ultimate god pack. Skins ca be used to make your character look like a true hero. My favorites include the Super Comando Ares and the luchador Hercules. By playing gods you get worshipers which level up your god. At level one you get a gold skin, level 5 a legendary sking and level 10 a diamond skin. Some skins are exclusive to get and need to be obtained through other means, such as the curse appollo skin. This game is extremely fun to play with firends and is a must get(why not its free to download and free to play). 9/10 a stunning game with plently of future potencial.

I have been playing this game since closed beta and have seen a lot of changes.  Out of all the other MOBA style games, Smite still has the best community and even the devs listen to the players if a problem happens or even adding content to the game.  They have multiple game modes besides the main mode that all MOBA players know.  The main thing that makes this unique over the other games in the same style is the 3rd person camera.  It makes you feel very involved in the game.  That and even the auto attacks are skill shots.  I recommend this game very highly!  Plus it is free!

I have only put 30 hours into this game, but have easily put 500 hours into the series in total. My opinion? Stay away. If you want large scale strategy based around modern/semi modern warfare, get Hearts of Iron 3. It is a better game in almost every way.
The SR series of games are large scale stragey games based in the 20/21st centruries.You control the economy, diplomacy, government and military of any nation you choose.
The problems with this game:
1)There is no tutorial (or at least not a very good tutorial). Be prepared to spend plenty of time trying to figure out how the game works (The economy is especially convoluted)
2)The territory system is a mess. conquering a country will often result in it being broken up and divided in the most nonsensical way possible.
3)The AI is abysmal. For Example: As Canada, I helped France obliterate Germany, barely having to cede land at any point (Hard/Hard/Hard), not because of skill, but because the AI does not understand how to use their armies properly.
4)As the game progresses, the performance gradually gets worse, until the game is unplayable. I have never been able to "finish" a game because of this, usually after 6 years the game runs so poorly that I have to quit.
The only positive thing that I can say about this game is that once you figure it out, the economic system is somewhat entertaining. You aren't able to transform a fledgeling nation into a super power overnight, and resources have to be carefully managed and balanced.
I like the concept of the SR series, but the games are not rewarding or challenging in a fun way. If you are thinking of getting this game, or any game in the SR series, make sure you try Hearts of Iron first. It is better in nearly every way imaginable.

If you like the survival/zombie genre then this game is a must buy! Fantastic game, with individual character development, tons of potential NPC allies and enemies, expansive map to explore, good story, etc. It goes on sale for a mere couple of bucks, often, which is really just stealing money from the folks who deserve more for a really well made game. If you are on the fence, then spend the few bucks to pick this up; you'll probably be surprised you hadn't discovered it sooner!
Pros:
+Interesting/original spin on the zombie outbreak scenario. Fast zombies suck but are awesome.
+Lots of NPCS hidden around the desert, mostly in small enclaves to interact with. Hostile humans can often be turned around to become neutral, or even join your group, if you play your cards right.
+Base building is balanced; the buildings and upgrades give benefits comparable to the work required to construct them.
+Finite, if generous, quantities of building materials rewards careful selection for base location and smart construction of buildings.
+Anyone who gets taken by an infected becomes an infected; you'll find former friends and enemies have become the very zombies that are now attacking you!
+Individual character development, with uncomplicated stats and skills.
+World changes as you play; NPC enclaves will eventually succumb to wandering bands of bandits and zombies, including side-quest locations and even groups of hostile survivors end up perishing over time.
+Reasonable graphics, the game has very modest system requirements.
+Good replay value; it is quite a long game and can be played through several times.
A real nice touch is that the NPC's appear to have the same rules as the player characters; everyone needs food, water, and sleep. If the NPC's that do the farming of an enclave or group die then the other members will start travelling the desert in search of provisions. It also usually leads to the death of everyone else in that group as their members individually run zombies they can't handle. Then they become zombies and help polish off the next desperate survivor who leaves the camp in search of food. The bandit groups might be an exception to this, hostile survivors that cannot be negotiated with, seem to never move and have no resources close by to sustain them. They stay awake for months at a time, with no food or water, the true zombies of the apocalypse!
Cons:
-Character development, while effective, is quite simple. It may be part of the charm but it feels like some lost potential.
-Base building can be pretty tedious when trying to gather resources from remote locations. Your runners either constantly run to the point of exhaustion(extremely vulnerable to zombies!!!) or walk about at a casual pace.
-Unable to create groups of runners for salvaging/gathering. Having to select each individual survivor and send them out to collect resources is a nuisance. These survivors all function separately, instead of working as team, out in the field. Lots of times a survivor gets mauled by a couple of zombies that they've encountered while one or two other survivors, also travelling to the same destination, are within a screen's distance and do not go to the aid of their fellow survivor. The only work around I found was to assign guards to each runner, which works, but wastes a lot of carrying potential.
-As above, you have to micromanage your survivors out in the field. Lone survivors are no match for two or more zombies at a time. Even teams of two, with a dedicated guard, tend to get overwhelmed pretty easily. It wouldn't be much of problem except they tend to be much less effective when AI controlled so you have to be quite vigilant. If your main group is also dealing with an encounter, it is very easy to miss a runner in trouble.
This is a great game and would easily be worth $20-$25, especially to fans of the genre! I've stayed up far later than I should on many a weekday to just get a bit more "Survivalist" time in!

Verdict: cautious recommendation. Buy it if it's on sale, but not at full price (for now, at least).
Upsides:
: Environment Design is mostly up there on par with Skyrim (and sometimes even more imaginative, as devs were not afraid to use the vertical space to their advantage). Textures are generally nice, though they could use an optional "HD texture pack". Though I also understand that said pack would make the installation weigh more than a hundred gigs, and would be a nightmare to update. Lighting system is quite impressive, and lits the interiors way better than, say, Skyrim engine would, shadows interact with lights in numerous ways and are always dynamic - all this results in a remarkable picture, even if some shaders are a bit basic.
: I can safely say that I met a whole lot more memorable characters in TES:Online than I had in TES5. Apart from defined characters, a good dose of humour is applied even in some dramatic situations, like, for example, when you meet a vampire cat /ahem, khajiit/, who tries to save last few villagers from being eaten alive, and she is distracted by a thought of yarn. In spite of some players crying "DEY BROKE DA LORE" "DEY RUENED DA ALDUR SCRULS" I didn't see many violations, more so considering how inconsistent the 'canon' lore is. Cyrodiil still has no jungles, but that has more to do with Bethesda's decision during TES4 development than anything else. The so-called 'Main quest' is used more like a plot device in order to explain some events in the game world, though it does have its
moments too.
: the amount of dialogue is immense, and it's fully voiced in its entirety. While there are few characters, who will make you cringe (that last Ayleid king, urrrgh), there are more than a few splendid jobs (even Sheogorath, which is not voiced by the original actor, but is still totally fine).
: Having a full-fledged war with melee weapons, siege machinery and thousands of participants - looks great on paper. Too bad that this concept is undermined by balance and stability issues. More on those below.
: TES5 had a fair share of UI mods (mostly due to its UI being console-oriented in the first place). TES:Online supports this kind of mods as well with per-character settings, so if you don't like something about the interface, there's generally "a mod for that": mini-maps, map markers, HUD overhauls, trading helpers, combat macros and whatnot.
: while you have to choose your starting ("home" so to speak) faction, you'll eventually get access to the zones of other factions as well. And it really does feel like three games worth of content (or time you spend on them at least).
Now on to some YMMW things (you might like these, you might hate these):
: it has its own upsides and downsides, huge upside being no teenage trolls spamming in chat or doing /playdead + /pushups on the town square (like they did in open beta). Downside being that by paying a fixed amount of money you won't necessarily get a steady amount of content (in fact, the only big content addition to the game was Craglorn). Arguably there's no better model choice - and most certainly I wouldn't want this game to become Free-to-Play.
: yes, mouth animations are finally added in Update 5, so people don't look like sock puppets. They still look like dolls, though. Just a pair of skin/eye shaders would work wonders here, but it seems like devs don't want to increase the budget even for close-up shots.
: five skills + Ulti, with additional second bar after Level 15. Unlike in TES5, you cannot dual-wield a spell and a weapon. In fact, you don't actually have any spells. Instead you have abilities, which might or might not be magical, and may produce various types of damage or have other effects on you, your allies or your enemies. So in short, Warcraft 3. DEY RUENED DA ALDUR SCRULS. Yeah, right.
: you heard it correctly, and no, it's not a LITERELY DED GAEM by any means. So good luck finishing any dungeon on your own - more often than not you'll get inside just to find half of it already decimated by players, who got in a few minutes before you. On the other hand, you'll have no issues with finding a party. Party will find YOU, comrade.
And at last, let's discuss the flaws:
. Your actions may have only a few different outcomes: a) enemies disappear from the area b) enemies become non-hostile in the area c) area is not changed in any way. No crumbling cities, no dynamic objects (the about only example of those is sky anchor, which pops every 10 minutes in predefined places), game sometimes tries to mitigate it by sending you into 'fake' zone, which becomes a 'true' zone once you complete the quest and return to it. To be fair, the devs did use a few dynamic objects in the main quest line, but that's far too few.
. Second-era Tamriel is populated with communists. No possession, no stealing, no jails. From each according to his ability, to each according to his need. This also means no Thieves Guild, no Dark Brotherhood, no Morag-Tong. Devs promised to introduce this system in one of the upcoming updates, so this might change in the future.
: when it works, it's an okay experience. You deploy siege machines, employ cover-up and deceit tactics, ambush the reinforcements et cetera. The key is 'when it works'. Game uses several servers (called Campaigns), with most players going to Thornblade. It's almost always population-locked on evenings, but that's not the main concern. Once you get inside, be ready to meet the almighty LAG. While the in-game counter breaks upon latency >1 s, the actual lag spike in >30 x >30 battles may freeze everyone in place (while you still can move around, that's an illusion made by lag compensation system) for up to several minutes. Thus taking any given fort may become an impossible feat even with prevailing forces. Currently some guilds have decided to just ditch the Thornblade and play on alternative servers. Though those might have some lag spikes time-to-time, but not any of same scale as Thornblade. Again, devs promised to fix these issues in upcoming updates, but until then this remains a flaw.
: this probably applies to the last two TES games as well, but yeah, it still is a flaw. Your choice is in most cases reduced to dialogue options before being given a reward, and generally only decides if that one character will greet you upon your final appearance in the current zone. Again, nothing out of ordinary for TES series, yet still.
. Okay, the TES4 was disliked by many for this, but TES5 used autoleveling to its advantage - if you go into a cave at Level 50, be prepared to meet bandits in glass armour or Draugr deathlords. In TES:Online if you go to, say, Glenumbra, to do some quests you missed, while you are already past Level 20, you'll find it extremely easy. In fact, many do miss the 'Bad man hallows' public dungeon, and when they return from the next zone to complete it, players just molest everyone inside. Another example: you completed every available group dungeon and played a few evenings in PvP zone. Then you return to usual questing and discover, that you are 5-6 levels above than the quest enemies/rewards. This means you get little to no items/experience for your activity, and basically robbed yourself of potentially good items, as they don't drop if you're more than 5 levels above your victims. The last update did fix some of the leveling issues, mainly with solo/group-only content.

I've never reviewed anything before, then I changed the view on Steam to the one that shows the number of hours played, and after a bit of a lie down to recover, I thought 'why not?'
I can only echo the other positive views. There is something so satisfying in ETS2, the surface simplicity hiding a rewarding, enjoyable experience. The simple pleasure of driving around, obeying traffic rules, avoiding the occasionally optimistic AI (no, I'm driving a heavy truck, I can't stop on a dime like you just did right in front of me), making crazy amounts of (virtual) money, is strangely relaxing.
I can often find other styles of game stressful, but the only time ETS2 worries me is after an update, when I have to figure out if any of the mods I use have been broken. But I can't complain too much, the fact that it is still being updated and supported by the developers after all this time is fantastic.
So, 631(!) hours later, do I recommend it? Um... well, OK then.

Highlights: Game is a horrendous, unplayable mess. Don't buy it, unless your life depends on it, or you want to pay 60 bucks for a game you most likely won't even be able to play until some undisclosed future date.
Pre-Summary: Disohonored 2 is a broken mess of a release that is all but unplayable by today's standards and expectations for a AAA title release, even on a machine that is arguably at the top end of the spectrum. Unless Arkane/Bethesda can make the game playable (I still haven't been able to successfully play the game past the first chapter), this is by far one of the worst releases I've dealt with in a long time. Like EA quality Battlefield broken, can't play for weeks after launch broken. Don't buy it. STAY AWAY. PROTECT YOUR CHILDREN! Also, be kind and rewind.
Details:
Pre-ordered the game (yes, I know that's not brilliant in the current world). I typically don't pre-order games, as a result of terrible releases of the past, but I said to myself "Come on, it's Dishonored. They knocked it out of the park on the first, how hard could it be to release at the worst case a 'good' game. Do it. DOOOOO ITTTTTT.". So I pre-ordered. Holy hell, I was so wrong.
I can't state whether the narrative, the gameplay, or the story is good. Why you ask? Because after leaving the first zone in the mansion (which ran beautifully mind you), I entered the second chapter, where you reach the 'open world' scenario. Immediately, the FPS was all over the place, screen tearing was rampant, and the game was such a mess that turning around and moving was so jarring visually, and so laggy that I felt as though I was trying to play the game on a box of rocks. I haven't been able to play the game since the first day it became 'pretend' playable. Don't even let me get started about mouse smoothing and the sh*t port that this is from controller to mouse/keyboard.
I've tried everything. I've downgraded graphics drivers, I've upgraded graphics drivers. I've changed from ultra, to very-high, to high- to medium and low. I've turned off AA in game, turned it on in the nvidia console. I've played with nvidia console settings. I've used process manager to attempt stop the Dishonored2.exe process from setting itself to 'low' all the time. I've messed with the config file to try and optimize. I've sacrificed at least 3 goats (one of them could have been a cat, at this point I'm trying anything), and I've prayed to all of the gods dreamt up throughout history. Regardless of all this, and some black magic sprinkled in, the game still runs like absolute sh*t. The last time I experienced a launch this terrible, was probably Battlefield 3, where the servers were inaccessible for over a week after launch and you couldn't even play single player because of DRM. Way to go Arkane/Bethesda. You just joined the ranks of EA level launches.
System Specs:
Intel i7-5930K
64GB DDR4
nVidia GTX980
Update 12/12/16:
After the latest BETA 1.3 Patch went public, and I've converted over to the public release of the patch, the game is running much better. I don't have an explanation as to what Bethesda/Arkane changed between the BETA 1.3 and the PUBLIC 1.3, but something changed. That being said, I can now run the game on high/ultra with minimal to no issues. While this is what one would expect with a AAA release, the fact that this came nearly a month after the actual release date is entirely unacceptable. Individuals who purchased the game at release (or prepurchased the game) effectively bank rolled a failed launch of a game, to a point that it was even worse than an Early Access endeavor given it was completely or nearly unplayable for the first 3 weeks for most PC users. I will not be changing my review of the game, as I believe fundementally this was a flawed product that gamed the system and took advantage of consumers and loyal members of the Dishonored fan-world. The fact that Bethesda has an embargo on early reviews of their releases only continues to support the fact that there was an effort to deliberately mislead the public upon release in order to reap financial rewards on a product that would have otherwise been widely panned by critics and would have had customers wait at least the first month until Bethesda/Arkane did the right thing and released a working product.
With respect to the game itself, it's an acceptable installment into the Dishonored franchise. It doesn't really break any new ground, and is more of the same you'd expect from what one could suggest as a full length expansion of Dishonored 1. It's storyline is mediocre, but fulfilling, and the voice acting is on par as well. I am enjoying the gameplay, as Dishonored is still one of the best stealth games to have ever been released, but in my mind the game itself will always be overshadowed by the shambling mess that was released to customers. What could have been an easy 7 or 8 out of 10, is now a middling 4 to 5 in my honest opinion given the entire picture of events.
If you buy the game, do it at a discount. If you don't buy the game, count yourself lucky you didn't have to deal with the horrendous launch and lackluster customer service/communication. You aren't missing much.

There were bad times though. The first few hours, I derisively referred to this game as Insulin Quest.  Watching my team split up and run off in four different directions because I was walking to close to a the edge of a cliff was a serious, recurring frustration. But nonetheless I couldn't put the game down until I had beaten it and replayed it, and I can't recommend it enough to anyone who appreciates those good qualities I have described.

FULL REVIEW:
At its best, Dark Souls II is just well... more Dark Souls. A slightly improved and better playing Dark Souls, but unfortunately lacking in a lot of the variety and creativity that previous entries in the series are known for. If you're already a fan and just want more Souls action, there's no reason not to hop aboard the Souls train for one more ride, but don't go in expecting to be surprised or as entertained.
Dark Souls II's world, story, and atmosphere all simply fall flat. In many ways, the game's trappings and incredibly repetitive and overused enemy and boss designs feel like a pale imitation of previous games' themes. The world's structure and design lack cohesion and focus, with progress through the game being a series of straight lines down a few pre-determined spokes from the hub world of Majula. The exploration that was encouraged in previous games is nearly absent here as the scale tips far more toward combat and less on the discovery, atmosphere, and mysteries unraveling of an eerie undead world.
Where the original Dark Souls felt like a grand adventure across a desolte and creepy undead wasteland and had a great sense of pace, Dark Souls II feels more like a collection of videogame levels thrown together for the sake of having a sequel. It's probably the safest game From Software could have made, and unfortunately, a sense of safety isn't what makes Souls games feel special.
It's still worth a play, but again, lower those expectations.

I was so close to not getting the latest in the Call of Duty series of games. But two days before the release I got caught up in the hype, and I'm glad I did. Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare is the best Call of Duty game to come along in a long time.

In my honest opinion, this is probably the best CoD in years, probably since MW1 as it was refreshing to play a CoD that tries to be different. There are some interesting weapons, such as EM-1 laser beam cannon that is inspired from Unreal Tournament's Link Gun which is a lot of fun to use while they also introduced double jumps, dodge moves, mid air dodge that does make this CoD a lot faster than its predecessors. The maps are generally well designed with some has gimmicks, like there is a map that is set under the Golden Gate Bridge where there will be a tsunami flooding the map half way which does make the pacing to be a bit different. Also, the maps also offers plenty opportunities to jump and vault around as they do offer more vertical than previous games which is a very welcome change.
However, I still would not recommend this game because of the peer to peer multiplayer systems it uses. The netcode seemed to be poorly implemented with a lot of inconsistency in ping and stability. At this time and age, I do think that games should be shipping with dedicated servers, not laggy inconsistent peer to peer. Due to the poor netcode, most multiplayer matches has been quite a frustrating experience. I could get a smooth game in one match, then, the next match becomes a laggy fest with a lot of minor teleporting and shots that isnt registered by the game.
The campaign is alright, as it is the same run of the mill CoD campaign you expected: Linear, explosive and occasionally surprises you with some smart gadgets. Dont expect much innovations or interesting changes in this one. Kevin Spacey's performance in the game is pretty good though.
At the bottom line, I do not recommend this game. As a game that is predominantly a multiplayer experience, one should not pay a fortune for a laggy and subpar experience.

The campaign had a mediocre plot but made up for in great acting, creative action setpieces, and it still gave the arcadey, break kneck pased action I enjoy in a Call of Duty campaign.
The Multiplayer is a huge improvement thanks to the new movement that effectivelyheightens the quick time-to-kill the series is known for with some fun weapons and gadgets. However, the Exo Survival is not nearly as fun as Zombies or Extinction mode and comes off as a lazy afterthought. Also the lack of dedicated servers is annoying, peer to peer multiplayer has it's lag problems and quirks that can effect enjoyment.
Despite the flaws, I still recommend it for fans of the series. It's not amazing, but it's pretty good.

I've been playing Smite for about three years now which is about 3500 hours of in game play (I have an addiction) and it's nice to see it finally hit Steam.  To begin, Smite is a Multiplayer Online Battle Arena.  It has a similar style to League of Legends, Heroes of the Storm, and Dota 2.  But, what sets Smite apart from other MOBA's is that not only is it 3rd person instead of top down play, but due to this, every single shot is skill besed.  Every auto attack, every ability, all skill based.  This makes for not only a much more diverse game, but one with a different skill curve.  League of Legends is a game with a steep learning curve that is hindered by millions of players who only care about winning and refuse to help lower level players develop.  Smite still has some of this issues, but with only having 10 million players, the community is a lot less toxic and this makes learning the basics a lot easier.  Ranked is easy to get into and by having the God Mastery system (yes, we had it first, Riot) it ensures your team will be competent on the God they are playing.  The meta changes weekly and characters fall in and out of favor fast helping you learn how gods play quicker and easier.  Breaking meta is largely accepted by the community allowing for variations on the tried and true style and providing a space to make your own comfort picks.  Smite is a diverse title in the MOBA series that is team based but isn't as toxic as other games in the genre.  The pro scene is massive and growing rapidly as well.  Give it a chance, it may be tough to start playing and be good but after about 10 hours Smite is easy to pick up and play.
