My First Impressions of Smite
[TLDR at the end]
So I played Smite on PC for the first time last night. I had heard many good things about it from friends, but I had also heard many negative comments from hardcore League or DOTA 2 players. “It’s not a real MOBA!”…“It’s so easy it’s boring!”…“Get gud nd play a real game, m8!”…etc ad nauseum. I wanted to form my own opinions. In the end, I was pleasantly surprised by the game.
Smite is a MOBA at heart, but it plays more like a third-person RPG (i.e. Skyrim). It’s definitely a more casual game with an extremely short learning curve; players of more hardcore MOBA’s will be able to pick it up in one night. Gone is the “clicking simulator” movement scheme coupled with QWER ability controls that most MOBA players hold near and dear; in Smite, you control your player with WASD and aim with mouse, which is much more familiar and comfortable for non-MOBA players. However, with this change comes a downside: I found the ability keys cumbersome and hard to reach in a frantic team fight while still trying to move my character. The camera is shifted from the obilgatory overhead view to a third-person over-the-shoulder view, which I found gives the game a more involved, more personal feel. Most of the same mechanics and metagames found in other MOBA’s can be found in Smite, but with small twists to make them more accessible to casual players.
Smite has three general gameplay modes that I discovered: The typical 5v5, three-lane map with jungles populating the remaining areas; a very fun, hectic 5v5 all-out brawl mode set in an open, circular arena, and “Joust,” a 3v3 mode similar to League’s ARAM maps, except with small “off-lanes” to either side with two jungle camps each.
The god characters are all extremely well researched, well designed, and well-voiced. There is an evident sense that someone put time and effort into researching a god’s lore to find the perfect design and ailities for him/her.
I held off buying the Steam DLC that unlocks all current and future gods, but after playing the game for about three hours, I came to the conclusion that the game was definitely worth at least $20, and I would be happy to pay Hi-Rez Studios to continue what they’re doing.
My general impression of the game was simply “It’s fun!” The game is easy to pick up, the controls are fairly intuitive, and it looks fantastic. Smite doesn’t require the finesse and involved strategy of other MOBA’s, but that is by design. It was a refreshing take on the genre, and I’m definitely going to play more.
[TLDR: If you’re looking for anther hardcore MOBA with a steep learning curve and high skill level, you’ll be disappointed. If you’re new to MOBA’s or just want a fun game to play, I think you’ll find yourself having a lot fo fun with Smite.]

TL;DR You should try Smite but be wary of the saltstorm.
(Salt/Being Salty: Being angry, agitated, upset.)
Smite is a great game. I've played it since the Beta and have done the 1-30 grind as well as a few ranked games last season.
Now that this has been made clear, i'll discuss what isn't so great about it. To be blunt, the community is♥♥♥♥♥♥ We could all agree that online video game communities are generally bad but in Smite more often than not, your game will have someone being salty towards another player for stupid reasons(anything from a teammate feeding, to someone not being able to take a joke or play along). The game has come a long way with all the visual updates and the god balance but the state of the community has just been getting worse every year. But of course, since you can just mute anyone who is fedora-neckbearding in the chat the gameplay doesn't really suffer unless you listen to their crap and let them get at you. In the end though, it's a team game, so you will have to endure some salt one way or the other.
The gameplay side of Smite is well executed and unique in the MOBA genre. The third person view and the familliarity of the gods to the common person makes the game more accessible in my opinion because not every player is interested in Lore and the bird's view in traditionnal MOBAs can be a barrier for the new player who has yet to pick up a game from the genre.
The last point that makes this game for me is the cheap god pack, in which you receive every god released as well as all future gods for like 20$USD. This method is far better than that of LoL/HotS, even though it's not nearly as good as the free DOTA 2 way of going.
Smite is at a great point in it's lifecycle for new players to join in, with the recent Steam addition and the game only being in it's second season of competitive/ranked play.
Overall, I would recommend playing Smite or simply giving it a try to see if you'd like it because it's definitely worth a shot.

Lets get this out of the way, it is not Skyrim Online! Most of these bad reviews on steam seem to be from people expecting to be Skyrim over the internet. Yes, the lore is the same and it takes place im Tamriel but its unfair to compare a MMORPG to a standalone game.
Elder Scrolls Online is a breath of fresh air in the MMO scene, it breaks the convencional class stereotypes of most MMOs. Yes, there is 4 classes to choose from but those are just templates, any class can use any weapon or be a tank, a healer, a dps or whatever kind of class you can think of (with certain limitations). You level up the weapon/armour/skill ability by using it but you are not restricted. Dont like that massive 2 handed axe you started with? Change to a destruction staff. You like the axe after all? No problem, go back to using it.
Storylines are really well done, main quest is amazingly good and the side quests can be more interesting than the main plot at times, im one of those persons who has little patience to follow all the plots and i find myself actually listening (yes, npcs are voice acted) to the story plots. Quests are the usual for a MMO, yet theres very few quests that tell you "Kill 10 of these, collect 5 of those", altough you end up doing that anyway in most cases, it is not the quest objective itself, so you dont feel like youre "grinding".
One little detail i like about ESO is that other people cant "steal" your quest objectives most of the time everyone sees their own stuff, with some exceptions. For exploration addicts like myself, ESO maintains what Skyrim did, hidden quests, lore objects, hidden books and skyshards to look for.
Group content is fairly good, ranging from world bosses, dolmens and the usual dungeons. Veteran dungeons can be really challenging and require team work and actual tactics contrary to some other MMOs. Its a shame they didnt made a better use of group tool as from my experience seems most people are either not aware it exists or simply dont use it.
So yes, its not Skyrim Online and it will never be, if you decide to play ESO thinking it is ,then you better save your money but if you look at it as a MMORPG and, like me, played and got bored of the usual standard type MMOs, then you might be pleasantly surprised.
UPDATE: Not only ESO is subscription free since the 17th March it also has two new systems, Justice and Champion System. Justice its the start of which i hope will be the coming of Thieves Guild and Dark Brotherhood, cause it allows players to steal, pickpocket and murder NPCs, still needs some minor improvements but it can be really fun.
As for Champion system its a whole new sets of passive skills basically increasing even more the possibilities on creating all different kinds of builds/classes, altough i hope they remove some useless passives and replace others in the future and for someone that completed all the quests only way to win Champions points,for now, its just brainless grinding of mobs,group content and not much else.
Finally the new Crown store that came with the drop of subscriptions sells pets, mounts, cosmetics and consumables, so far nothing that allows players to have advantage over others.

I rarely play COD games because I am sick of the same thing many of the gamers have complained about for years.  The publisher makes the developer re-create the same game for it's annual release.  It sells HUGE because the franchise name, and good marketing to gamers. When I DO play them, I  mainly play for the career mode, storyline, and eventually the multiplayer.   As it stands right now, the lack of dedicated servers and my personal sluggish DSL, I mainly got the game because:
- I got a great deal of a discount off the current price and,
- The promos gave a feeling of newness to this AW installment... so I gave in because I really wanted to check out
Advanced Warfare's career mode play.
Win7 pro x64,
2-way SLI  EVGA GTX 660's (2g Vram),
overclocked i5 3570 with a max speed-boost of 4.9Ghx.
I have the game installed on a Samsung Evo SSD.
It's been startup-stuttering which seems to fix itself when I notice and hit the "Windows" button, then switch back to the game by selecting its window tray icon.
I did need to tweak the video graphics settings because the default detection must have expected more out of my components, however I only lowered motion blur quality one notch, tweaked the refresh rate and turned on the game's version of VSync, and gameplay has smoothed out quite nicely.
As far as the campaign goes, it does have that, "I am a Call of Duty game," feeling- but I really like the newness of the boost-pack for jumping and slowing your falls.  The story itself is very epic and dramatic-  some people have pointed out that the dialogue is just horrible, and I concur that the writing for acted parts could have been a lot better.
All in all- it's a vidoe game.  It's a fun, action-packed video game.  If you want the eye candy to be top-notch, using a new-gen 4gb + card would be a great way to enjoy it maxxed out.  As far as my dual 2Gb 660s- I have to say they are doing an excellent job rendering some high quality next-gen graphics.  That's plenty good for me- since I don't have the money for a GTX 980 or Titan Black.   If you want to compete with the new-gen consoles, the more rendering units and VRAM in your graphics card(s), the better- since the VRAM and GPUs in the consoles have been beefed up tremendously.
I can understand people for buying the game and being upset because the online multiplayer is in♥♥♥♥♥♥poor shape for an epic new game launch.  I can't understand why the groundwork for a dedicated server system suffered from lack of focus on the part of the publisher/developers?  I don't know.   It does make me wonder why these big-name companies continue to slack on the details of game launch success, especially considering how they hype these titles up- ramping to launch day.
I think gamers who pay 60+ dollars to pre-order a game they've anticipated have a thorn in their sides, put there by the lack of focus required to prepare a successful game launch.  I do blame the deadline and budget guys who work at the publishing companies for this- but when everything is in-house, when you're working on a reputed franchise, you want people to keep wanting to pre-order your future releases, right?  And what have they been doing as of late?
-- They've been releasing un-optimized ports to PC versions, like they couldn't give NVidia or AMD the time to fully adapt game drivers before they launched.  They've been pushing games with MP online modes without the server capacity or proper anti-cheat protocols in place for launch success.    Thus, they will begin to see a significant drop in pre-orders and launch-week sales.   They will see their reliable fan-base dwindle down.
I'm not tryin' to be a hater by addressing an inevitable reaction within the communities of gamers who like to buy a new game and enjoy playing it right away.  (Look at the average user rating of this title. (11/24/14))
That being said, I do recommend this game for people who have removed themselves from the COD franchise because of repetitive gameplay- the dynamic of this game has a post-modern military-industrial science-fiction appeal-  and the action in the career story makes it very fun to play.  If you can get a deal where you aren't paying full price, and feel like I did about checking this one out- I believe you could find it worthwhile, as I have so far (I'm not very far progressed yet.)
If you are interested in Multiplayer mode- I guess I should say, Don't.  Wait for a dedicated server to be released, then when people are actually having fun and reviewing this as an epic multiplayer fiesta, THEN you cave and buy it!   If they get a dedicated server with anti-cheat and subsequently you happen to notice that it's 50% off-- then you should buy it ;)
If you have any qualms about not being able to play it on ULTRA graphics settings- you will want a HIGH end GPU. Plain and simple.   An SSD is recommended by me for faster loading and processing.  I'm just happy my rig is capable of playing next-gen PC ports.

I've been playing Smite for about three years now which is about 3500 hours of in game play (I have an addiction) and it's nice to see it finally hit Steam.  To begin, Smite is a Multiplayer Online Battle Arena.  It has a similar style to League of Legends, Heroes of the Storm, and Dota 2.  But, what sets Smite apart from other MOBA's is that not only is it 3rd person instead of top down play, but due to this, every single shot is skill besed.  Every auto attack, every ability, all skill based.  This makes for not only a much more diverse game, but one with a different skill curve.  League of Legends is a game with a steep learning curve that is hindered by millions of players who only care about winning and refuse to help lower level players develop.  Smite still has some of this issues, but with only having 10 million players, the community is a lot less toxic and this makes learning the basics a lot easier.  Ranked is easy to get into and by having the God Mastery system (yes, we had it first, Riot) it ensures your team will be competent on the God they are playing.  The meta changes weekly and characters fall in and out of favor fast helping you learn how gods play quicker and easier.  Breaking meta is largely accepted by the community allowing for variations on the tried and true style and providing a space to make your own comfort picks.  Smite is a diverse title in the MOBA series that is team based but isn't as toxic as other games in the genre.  The pro scene is massive and growing rapidly as well.  Give it a chance, it may be tough to start playing and be good but after about 10 hours Smite is easy to pick up and play. My First Impressions of Smite
[TLDR at the end]
So I played Smite on PC for the first time last night. I had heard many good things about it from friends, but I had also heard many negative comments from hardcore League or DOTA 2 players. “It’s not a real MOBA!”…“It’s so easy it’s boring!”…“Get gud nd play a real game, m8!”…etc ad nauseum. I wanted to form my own opinions. In the end, I was pleasantly surprised by the game.
Smite is a MOBA at heart, but it plays more like a third-person RPG (i.e. Skyrim). It’s definitely a more casual game with an extremely short learning curve; players of more hardcore MOBA’s will be able to pick it up in one night. Gone is the “clicking simulator” movement scheme coupled with QWER ability controls that most MOBA players hold near and dear; in Smite, you control your player with WASD and aim with mouse, which is much more familiar and comfortable for non-MOBA players. However, with this change comes a downside: I found the ability keys cumbersome and hard to reach in a frantic team fight while still trying to move my character. The camera is shifted from the obilgatory overhead view to a third-person over-the-shoulder view, which I found gives the game a more involved, more personal feel. Most of the same mechanics and metagames found in other MOBA’s can be found in Smite, but with small twists to make them more accessible to casual players.
Smite has three general gameplay modes that I discovered: The typical 5v5, three-lane map with jungles populating the remaining areas; a very fun, hectic 5v5 all-out brawl mode set in an open, circular arena, and “Joust,” a 3v3 mode similar to League’s ARAM maps, except with small “off-lanes” to either side with two jungle camps each.
The god characters are all extremely well researched, well designed, and well-voiced. There is an evident sense that someone put time and effort into researching a god’s lore to find the perfect design and ailities for him/her.
I held off buying the Steam DLC that unlocks all current and future gods, but after playing the game for about three hours, I came to the conclusion that the game was definitely worth at least $20, and I would be happy to pay Hi-Rez Studios to continue what they’re doing.
My general impression of the game was simply “It’s fun!” The game is easy to pick up, the controls are fairly intuitive, and it looks fantastic. Smite doesn’t require the finesse and involved strategy of other MOBA’s, but that is by design. It was a refreshing take on the genre, and I’m definitely going to play more.
[TLDR: If you’re looking for anther hardcore MOBA with a steep learning curve and high skill level, you’ll be disappointed. If you’re new to MOBA’s or just want a fun game to play, I think you’ll find yourself having a lot fo fun with Smite.]

Combine the water, sugar and kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer and sprinkle the yeast on top. Allow to sit for 5 minutes or until the mixture begins to foam. Add the flour and butter and, using the dough hook attachment, mix on low speed until well combined. Change to medium speed and knead until the dough is smooth and pulls away from the side of the bowl, approximately 4 to 5 minutes. Remove the dough from the bowl, clean the bowl and then oil it well with vegetable oil. Return the dough to the bowl, cover with plastic wrap and sit in a warm place for approximately 50 to 55 minutes or until the dough has doubled in size.
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees F. Line 2 half-sheet pans with parchment paper and lightly brush with the vegetable oil. Set aside.
Bring the 10 cups of water and the baking soda to a rolling boil in an 8-quart saucepan or roasting pan.
In the meantime, turn the dough out onto a slightly oiled work surface and divide into 8 equal pieces. Roll out each piece of dough into a 24-inch rope. Make a U-shape with the rope, holding the ends of the rope, cross them over each other and press onto the bottom of the U in order to form the shape of a pretzel. Place onto the parchment-lined half sheet pan.
Place the pretzels into the boiling water, 1 by 1, for 30 seconds. Remove them from the water using a large flat spatula. Return to the half sheet pan, brush the top of each pretzel with the beaten egg yolk and water mixture and sprinkle with the pretzel salt. Bake until dark golden brown in color, approximately 12 to 14 minutes. Transfer to a cooling rack for at least 5 minutes before serving.

It's like Dark Souls 1 except without all the crappy design choices. It doesn't have a brick wall learning curve like the first did and it didn't even skimp on difficulty in order to achieve this.
If you're like me and couldn't stand the way Healing items / Kindling / Transient Curse / Divine weapons / Curse / Every other useless mechanic used to pad out one area with an annoying gimmick worked, then this game is a breath of fresh air.
The bloody thing works, for a start. Runs smoothly in 1080p. Admittedly you're still going to want to use a controller but you could probably use a keyboard if you're insane / superhuman.
Builds & weight system seem a bit more balanced this time around. PvP doesn't seem to be 'Katana / Dark Magic in light armour or GTFO' anymore and you actually get a bit more choice in what you want to wear, though PvP does feel slower. Judge that how you will, it's not always a downside.
One gripe many people might have is the lack of creativity when it comes to boss design. Let's be honest, it's an array of guys wearing heavy armour and then the odd dragon and demon. In fact, I think about half of the bosses boil down to 'guy in armour.' Arguably makes the game easier since 'Hold up your shield and rub against him' is a viable tactic for half the boss fights in the game, but to be fair there are a few curveballs thrown in there that completely decimate people who sit behind shields.
Probably a biased review considering I had little love for Dark Souls due to many of the mechanics listed in the beginning of the review, but I definitely think that from a mechanical and gameplay standpoint, this is a superior game. It's still as difficult while being less frustrating due to the simplification of mechanics and better bonfire placement.
TL;DR Got rid of all the bad bits of Dark Souls but unfortunately dropped a lot of the world, enemies + exposition in the bin with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanics. Better gameplay experience, mechanics better designed, would recommend to anyone who doesn't get stressed too easily.

The best MMO since early WoW days.
I can't remember having this much enjoyment in an MMO since early WoW.  Let me just briefly describe why in point form...
1)  The world of Tamriel is huge, and between the 3 factions (each having their own areas, but eventually you can cross over) there is plenty of questing, exploration, dungeons, and other secrets/goodies to find.
2)  Every single NPC is voice acted, with mostly interesting narrative that plays into a bigger plot line for your faction.  This means the days of kill this, collect that are over.  While questing is relatively similar to most MMOs in that you do need to still kill or collect something, it's done so in a way that falls into a bigger quest-line with a background story.
3)  The UI is simple, and doesn't get in the way of your adventures, yet includes most of the functionality you need.  If you want more, there are add-ons for those end-game enthusiasts who need every stat and percentage displayed for them.
4)  The classes and skill system play out in a way where any class can wear whatever armor they want and wield any weapon they want, but have class-specific skills to complement it.  Want a 2H heavy armor sorcerer with storm magic or the same 2H heavy armor Orc Dragonknight with draconic powers and defense mechanicsms?  This makes the combos limitless.
5)  Progression.  This game feeds on your eagerness to progress in so many ways.  Great for completionists or those looking for more challenge.
6)  Crafting.  This is the first MMO in a while that made crafting fun and rewarding.  I won't go into specifics, but if interested, look into how cool the crafting is in this game, and the rewards sought after by many players, even end-game.
7)  The world and exploration.  One thing that awed me when WoW first released back in 2004, was the world everyone loved had come to life, and you can find things that made fall in love with it even more.  Well in ESO, the exploration of hidden tombs, locations of interest, delves, dungeons, towns, etc. has the same effect.  Not to mention the amount of lore, books, notes, and scrolls that come with the other elder scrolls games.
8)  Combat.  The combat is pretty close to that of Guild Wars, but enhanced in the art of blocking, dodging, and prioritizing the use of your magicka/stamina in battles.  Gone are the days of auto-atk and standing in one spot mashing buttons, yet this game also eliminated all the boringness of mashing hotkeys while running in circles like other modern MMOs.
9)  Social aspects.  You can belong to 5 guilds for multiple purposes like socializing, trading with guild auctioneers, PvE, PvP etc.  Given the amount of guilds you can belong to, and one giant clustered server housing all players, there is enough social activity during most times while playing.  You can literally play in a group or solo and still feel like you are just a part of the bigger picture in the world around you.

Very interesting game. As soon as I began, the impression which I was given amazed me. The graphics, story, physics, atmosphere and lighting all contributed to my liking of Blameless. Gameplay was smooth, I experienced only one bug which was when I jumped off the scaffolding, however it was minor.
In Blameless, you play the role of a freelance architect who is offered a job in an isolated area, which you ultimately take up. You attempt a schedule, but the advertiser insists you come earlier than you expected. You arrive at the house, where you are given instant bad vibes as the entrance is hidden behind a stack of cargo holders. More insight is given until you are hit over the head and wake up with blood stains surrounding you.
Blameless offers realistic, high quality puzzles which add to the atmosphere. You can approach these puzzles in multiple ways, providing a unique experience. The physics are brilliant, especially for a free game. But what surprised me the most were the graphics. The graphics and textures are dark but beautifully done. They combine very well with the theme. I adored them! ^_^
The ending was suspenseful, and the chase got my heart pumping. The sound effects chosen were perfect and the voice acting was a major add on to my liking. Overall, the only suggestions I can give would be to close off the ability to investigate items when they have been fully investigated - In the first scene, I repeatedly checked the blood stains as I thought there was more to offer, only to realize I found everything I needed. A worthy entry into the horror genre,
is a first-person adventure that offers good elements of tension and a mysterious atmosphere. As a free to play game designed and created entirely by one person in Unity, this game is great! It is a short game with a story that places focus on puzzle solving and progress via exploration. You will most likely get an hour or so of 3D adventure gameplay inspired by the likes of Condemned and the Slenderman series – combining good story, atmosphere and investigative gameplay!
You play a freelance architect who takes up a mysterious offer to discuss renovations for a stranger’s unfinished house. You offer to schedule a visit in the next few days, but you are cut off as the stranger insists you come over right away and promises to pay in cash. You look at your watch, it’s 2:36am – it’s late, and you’re already drowsy, but you haven’t had a gig in over two weeks so you could really use the money. It’s a 30-minute drive into the middle of nowhere and once you get there, nobody seems to be present. The house is dark, and it looks abandoned. You decide to get out of your car and next thing you know you are waking up battered on the floor with blood stains all over a mysterious room. What’s next?
The puzzles are realistic and offer multiple approaches to solving them. They’re organic as well, so they’re not just crossword puzzles you need to solve in order to unlock a door. The graphics are good – gritty, dark and suspenseful. The game is a fast download and has four achievements that are relatively easy to obtain. This game showcases great potential from the developer and judging from its overwhelmingly positive reception, it will most likely get a sequel – and I’ll be looking forward to that because the story has twists and events that, for better or worse, remain unexplained.

My First Impressions of Smite
[TLDR at the end]
So I played Smite on PC for the first time last night. I had heard many good things about it from friends, but I had also heard many negative comments from hardcore League or DOTA 2 players. “It’s not a real MOBA!”…“It’s so easy it’s boring!”…“Get gud nd play a real game, m8!”…etc ad nauseum. I wanted to form my own opinions. In the end, I was pleasantly surprised by the game.
Smite is a MOBA at heart, but it plays more like a third-person RPG (i.e. Skyrim). It’s definitely a more casual game with an extremely short learning curve; players of more hardcore MOBA’s will be able to pick it up in one night. Gone is the “clicking simulator” movement scheme coupled with QWER ability controls that most MOBA players hold near and dear; in Smite, you control your player with WASD and aim with mouse, which is much more familiar and comfortable for non-MOBA players. However, with this change comes a downside: I found the ability keys cumbersome and hard to reach in a frantic team fight while still trying to move my character. The camera is shifted from the obilgatory overhead view to a third-person over-the-shoulder view, which I found gives the game a more involved, more personal feel. Most of the same mechanics and metagames found in other MOBA’s can be found in Smite, but with small twists to make them more accessible to casual players.
Smite has three general gameplay modes that I discovered: The typical 5v5, three-lane map with jungles populating the remaining areas; a very fun, hectic 5v5 all-out brawl mode set in an open, circular arena, and “Joust,” a 3v3 mode similar to League’s ARAM maps, except with small “off-lanes” to either side with two jungle camps each.
The god characters are all extremely well researched, well designed, and well-voiced. There is an evident sense that someone put time and effort into researching a god’s lore to find the perfect design and ailities for him/her.
I held off buying the Steam DLC that unlocks all current and future gods, but after playing the game for about three hours, I came to the conclusion that the game was definitely worth at least $20, and I would be happy to pay Hi-Rez Studios to continue what they’re doing.
My general impression of the game was simply “It’s fun!” The game is easy to pick up, the controls are fairly intuitive, and it looks fantastic. Smite doesn’t require the finesse and involved strategy of other MOBA’s, but that is by design. It was a refreshing take on the genre, and I’m definitely going to play more.
[TLDR: If you’re looking for anther hardcore MOBA with a steep learning curve and high skill level, you’ll be disappointed. If you’re new to MOBA’s or just want a fun game to play, I think you’ll find yourself having a lot fo fun with Smite.]

Alright boys and girls, it's your favorite person here to correct all of your silly mistakes. Preface: This game is easily a 9/10. Let's begin with what you all assume and get wrong.
1. For whatever reason, I see the complaint about a monthly subscription. I really shouldn't even validate these complains with a responce, but I feel the need to remind you all that this is an MMO, and all the best MMO's are sub games. It's what pays for the amazing content updates you really don't get in FTP. (Free to play)
2. "Skyrim Online" I really kinda wish this wasn't a complaint, but people seem to have gotten under the impression that this game was going to be Skyrim Online. Now, I don't want to insult anyone, but I have to assume everyone who thinks this is a little kid. First off, the game was designed by a completely different studio, during the time when Skyrim was in development (or even before that), so there is no reason to link these games together, they only share the same Lore Universe. Second off, the concept of an online Skyrim, even just a co-op one, we are not near that capability. The game would have to be tiny or look like crap.
These are some huge issues players have with the game that lead to negative scores the game doesn't deserve. It doesn't help the game or the community when misinformation and shallow reviews muck up sites like Steam and Metacritic, because unfortunately people are affected by others opinions. It drives away people who might genuinely enjoy the game if they see consistently low reviews, but for reasons that don't really exist or may be misconstrued.
Now on to the really good part. The game itself.
1. This is a beautiful game. The developers really cared about how the world looks and feels, so you're gonna get some magnificent backdrops, weather, water effects, armor, spell effects, creatures, and more. It runs fine on my mediocre system, and I still get great lighting effects, nice looking water, and decent draw distance.
2. The combat. People who have played both classic trinity games (WoW) and more action oriented MMO's, (Wildstar, GW2) will both feel at home in ESO. The game utilizes and system eerily similar to the classic TES system of click swinging and blocking, but gives you the added bonus of skills that define your playstyle. This is where it gets fun. On top of the three skill trees you get from your chosen class (Sorcerer, Dragon Knight, Templar, Nightblade) you also pull from trees dedicated to each weapon type, soul magic, guilds, PvP, and a few extras I won't spoil. This gives your character amazing possiblities, enhanced by skill morphs, which gives you the choice to alter your skills with new benefits. The in game combat is akin to the Guild Wars 2 style, with more mobility and positioning, but the trinity is very much alive, parties will want dedicated healers and bulky tanks. The class system does not limit your role however, Sorcerers can easily don heavy armor and a shield and tank with the best of them, and Nightblades can heal as well. The game is incredibly flexible, and gives you freedom. While there are a few skill imbalances, nothing sticks out, and its contstantly tweaked by developers.
3. The game itself is set in a few different locations which TES fans will be able to identify easily, with each faction getting access to different provinces. The Ebonheart Pact, a patchy alliance of Argonian, Dunmer, and Nord find themselves defending Morrowind and Skyrim from opposing forces, for example. A few raise concerns about all the areas unavailable, but I feel like I should remind you that for an MMO the game is very young, and future updates promise increased world size.
4. Updates, updates, updates. This game is being updated and improved constantly. Many of the original issues have been patched already, and the future updates bring even more fixes and improvements. Soon the game will have a justice system akin to classic TES games, with stealing, fences, fines, and even allowing players to hunt down criminals. The game has limitless possibilities, and is being made even better as we speak.
I write this mostly for my fellow gamers who need only one good review from a regular guy to take the plunge and buy the game. The bad reviews are daunting, but if you're a real TES fan and not just a Skyrim bandwagoner, you will be right at home in ESO.

TL;DR You should try Smite but be wary of the saltstorm.
(Salt/Being Salty: Being angry, agitated, upset.)
Smite is a great game. I've played it since the Beta and have done the 1-30 grind as well as a few ranked games last season.
Now that this has been made clear, i'll discuss what isn't so great about it. To be blunt, the community is♥♥♥♥♥♥ We could all agree that online video game communities are generally bad but in Smite more often than not, your game will have someone being salty towards another player for stupid reasons(anything from a teammate feeding, to someone not being able to take a joke or play along). The game has come a long way with all the visual updates and the god balance but the state of the community has just been getting worse every year. But of course, since you can just mute anyone who is fedora-neckbearding in the chat the gameplay doesn't really suffer unless you listen to their crap and let them get at you. In the end though, it's a team game, so you will have to endure some salt one way or the other.
The gameplay side of Smite is well executed and unique in the MOBA genre. The third person view and the familliarity of the gods to the common person makes the game more accessible in my opinion because not every player is interested in Lore and the bird's view in traditionnal MOBAs can be a barrier for the new player who has yet to pick up a game from the genre.
The last point that makes this game for me is the cheap god pack, in which you receive every god released as well as all future gods for like 20$USD. This method is far better than that of LoL/HotS, even though it's not nearly as good as the free DOTA 2 way of going.
Smite is at a great point in it's lifecycle for new players to join in, with the recent Steam addition and the game only being in it's second season of competitive/ranked play.
Overall, I would recommend playing Smite or simply giving it a try to see if you'd like it because it's definitely worth a shot.

First of all, the game is generally a good strategy game, eventhough there are several weak points.
I would like to point out some of the weaknesses that I think need attention:
1. The game is running too slow, though you have the option to change the time cycle, but it is still not significatly helping the game's time frame. When it is running slow, it can make you bored at some point.
2. You will find it hard to replenish or reinforce your current forces, as it takes a while to train and produce your war machines.
It will be better to shorten the time needed to produce a unit.
3. Battle could be pretty boring, since there is no option for you to have a detailed direct control of the units while battling the enemy.
4. Relationships between countries could be tricky to maintain and I could say that it is not historically correct. For those who prefer their own stories, then it does not really matter, but if you are looking for something that historically accurate, then the game should have an option for that.
In conclusion, the game is pretty good, though it has several weak points, but I still recommend this game to anyone who loves strategy game.
Developer please improve the game wherever possible! Thank you.

Hard and unforgiving but fair at the same time, Dark Souls 2 is so far the best game iv'e played this year and one of the best RPGs iv'e experienced in my life.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A small WARNING :
The PC controlls of Dark Souls 2 are very,very bad, it's strongly suggested to use an xbox360 controler to play the game otherwise you will be severely handicapped, please if you do not have a controller around do not buy Dark Souls 2.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
In the other hand, the x360 controls in Dark Souls 2 are very responsive and good, only time they don't feel all that great is in the occasional moment when you have to do some minor platformig , the jumping controlls are weird in the game, they  require you to hold down the B button to run and than click in the left analog stick while running towards the direction you want to jump which is a bit of a b***h to do when you don't have much space around yourself.
The PC version runs in a silky smooth 60 FPS on max setings even on a mid range PC, the game is optimized pretty damn good, even a low end laptop should be able to run the game on lower setings with a playable frame rate.
The graphic options are far better compared to it's predecessor, you have a large variety of resolution options, VSYNC, texture quality, SSAO, shadow quality, anistropic filtering, FXAA, water quality, motion blur, deph of field, high quality character rendering, model quality and effects quality, however sadly the amazing lighting we saw in preview builds of the Alpha and Beta stages of the game is not here, so the lighting in the game feels pretty flat, only in some areas of the game such as the main hub area Majula and a few others have actual good dynamic lighting, still even with the graphical downgrade they had to do because of frame rate issues on the old last generation consols it still looks better than the previous game which had very simple dynamic lighting and shadows.
The gameplay in Dark Souls 2 is the most satisfying and rewarding experience iv'e ever had in any game, fighting the large variety of unique enemies and bosses is a blast, learning their attack patterns and their weaknesses so you can be victories is great and pretty much every death in the game almost never feels cheap, the game rewards patience and smart players and punishes does who try to play it mindlessly, the level design is great and the game offers you a large quantity of multiple paths you can chose from the very start, every area in the game holds secreats to be discovered, some secreats you might never even find in your first playthru which makes multiple playthrus still intreasting.
I don't want to spoil much but one my favorite and i think the best boss fight in the game is against a boss named the "Looking Glass Knight" who can use his mirror shield to summon other players from their worlds into yours to kill you during the boss fight, this isn't done willingly by the players it happens randomly to the people who are infront of the gates of the looking glass knight boss which leads to a very intreasting fight as you're fighting this big knight as he summons other players to help him defeat you.
The way multiplayer works in Dark Souls 2 is, it's always connected, you occasionally see white spirits walking around which are other players who are playing at the same time, you can touch bloodstains in the game which will show you a memory of sorts of the last few seconds of a player that died in that area which can be usefull to check if there's something dangerous around, it can also be quite amusing as you can watch a guy roll off a cliff by accident.
Other players can also invade your world using specific items in the game and than try to kill you, you can also do the same to other players however the more you invade the more likely you will get invaded and there's groups(covenants) that punish people who kill innocent players and friendly NPCs, you can also summon and or be summoned by other players for some jolly-cooperation to help each other in the game.
Covenants in the game could be considered like guilds, you can only be in one at a time and each one has it's benefits, there's one for people who like to invade other players and kill them, there's a covenant for people who want to punish invaders by invading their worlds as a good blue sentinal to pass judgment onto the them for theirs sins, there's a covenants that primarly focuses on helping each other in the game and the list goes on, i don't want to spoil all of them but each covenants will rewards you with alot of items as you rank up, also you can leave a covenant and join another one without any issues and you can easilly join back to the covenants you left without any consequences, a fair amount of people like to get to the max rank in one covenant and than move on to another they're intreasted in.
When you die in Dark Souls 2 you will lose all of your currency in the game which is Souls, however you can get your Souls back by going to the exact spot where you died and simply picking it all back up, the spot is marked with a big green glowing orb however if you die before doing so, all of those souls are gonna be long gone.
One tip, when you have no humanity (when you're hollow/undead) you cannot summon or be summoned to do co-op in the game, the reason i'm explaining is because alot of new players don't know this and get confused why they often can't find others players to help em out.
You get humanity back by simply using an item called Human Effigies.
My only big issue is primarly related to the online experience , it's the weird lagg you'll get in some co-op and PVP sessions which can be extreamly infuriating at times as you magicly get hit my attacks which compleatly missed you on your screen.
So my final verdict is, the game is awesome, the game has so much good content it will keep you busy for a long time and once you beat the game, starting it over again in New Game+ adds new and exciting enemies, some different A.I. behaviors, new loot to get and of course new challenges to overcome.
Dark Souls 2 is worth buying even at full price, just note as i told you at the start the M&K controlls are terrible so don't buy DS2 if you don't own a controller.
Also i don't suggest to waste your time to much in PVP , it can be fun and it adds a cool experience to the game of being invaded or invading other people but it's obvious the game was not balanced around it and the large lag issues it has destroys any type of real competetive play.

I personally think the 60 dollars you have to pay for on this game is you paying for the Bethesda name and the Elders Scroll feel, and as I will admit it DOES have the Elders Scroll feel to it, that does not make up the fact that behind the HUD and the gameplay mechanics, it's a regular ol' run of the mill MMO. I've been a huge fan of The Elder Scrolls game since I first played Morrowind at a friends house on his pc. I remember as a kid begging my parents to buy it for me once it was announced for Xbox. The world, the characters, and the stories that you could create were some of my most cherished gaming moments. I've continued to play each Elder Scrolls game thats been released since and probably know more about the lore of these games then I do actual world history. Now that I've had the chance to put a significant amount of time into ESO, I think I can fairly review it.
First of all, let me address the monthly fee. I think that it is beyond unfair to ask $15 a month plus the full retail price of the game. With the base price included, the game adds up to be about $250 for your first year. That is unacceptable for any game, regardless of the quality. There aren't any pay to win features of the game, but they still need to come up with a better model then this if they want people other then the most die-hard Elder Scrolls fans to play their MMO.
Let me just  quick fire the rest of my negative opinions before moving on to the many positives of the game. It's hard to group quest when your friends disappear because they are at a different part of the quest then you. The horses in the game are overpriced beyond belief. I played for almost 100 hours with one character and still couldn't afford a damn horse. Not cool...not cool. Also, some of the zones in the game look very similar to other zones when they should not according to the lore. That one is a nerdy complaint, but it still sort of irked me.
Now for the positives. The game looks very pretty for an MMO. I liked most of the art style and had some moments when I was just running around where I had to just stop and enjoy the scenery. The one exception to this is Cyrodil (where all the pvp takes place). While I didn't spend much time there, it was huge space that was populated with almost nothing interesting to see. Other than that, the dungeons and the effects in the game are great.
The fact that everything is voice acted is another amazing feat in an MMO. I know that Bioware already did this with The Old Republic, but here it is done really well. It makes the quests feel like  single player quests and makes the game a bit more immersive. Along with this, the quests are pretty good for an MMO. Compared to other games in the genre, ESO has great variety and made me wonder what cool thing I might stumble upon next.
The community was also pretty good for ESO (at least when I played over the summer). I ran into alot of cool people and most were willing to help out or just have dance-offs at least. This may be related to the fact that the game is subsription based, but I'd be willing to endure a few ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s if it meant not taking out a small loan to access the game.
I think the game itself deserves to be played. The developers crafted a fun and beautiful game. I am conflicted though. Im not sure whether to recommend it or not. If you want to play something a little different than your standard MMO, give ESO a shot. However, be prepared to spend a lot of money on the game.

This game is all about shooting monsters with awesome, big and destructive guns while you are walking through the beautiful landscapes of Ancient Egypt, Mayan Civilization, Persian Empire and Medieval Europe.
The game features over 25 levels, where you can find a lot of secrets.
Serious Sam is an old-school game, this means that you fight without cover against serious masses of enemies. There can be over 100+ enemies rushing towards you! To stop them, you get to fight with a minigun, a laser, a cannon and many more weapons!
You can also choose to play with other players together or play against them in some serious deatmatch.
Serious Sam Revolution merged the two original games The first Encounter and The second Encounter into one game. It also features more weapons, secrets, monsters and gamemodes.
Positive:
- Tons of enemies, weapons and levels.
- Modding support.
- Singleplay, co-op, versus modes.
- Support for modern computers.
- Still great graphics for such an old game.
- 10h of serious destruction!
- Leaderboards.
- Ongoing support by the developers, though it's slow.
...aaannnddd it features both original games (Serious Sam TFE Classic and the Second Encounter Classic) too!
Negative:
- There are some bugs.
- Multiplayer doesnt have many players.
- Savegames are broken after each update. (You can still load them, you need to enable this in the options menu.)
- Will probably still remain some time in early access...
TL;DR:
You fight monsters with big guns in a lot of levels. There's no cover, just you against them.

Don't dismiss this as yet another zombie survival game - this is a hidden gem which is well worth a look.
There are so many great ideas - recruiting survivors, building a community (each of whom you can give orders to or control directly) relationships with every character which are tracked and affected by your actions, a variety of quests, building, crafting...
While the game is somewhat linear, there are a few different endings and various ways to achieve them which adds replayability to a game which already has plenty of playtime potential.
The graphics are functional, and while the isometric view is a bit limited, the cinematic window is a great touch. Some of the music tracks are earworms, if a bit grating after a while. The best bit is the writing, which is often amusing and occasionally touching.
There's plenty of content and good ideas here for a low price.

Okay, so I was hunting around Steam for a relatively cheap game because I had $5 left in my wallet and wanted to make the most of it.
I sure did.
Survivalist is quite frankly the most modest/fulfilling game I have found in a long time, in all honesty it should be raised to the $7.50-$10 price range, and I shall tell you why soon.
Okay so basically TL;DR Survivalist is a post-apocalyptic zombie survival game that orientates you a year after the outbreak, all the whilst you have been barricaded inside a bunker you bought for absolutely no reason (quite coincidental if you ask me). You begin the game exactly one year on as a rich, cheesy character who emerges from his bunker looking for other signs of life, and then the adventure begins.
Before I mention about the storyline (I don't want to spoil it so I will only provide vague details) I want to talk about the general gameplay. The closest I can liken the camera angle to is Diablo, fixated roughly birds-eye but angled slightly towards the player. This allows for a good view of the surrounding area, but doesn't impede imersion at all. Your character also follows the direction of your mouse, which is a good quality as you are easily able to pick off zombies as they come screaming towards you. The aiming aspect of the game I believe is unique, yet brilliant; your accuracy is basically zero if you are 'run and gunning' so to be able to kill zombies you need to stay still, juke side to side while plinking them off. The sound is also relatively ambient, however after a fair amount of time the footstep sound can get a little repetitive, but don't get me wrong it definitely adds to the realism of the game. Occasionally you hear the words "Eeeviillll" coming from a zombie somewhere in the close vicinity, but I love this cheesiness considering the game only costs $5, and I have absolutely no problem with it. Although the only aspect of the sound that I consider irritating is when you over-encumber/fatigue; the heavy breathing your character embodies (despite realism) is loud and kind of annoying but oh well, thats a minute flaw in a brilliant game.
Now basically this game grasps every concept of a fantastic zombie survival on a minimalistic, but perfect scale. You cannot carry over a certain weight in items, but this can be enlargened through increasing your fitness skill (by running) or by obtaining different backpacks. You have a constant need to find water and food but on top of that ammo is relatively scarce so you need to make use of it considering zombies take a fair amount to bring down. You can also band up with other survivors to create a community, each with different assets like construction/medicine that can help improve your chances to survive. That brings me to the point of base-creation, which in this game is just amazing; you have to collect building resources such as wood and concrete to be able to fence off an area and construct buildings/defenses for a good defense agaisnt the undead. I love this aspect of the game, I didn't expect it to be there at all considering the price but oh boy does it make the difference. However early on you are established as the alpha of the group, and that means catering to the Type-1 Diabetic who requires Insulin constantly, which in this world doesn't come cheap at all.
The one thing that really impresses me though is this game is made by a single guy. Just one developer, who hasn't given up on the game (online co-op is in beta now with constant updates) which brings happiness to my heart considering most developers these days give up on early-access. For this guy to be able to create such a simplistic, perfect zombie survival is beyond me, and that is why I believe the price should be raised.
I definitely recommend this game 100%, and at this point I only have 3.5 hours but I feel like that number will just skyrocket.

I got this game for 3 Euro during it's most recent sale and I'm glad I did. It's a really fun, open world game that feels quite unique compared to a lot of zombie games I've previously played.
There are plenty of quests to keep you busy and you will also need to build defences at your base to keep looters and undead hordes away. Switching and controlling different characters is fairly straight forward and allows you to multi task with the members of your group with ease. Sometimes leaving group members to do tasks you've given them can get put off due to the character deciding he/she needs to find food/water first before continuing their task even when they're not overly hungry or thirsty. However, I think it's fair to say that this is the biggest problem I have with the game which isn't much of a problem, just a nuisance from time to time. I would highly recommend this game to anyone who's looking for a simulation zombie game to put a decent amount of time into. To anyone who is interested in the game but not entirely sure on whether to buy the game or not, be sure to try the demo. It's what made my mind up.

Dark Souls 2 is an action RPG for those that are looking for a serious challenge.  While at current I have only played throug hthe first couple of areas, The sense that i have of the games direction was a war of atricion with a steep learning curve  and us very unforgiving.  Make no mistake about it, you will die in this game, probably more than yu have in any other action RPG, but the idea is to take that death, and make a strategy in order to keep it from happening a second time, else you lose all of the souls you have not spent.  The situations that the game sets you in, whether it be through monster mechanics, or tricky terrain navigation, is set up in order to maximize difficulty given the progressioon through the game. The areas are not so difficult that they are unmanagable, but the game and its controls are very unforgiving when you make a miscalculation.  To some this may seem harsh, but it is the one true RPG in some time that has something more than "You can die, spend a little bit of money and repair and its okay" vibe to it, and at the same time your character is not losing experience that they have already attained as in games such as Everquest and the like.  This particular mechanic adds a layer of "should i wait on getting more souls for something more powerful, or spend them now in case i run into something I might not be able to handle" ideologies.  If your a controller launcher upon death, this game is not for you, however, if you are a person that takes a look at the things surrounding said death and enjoy a thorough challenge, this game is perfectly suited to you.

Gameplay - The gameplay takes all the great things from the original and makes them more refined and balanced, for the most part anyway. Rolling now actually requires skill rather than just rolling past everything, and it is assumed that you learn it to get far in the game at all, as the some of the most powerful attacks in the game can only be countered by doing so (Dark Magic, Great Hammers/Swords just to name a few). Where this game fails in some respects is the boss and enemy design. In the original there would be a few tough enemies in one area with heavy swings and low mobility, and the object of play was controlling their attacks and anticipating their next move, Dark Souls 2 seems to forget that this is where the combat system shines the brightest a lot of the time though, placing many enemies in one room just so they can stunlock you to death. And Bosses like the Royal Rat Vanguard and Belfry Gargoyles are just great bosses from the last game with a tonne more enemies shoved in for more artificial difficulty. This is my main gripe with the game, most of it isn't skill, it is just waiting until a set of enemies have completed their attack animations and taking a few safe hits in the downtime between the next (An example of this would be the set of three knight enemies in Heides Tower of Flame). This doesn't play to the strengths of the combat system and makes the game less fun overall. Speaking of boss designs, most bosses are predictable, humanoid Strafe/Roll fests with little to no substance, the ones that aren't are usually filled to the brim with enemies. Usually. There is one boss encounter that is true genius, and he is optional and out of the way for no particular reason, Darklurker. This boss is brilliant, seemingly easy at first, he has slow, easily dodgable attacks with long windups, but then, he suddenly splits into two. And usually this would be a problem like a said before, having you wait out his attacks and such but not this time around, it turns into a beautiful almost dance-like pattern that takes much more skill than most bosses to complete. This is how the whole game should have been structured, but it seems to have fallen off mark. That said, it was still thoroughly enjoyable and i would recommend an all-bosses run to anyone with the time, you get this game for the gameplay. Thank god it is good. Score: A-
Story - The story is an abstract piece to many people. Instead of the game just outright telling you the legends of people and places, you are meant to piece together it's tale using a plethora of techniques, in-game descriptions for items, talking to people and the environment being just a few of the ways you can go about it. The game begins with a short cutscene of your player being told that you are cursed, that your timelines and sense of self will have no meaning, that you will become a wretched hollow come time past, and that you will "stand before it's decrepit gate without really knowing why". These things are left as speculation for the player for the most part. And are never answered directly, adding to the nature of the game. While it isn't the best story for your main character it is passable, but the legends and stories of people scattered across the land are really where the brilliance is at. Score: B
Controls - Ahh controls. The first game was a horrible port to PC, suffering disgusting mouse issues, keyboard mapping not working most of the time, and just being a disgusting experience without a gamepad. Dark Souls 2 addresses the most major problems, but still leaves a few glaring issues. The mouse is actually amazing this time around, working like you would expect. The movement can be done fully with WASD and sprinting by pressing X. The only problem with playing with the mouse is that there is major lag when attacking, being as the two attacks for each hand are mapped to the same mouse button. Thankfully, all of these problems can be fixed with a script you can find on the PC Gaming Wiki, you can even edit the prompts to show PC buttons in place of Xbox buttons. While it isn't as easy to setup a M+KB with this game, it is definitely not a disadvantage once you set up the scripts. Gamepad controls are the same for the most part, with a few minor changes to make movement easier. You can now sprint up ladders by holding B, slide down ladders with the same button, and if you really want to, completely let go of the ladder and fall by double tapping B. Jumping has been changed to L3, and this is for the better, as in the last game triple tapping B was extremely unwieldy, and lead to many a death. All in all, great controls, but could have done a little better with Keyboard and Mouse bindings. Score: B+
Sound - The game was composed by Motoi Sakuraba, the man behind games like Braverly Default, Golden Sun and Kid Icarus: Uprising, and it shows. The game is filled to the brim with memorable themes and soft tunes while on your journey, making for a truly brilliant game to listen to. Themes to look out for are Majula main theme, Flexile Sentry boss theme and Tower Knight theme. Nothing much else to say really, brilliant sound design all around. Score: B+
Multiplayer - I felt this needed it's own segment because it is extremely important, for PVE, you summon phantoms to help you on your journey, this can make many bosses trivial by splitting the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s up, I recommend playing through the game once without summoning anyone, as it ruins the difficulty. But it is overall fine and has no massive issues. PVP on the other hand.. It honestly depends on the time of day or the weather or how the game feels most of the time. Getting lagstabbed is extremely common and is not fun to fight against. There is a region setting, but it is literally 'Japan' and 'Not Japan', making many of your fights a battle of who can lag the hardest and backstab the other first. If you want this game for the PVP, get it on consoles. Because the matchmaking for PC is atrocious, FROM should be ashamed that they shipped the game like this for PC. Not to mention a cancer that plagues everyone, Soul Memory. Soul Memory means that builds become complete meaningless, where in the original many people would limit themself to Soul Level 125 to keep challenge in the PVP, that doesn't matter anymore. If you have a high enough soul memory you will get people wearing the best armor, best weapons and people that have to ability to use every spell in the game. This needs to be fixed with the new DLC or something, because right now going into areas such as the Bell Tower are bound to get you killed by lag. Score: D
Overall, it is a great game with amazing gameplay, but if you have to choose between this or the first one, get the first one. Dark Souls 2 just doesn't live up to it's name. If you play DaS1 and want some more action do get this though, as it is still a brilliant game.
Final Score: B-

This review contains only mechanic spoilers. No location, enemy, or item names are found below.
Dark Souls II is the second game in the Dark Souls series, third game in the Souls franchise as a whole, and doesn't change too much from the formulas of its predecessors. The combat is still excellent, the enemy design still fresh and unique, and the difficulty is still intense. However, FROM Software has opted to change a handful of things with this entry, and for the most part they're well thought-out, smart changes, though some of this is down to personal preference. If you were a fan of the inconvenience previous Souls games had as a facet of added difficulty, you may be disappointed to learn that Dark Souls II is the most convenient, though not easiest, Souls game to date.
WHAT'S GOOD:
-Loads of new and interesting locations, some that are straight out of Dark Souls, with some being more reminiscent of Demon's Souls
-A cavalcade of interesting and difficult bosses, some that are nods to bosses from previous games while others are wholly original
-Lots of new weapons, a handful of new weapon types, and a revamped magic system that now includes Hexes as a fourth magic type
-A stunningly good soundtrack, with some of the most intriguing and haunting music to date
-Sweeping changes to how covenants work, entirely for the better; you can now leave your covenant to join another one effortlessly and with no penalties; you'll keep your rank in the first covenant and can swap between multiple covenants at any time
-Vastly improved handling of how co-op works, with multiple changes to make playing with your friends, or just helping out others, much easier
-THE PC PORT IS INCREDIBLY WELL-HANDLED. For those of you who played Dark Souls on PC, you'll remember that it was only playable thanks to third-party modifications. No more. Dark Souls II is one of the best and most consistent ports I've ever played, with not a single noticeable framedrop that I can remember. Blazing fast 60fps, incredibly consistent, and with pretty good image quality and overall graphical fidelity. The textures look nice, the characters look good.. it's a good version of a great game.
-Any enemy that you kill 15 times will stay dead, allowing you to grind a certain section down in order to make paths easier for you. It's a good change that allows even people who have trouble with a huge amount of enemies in a row to still enjoy the game, letting you set the difficulty of paths yourself.
-You can, through the use of consumable items, set an area's level to NG+(...) even without going into NG+ proper. This respawns the boss, any enemies that had been killed 15 times, and some of the items and chests, while setting the area's difficulty up a notch. It's a welcome change so you can kill a few bosses again without having to go through the whole game again, and it allows you to grind for souls/get some items again/get certain items that need a certain NG+ level, all without having to beat the game and start over.
WHAT'S BAD
-The hitboxes are not quite as accurate as they were in previous games; a few times during this game, you'll feel cheated by an attack that clearly missed you, even if only just, and it's a rare but disappointing thing to happen in a game that's heralded as being difficult, but fair
-A couple of the bosses get reused, and some of the bosses spawn multiple enemies; this can be a pain to deal with and often just feels like a cheap way of adding difficulty. I never had too much trouble with these multi-enemy bosses, but I felt like FROM used too many of this type of boss fight this time around
-Some late-game hexes are ♥♥♥♥ing broken in PvP
WHAT'S CHANGED
-To go from hollow to human, you need to either be summoned and help the host out or use a human effigy. This is a lot different and, in my opinion, much better than Dark Souls' humanity system, which felt like a couple steps too many. In DSII you can go from hollow to human anywhere, and that's a great change that only helps make things more convenient.
-Estus Flask uses no longer depend on how much you've kindled the bonfire you last rested at, but are a flat value that you upgrade over time with items. I think this is a better change because it's a more universal progression. In addition, you level up the strength of your estus flask with items you burn in bonfires, as opposed to fire keeper's souls. It's not too different, but I prefer DSII's implementation.
-Durability is restored to 100% every time you rest at a bonfire, unless the item is broken. This is overwhelmingly better as it does the same thing (keeps you from spending too long fighting) but without making you go all the way to a blacksmith every so often.
Overall, I enjoyed Dark Souls II much more than Dark Souls, even with the hitbox issues, and I have a hard time picking a favorite between it and Demon's. Whether you're a Souls veteran or a newcomer looking for some fun-but-difficult action, Dark Souls II is a must-play.

This is the first MOBA I tried and it just might be that.
The first thing I see when I get in to the tutorial is Neith. Oversexualized(not just the character model but the animations) ranged character. But what the hell... This isn't the first F2P game I see this.
The tutorial explains me how to move and... Is it just Neith or is every "god" as slow as a turtle? Mving on - > It shows me how to attack and... Wow... This game isn't 3rd person after all. It's just Isometric with changeable camera angle... Then it show me the skills and damn they feel dull... 1 of the skills shoot through enemies and others were just for damage.
Before I complete the tutorial I press "space" and see the jump... Is it actually used somewhere? Why can the characters jump? I don't get it...
After the tutorial I decide to try singleplayer match with some bots. Ra was one of the available characters, one of my favourite gods and my favourite class: mage. First thing that pops up is a introduction video for Ra. After the video ends I realise that the match has already begun...
Around halfway match I press ESC, click the quit and tell my wife who was eager to play with me if it's any good, to uninstall it from her computer.
TL;DR:
Smite is an isometric PVP game with camera that may fool you that it's 3rd person. Gods lack interesting skills and feel sluggish. Almost every female god is overly sexualized.
Pros.
+ Good graphics
+ Lots of different gods
+ Tutorial
Cons.
- Wonky camera
- Preparation based combat(No skill involved)
- Sexualized gods
- Incredibly slow based
- No impact in skills
I might change this review after I try other MOBAs but for now this feels like a game that I played in early 2000.

Oddly satisfying game for just zoning out to while watching a movie in tandem.  There can be some intense moments but for the most part, if you enjoy exploration games with a hint of survival and a bunch of building; you may enjoy Astroneer.

Overall, an fun and solid experience.  This game really apeals to the exploration aspect, in ways that games like No Man's Sky attempted to do, and failed.  The enviornments are colorful, the content good for Pre Alpha stages of development, and the gameplay smooth and almost therapeutic.  The development team is very responsive and seems to consistently work towards improving the game and releasing the next big update, or weekly vlog highlighting their latest work.  They communicate with players and are a frequent sight on the reddit page.
While currently there is a less than optimal amount of content, a certain suspension of critiscism must be employed because the game is still very far from completion.  Saying that, I apriciate the studio's willingness to allow the community to review, critique, give feedback, and be very involved in the game's progress.
In conclusion, I would recomend this game to anybody wishing to have an experience unlike most other games on steam!

tl;dr: It's a fun game that takes a bit of teamwork and cooperation to play.
Actual review:
A more slow paced survival horror game that sticks to the traditional slower moving undead called "shamblers" with a few twists, such as child zombies and runners. You and a group of survivors try to either hold out against the undead hoard in survival mode, or escape from them in the objective game mode. Overall the game is amazing, built in source, and molded to near perfection. Coming from someone who has played this since before it was on the Steam Store, I'd say it's worth a download. Just be weary when you first start out. The game revolves around a small amount of realism, meaning you'll have to scavenge ammo and medical supplies. Certain ammuntion only fits to certain guns, and you don't have infinite stamina. So if you're a melee weapon user, be cautious. Any long-time player, or even a quick learning one knows the ins and outs of the game. What to look for and where. What places have weapons and ammo and how to access them. The most interesting feat of this game is the ability to get infected and actually turn if you don't get treatment. In this case, pills. If you get hit by a zombie you also have a chance to bleed, which can be fixed by either first-aid kits, or bandages. Due to there being so many inexperienced people on this game, there tends to be a lot of wipes. Don't get discouraged. The game is hard, and you will get frustraited. That's the nature of the game. Most think you can pick up a shotgun and be set, sadly this isn't the case, as you have to go for headshots as well for an instant kill. It's unique and once you know what you're doing it's very enjoyable.
In all I give this game a 9/10, for what it is and how it plays, not to mention new updates adding more maps, characters and guns. Definitly recommended.

This is an excellent match 3 game.  It has earnable power-ups, match 3 combo upgrades, and interesting challenging mechanics.  These challenges are presented as bugs that need to be removed.  Bugs can do different things like clog up the board, prevent tiles from moving, etc.  There are helpful items, too, that help destroy bugs.  Matching medkits charges up your powerups.  A medkit with a symbol on it will supercharge that particular powerup.
The theme is not disturbing or sickening at all.  In fact, with every problem you cure on the patient, you can watch that part of the patient get better!  This is actually quite satisfying.  More so than saving the world, honestly, which seems so far fetched. It's quite addictive, and I want to bail on this review to finishing curing the patient (the ultimate goal, I believe).
I always play on the harder difficulty, and this one is just two - timer or casual.  The timer hasn't been an issue so far ... it just dictates how much extra points and cash is received for upgrade purchases.
All in all, a very fun game!

This review contains only mechanic spoilers. No location, enemy, or item names are found below.
Dark Souls II is the second game in the Dark Souls series, third game in the Souls franchise as a whole, and doesn't change too much from the formulas of its predecessors. The combat is still excellent, the enemy design still fresh and unique, and the difficulty is still intense. However, FROM Software has opted to change a handful of things with this entry, and for the most part they're well thought-out, smart changes, though some of this is down to personal preference. If you were a fan of the inconvenience previous Souls games had as a facet of added difficulty, you may be disappointed to learn that Dark Souls II is the most convenient, though not easiest, Souls game to date.
WHAT'S GOOD:
-Loads of new and interesting locations, some that are straight out of Dark Souls, with some being more reminiscent of Demon's Souls
-A cavalcade of interesting and difficult bosses, some that are nods to bosses from previous games while others are wholly original
-Lots of new weapons, a handful of new weapon types, and a revamped magic system that now includes Hexes as a fourth magic type
-A stunningly good soundtrack, with some of the most intriguing and haunting music to date
-Sweeping changes to how covenants work, entirely for the better; you can now leave your covenant to join another one effortlessly and with no penalties; you'll keep your rank in the first covenant and can swap between multiple covenants at any time
-Vastly improved handling of how co-op works, with multiple changes to make playing with your friends, or just helping out others, much easier
-THE PC PORT IS INCREDIBLY WELL-HANDLED. For those of you who played Dark Souls on PC, you'll remember that it was only playable thanks to third-party modifications. No more. Dark Souls II is one of the best and most consistent ports I've ever played, with not a single noticeable framedrop that I can remember. Blazing fast 60fps, incredibly consistent, and with pretty good image quality and overall graphical fidelity. The textures look nice, the characters look good.. it's a good version of a great game.
-Any enemy that you kill 15 times will stay dead, allowing you to grind a certain section down in order to make paths easier for you. It's a good change that allows even people who have trouble with a huge amount of enemies in a row to still enjoy the game, letting you set the difficulty of paths yourself.
-You can, through the use of consumable items, set an area's level to NG+(...) even without going into NG+ proper. This respawns the boss, any enemies that had been killed 15 times, and some of the items and chests, while setting the area's difficulty up a notch. It's a welcome change so you can kill a few bosses again without having to go through the whole game again, and it allows you to grind for souls/get some items again/get certain items that need a certain NG+ level, all without having to beat the game and start over.
WHAT'S BAD
-The hitboxes are not quite as accurate as they were in previous games; a few times during this game, you'll feel cheated by an attack that clearly missed you, even if only just, and it's a rare but disappointing thing to happen in a game that's heralded as being difficult, but fair
-A couple of the bosses get reused, and some of the bosses spawn multiple enemies; this can be a pain to deal with and often just feels like a cheap way of adding difficulty. I never had too much trouble with these multi-enemy bosses, but I felt like FROM used too many of this type of boss fight this time around
-Some late-game hexes are ♥♥♥♥ing broken in PvP
WHAT'S CHANGED
-To go from hollow to human, you need to either be summoned and help the host out or use a human effigy. This is a lot different and, in my opinion, much better than Dark Souls' humanity system, which felt like a couple steps too many. In DSII you can go from hollow to human anywhere, and that's a great change that only helps make things more convenient.
-Estus Flask uses no longer depend on how much you've kindled the bonfire you last rested at, but are a flat value that you upgrade over time with items. I think this is a better change because it's a more universal progression. In addition, you level up the strength of your estus flask with items you burn in bonfires, as opposed to fire keeper's souls. It's not too different, but I prefer DSII's implementation.
-Durability is restored to 100% every time you rest at a bonfire, unless the item is broken. This is overwhelmingly better as it does the same thing (keeps you from spending too long fighting) but without making you go all the way to a blacksmith every so often.
Overall, I enjoyed Dark Souls II much more than Dark Souls, even with the hitbox issues, and I have a hard time picking a favorite between it and Demon's. Whether you're a Souls veteran or a newcomer looking for some fun-but-difficult action, Dark Souls II is a must-play.
