While i enjoy the lack of voice acting, the dialogue is mediocre and the characters feel as bland and lifeless as the undead they are fighting off. The least you could do is give each character a personalty, as they aren't randomly generated and you will run into the same people time and time again.
I also feel that the game forces you along certain paths, and here's an example of what i mean: I was doing a quest for someone at one of the forts, she wanted to go see some guy she left at a police station. I liked the guy better then i liked her, as he seemed pretty polite and would make a better addition to my group. So i shot her and recruited the guy. I saved in a different slot and started my way back to my base. Half way home my people at my bunker kept getting killed. So i set the main guy on the course for home and switched back to the carpenter at my base. Turns out, the people from the fort of the woman i shot sent a death squad to my base. It may sound logical at first, but i was halfway across the damn map when i shot her! HOW ARE THEY GOING TO KNOW?!? It wasn't even a little while after either, it was right when it happened! Unless you're armed to the teeth, you are going to get annihilated. So i you even stray a little of the path the game thinks you should go on, you get severely punished.
Over all, it's a mediocre survival game with decent potential, but poor execution. I'll give this game another shot down the line to see if it is improved, but in it's current state, i strongly reccomend spending your money elsewhere.

Maybe its because I´m new to the Supreme-Ruler-series, but I cannot recommend this game. For long-time strategy players like me its just to arcade-like in its warfare part. But its easier to make a list anyway.
PROs
- the economic side is cool. You can built and reinforce your economic sectors in six categories and three manufactured goods. Plus you trade surplus and buy things you lack with ease.
- the builtup for war is easy. Units are built with land-/naval-/aircraft-factories in different cities. Plus you can hold them in reserve so they don´t clutter the map and cost immense resources
- I like the importance of recon units and the extra range of artillery. Makes the tactical combat fun.
CONs
- research is far reaching, but the easy way to trade it, destroys the fun. If you have researched the general tech, you can trade or buy unit-schemes from friends (or just anybody) for next to nothing. As Italy I ended up with advanced carriers of Japanese design and cool German recon units. Plus I think that there should be far more not tradeable research areas, so it´s more difficult to excel in research as a minor nation.
- producing units is very cheap, so you end up piling up units in reserve. which leads to:
- in my view your armies are far to vast to really control them properly in all theatres. So you end up losing small or prestigious units somewhere without even noticing it right away. Even units like carriers can be destroyed in seconds (which I did) or four submarine in a wolfpack are oblitarated in a glimpse. Its better in land and air combat, but naval combat just goes on to fast.
- the AI is not useless, but not very clever either. For example: As Germany attacked Poland the Western front to France was unguarded. Later it tried an invasion of Britain only with (zillions) of transports risking a good portion of its army. Fortunatly for Germany the British navy drove around aimlessly.
- the manual does not explain very much. So I looked in forums and learned much the "hard way" via losing.
For me Supreme Ruler 1936 has many fun aspects, but it´s not properly balanced and too confusing in large scale combat. The AI is not clever enough to watch theatres for you (not mentioning your Allies) so you win mostly by sheer numbers.

I'm a long time Civ player but SC36 takes the prize as the ultimate management game imo.  It's so complex that it takes a while to figure out but it's worth it.  Players have complete control over every aspect of the game: industrialization, research, social investment, diplomacy, espionage, militarization, theater strategy, tactics, and more.  You can play as whichever country you want (Uruguay, New Zealand,...), however you want.  The game has an outstanding underlying economic model that's intricate, well balanced, and challenging to manage.  Nation development is throttled but in a realistic way rather than the "you're just holding me back" methods other games use to slow us down.  The enemy AIs are also fairly decent though I've not let my advisors have much control so I can't speak for the intelligence of your helpers.  With this level of complexity, the UI can be clumsy at times but Red Goat seems to be improving it with intelligent patches.  In the meantime, you'll want to save often because one mis-click can completely ruin a game and if you like to control every aspect of the game like I do, a game can take a very long time.  Overall, it's just a very challenging, very fun game!

Grapple is a hard game. The point of the game is iteration, doing the levels over and over until you understand what to do and until you get better at doing it. The camera is close to the actual "ball" that you're playing, which makes it difficult sometimes to see where you're supposed to go, and the game's visuals plays into this with its aesthetic and actual, invisible platforms in many levels. Don't expect to be able to do all levels in the first try; again, the game is about iteration and learning-through-doing. If you like games that will frustrate you a lot at times, then Grapple is a pretty damn good experience. If you don't, you will hate it and probably not finish it, because there is nothing else but the gameplay to get you through the game (meaning, there is no story).
As for my recommendation, I personally liked it, but I can see it being kind of a nieche experience. I would suggest getting this game if you like the core principle of grappling/swinging, because it does work very well in this game. I would suggest getting it if you like difficult games and overcoming them. I would suggest getting it if you like 3D platforming, and can oversee your perspective being limited while playing. If there is one of these three things that you find very unappealing, I would not recommend this game for you. It's that simple.

I loved Dark Souls one, and I wanted to love Dark Souls Two. But they changed several mechanics in this game, One being that enemies stop spawning if you have killed them 10+ times. This makes the areas feel empty if you are stuck at a boss for a while and are unaware of this change. It makes farming enemies for souls and items impossible at a certain point. The only way to respawn the enemies is by using an item which makes the enemies respawn (as well as the bosses) but it permanantly increases the difficulty of the area you used it. Which could make an already difficult boss fight nearly impossible. I really hope that they give us an option to change this in the future or patch it. But until then I still reccomend Dark Souls one as I believe it is a superior game. While this game isn't bad (far from it) It's just not the sequel that I was hoping for. The graphics are beautiful, some of the best I have seen in a long time, and the combat is still hard but fair as it was in the first game.
P.s. Do not play this game without a controller.

As most people by now already know it is possible to play as either Corvo Attano or Emily Kaldwin (and even without any powers if you feel masochistic and "hardcore").
So far I only played through the game as Corvo which while very similiard to the gameplay in Dishonored 1 each ability got some more upgrades to unlock so it can play different depending on how you skill your character. Also artifacts can now be crafted yourself which sounds like it could be fairly powerful if you do it enough though im not a patient person when it comes to these things.
From a tool standpoint Corvo mostly has the same things as in the first game, at least I cant remember anything so memorable that it would be worth noting here. (Though you can upgrade your gear a bit further in some regards and there are some new bolt types avaiable I suppose.)
I played the game on the second hardest difficulty and it can be said that the game is fairly challenging which of course is completely justified with the quicksaving and quickloading beeing as quick as it is.
Enemies are very attentive and can spot you very, very quickly if you mess up. They also do deal a fairly big ammount of damage if you get hit, yet often enough you can avoid damage if you fight skilled enough.
While I obviously wont spoil anything about the story itself I would say that it felt to me that overall it kind of "lacked something" though im not sure why. I liked it and yet it just didnt feel as purposeful as Dishonored 1 to me.
The setting of course is as dark and grim as always.
I'm just gonna leave it at that.
Overall I would recommend the game as it plays very good and the story, while lacking in some regards (in my opinion), was fine as well.
Since the Performance Patch the game is in a better state (for me at least), though to be frank it should have preferably been this way from release.
tl;dr : Game is pretty good, yet subjectively not as good as Dishonored 1. Performance isnt perfect but since the patch Bethesda released it seems to be better.

If you're a fan of platformers but are getting bored of those 2D sidescrollers, delightful staples of the genre though they may be, then Grapple will be a breath of fresh air.It is an extraordinarily unique take on platforming, with the grapple mechanic being as revolutionary to the genre as a portal gun was to that other, admittedly more-polished series.  Though this game lacks any kind of story element or graphical marvels, its simplistic yet unique aesthetic keeps the focus on the gameplay, which perfectly suits it.
Every level uses the same dozen-or-so assets in the same way van Gogh uses the same dozen or so colors in any one of his paintings.  That is to say, each level is a breathtaking mesterpiece of design that leverages a few basic elements to create 90 unique puzzles, often challenging you to come up with new and provocative ways to utilize the tools you're given.  Naturally, at least the first half of the game is relatively accessible and doesn't require too much thought or effort, but towards the end, especially the last ten levels or so, you'll run into some very rough challenges that require a fair bit more precision than the rest of the game.  With that said, it should still be completable even by someone who's a bit more casual.  Just don't ask me about the time trials, those are for a different breed of platformer enthusiast altogether.

One of the more unique platforming gameplays you'll encounter out there.
You're a ball of goo that wanders through space, seeking the portal in order to advance to the next stage.
To get there you'll have to slime your way and use your grappling ability on all sorts of surfaces.
This game puts a heavy emphasis on momentum and creating your own way of dealing with obstacles.
Every stage got a "proper" way of beating it, and the "thinking out of the box" way of beating it, which is totally up to you and your own skill.
What hooked me the most was the fact that I never felt restrained as to how I'd like to complete every level, since the amount of freedom you get is incredible.
Grapple has:
- 90 stages.
- Time attack for each stage.
- Speedrun mode.
Pretty much all you need out of a small indie.
I've also seen some people complain about the camera angles, but if you ask me that is also an acquired skill, as the camera play is definitely something that you'll have to master as well.
As a platformers addict, this was a very unique experience that gets my two thumbs up for innovation and fun. 👍👍

Though this game can probably be very enjoyable, in it's current state I don't recommend it to new players to the Supreme Ruler series.
Basic game mechanics are explained only superficially in a short tutorial. Understanding warfare, diplomacy, research and how to manage your economy and population will require you to wade through a wiki made for other games in the Supreme Ruler series, which isn't completely applicable to Supreme Ruler 1936. The Steam community luckily is helpful to a point, however a game company can't just leave the responsibility of getting to know the basics of a game to the community.
IMHO a game company delivers an incomplete product, when it doesn't give you an adequate manual or at least a decent tutorial with the full release of a game. This holds especially true for a complex game like Supreme Ruler 1936. Instead you are left to mostly figure the game out for yourself.

The game is very difficult to understand.  The Tutorial mission is kind of pointless as in it tells you to do a few varied things but doesn't really explain why you should be doing them.  You don't have a feel for how long it takes things to construct, or what order they're going to contruct in.  I set up 10-15 things to build and had no idea what order they were going to happen.  As for the buildings, what are the benefits of each and why should you build them?  I was looking for something a bit more straight forward for construction management such as in the games Civ. 4 or Civ 5.  After spending 3 hours with a game I expect to understand the basic game mechanics... but this game still eludes me.  The "manual" off the website does little to clear up these issues and is far from complete.
The concept has promise.  With a drastic overhaul to the menu system it might be enjoyable.  As is, if you've never played this series before DON"T BUY IT because you won't understand how to play.  I rate this game a 4 out of 10.

Despite its sickeningly cute look, Slime Rancher is a great game to waste away the hours with. There will always be something that's in need of being upgraded, restocked, or, in some cases, recaptured, and it's FUN.
Taking the position of Rancher out in the Far, Far Range, you have an entire world to explore, and a small arsenal of tools to help you do it. Vac up slimes, cram them into corrals, feed them, and grab up the plorts they drop. Sell 'em off for some sweet sweet cash!
Some slimes can only be found in certain areas, which requires some exploring. Some areas are locked behind doors that require keys, some of which are hidden inside Gordos (basically really big slimes), which requires you to start jamming as much of their favorite food type down their gullets until they eventually explode, dropping a key, possibly some loot crates, or uncover a tele-pad to help you get around faster.
And that's just exploring. The Plort Market will change from time to time, meaning that cheaper plorts become less profitable. If you want those upgrades, your lab, and your Range lots to be at their best, you're going to need money. That's where Largos come in, and they'll be your bread-and-butter slimes for a fair portion of the game. Mix two profitable slimes together by lobbing a plort at the 'base' slime (Boom Slime + Hunter Slime = Boom Hunter Largo, for example), and you'll have a Largo that will spit out a Boom AND Hunter plort when fed. Rinse and repeat, and you'll have plenty of plorts to sell!
Being a Slime Rancher, however, does have its dangers. You don't take any fall damage, but falling off a cliff into the Slime Sea, taking too much damage from certain slimes, and taking too many rads will knock you out for a period of time, AND force your inventory to empty out (save for your money). And that's just the stuff that's right in plain sight. The biggest (not to mention most chaotic) threat comes from the slime know as a Tarr. Tarrs are born when a Largo eats a plort of another slime that doesn't match its make-up (Boom Hunter + Pink Plort = Tarr), and they are hungry for everything, including you. Slimes, chickens, their young, fruits and veggies, they'll clear out entire zones if you let them, and can quickly turn a peaceful stroll through the canyon into a full-scale fight to keep everything from getting devoured. Splash some water on them, or toss them into the Slime Sea or a pond to get rid of them, though, and things will settle down quickly enough.
Despite the fun, there are a few issues that I ran into, ones that concern certain elements of the game, or, in a few cases, concern a lack of elements.
1. Puddle Plorts missing the Market intake cause them to be destroyed. This can get annoying quickly, as it'll sometimes happen randomly. That means lost income, and a wasted plort. Puddle plorts an't be made to create Largos, either, which is a shame. A Phospher Puddle Largo would be kinda pretty.
2. Tarr attacks aren't all that damaging, even at the beginning of the game. They only deal a little damage, making them more of an issue when you're dealing with a mob. Their attack animations also cause any attempt at launching them to immediately fail, which can be a little tedious.
3. The lack of inventory space gets a little annoying once you get into the late-game. You can increase the AMOUNT of an item you can carry, which is handy for withdrawing from a silo, but the NUMBER of items you can carry is limited to four, plus a dedicated water slot.
4. There's very little story once you reach the last email you recieve from your Range Exchange clients. I would love to see some story get added to the game, even if it meant starting all over. That's just how much fun I find the game.
5. This is more of a gripe than an issue, but I would love to see Tarr cleansing or Triple-Type slimes become a thing. It could be a lab-related feature you unlock at some point, requiring you to contain a Tarr in a maximum-upgraded corral, meaning you either have to risk some of your other slimes, or find one out in the wild. It would be neat to see Rad Hunter Boom slimes, or Pink Phosper Rock slimes...Really, ANY Triple-Type slime would be neat.
6. In the same vein as #5, I wouldn't mind seeing the ability to raise Gordos. They could be used to rake in one specific type of plort (to an extent, of course), and would eventually explode, releasing about a quarter of the number of slimes needed to create another one, plus whatever it was you fed them last. More of a feature thing, but it would dope to have one around.
7. Last one, I promise. COMPANIONS. I would love to be able to train a base slime or Largo, and have it join me on a trip out. It would make trips through the Quarry a lot less lonesome. Plus, with some Lab-based perks, it could help you run off Tarrs and help scavenge up plorts and drops. Devs, if you're reading this: I'd love to see Pet Slimes become a thing. :)
TL;DR
Slime Rancher is fun, and it's a great game, even if it's in Early Access. Stop thinking about buying it and just do it!

is a dark fantasy puzzle-platformer that reminds me Tim Burton's work. Obviously, any black/white platformer gets compared to Limbo which really isn't a good comparison beyond surface level features. It is not a bad game but I feel like toward the second half there is more frustration than fun (mostly do to poor hit boxes, combat, and time-consuming respawns) While I feel that game could be sufficient with few updates I was forcing myself to enjoy it.
The first Act focused primarily on puzzles, story, and platforming which was very enjoyable. I only died few times and felt like I was playing a casual, sinister looking puzzle game. Then it starts snowballing downhill almost to where I considered refunding it. In next few Acts, generic combat becomes a big part of the experience. Game has a lot of insta-death so you constantly replaying 2-4 minutes sections between checkpoints. I died at least 100 times to just poor visual hit boxes. The combat system gets really boring and just feels like a massive waste of time when you die in an unfair way.
For me, one of the biggest problems is the visibility. There are many parts of the game where I had to move my head toward the screen just to see the enemy in dark corridor. Other times I just wander around the area for 20 minutes because I can't see the interactive object blending into the environment. Part of the problem is just the fact that game has no zoom options (maybe will be added later?) I definitely feel that developers need to do a better job showing points of interest and maybe give some tool tips when new mechanics are introduced. In general, I would even enjoy the aesthetic more if only I could look at world's detail closer.
+ very enjoyable aesthetic
+ many unique mechanics
+ interesting puzzles
+ good amount of content
+ soundtrack
- visibility problems
- problematic hit boxes
- a repetitive and frustrating combat system
- beginner traps that make you replay from poor checkpoints
- no zoom options
- relatively weak story
- limited platforming elements
I can't deny the effort that went into making the game look the way it does. There is clearly a lot of thought that went into making each object, enemy, and background. Unfortunately, to me, this is a case of an identity problem toward gameplay. It starts as a casual puzzle game only to become Meatboy with more punishing deaths do to checkpoints. The game keeps adding things that instantly kill you but it does not give you more mobility tools. Crapy combat+begginer traps+poor hitboxes+instadeath+uneven checkpoints+visibilety issues. It legitimately becomes a hard game except that you get good at it by learning how to adapt to its flaws.

The graphics are fine and I enjoy the atmosphere so far, but overall the game leaves a bad taste.
The puzzles are kinda dull, the hitbox detection (of your attacks) simply sucks and the controls are clunky as hell. In addition the gameplay feels repetitive, at least I can't recommend this title.

Zombies? Check.
Post-Apocalyptic Wasteland? Check.
Base Building? Check.
It all sounds very cliche, but it's pulled off - well. Instead of being focused on 1 area, it takes bits and pieces from each genre and creates a game that's worth playing, and definitely worth the price tag.
★★★★☆ [4/5]
Well constructed music and sounds' guns sound like they pack a punch, panting when fatigued, the grunts and shuffling noises of the undead, lurking in the fog. The music is good, however some seems misplaced (too upbeat when you've just seen your community slaughtered, for example)
★★★★☆ [4/5]
Obviously, nobody is expecting top of the line graphics here, yet doing it like this has it's charm. It's cartoon-like appearance helps take away from the harshness of the surroundings, whilst still immersing you in what's going on around you. Some of the animations could of been improved though, however, for an indie game, personally graphics don't matter too much.
★★★★★ [5/5]
Gameplay is a very important feature; the most important you could say. The gameplay is done flawlessly. Base building, whilst it could be expanded, is simple. The UI is easy to navigate, which is handy when you've got zombies swarming around you, with that looter party in the horizon getting ever closer. Guns are well thought out, and whilst slightly limited, each serves a role with perks and drawbacks for each. The RPG elements keep the game fresh, and keep you on your toes as to who is the best man for the job.
★★★☆☆ [3/5]
A range of languages to choose from and rebinding keys are big pro's for an indie game. However, the options menu's are let down by the lack of Graphical options (Resolution, Full-screen, and 60fps are your only options) and the sound sub-menu, whilst efficient and clear, when turning everything down to 0, some noises are still audible (such as panting).

This is a borderline-positive review, as Blameless (as it currently exists) seems like a promising demo for first-person adventure storytelling, but lacks polish. The environment delivered here is exquisitely detailed and feels solid, but persistent clipping bugs and other small issues keep it from feeling ready. The story fragment that this game tells certainly rouses interest and curiosity, but the continuation feels a long way off, if it'll ever come. The puzzles are reasonable, sometimes offering multiple solutions, and the presence of non-helpful items gives the game, on the one hand, a realism that few adventure games offer (in the sense that every object you can interact with has its use somewhere), and on the other hand, can be frustrating as you wonder why more parts of the environment aren't available for interaction. Voice acting is passable at best, and cringe-worthy at worst. If you spend half an hour on this mini-game, I doubt you'll regret it, but you may be left wondering at the potential left unfulfilled.

The Supreme Ruler series is one of the best grand strategy games you can find on Steam.
I started out with Supreme Ruler 2020 and played the hell out of it before and even after the Gold version came to Steam. With Supreme Ruler 1936 you not only get a better optimezed engine that can handle even more units and events than the previous one, but you get a time period that is extremely interesting to play in the Grand strategy scenario.
While the game might not look like much (graphics wise), it makes up for it with its superb and in-depth gameplay. You are the ruler of a nation, you take all the important decisions and even command your troops into battle as you take the territory of your enemy bit by bit.
What I like about this game compared to other Grand Strategy games is that while it is hex based, the style in which your units or the enemy units capture a territory is shown in a more interactive way making it feel like your actions truly have a great impact on the world.
The tech tree is also something to be amazed of, each tech you unlock as you progress through the years has a significant impact on the game and how you play the game and if you are able to survive the onslaught of enemies.
The economy is also complex and at times quite hard to manage, luckily the difficulty level can be adjusted to give new players an easier start on managing their resources. The buildings you can construct to help your economy range from simple wood managing complex to uranium mines. The economy also plays an important role on your armies, without petroleum your units will not move, without ammunition they will not fire, without construction materials you will not be able to build new structures and without food your population and army reservers will die.
The game is a must own to all Grand Strategy players, the game not only offers a singleplayer campaign and different skirmish / scenarios to play but also a multiplayer mode where you can fight with other players that control their own nations in real time.
You can play as Hitler or Stalin!
8.5/10 - Highly Recommend - every single next Supreme Ruler is getting better and better. This game will undoubtetly give you fun when becomes fully developed.

After playing this game for a long time, even way before the steam version, I think I can make a valid review of the game.
Smite is a moba that seems very different from other mobas and it is in some aspects. It is far more casual than dota or league with all its game modes but it can also be very competitive with a ranking system just like any other.
Pros:
- 3rd person perspective
- Extremely enjoyable progression and generous rewards compared to other big mobas
- Many game modes that fit your casual and competitive needs
- Decent pro scene and smooth learning curve
Smite is a lot of fun early on and you will be having a blast learning how the game works. It is fairly easy to get "good" at the game and that is enough to win most of your casual games if you are careful and have an average team.
Cons:
- Terrible and I mean TERRIBLE balance. If you play smite for a while you will notice that some gods are just too good and some items are pretty darn useless. In solo lane for example, you have at most two builds that everyone goes with and if you try and be "creative" you will lose the matchup. Some gods are absolutely terrible compared to others. The more you play, the more you notice how broken and linear the game is. The main problem stems from the conquest map (main competitive map) itself. So much focus is on early game and snowballing cannot be dealt with. Even the devs mentioned that and are working on changes. Unfortunately, Hirez seems to never get things right. There are always problems.
- Relatively toxic community and this is to be expected from any game. However, you will always have a player that thinks he is too good and starts trolling or DCs. If they were actually good, they would focus on carrying the game and try to help out bad teammates.
- Matchmaking. Oh boy. I really don't know what to say about that. 3 years ago the game had some really good players. You would queue in a game where everyone played their  best and knew what they were doing. Nowadays, you almost always get a meh team with one guy that lags all the time and/or is very unexperienced. This is applicable to both ranked and casual. Instead of queuing up 5 v 5 players of the same level, smite decides to queue up excellent players with trash players to "balance" things out.
- Learning curve. While for most of the game, the learning curve is smooth, you get to a point where it gets REALLY steep. Most players never climb the rest of the curve and this is because of limited learning sources. Watching pro games is almost useless because pro games are so drastically different than ranked and casual games. The only thing you learn from those games are good combos but it is definitely not enough. There a few youtubers and streamers out there who are actually good at playing and teach you how to play ranked effectively: How to control lanes, how to rotate, how to teamfight...concepts that are often ignored by players.
All in all, I recommend that you at least try out the game and judge it for yourself. I am sure that it will be a blast for you, especially with some friends. However, be warned that the game is not as good or deep as it seems to be and this is caused by developers who lack originality and only seem to care about gems. If the time spent on making these stupid events was instead invested on making better maps, better balance and advanced mechanics, smite would be on a whole other level. (They literally made a terrible mario kart knock-off...unbelievable).

Amazing game! Not as immersive or difficult as the first but, without Hiyao Miyazaki, who can seriously judge them accordingly? From Soft knocks it out of the park to trifect the souls anthology. Beautiful scenery, a vast array of weapons and armor, and a library of spells to cast on your unfortunate foes. A must play for any RPG gamer seeking a challenge.

This game is intoxicatingly good. There are moments that seem to lean heavily on inspiration from the original Dark Souls, certain areas are strongly reminiscent of those from the preceding game, and the fast travel system being available from the start means there are no architecturally genius shortcuts similar to the routes that linked the Firelink Shrine, Undead Burgs and Undead Chapel in the first game. Nonetheless, Dark Souls II is one of the most thoroughly engrossing games it's been my pleasure to play in recent history. The world is beautifully realised, I found myself quick to connect with many of the NPCs (the voice acting is evocative and brilliant), the combat and character development are detailed and rewarding to dive into. Stepping through the fog to face a new boss for the first time was always exciting, summoning other players to take down tough bosses was fun, and exploring every nook and cranny of the world was rewarding. If you haven't played Dark Souls, the ending will confuse you, but the overarching themes of death, darkness and sin are things that prove surprisingly relatable.
If you don't mind or actively enjoy difficult games, and consider yourself an RPG fan, this game is a must have.
These days new games are liable to run you $59.99 and will provide maybe 10 hours of game play barring some kind of inherent replayability or multiplayer. Dark Souls II is only $49.99 and my first play through took me nearly 70 hours, with the possibility of NG+, a new character or further engagement in PvP promising even more value. Definitely worth its full price.

Dark Souls II, like its predecessor, is a powerful allegory, and a profound inqury into our current social structure, and the meaning of existence. This magnum opus takes you on an emotional journey through the planes of despair, and desolation, offering very little solace, even at its conclusion.
The events of the first game is long forgotten. This tenuous nature of historical events in the Dark Souls universe calls into question the (in)significance of human existence. The players are forced to confront the question: if what I do has so little impact, what is the purpose of this journey? What is the purpose of existence? The answer is there is none. The protagnist's quest for a cure for undeath, is a symbolic search for existence/identity. And this pursuit of identity ultimately leads to existentialism.
The protagonist journeys on to obtain existence, we (in real life) work to sustain existence. The parallel between the protagonist's journey, and our engagement in social activities for monetary remuneration, forms a potent critque on (and perhaps lampoons?) our current socio-economic structure: are we really alive, or are we like the undead, automatons lost in this systematic desire for something that is seemingly meaningless.
Perhaps the end result is meaningless, rather it is the journey that is invaluable. 10/10

Survivalist is a open-world RPG set one year after the zombie apacalypes. The game focuses on a business man named Joe Wheeler, who emerges from a underground bunker in the middle of a desert. Here are some Pros and Cons of the game.
PROS:

First of all I want to say… this game was just not for me, and so to people who know my likes well and have similar tastes, I would not recommend it. However, I can appreciate that although it may not be for me, it is actually a fairly good game and people who don’t have the same miffs with it that I do might really enjoy it (and actually have).
That said, let’s get on with the review.
Joe Wheeler, a self-centered businessman, leaves the safety of his bunker in search for food just about a year after the zombie apocalypse. The game is actually pretty run-of-the-mill post apocalyptic survival game, you have to scavenge, avoid looters, kill/escape zombies, build your own place in the world and overall just survive.
The graphics are pretty good, not 3D masterpieces but I rather like the look of them; the game runs perfectly on older computers and the sounds and music are pretty alright as well.
The Good:
The game has lots of potential, and for being a one-man job, it’s really an amazing accomplishment on the developer’s part.
The world seems to be quite large, the quests, although rather typical, are alright; the quest givers do remember your actions and any misstep will have consequences. You can go to war with factions, recruit people to your side, etc. You can use diplomacy, buy, sell, trade…
The characters do seem to have some form of distinct personalities, and they are flawed in them. I really loved the touch of one of them having diabetes, it brought realism to the story. That there is a limited supply of insulin you must find/trade for also made it more realistic. But it also has the downside of making you feel truly rushed…
You can split your party and give everyone commands. You can build things and plant crops.
It has a fatigue system so you can’t just run forever, and I rather like that they added a needed sleep schedule to the hunger/thirst part of surviving.
People can actually leave your party/settlement/faction when they don’t like you anymore.
You can save at any time during the game, something that always wins my heart.
The Bad:
The default controls are super uncomfortable to me. Having to click F1 for the inventory is a stretch, using the middle button (mouse wheel button) to skip text is super uncomfortable. Entering a building is done through clicking with the mouse, but so is talking, and the menu for talking pops up as soon as someone is next to you, so sometimes the characters would stand right next to me when I was trying to enter a building which ended up in me talking to them when I didn’t want to.
Overall it was a pain to do half the things I had to do.
The characters who didn’t have a high shooting skill couldn’t shoot straight worth a damn. I get it this was probably going for realism, even Joe outright admits that he’s a bad shot. But there’s a bad shot, and there’s I-can’t-hit-a-target-even-when-it’s-on-me. The zombies were just way too fast and the aiming did not work quite as well when you had to be moving around all the time to avoid them jumping you from far too far. I found 0 melee weapons on the time I played (I honestly don’t know if there’s any), which admittedly wasn’t much. It was disturbing. I’d expect you’d find a baseball bat to smash a zombie’s head with before you’d find a gun…Then again I suppose since it’s a year later most people would be carrying guns… all the same, a backup melee weapon would have been nice to find.
The game’s inventory is handled by a weight system, which is alright. However, it feels like you can’t really accomplish anything because everything you find to carry weighs too much and you end up having to make some very tough choices. This could be fine if you like a hard challenge, I’d rather get a bit more time to enjoy the game while surviving…
Resource hunting is mind numbingly boring. Just getting the things to start building a fence took forever. Even with a backpack, because of the weight issue, the character can only bring one or two pieces of wood at a time. While realistic, this was also terribly frustrating - It takes longer to bring a piece of wood back to the shelter than it takes my characters to start getting hungry and sleepy and thirsty.
The need for food/sleep/water/insulin seems too pressing. Again, good if you’re playing say, hard mode, but it doesn’t let you (or at least, wasn’t letting me) enjoy the game. I wasn’t even done figuring out a quest, and already they were starving. (Ok, not starving-starving, but already quite hungry).
The AI seemed clunky when you left your guys alone. I left one doing the supply runs for wood so I could start building up something, he was attacked and bitten because I wasn’t there to press space when he got jumped. Had to restart because I was unable to get the needed antigen and I was fairly sure I couldn’t lose my only builder so far.
All in all, while I loved the general premise and style of Survivalist, I couldn’t bring myself to fully enjoy the game as I felt rushed to get through it, and annoyed with the controls; yet I can see lots of potential in it. I was pretty split on recommending this game or not. In the end I’m going with a tentative “no” because to me the cons are a bit more annoying than the pros. Still, I can admit it's not a bad game.
So, if you like a challenge in your survival games, then I would definitely recommend Survivalist to you. For the price it can be a great game. If you were expecting something a little more relaxed, I wouldn’t recommend it.
There is word that there might be a multiplayer mode added, and I’m looking forward to see if it makes it any easier on the players by teaming up.

There's other communities around, each with their own ways of running things. You can trade with them to get your precious backpacks and medical supplies or look for loot in the surrounding zombie-infested towns.
You can literally build a community with the ability to loot wood, cement, and chicken wire and then construct fences, defensive structures, and wells for water. There's not a whole lot you can construct but it's enjoyable to see your community come together. You assign roles to the members of your ever-growing community, they can guard, make loot runs, build, or farm.
The quests are in-depth, extensive, and frankly quite interesting and unique. Each one usually gives you different ways of completing them and you can chose who to side with.
The controls are decent once you get used to them. Your view range is limited which is for the most part realistic but can be annoying at times. Combat is difficult to get used to but relatively easy after you learn the basic tactics. The AI of the zombies and various NPC survivors is not bad at all, their path-finding is pretty good and their combat isn't too good nor is it terrible.
You can switch between the various members of your community at any time if they're stuck or you want to do something for them, but if the main character, the guy you start as, dies then you lose.
You have one main objective to work towards shortly after starting. You can chose if all you want in life is love, money, or power and the "Complete the Game" quest will be altered accordingly.
The developer is still working on the game despite it being finished and is active on the forums. He's going to be adding co-op soon which will really make this game a gem.

Combat is fast, though predictable. Each fight basically comes down to trying to keep your stamina high enough to knock away Zombies that grapple you while trying to aim at legs to make them stop running or heads to just kill them quicker. One thing I don't like is there's basically no melee option, the only weapons are guns and there is a limited amount of ammo available even from traders but to be fair it's a hell of a lot, more than enough to finish the story even if you take it slow.

Initially, Grapple comes across as a very simplistic puzzle-platform game that's a throwback to earlier arcade-style games. But it's also addictive. Though the graphical elements aren't complex enough to challenge many computers, the game relies on the strength of the puzzle elements, which translates to the timing of the grappling and jumps to race across the levels as quickly as possible. This is a game that asks players to think and doesn't punish them for ill-fated leaps. Fall into the void of space? No problem -- just hit the R key and start again from the last save point.
Grapple bills itself as a sandbox game, and players can select how to get from beginning to end (except early on, and those levels are very straightforward, but they do teach players the moves and skills that will be necessary later on). Where the game falters a bit is in its 90 levels not being randomly generated, which may affect replayability. At least the easy controls make it accessible, and the affordable price should appeal. Grapple is a pleasant diversion.

It's been a while since I played a 3D platformer that was both well-designed and fun to play. Some are great in concept, some have excellent mechanics, and some have good level design, but rarely do you come across a mix of all three (especially in the indie space, where 3D platformers are an underrepresented genre).
So I bought Grapple expecting some mindless fun while I waited for bigger, brighter, more well-known indie 3D platformers to come out (Yooka-Laylee, A Hat in Time), thinking that even if the game was bad, I didn't spend too much on it and it was worth a try.
So I was blown away to find a true hidden treasure, especially one with such a (sorry!) horridly bland name. The very first level lets you know this game has true effort put into the controls. Responsive, easy to understand, and simple, you'll be using the same three buttons the entire game: Jump, attach your grappling hook where your cursor is pointing, and drop from a surface you're attached to (not counting movement, obviously). That's it.
So, how can three buttons carry you through ninety unique levels, each with its own collectibles for the completionists out there?
A Nintendo-like approach to introducing new concepts, teaching you how to master them, then testing you on them, as well as everything you've learned before. The gameplay loop might look simple, but there's enough added as the game progresses, just in level design, to keep you interested even after the fiftieth (!) level. Jump pads, launch cannons, walls you can stick to but not grapple to, walls of death, invisible walls that only appear as you get close... It's brilliant design and doesn't outstay its welcome for a minute, even though some of the levels in the last set of 10 made me try for longer than dozens of the other levels combined. Especially the end level: that's a doozy.
I bought the game and started it up the next day expecting to play a bit. I played for eight hours that day across a few sessions and finished it. The light sprinkling of puzzle elements on top of 3D platformer was just what I needed, and if you're a fan of Portal, Super Mario 64, the F.L.U.D.D.-less levels of Super Mario Sunshine (It can't be just me that loves those), it might be just what you need too. I've never seen a single person mention this game before, even on places designed to spotlight unknown indie games.
I want that to change. I want more people to play Grapple, to see that 3D platformers in the indie space exist, can work, can be great. Artistically, sure, it's not the best. A ball, some walls, and a hook, all in the empty expanse of space? But it doesn't need anything more. Even with that said, I would be remiss if I didn't point out the soundtrack. It's great, calming but engaging, and helps put you into that flow state as you swing yourself around at dizzying speeds, calculating trajectory on the fly, missing the hook by inches and searching desperately for that one last place you can hook to.
There's really only a couple complaints I have with Grapple: The invisible maze sections are the main one. They're designed to teach you tight, small swings, really precise hook control, and to not overswing confidently into the unknown. But they're mostly dizzying annoying bits of trial and error. The second is a late-game stage where you're flinging yourself skyward in the midst of pure red blocks, trying to get to launch-cannons but without easy ways to get momentum. It's frustrating, boring, and doesn't feel like it has the same sense of speed. Everything else, though? :starfull:
Grapple is an excellent game. Everyone should at least give it a shot (more so if you like those games I said above or are looking for something unique in the indie space), because it's worth experiencing. Some of the levels are brutal, but they will reward your patience and perseverance, because it's not the game's fault you're failing: it's you. Analyze your swing, perfect your hook anchor, and fly.

This is a fun little platforming game. The swinging mechanic works well, and it  can be really fun flinging yourself around the environment. There are a ton of levels, and it has nice relaxing music. A few problems. It would be nice if there was more variety, as ou see the same 4 shapes or so, and theres only 3 different types of blocks. Spinning blocks, moving blocks, etc, would provide new and interesting challenges. The camera is completely awful. Its way too close, and when looking up, which makes you go up, you can't see how close you are to what's above you, and you can't see how close you are to what's below you. Since you need to look up constantly to grapple this can lead to many deaths. Also since its soo close when youre flinging around an object or moving quickly it can be hard to see what's around you. Another problem is the controls. The controls aren't specific to your position. If you are on the side of an object, pressing side doesn't move you to the side. You have to turn your camera so its behind you on the wall and you press forward to move that way. They should be structured moreso to your position and be consistent, as it can be confusing and finnicky. The other big problem is the attaching to objects. There seems to be no rhyme or reason when it happens. Sometimes i would be really close and it would suddenly not let me latch on, other times it would say I could, then as I got closer it would say I couldn't. Other times It would say I could, I would shoot and then I would keep falling and it wouldn't latch on. It's super erratic and I died so many times I shouldn't because it wasn't consistent. So there were some things holding this back from being higher, but all in all it's still a fun game.

Decided to edit a little bit after 85-hour in game play.
-----
I read quite some reviews before I grab a copy.  I was hesitating at first, after reading all those negative reviews.  But since everyone has different preferences toward a game, I decided to give it a try.  Although it's not like the Skyrim we have played, it's definitely not your typical MMORPG either which you are asked to "kill X amount of Y", everytime, from level 1 till cap.  It's not a game that encourages you to rush to max level in couple days, and it's not a game which you may go out of quests and have to grind like no tomorrow just to up a level.
The game has its own unique features compare to most MMORPGs out there, which I find very interesting.  To name a few, for example, crafting, you are not forced to choose a profession.  Instead, you can basically craft as long as you have gathered all the required materials.  Not something like you have to be at certain level before you can choose a "job", or to pick a plant and ore mining.   Besides, there is no auction house, but guild store for members in the same guild.  And you can join up to 5 player-guild (there are NPC-Guild which you can join for quests and additional skills).
Throughout the world, you will find lots and lots of crates, barrels, back packs, wardrobes, drawers furnitures, and etc. Loot them all, just like how you play an RPG!  Besides, you can adjust your perspective view (from 1st to 3rd person) with the mouse scroll wheel.
Graphics quality, sound effects, voice acting, quest stories, combat are all excellent!  While they may not be the best in the market, everything blends in perfectly in all aspects.  Not to mention it has wonderful weather effects too.  I particularly like the voice act, which I personally feel it's always one of the important game features to keep players immersed.  If it's done right, of course.
In short, although the game still have some glitches/bugs (which game doesn't anyway), it is unique in its own way, and you'll either love it or hate it.  For me, money well spent and no regret!

Worth $8, a steal when on sale, Grapple is the most fun I've had platforming since Portal 2. With only a scattering of the absolute mildest cartoon violence and virtually no language dependence, this game is great for a wide range of audiences; yet the optional challenges of time trials and hidden item collection keep it engaging for more skilled players. While the "walking" controls can be a little clumsy, that's not really a problem because you'll spend most of your time swinging and flying around the level and those mechanics are great - sometimes I like to take a break from the objectives and fling myself about the stages like Spider-Man turned up to 11. The introduction of new elements and challenges is well-paced, keeping it interesting but not frustrating. The sound design, music, and visuals of the game are perhaps mediocre, but it's well-polished and the music changes enough as the game goes on so as not to become stale.
I'm lovin' it. Would love to get more games like this to play and review.

Here we are with yet another free-to-play survival horror FPS. It may be free, but, is it worth installing to your computer?
"No More Room in Hell" is a standalone mod for the game, Half Life 2. The game provides a simple startup, character selection, and server selection. Before heading into the zombie apocolypse, you need to find the right character that suits you best, right? Unfortunately enough you chose from one of four different avatars to use. They aren't any different aside from looks.
But, let's forget that and talk about the real reason you're reading this:
How is the gameplay? When you finish loading a game session, you and all the other players will start unarmed. The round then begins and you will have to rush to find randomly spawned weapons, medicine, and tools. Once you are all geared up, your team must band together to fight off the appending zombie forces.
There are three game modes. One involves you and your teammates defedning certain area's from being overwhelmed. Secondly, there are mission objectives where you must use problem solving, and sheer wits to make yourself to extraction. Thirdly, there's plain survival.
Each is fun, that is, if you have a decent team around you. There are several locations that suit the tone of the game perfectly. Each is unique, and have there advantages and disadvantages. From croakers, to runners the actual zombies, when at high graphical settings, are quite disturbing :)
From shooting my friend after he got the infection, to reaching the extraction chopper just in time, "No More Room in Hell" is a good, fun, and satisfying experience.
Final Verdict: 7/10
Pro's:
*Requires a TEAM
*Great map variation
*Good visuals
*Good amount of weapons
Con's:
*No real customization
*Lack of lasting content

Most reviews that i've read are from people who either didn't even hit level ten or spent 40 hours thinking they could speed level through the game and found it impossible. Also to really understand this game you have to completely cut it away from the main series games. THIS IS NOT AN ELDER SCROLLS GAME. It is an MMO game with an elder scrolls theme and overtone. Also in the time since launch this game has drastically evolved. a substantial patch is added nearly every month with new content, systems, and fixes.
(REVIEW)
Graphics- I'll start with the obvious. The graphics in ESO are gorgeous. You can really see the hard work that went into making tamriel a truly breathtaking world. From The snow in Eastmarch and The Swamps in Shadowfen to the A'likr Desert each environment was crafted in a way that makes you want to see whats next for your journey.
Game World- While on the subject of the Environments the scope of Tamriel is insane. It is easily one of the largest Game world i have ever seen. Also the difference between zones is quite drastic. Sure you might see similer buildings in the same zone but that is to be expected in a game of this size.
Character Creation/Development- The Character creation in ESO is probably the most robust and fluid system i've seen in an mmo to date. You have 3 alliances each with 3 races (And imperial as the tenth for an upgrade fee) and the choice between 4 classes. The thing that sets ESO apart is the fact that these classes are not constarined whatsoever. You Want a Sorcerer with medium armor that wields two swords? go for it. Every class can use any type of armor or weapon the want with out specializing in any. The only constriction your class sets on use is the specific skill line you will use.
Skills- Logically the next step is skills. In the game you don't have a typical mmo skill tree. There are an assortment of skill lines  including class, weapon, armor, racial, world, guild, and crafting skills. You literally have hundreds of options for where to invest your skills. some being active hot key skills for combat and others being passives to buff your stats. This system gives you more freedom then any previous mmo i've played.
Crafting- As an avid crafter i absolutely love the crafting system. A player is'nt confined to any one profession. I can use my blacksmithing skill to craft my weapons and armor, my woodworking skill to craft my shields, and my enchanting skill to craft runes to enchant my weapons and armor. Also the system is quite robust. You earn experience in your crafting skills by crafting(obviously), Deconstructing(which gives you materials as well), Improving items, and researching(which gives you traits). On weapons and armor you can research about 20 different traits which you can then use in your crafting recipes to recieves buff from increasing attack and defense to adding critical chance or increasing skill line experience.
Questing- Questing is one thing most people are uninformed about. Some reviews make it out to be bland basic quests. In fact it is the opposite. Gone are the collect 10 of this for no reason and kill 20 of these because i'm bored quests. Sure some quests have those aspects but every quest has a story. You might be setting up a ritual to stop a nechromancer or finding out who killed a local merchant or helping soldiers take control of a fort. every quest has some reasoning that makes it interesting and makes you want to know what happens. also many quests can completely change whats happening in an area.
Economy- This is one point that has really annoyed me. Many people are calling for a public auction house but the fact of the matter is that in a game like this Thats impossible. Eso is not based on servers. There are 2 Mega servers. With the immense population of a mega server an auction house would become bogged down with high level items which would lower the value and in turn ruin the reward of earning top tier gear. The way it is set up with guild stores makes it much more accessable. Also with the last update guild merchants have been added so that you can buy items from other guilds members. most large cities have a handful of guild merchants that will have completely different wares to choose from which helps keep the value of items.
Pvp- I am not much of a pvp player so i don't have much sway on it. but from what other players have told me it is better at higher levels and always more fun in a group.
Endgame- Now that i have Passed the level cap of 50 and entered the veteran rank system it really adds a lot to the game. After beating your factions story and the main story you are able to play through every quest from the other factions scaled up to your level. The content gets much harder but also much more rewarding. I am Only veteran Rank 1 out of 14 after update 4 released today But i will Update as i move forward.
So all in all The Elder Scrolls Online has been a wonderful Journey for me. If you go into it expecting to play skyrim you probably will not enjoy it but if you go into it looking at it as an MMO its a very rewarding experience. PLAY THIS GAME!
SCORE- 8/10
(p.s. I've played this game for almost 140 hours as of this review. if your going to take anyones word for how the games is don't listen to the guy with under 10 hours. It took me 120 hours to hit level 50. I might be subjective in my review but at least let my experience speak for me and anyone else with substantial time in the game. It gets better every update!)

Despite its sickeningly cute look, Slime Rancher is a great game to waste away the hours with. There will always be something that's in need of being upgraded, restocked, or, in some cases, recaptured, and it's FUN.
Taking the position of Rancher out in the Far, Far Range, you have an entire world to explore, and a small arsenal of tools to help you do it. Vac up slimes, cram them into corrals, feed them, and grab up the plorts they drop. Sell 'em off for some sweet sweet cash!
Some slimes can only be found in certain areas, which requires some exploring. Some areas are locked behind doors that require keys, some of which are hidden inside Gordos (basically really big slimes), which requires you to start jamming as much of their favorite food type down their gullets until they eventually explode, dropping a key, possibly some loot crates, or uncover a tele-pad to help you get around faster.
And that's just exploring. The Plort Market will change from time to time, meaning that cheaper plorts become less profitable. If you want those upgrades, your lab, and your Range lots to be at their best, you're going to need money. That's where Largos come in, and they'll be your bread-and-butter slimes for a fair portion of the game. Mix two profitable slimes together by lobbing a plort at the 'base' slime (Boom Slime + Hunter Slime = Boom Hunter Largo, for example), and you'll have a Largo that will spit out a Boom AND Hunter plort when fed. Rinse and repeat, and you'll have plenty of plorts to sell!
Being a Slime Rancher, however, does have its dangers. You don't take any fall damage, but falling off a cliff into the Slime Sea, taking too much damage from certain slimes, and taking too many rads will knock you out for a period of time, AND force your inventory to empty out (save for your money). And that's just the stuff that's right in plain sight. The biggest (not to mention most chaotic) threat comes from the slime know as a Tarr. Tarrs are born when a Largo eats a plort of another slime that doesn't match its make-up (Boom Hunter + Pink Plort = Tarr), and they are hungry for everything, including you. Slimes, chickens, their young, fruits and veggies, they'll clear out entire zones if you let them, and can quickly turn a peaceful stroll through the canyon into a full-scale fight to keep everything from getting devoured. Splash some water on them, or toss them into the Slime Sea or a pond to get rid of them, though, and things will settle down quickly enough.
Despite the fun, there are a few issues that I ran into, ones that concern certain elements of the game, or, in a few cases, concern a lack of elements.
1. Puddle Plorts missing the Market intake cause them to be destroyed. This can get annoying quickly, as it'll sometimes happen randomly. That means lost income, and a wasted plort. Puddle plorts an't be made to create Largos, either, which is a shame. A Phospher Puddle Largo would be kinda pretty.
2. Tarr attacks aren't all that damaging, even at the beginning of the game. They only deal a little damage, making them more of an issue when you're dealing with a mob. Their attack animations also cause any attempt at launching them to immediately fail, which can be a little tedious.
3. The lack of inventory space gets a little annoying once you get into the late-game. You can increase the AMOUNT of an item you can carry, which is handy for withdrawing from a silo, but the NUMBER of items you can carry is limited to four, plus a dedicated water slot.
4. There's very little story once you reach the last email you recieve from your Range Exchange clients. I would love to see some story get added to the game, even if it meant starting all over. That's just how much fun I find the game.
5. This is more of a gripe than an issue, but I would love to see Tarr cleansing or Triple-Type slimes become a thing. It could be a lab-related feature you unlock at some point, requiring you to contain a Tarr in a maximum-upgraded corral, meaning you either have to risk some of your other slimes, or find one out in the wild. It would be neat to see Rad Hunter Boom slimes, or Pink Phosper Rock slimes...Really, ANY Triple-Type slime would be neat.
6. In the same vein as #5, I wouldn't mind seeing the ability to raise Gordos. They could be used to rake in one specific type of plort (to an extent, of course), and would eventually explode, releasing about a quarter of the number of slimes needed to create another one, plus whatever it was you fed them last. More of a feature thing, but it would dope to have one around.
7. Last one, I promise. COMPANIONS. I would love to be able to train a base slime or Largo, and have it join me on a trip out. It would make trips through the Quarry a lot less lonesome. Plus, with some Lab-based perks, it could help you run off Tarrs and help scavenge up plorts and drops. Devs, if you're reading this: I'd love to see Pet Slimes become a thing. :)
TL;DR
Slime Rancher is fun, and it's a great game, even if it's in Early Access. Stop thinking about buying it and just do it!

This game is the standard Call of Duty Experience with some added Titanfall-esque movement abilities. If you consistently enjoy Call of Duty games, You'll enjoy this one too. But if you want something genuinely new from the franchise, you'll have to keep waiting. This game plays and feels very similar to previous games of the series.
Singleplayer Campaign:
The visuals are much improved over Ghosts, with some beautifully rendered cutscenes. The voice acting is very good, with a great performance by Kevin Spacey. The writing however leaves a lot to be desired. There is some added RPG elements with the ability to collect experience and upgrade your character's skills as you progress through the story. The amount of customization that can be done is very little however and should have come to COD a lot sooner.
Multiplayer:
The only thing new here is the movement abilities. The maps are still small. The amount of players in a game is small. They did add "Ground War" to this game with slightly more players on a map, but it's a joke compared to Battlefield's 32v32. The wait times for certain game modes are very long (Most everyone plays Deathmatch or team deathmatch). The available weapon pool seemed to get smaller, unfortunately. I do have to say the Multiplayer as a whole is a little better and a little more fun than recent installments of the series. But not by much.
Bottom line: Not much new here. It is Call of Duty done decently with a slight futuristic spin.

Security for your account is OK, but you should demand more these days. No matter how much you tell people to not use the same password across different sites, people don't learn. Your HiRez account is protected only by your password. Your email address has nothing to do with your account security. If someone gets your password, they can log-in to your HiRez account, change the password, and your email address. There is no email verification required when changing account information, let alone security questions. Their response to account compromise is, to get a stronger password.
That's all fine, and there are obviously other forces at work. Account security needs to be as much a personal responsibility, as much as a level of trust between the service you are using. That is, until you have to prove you are the original owner of the account. The question they ask? "Please provide information on financial transactions made on this account." - If you haven't spent money on this game, they don't care about you. I know this, because a smurf account used to play with new-playing friends, was compromised. (If you use your main to play with them, they will get matched with full-ranked players, and get destroyed. Not a fun first experience) : That smurf account is lost, because I spent no money on it. No big loss, but being told that I can't prove I owned the account, without some sort of money exchanging hands, is ridiculous. They obviously had no record of the original email address on file, even if they could tell the email had been changed recently.

I reviewed this for Two Credits. You can find the full review, the score I gave it, and some cool screenshots from my time playing here:
Summary:
When World of One sticks to puzzles and dealing with enemies by avoiding them, a bright light begins to shine in its dark world. Puzzles are varied and many have multiple solutions. They are also surprisingly nuanced; simply solving some of them incorrectly will solve them, but it will also lead to your death. The experience falls apart a bit when it begins to focus on combat, but it should be noted that, despite that fact, I played through practically the entire game in one sitting, which took around seven hours, a testament to the fact that the game was still enjoyable long after the focus had shifted slightly. It’s a game that I wish had focused more on its puzzles, bringing back some of its mechanics in new and interesting ways more often, but one that still manages to remain interesting and present challenging puzzles throughout despite the fact that it does not.

Outcome: 8 Pretzels
Combine the water, sugar and kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer and sprinkle the yeast on top. Allow to sit for 5 minutes or until the mixture begins to foam. Add the flour and butter and, using the dough hook attachment, mix on low speed until well combined. Change to medium speed and knead until the dough is smooth and pulls away from the side of the bowl, approximately 4 to 5 minutes. Remove the dough from the bowl, clean the bowl and then oil it well with vegetable oil. Return the dough to the bowl, cover with plastic wrap and sit in a warm place for approximately 50 to 55 minutes or until the dough has doubled in size.
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees F. Line 2 half-sheet pans with parchment paper and lightly brush with the vegetable oil. Set aside.
Bring the 10 cups of water and the baking soda to a rolling boil in an 8-quart saucepan or roasting pan.
In the meantime, turn the dough out onto a slightly oiled work surface and divide into 8 equal pieces. Roll out each piece of dough into a 24-inch rope. Make a U-shape with the rope, holding the ends of the rope, cross them over each other and press onto the bottom of the U in order to form the shape of a pretzel. Place onto the parchment-lined half sheet pan.
Place the pretzels into the boiling water, 1 by 1, for 30 seconds. Remove them from the water using a large flat spatula. Return to the half sheet pan, brush the top of each pretzel with the beaten egg yolk and water mixture and sprinkle with the pretzel salt. Bake until dark golden brown in color, approximately 12 to 14 minutes. Transfer to a cooling rack for at least 5 minutes before serving.

Love 'splosions, slaughtering loads and loads of bad guys, only differentiated in their class, showers of blood and 80's/90's action movie heros? You have come to the right place, brother or sister, Broforce deliveres this all in truck or helicopter loads, fueling your power fantasies, one shell at a time.
But to be more serious, Broforce is a really fun game, lots of eye candy all over the place.
Thanks to next-gen particle effects and the pure amount of explosions being able to be rendered all over your screen, it can get rather confusing at times but i'm not saying thats even a bad thing.
In short: very nice to look at.
The movement system allows for a bunch of ways to swing you butt over all that non-american soil and if all your gracious parkour moves fail, you can still blast your way through that pesky terrorist wall, keeping you from turning the bad guys on the other side to a red pulp on the temporary floor.
Thanks to hords of enemys and lots of bros to play as, variaty is guaranteed for
the first hours of playing, up until you've unlocked and figured out the best way to play as every bro and can speedrun your way through all story missions.
But thats the part where the level editor comes in.
Are you creative? Like to build 2D levels? Like to add tiny details that oh so often slip by most players in their unsadisfiable thirst for blood? Good, because Broforce got you covered, althought in it's current state the level editor isn't all that userfriendly, so i hope you like exploration too.
But lets say you don't feel very creative or are just plain lazy.
Not a problem, you can play levels, other Bros put together and uploaded for public enjoyment and there are levels being added every couple of days, just don't expect there to already be a new level uploaded as soon as you reload the level browser (yet).
What gets on my nerves, and thats not even the developers fault, is that there are so many co-op exclusive modes that i can't play because non of my friends can handle the freedom being dealt out in here.
This means, people like me will feel like missing out on maybe 25-30% of extra game content.
But hey, there is a way around that if you aren't entirly like me and don't mind playing with strangers around the globe, because there is actually the option to play online!
The worst thing i could honestly say about this game is that, even thought it has a level editor and an active community building new levels
the possibility to play online with friends or strangers, it can get stale after some time of playing, so taking a break for a few days or even weeks after you got bored is advisable, wouldn't want you dragging your gun along the ground, out of pure unmotivation, while boredly stabbing Terrorist #1369 again.
So all in all, if you've got some money to blow on games, why not give this very entertaining and gory, if a bit mindless at times, Freedom Simulator a chance?
If you don't like this game, maybe you just aren't free enough yet.

Now that i've reached the endgame and spent quite sometime with this game i wanted to leave a review. Most reviews that i've read are from people who either didn't even hit level ten or spent 40 hours thinking they could speed level through the game and found it impossible. Also to really understand this game you have to completely cut it away from the main series games. THIS IS NOT AN ELDER SCROLLS GAME. It is an MMO game with an elder scrolls theme and overtone. Also in the time since launch this game has drastically evolved. a substantial patch is added nearly every month with new content, systems, and fixes.
(REVIEW)
Graphics- I'll start with the obvious. The graphics in ESO are gorgeous. You can really see the hard work that went into making tamriel a truly breathtaking world. From The snow in Eastmarch and The Swamps in Shadowfen to the A'likr Desert each environment was crafted in a way that makes you want to see whats next for your journey.
Game World- While on the subject of the Environments the scope of Tamriel is insane. It is easily one of the largest Game world i have ever seen. Also the difference between zones is quite drastic. Sure you might see similer buildings in the same zone but that is to be expected in a game of this size.
Character Creation/Development- The Character creation in ESO is probably the most robust and fluid system i've seen in an mmo to date. You have 3 alliances each with 3 races (And imperial as the tenth for an upgrade fee) and the choice between 4 classes. The thing that sets ESO apart is the fact that these classes are not constarined whatsoever. You Want a Sorcerer with medium armor that wields two swords? go for it. Every class can use any type of armor or weapon the want with out specializing in any. The only constriction your class sets on use is the specific skill line you will use.
Skills- Logically the next step is skills. In the game you don't have a typical mmo skill tree. There are an assortment of skill lines  including class, weapon, armor, racial, world, guild, and crafting skills. You literally have hundreds of options for where to invest your skills. some being active hot key skills for combat and others being passives to buff your stats. This system gives you more freedom then any previous mmo i've played.
Crafting- As an avid crafter i absolutely love the crafting system. A player is'nt confined to any one profession. I can use my blacksmithing skill to craft my weapons and armor, my woodworking skill to craft my shields, and my enchanting skill to craft runes to enchant my weapons and armor. Also the system is quite robust. You earn experience in your crafting skills by crafting(obviously), Deconstructing(which gives you materials as well), Improving items, and researching(which gives you traits). On weapons and armor you can research about 20 different traits which you can then use in your crafting recipes to recieves buff from increasing attack and defense to adding critical chance or increasing skill line experience.
Questing- Questing is one thing most people are uninformed about. Some reviews make it out to be bland basic quests. In fact it is the opposite. Gone are the collect 10 of this for no reason and kill 20 of these because i'm bored quests. Sure some quests have those aspects but every quest has a story. You might be setting up a ritual to stop a nechromancer or finding out who killed a local merchant or helping soldiers take control of a fort. every quest has some reasoning that makes it interesting and makes you want to know what happens. also many quests can completely change whats happening in an area.
Economy- This is one point that has really annoyed me. Many people are calling for a public auction house but the fact of the matter is that in a game like this Thats impossible. Eso is not based on servers. There are 2 Mega servers. With the immense population of a mega server an auction house would become bogged down with high level items which would lower the value and in turn ruin the reward of earning top tier gear. The way it is set up with guild stores makes it much more accessable. Also with the last update guild merchants have been added so that you can buy items from other guilds members. most large cities have a handful of guild merchants that will have completely different wares to choose from which helps keep the value of items.
Pvp- I am not much of a pvp player so i don't have much sway on it. but from what other players have told me it is better at higher levels and always more fun in a group.
Endgame- Now that i have Passed the level cap of 50 and entered the veteran rank system it really adds a lot to the game. After beating your factions story and the main story you are able to play through every quest from the other factions scaled up to your level. The content gets much harder but also much more rewarding. I am Only veteran Rank 1 out of 14 after update 4 released today But i will Update as i move forward.
So all in all The Elder Scrolls Online has been a wonderful Journey for me. If you go into it expecting to play skyrim you probably will not enjoy it but if you go into it looking at it as an MMO its a very rewarding experience. PLAY THIS GAME!
SCORE- 8/10
(p.s. I've played this game for almost 140 hours as of this review. if your going to take anyones word for how the games is don't listen to the guy with under 10 hours. It took me 120 hours to hit level 50. I might be subjective in my review but at least let my experience speak for me and anyone else with substantial time in the game. It gets better every update!)
(EDIT)- Seeing as no one is really understanding my meaning i thought i would add to this. When i say its not an elder scrolls game i mean that as in it is completely different then the main series games. It is a new take on the series but it still has all of the original areas, lore, creatures, etc... Giving a game that gave fair warning that it would be completely differentt a bad rap for only the fact that its different isn't right. If its too risque for you because your an elder scrolls fanboy that thinks this game tarnishes their reputation then the easy thing to do is just not play it. Don't tell everyone else that they are wrong in playing it when you won't step out of your comfort zone and try something new. Now enough ranting. PLAY IT. HAVE FUN.
