Some things I've found:
- When you play as a country that isn't a known tech powerhouse, you are limited. I'm not sure if this is a bug or not, but playing as Mexico, I have not been able to get tanks. I can't even trade for them.
- I wish I could minimize the tool bars. I play on a 14" alienware and with all the clutter I don't have much of a window to see things.
- Somtimes things just seem to pause when building. Buildings, tech research, and unit building. They just freeze. I found if you pause, then unpause or save and then resume it fixes this.
- A lot of pathing issues to resolve yet I see too. As Mexico I was invading Germany, then I invaded Romania. I was then attacked by France, so for some reason, my units decided to hit the coast near Constanta and turned into merchant vessels and just sat there spinning. I clicked on them and told them to unload at the port there and everything was fixed at that point.
- The BG forums themselves are having problems these days too. I went to log in and it said there was no record of my account. So I made a new one. I never got the activation email after 12 hours so I clicked to send a new one. Again it says no record of account. So again I try to make a new one and now it says I can't cause an account already exists. It's a circle of frustration.
- The next game, I'd like to see this SR format where you can go from a caveman society to future tech. With expanding influence/country borders like SR offers.

Rarely does the sequel ever live up to the original - Dishonored 2 goes one step further and actually surpasses the first game.
Two playable characters that are both a lot of fun: Corvo has the same abilities but they feel as good as they did before (better, once you've upgraded them), and Emily brings a totally new set of skills that feel great too. The levels in this game are unbelievably well designed. You have so many ways to approach any given situation that even though the game is not really 'open-world', it still provides an unparalleled sense of freedom.
New features really help add depth to the game - each ability now has 3 or 4 potential upgrades to further diversify gameplay. A bonecharm crafting system fits perfectly in the game and adds a bit more customization to your character. My only criticism really is the story - I didn't really care about any of the characters I was hunting down. I was also slightly disappointed that there only seemed to be one kill animation for assassination targets, but that's not a big issue.
Why can't I recommend this game then? Because supporting something that was released in such a pitiful state is just not right. I appreciate that Arkane have been open in acknowledging these issues and promising a patch 'soon', but still. How any game can make it to release when some areas are borderline unplayable is beyond me. I have an RX 480 and was dipping to 15-20FPS in outside areas. Combat felt clunky most of the time because of the poor framerate. Such a shame as the actual game is awesome. Wait for a patch before buying.

I don't really know what to say other than this game is just terrible.  First off I have been playing CoD since CoD 2 and they have just been getting worse and worse.  CoD4:MW was probabably the only good one that happened in the newer gen line of games but anyway... If you are buying this game for the campaign then i have nothing bad to say about it.  For a call of duty game the single player aspect was action packed (except for those boring follow the really slow moving guy to draw out the level parts) and actually had a decent story.
But lets face it, no one buys CoD for just the single player.  I have honestly been trying to give this game a fair chance but the 2 biggest set backs right now are the level design... not 1 single map in multiplayer seems like it was thought out at all and instead feels like it was just thrown together by a team who eats too much paint.  The other flaw that goes hand in hand with the bad level design is the exo movement.   This ascpect of the game has no reason to be in a multiplayer game.  It is not fun, it is not creative at all and with the terrible layout of the levels can turn intense battles into boosting off the level completely and dieing.
The co-op is entertaining for about 30 mins or 2-3 rounds before you realize there isn't enough variety and it is just MW3 survival with mini games in certain waves... on the same dumb levels.
In the end i purchased the season pass and the base game because the trailers and the hype got the best of me.  It was over-promised and way way way under-delivered.  Stay away unless you literally have nothing else to waste your time on.  There are far better uses for both your money and time though and this is definately going to be a skippable CoD game, unless they do something miraculous with the DLC but i wouldn't hold my breath on that one.
Personally i will probably just leave it installed and see what happens but as of now i just can't recommend it.

The reason I loved the original Dishonored was because I love games that give you choices, to "play your way," and they combined it with a well told story, beautiful art style, and engaging gameplay. You will find all of these things in Dishonored 2. I never felt as if they sacrificed something for something else. Bethesda stated themselves that it is not an open world game, but they wanted it to feel like one. And it does, to an extent. The level design is fantastic in a way that they managed to create huge levels without any of it feeling pointless. It doesn't exactly feel like open world but your first few playthroughs will result in hours being spent on just one mission if you want to see it all. If you really want to see it all, you'll need to play it multiple times on both playable characters. Replay value feels slightly higher than the last game.
The magic abilities in this game have their own sort of mini upgrade trees and some of them get really interesting. Corvo retains his old powers from the previous game and Emily has her own set of unique abilities. Even though Corvo doesn't have any brand new powers, it was still a refreshing playthrough. Both Emily and Corvo seem to have picked up a small amount of Daud's powers from the original game's DLC, Corvo gaining a "stop time" while aiming blink, and Emily gaining a pull-items-and-bodies-to-me with her Far Reach. The most notable changes are to Dark Vision as it is very different than the original game.  It's less OP and, if you're used to the original, it's a bit annoying to use at first. I adjusted rather quickly and after adjusting it actually makes more sense to work this way.
The passive abilities received some minor changes and a few were added, but I found myself not using any of them besides agility pretty much at all. They're by no means useless but perhaps unnecessary. How good bone charm crafting is completely depends on what you find. If you only find charms you won't use, you won't need to combine any. My first playthrough saw heavy use of the crafting system, but my second playthrough barely even touched it.
The final upgrade of Shadow Kill is amazing for high chaos runs. :)
Enemy AI has seen a large improvement. Guards are smarter when they search for you and have smoother animations. They also act a lot more realistic when they're confused, such as when you inevitably fall on their face because you miss an assassination cue and promptly blink away. Their guard-to-guard banter is just as entertaining as well.
Well, that's about it. The rest you should find out for yourself. It's a worthy successor.

I love the Elder Scrolls games. The huge open worlds, the freedom to create the character you want and to go and do whatever you please, the awesome modding scene etc. We all love that right? But not everyone loves MMOs, or at least themepark (WoW-style) MMOs. The restrictions that come with the genre don't really sit well with the freedom that Elder Scrolls games traditionally offer. And perhaps this should have been more of a sandbox game.
That said, this game does a very good job of allowing a remarkable degree of customization when it comes to building your avatar. And the world does have that Elder Scrolls vibe. If you appreciate the details, you'll find a lot to enjoy here. Visually the game is a notch above anything else in this series. On ultra-high settings, it looks fabulous. The combat is fast paced and fun. You can play in first-person or third-person as you like. The music, featuring tracks by Malukah, is excellent. Crafting is solid. The zones are huge with lots to explore. I bought this game on Steam and I have played nothing else since.
Note - the game does require a sub to play. Some gamers do not like this. Personally, I'd much rather pay a sub than put up with cash shops, lockboxes and the rest of the crap that comes with F2P, but YMMV.

I immediately fell in love with the idea of the game. Who among us, who grew up in the GTA generation, could refuse a massively multiplayer simulacron? A game where you could run rampant in a bustling city, breaking the law or thwarting lawbreakers. A game where you could make your own theme music, graffiti and design your cars and clothes. A game with a thriving community-driven marketplace.
It wasn't hard to crush those dreams, as the current developers and community have done. The game makes you hate each other. It makes you hate the people hosting and developing it. Matchmaking forces you to discriminate against weaker players being on your squad. Mission types devolve into hateful grudge matches that will make you twitch, sweat, and curse. The low population and broken ranking system will ensure that certain notorious individuals will become your personal arch nemeses. The laughable price point at which gear is pushed by the marketting department will have you cringing. The balancing of weapons, and the steep skill landscape will ensure that every now and then your weapon, no matter how spectacular or expensive, will feel like a capgun or limp noodle in your hand.

Serious Sam will always hold a special place in my heart as a series that kickstarted my love for...well, games, to be completely honest with you (Timesplitters was the series that kept my interest for the long term.) I highly doubt that I would be enjoying games if Serious Sam and Timesplitters didn't show me just how fun, crazy and satisfying it can be. But I don't necessarily want to be reviewing Serious Sam as a game here, as chances are if you're reading this review you've already played a Serious Sam game. Instead, let's focus on the fan-remake, Classics: Revolution.
There isn't much to say really. The gameplay is near-identical to how I remember it on the original Xbox, and since the Xbox version I played was pretty different to the First and Second Encounter I was somewhat surprised. If, like me, you've never played the original on PC, the workshop support will allow you to change the enemy models and HUD to something you remember. The workshop support also helps enhance and prolong the replayability, as custom maps are actually still being added and the ones I've played have all been excellent. The engine is smooth and well-optimized, and if any graphical tweaks are needed then you're at full liberty to do so with an expansive options menu (that can be somewhat confusing to navigate) This game may seem a bit pointless considering there are HD editions, but I found that Classics: Revolution has the most resemblance to the Serious Sam I know and love. Plus, the First and Second Encounters are conjoined in this game, whereas the HD versions are split and have different features in both, which is frustrating to say the least.
Onwards to the negative. Yes, this is Early Access. Yes, this is fan-made. As such, there are a number of bugs that are annoying but rarely game-breaking. They are still there, however. Some issues I've ran into are enemies getting stuck behind objects and walls frequently, which makes it a lot easier to shotgun them to pieces, some buttons required for puzzles and secrets actually won't work depending on what gun you're holding, and graphical glitches such as clipping through the wall ever so slightly if you brush against one (this one is perfectly manageable, since it happens on other games frequently, such as Skyrim, and doesn't take up a lot of screen space) I've also experienced crashes, especially every time I tab out.
However, these negatives are still minor because this Early Access game is feature complete as hell. I haven't yet had the chance to try out online multiplayer but I've tried local co-op and it works fine. I really like this game. It's incredibly smooth and fast paced. I find in this game you can be quite flexible in how you reach the goal most times. It's incredibly easy to start picking up and it just feels so good to be good at it.

Just a bit of advice too. Try not going for the little point blocks every chance you get. The game is much more fun when you're just flowing through, and the point blocks don't do anything special. Keep them in mind when jumping, but don't ruin your run trying to get them.

It's a great platforming experiance, but offers very little in terms of aesthetics but does rather well for how simple it is. For the price of 2 dollars i got it for, I think it was really worth it.

After 20 minutes of gameplay, I feel as if I've experienced a good portion of the mechanics of the game. This isn't a bad thing; this game is about the application of those mechanics. However, two small issues present themselves:
1) The camera is too close to the player
2) You need to click at the right time in order to grapple
If these two issues were addressed, the game would be far easier to play. While this may seem like a detriment, the increased view and an ability to hold down the left mouse button to grapple at the first opportunity would be fantastic QOL improvements, and leave an opportunity to faster paced, more technically complex levels. Additionally, knowing the solution to a puzzle but being unable to execute it because of finicky controls can be very frustrating.
Overall, for the price, this is pretty good. If you like this kinda game, you'll like this game. Just keep an eye on the potential motion sickness.
EDIT: I've now finished all 90 core levels. Enjoyable, definitely. Some of the later levels can be cheesed, which is nice.

This is my secong review. My first attempt was perhaps too vague and came off way harsher than I anticipated.
The games starts great. You awake in the basement of a house undergoing a rennovation. You must engineer an escape using the objects and environment and the game does this very well. As you progress, you learn that something is definitely wrong with this house and we hit on another plus point, the game's atmosphere is actually pretty good for a free game. You're constantly looking over your sholder as you attempt to break free. And what's more, there is more than one escape route. All this is cool.
What I always ask myself when writing a review is this: Would I reccomend this game to friend? And the answer is sadly, no.
My reason for not reccomending this game is down to the fact that the game's ending feels thrown together and almost idiotic. A few tweeks to some mid game elements and some improved dialogue is all that's needed. It's difficult to discuss the ending of a game in a review. Just because I don't reccomend it doesn't mean that I want to spoil it for other people. All I can say is I found the conclusion requires you to not ask any questions and to just except it at face value. For me, the way a game ends is very important. I expect a revelation or a pay-off or some closure. What I found in place of all those things was some lousy voice acting and an unbelievable conclusion.
As I said, the game has strengths and the ending could be saved to feel and sound as believable as the events leading up to it.

I have played through the game once so far, and I am about to do a second playthrough to get to the ending with an alternative path, and to get the last achievement, so please forgive my 0.9 hours in game.
So, a basic summary of this game is that it is a very short game that delievers a sub par story with sub par voice acting with good visuals and amazing optimization. Also, the game was only made by one person, with a few other people providing music and the voice acting.
So first off, the length. If you know what you're doing, you can beat this game in under 30 minutes. If you have no clue what you're doing, then it could take longer. Also, depending on how you solve the puzzles, it could be longer or shorter.
Secondly, the puzzles. They are pretty good. None of them are too hard, but you definately will get stuck if you don't think of everything that is around you. For instance, the first area hase a puzzle that you have to pull down the ladder actic. You can either bend a pole using a pipe and the wench on the table, or you can attach the pole and use pliers to twist it. Each puzzle has two ways to go about it, and I enjoyed being able to solve it how I saw fit, more or less.
The voice acting leaves something to be disired though. The main characters voice actor is decent enough, but the other actors can be a bit cringey. That being said, it doesn't really take anything out of the game itself, which is essentially just an environmental puzzle game.
The Story. It is decent enough. A person calls upon a construction worker (or something along those lines) to help with the construction of a house. You get knocked out and then you have to escape. It's simple, and the game doesn't really need a good story for playing it either. The story is really just their to give us the environment for the puzzle.
Really the last thing to talk about is optimization, and holy crap is this game optimized. I currently have an Radeon RX 480 8GB and an OC AMD FX 8320, and I was able to play this game at 4k, whilst recording, and it never dipped bellow 60 fps. You would probably be able to play on a potato laptop and still have the game look nice and play smoothly.
Price. It's free.
Honestly this is a nice game to play. It is free to play, and it has 4 easily achieved achievements, so you can get another Perfect Game in less than an hour. I'd not only recommend the game, but I'd recommend playing it through twice to do each puzzle in a different way than your original playthrough. There is no reason to not at least give the game a try considering it's free, and only 1 GB in size.

The main draw of this game, like it's predecessor, is the difficulty. Common trash mobs present challenging affairs, often best engaged one by one. However the feeling you get upon clearing an area after cautiously inching through it is amazing, and later still, after you've beaten the game and started New Game+ and perhaps want to create a new character concept and begin anew, you will feel like a GOD OF VIDEO GAMES as you go through the starting areas and easily dispatch enemies.
That's Dark Souls in a nutshell, really; escalating and de-escalating between "this is hard" to "this is ♥♥♥♥ing hard" to "THIS IS IMPOSSIBLE" to "Oh, I get it" to "I am the best there ever was. Clearly, Dark Souls is a easy game and I am the apex gamer."
This game has great replayability, with the option to continuously start the game anew and face increasingly difficult opponents. Or if PVE isn't your thing, multiple PVP options are available to prove your dominance. Rerolling is also an option, as designing new characters is fun, and often the choices you make in equipment matter as much as stats: do I make a katana wielding wizard? Or perhaps this time i'll go naked with dual greatclubs? The choice is yours.
For newcomers, previous experience is not needed. There are some character cameos and references to older concepts, but the world of Dark Souls II is seperate from Dark Souls I. Lore in the game is elusively teased out through NPC conversations and item descriptions, and as such, must be sought out by a player in order to be known.
The multiplayer appears to be working much better in this sequel, and over my time playing I never had any problems connecting to friends for jolly co-operation. There is, however, a tiny bit of delay that may throw off parries, but not due to any hosting issues.
The one major flaw of this game is the controls; specifically, for mouse and keyboard. I'm of the opinion that From Software purposely made learning the controls for keyboard as hard as possible, as an extension of their "hardcore" game design. My friends that play without gamepads lament the difficulty at switching targets, but otherwise after a period of time were able to get used to the layout.
If you are curious about all the Dark Souls hype, Dark Souls 2 is a perfectly acceptable entry point; although since the game is about living in constant terror and exploration, for the love of God do not use a guide for your first playthrough. For returning players, Dark Souls II changes just enough game mechanics to make the game feel like a different game, without losing the Dark Souls flair.

Love 'splosions, slaughtering loads and loads of bad guys, only differentiated in their class, showers of blood and 80's/90's action movie heros? You have come to the right place, brother or sister, Broforce deliveres this all in truck or helicopter loads, fueling your power fantasies, one shell at a time.
But to be more serious, Broforce is a really fun game, lots of eye candy all over the place.
Thanks to next-gen particle effects and the pure amount of explosions being able to be rendered all over your screen, it can get rather confusing at times but i'm not saying thats even a bad thing.
In short: very nice to look at.
The movement system allows for a bunch of ways to swing you butt over all that non-american soil and if all your gracious parkour moves fail, you can still blast your way through that pesky terrorist wall, keeping you from turning the bad guys on the other side to a red pulp on the temporary floor.
Thanks to hords of enemys and lots of bros to play as, variaty is guaranteed for
the first hours of playing, up until you've unlocked and figured out the best way to play as every bro and can speedrun your way through all story missions.
But thats the part where the level editor comes in.
Are you creative? Like to build 2D levels? Like to add tiny details that oh so often slip by most players in their unsadisfiable thirst for blood? Good, because Broforce got you covered, althought in it's current state the level editor isn't all that userfriendly, so i hope you like exploration too.
But lets say you don't feel very creative or are just plain lazy.
Not a problem, you can play levels, other Bros put together and uploaded for public enjoyment and there are levels being added every couple of days, just don't expect there to already be a new level uploaded as soon as you reload the level browser (yet).
What gets on my nerves, and thats not even the developers fault, is that there are so many co-op exclusive modes that i can't play because non of my friends can handle the freedom being dealt out in here.
This means, people like me will feel like missing out on maybe 25-30% of extra game content.
But hey, there is a way around that if you aren't entirly like me and don't mind playing with strangers around the globe, because there is actually the option to play online!
The worst thing i could honestly say about this game is that, even thought it has a level editor and an active community building new levels
the possibility to play online with friends or strangers, it can get stale after some time of playing, so taking a break for a few days or even weeks after you got bored is advisable, wouldn't want you dragging your gun along the ground, out of pure unmotivation, while boredly stabbing Terrorist #1369 again.
So all in all, if you've got some money to blow on games, why not give this very entertaining and gory, if a bit mindless at times, Freedom Simulator a chance?
If you don't like this game, maybe you just aren't free enough yet.

So first off I actually started playing this game 6 years ago, but only connected it to Steam recently so that's why my play time is only said to be 100 odd hours. Now honestly I didn't play for all of those 6 years and for the reasons I am about to cover...
The game has some heavy pay to win issues, now some people (usually those who pay actually...) defend the game and say that if you earn enough 'joker tickets' you can buy these OP premium weapons for 7 days. The problem I'd argue is that it takes about a week for doing specific missions known as 'fight club' missions to actually achieve the joker tickets necessary in the meanwhile you are facing off against opponents whom oay for premium weapons and I have always played without paying any money so I can most defintley confirm that premium weapons absolutley out class their standard counter-parts and only after heavy modification after loads of playing time can one even stand on the same level as a premium weapon. Of course natrually a premium assault rifle will still lose out to a standard shotgun at point-blank range assuming the shotgun is being used well as it is not unheard of for a shotgun to lose in this scenario. I have played with the regular weapons then one-day trialed their premium counter-parts and it is very easy to notice the difference.
Another issue is that the community are generenally♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like if you've ever thought a community in a game like LoL is bad then wait till you see APB. But yeah people won't be kind to you. Also this has been massively improved upon (as once this was literally no exaggeration a problem every other match in a standard district) but there is still the occassional hacker that ruins the game. But I am thankful as this is way less common than before.
On the flip-side the customisation is better than any game I have ever seen ever and I do love it. It is incredibly in-depth and you can truly create your own identity, both in your character and vehicle. However once more customisation is better with premium allowing you to obtain a few more pieces of gear that are usually impossible to get due to pricing and also more decals are allowed on you and your gear and vehicles if you are a premium member.
Also I generenally find the combat fun, hit detection can be quite bad. But if you aren't playing against a load peeps using premium weapons, which makes up a large amount of the community, then it is quite fun and skill based. But as I said no matter how skilled you are your assualt rifle will lose out to a premium assualt rifle at almost any range. Except there does exist the odd bad premium weapon.
Overall I wouldn't recommend. Unless like me you love customisation and the game can be very fun, it has a few interesting gameplay features/ the game just feels unique in it's gameplay despite just being a third person shooter. But if you play for free you'll find yourself heavily disadvantaged and will recieve slightly limited customisation options. Having said that the customisation is still truly amazing and it's weird to think that a not so good game can nail one mechanic so much better than any other I've ever seen.

Hello and welcome to this review of Slime Rancher, an adorable FPS RPG about corralling slimes and stealing their poop for sweet sweet profits! Let's get started.
So the meat of Slime Rancher is in its gameplay, where you explore, discover, and...ranch slimes. You can corral them, free-roam ranch them, or let them hang out in their preferred areas and clean up their droppings to your liking.
So first off, there are small slimes that are manageable and come in a simple variety, larger slimes that are a combination of more than one, and giant stationary slimes you have to feed to break apart and get rewards from. Apart from the giant slimes, Gordos, you get plorts from the small and large (Largo) slimes, which are their magical poops that feature a wide variety of uses in technology and are considered quite valuable. As a slime rancher, you collect slimes and feed them so you can collect their plorts.
There's a lot of exploration in Slime Rancher, with 4 huge areas and many sub-areas and passages between them. There's also a lot of content. While the game is simple to play and the goal is simple, there's all manner of upgrades to unlock from teleporters to health and jetpack efficiency increases. You can upgrade your corrals and farms and coops to make things run smoother, too.
Not everything has to be purchased though. Fruit and vegetables grow in the wild, and there's boxes with random goodies and treasure capsules waiting to be discovered, too!
I don't want to say too much, as this is a wonderful and magical feeling title and I'd hate to spoil that for anyone, but it's a great game that's fun even though a lot of the gameplay boils down to sucking things into your vac-pac or shooting them out. This is a case where even though what you're doing may be a boring action, the way you do it and the reasons for doing so make the game a real treat.
So the graphics. My god the graphics. This game is gorgeous, from its great execution of the realistic turned cartoony style to it's crisp design and great use of vibrant and varied color. The whole game is a visual treat full of varied VFX and unique areas with distinct identities. Oh, and did I mention everything everywhere is freaking adorable? Absolutely anyone can find something to enjoy here, gameplay and graphics-wise.
The audio in Slime Rancher is fantastic. Each area has its fair share of unique ambience, but since so much of the game involves the wildlife, each area gets its own sort of unique sound through the foreground noises it produces also. Most sounds are concise and satisfying, and have the feel of a happy birthday celebration. Streamers and confetti shooting off, joyous laughter, plants and wildlife being spit out of the ground with a fun popping sound, plorts clinking around, etc. The music is just as happy, and just as stellar. Maybe after 10 or 20 or 50 or 100 hours you'll get tired of it, depending on your tastes, but until then it's a blast.
So if you somehow didn't see this coming, I can safely recommend Slime Rancher at:
Full price.

The COD franchise is one to both love and hate.  I think the PC versions have suffered from neglect since consoles started to dominate and some of the content has just plain not worked for me.  The last co-op that worked for me was MW2.   I haven't tried co-op on this one yet.  It's the same COD we know and love.  We know we'll get something similar to last time, similar controls and actions.  The new engine seems to make prettier graphics, more detailed.  I never had a crash in game and installation was smooth.  That was an improvement over previous games.  The single player was of similar length to past games and it was good.  Kevin Spacey was a nice addition.  Multiplayer:  Now we have these exo-suits where you can double jump and also thrust in any direction briefly while in the air.  What does that mean?  Now we have 3-d bunny hopping.   Very annoying!  OMG, the most annoying thing in this whole game.  Still, shooting someone down like a clay pidgeon is satisfying.  Using your suits strength the melee kills are also entertaining as sometimes people go flying.  The MP maps are on par with past games with interesting variety for snipers, run and gunners, campers, etc.  Nicely done.  I have grown annoyed with the season pass model where content such as maps I feel are held back so they can ask you for more money for them later.  I never have bit on that one.  Especially with original content on most games not even working correctly for me.  Sadly, I buy each COD that comes out each year.  Some of the single player has excellent replay value and I like the single player.  I rank up on MP and then don't prestige and wait for the next game.  Sometimes I play with friends so MP has a particular value there.  And I'm talking MP team deathmatch as I've said previously co-op has been very hit or miss in working for me, mostly miss.  A nice working co-op like MW2 would add a lot of value for me as my brother and I love that one.  I recommend this game if you want to do MP online.  The single player alone is too short for the cost, so if that's all you want, wait for it on sale.

Combat is a bit simple, kick down a zombie, shoot it in the head. Or stomp him to "death". It gets old quickly, but you *can* actually clear area's, suffering only the occasional pach that's caught your scent.
I'm continuing with some serious expectations!

I cannot believe how great this game is, and especially at this price. I'm 42 hours into it and not yet near the end. At least I don't think so. I'm the type that likes to take my time and explore slowly, finding everything. This game has a lot to explore and you can pretty much pick your own pace, at least until you run out of insulin which hasn't been a problem so far.
I found the game challenging at first, mainly because I didn't understand the dodging mechanic and I didn't realize all the options that are available to you. There are a lot of things at play here and they are not obvious at first but once you understand how things work you begin to see the simple genius behind the design. I'm only just now realizing different ways use the command interface to multitask my group far beyond simply fetching supplies.
The story is interesting and the characters have just enough individualism that I know who I like and who I send out to fetch things with low ammo and no escort :) The world feels real enough as you see NPCs in other communities relying on each other for food, bandages, water, etc.
My favorite example of NPC behavior was when I had a fist fight in a small camp of looters. After the fight, my opponent was bleeding but nobody in the camp had any bandages left. He went running off and I followed him. He made it to an abandoned car, got bandages, and stopped his bleeding. But he then ran into a zombie and got infected. He ran back to his camp asking his people for antidote but turned into a zombie before he could get help. I gained respect from the people in the camp by helping them kill him :)
I can't recommend this game enough. This is a lot of entertainment for the price of lunch.

I'll be honest: My interest in this game is based purely on the soundtrack by HOME. I also happen to love the occasional puzzler. Long story short? The most talented of artists don't always sign off their music to quality products
Matris' gameplay could be best described as... the painters version of Tetris? Although I'd more say it was the Duplo or Mega Bloks of Tetris games, but even with that comparison, I think in some ways that's giving this game more credit than it deserves, as it would justify why it was made. Matris lacks that certain raison d'être, both in design and its gameplay. You kind of just stick puzzle pieces into place, and that's really it. None of the other game modes take it in an interesting direction either, as you lack that reason to care about your placement like in real Tetris when you fear your blocks touching the top of the screen. You have all day, really, and you could think out your moves precisely, and that's just not exciting.
Classic puzzle games like Tetris or Columns are about a constant assault on the player. How will you deal with what the game throws your way next? Matris (like a mattress, as in, the game will put you to sleep because it's so boring) isn't interested in asking you that question. I don't even think it's even that interested in itself with its colorless, grey and plain design. Yes I know I can customize it myself, but it says a lot when not even the designers thought fit to make the presentation eye catching for people that you know, might REFUND the game, cause you could get everything you need within five minutes.
The soundtrack by HOME, while great, just doesn't fit. The gameplay is too slow. Even in time attack - where you're given a way too generous (I'd actually call it laborious) 10 minute limit - never do I ever feel compelled to race the clock. It'd be like if Jeopardy had the Duke Nukem theme playing throughout the entirety of the show. Does it make Jeopardy more exciting? No. It'd still be the same old sassy molassy Trebek askin' questions. HOME's music deserves a better home in a moderately faster paced game.
The game reeks of mobile phone game design, where if you give the game your undivided attention, you get nothing in return, because it's just not that taxing to play. It needed something to drive the gameplay, but maybe like myself, the devs were too excited about licensed music and not the actual content of the game.

For those who missed the original Serious Sam games, Revolution is the best choice right now: by combining both Encounters and updating them to meet today's technical standards, it lets everyone equally enjoy this old-school shooter series, testing their abilities (and the power of their serious arsenal) against hordes upon hordes of monsters.

When the original Serious Sam games got too outdated to play them without issues on modern systems, the developers decided to just remake them entirely in their then-newest engine as HD editions. There were some players though who preferred the original– either for the lower requirements, the old-school looks, or because they didn’t like the small level and gameplay changes. So, they disassembled the old engines and completely remade them as a single package, completed with a series of bug fixes and some community levels.
The result was Revolution, which turned out to be so good that now it even replaced the original First and Second Encounters in the Steam store.
If you never met this series, then buckle up, because Serious Sam is a very old-school FPS. There are no covers or health regeneration (unless you play the sissy difficulty), and the enemies won’t stop in the distance to make sure the player has time to kill them at their leisure. Here, you have to gruellingly cut, burn, slice, shoot, and explode your way through courtyards upon courtyards of alien monsters in ancient Egypt, the Maya Empire, Babylon, and medieval Europe.
This may suggest some grim and gritty tone, but Serious Sam is also known for its cheesy humour, usually in the form of corny one-liners– mimicking the worst of 80s action movie clichés– or goofy secrets. This combination of hardcore action and nonsensical writing was one of the reasons Serious Sam reached its cult classic status, and the reason anyone who never played it should do so at least once.

So first off I actually started playing this game 6 years ago, but only connected it to Steam recently so that's why my play time is only said to be 100 odd hours. Now honestly I didn't play for all of those 6 years and for the reasons I am about to cover...
The game has some heavy pay to win issues, now some people (usually those who pay actually...) defend the game and say that if you earn enough 'joker tickets' you can buy these OP premium weapons for 7 days. The problem I'd argue is that it takes about a week for doing specific missions known as 'fight club' missions to actually achieve the joker tickets necessary in the meanwhile you are facing off against opponents whom oay for premium weapons and I have always played without paying any money so I can most defintley confirm that premium weapons absolutley out class their standard counter-parts and only after heavy modification after loads of playing time can one even stand on the same level as a premium weapon. Of course natrually a premium assault rifle will still lose out to a standard shotgun at point-blank range assuming the shotgun is being used well as it is not unheard of for a shotgun to lose in this scenario. I have played with the regular weapons then one-day trialed their premium counter-parts and it is very easy to notice the difference.
Another issue is that the community are generenally♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like if you've ever thought a community in a game like LoL is bad then wait till you see APB. But yeah people won't be kind to you. Also this has been massively improved upon (as once this was literally no exaggeration a problem every other match in a standard district) but there is still the occassional hacker that ruins the game. But I am thankful as this is way less common than before.
On the flip-side the customisation is better than any game I have ever seen ever and I do love it. It is incredibly in-depth and you can truly create your own identity, both in your character and vehicle. However once more customisation is better with premium allowing you to obtain a few more pieces of gear that are usually impossible to get due to pricing and also more decals are allowed on you and your gear and vehicles if you are a premium member.
Also I generenally find the combat fun, hit detection can be quite bad. But if you aren't playing against a load peeps using premium weapons, which makes up a large amount of the community, then it is quite fun and skill based. But as I said no matter how skilled you are your assualt rifle will lose out to a premium assualt rifle at almost any range. Except there does exist the odd bad premium weapon.
Overall I wouldn't recommend. Unless like me you love customisation and the game can be very fun, it has a few interesting gameplay features/ the game just feels unique in it's gameplay despite just being a third person shooter. But if you play for free you'll find yourself heavily disadvantaged and will recieve slightly limited customisation options. Having said that the customisation is still truly amazing and it's weird to think that a not so good game can nail one mechanic so much better than any other I've ever seen.

This game costs only £4, but it contains hours of fun for those who want to enjoy a zombie apocolypse game where you build your own community.
I adore this game. The choices you make can define how your gameplay is, such as: Should I recruit this group of five to my community? They could be used for guarding, farming or constructing buildings, but they also need to be fed which can drain my supplies and risk my other survivors' lives if they venture out to get more food for them.
I am very impressed by this game, considering that it costs such a small price is a big surprise for the quality of it. I wish we could see more games like these more and State of Decay. I adore a game where you build a community during an apocolypse or other circumstances.
The only cons I would say about this game is that the camera angle and this 'fog of war' that limits your visibility to such a small sight, by the time you've seen a group of infected and raised your gun, they're already on top of you and infecting you. I have had this happen quite often, which is an annoyance. The other con would be the unecessarily fast zombies in this game, there is nothing that has annoyed me more than having one of my runners ambushed by a group of infected and then constantly caught by them when they try to outrun them, eventually they either get caught and bitten due to the poor fatigue that takes a long time to improve or they waste all their ammo on shooting them whilst moving, which is irritating due to the poor accuracy when moving even when a survivor is right in front of them.
Overall, there are improvements to be made, but this game at the current moment is great in my opinion.

Breaking the review into two parts, SP and MP; I'll be trying more multiplayer and might update part of the review:
SP:
The story is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Nothing about it is redeeming, not even Kevin Spacey.  There are lines of dialog that don't make sense (to name one, the two "best friends" have a conversation in the first cutscene that only non-friends would have), there are actions that simply don't make sense (One hilarious example: The female chick has a fight with a guy who doesn't have an EXO suit. Even though she punches a dent into a car's hood, she can't overpower the guy), and the set pieces are too... restrictive.
It seems like whenever a COD game wants to introduce something it can only do it for 5 minutes. Assassin's Creed does this and it is getting really, really annoying when something that is generally fun is only used for 5 minutes.
Now, why do modern shooters feel the need to tell me to "Follow" a character? For 90% of the game, I was able to run ahead of characters, only hitting an invisible wall, while they yapped about stuff that was unimportant.
And the last thing I wanna ♥♥♥♥♥ about is this EXO suit. Do not compare it to the suit from Crysis or the jump pack from Titanfall because it certainly is not. Just like other COD games, the EXO suit feels like a knock off idea that never goes anywhere. I never used the suit's powers once during the story mode unless it told me. Unlike Titanfall or Crysis, the suit used really does feel tacted on at the last minute.
MP:
Let's talk about this EXO suit a little more because the faults become a lot more glaring in multiplayer. Pro tip for the devs: Don't say "parkour" then add ledges to a map which you CANNOT grab. Every single map in this game was designed WITHOUT the EXO suit in mind. I can't tell you how many times my EXO suit jump couldn't reach a ledge or tried to grab a ledge that was just decoration.
The maps are too small. Titanfall had larger levels with the same amount of people, 6 on 6. THe chances of getting shot in the back were lower to almost non-existent due to the distance between respawn locations. This just isn't the case with this COD. I think 70% of my deaths were respawn, wait 2 seconds, get shot in the back.
Nothing about the weapons or EXO suit 'abilities' are unique. Again, let's look at Titanfall! There are three abilities: Cloak, Sprint, and Wallhack. Cloak isn't too great on players, but makes you invisible to Titans; Sprint lets you run faster for a bit and regen faster; and wallhack lets you... wallhack for a bit. There are nearly triple abilities in COD:AW, yet none of them are special while some are outright useless. Do you want extra health that doesn't help, or what about an ability that makes you hover slowly for an enemy to kill you? No, of course not.
There are a lot of weapons and, just like the previous CODs, a lot of them could have been cut from the game. Some are better than others right out of the box, which makes me wonder why bother putting them in.
Oh, and I hope you like Team Deathmatch, because that's all people play and there are 0 unique modes which are worth it.
Final thoughts:
This is a $20 game. If the asking price is higher, don't bother. If you want a real parkour game with innovation to the COD formula, go get Titanfall.

I was skeptical at first, but Sledgehammer did a pretty decent job here. Though it's still not as optimized as the Black Ops series, it can still proud itself of being a far more superior COD than Ghosts. The exo abilities are a big welcome to this rather stagnant franchise. It's innovative and that's what we gamers want. The only downside would be the same awful P2P sytem found in MW and Ghosts. If you're playing from South East Asia like me, then I would advise you to play with a party. On top of that, annoying lag spikes and stutters can sometimes appear. A few of the maps are broken e.g Defender, Recovery, Instinct and such. You would simply lag to death, specially when you're not playing with a high end rig.
With Black Ops 3 revealed, this COD franchise would probably be the one and only peculiar incarnation due to the aerial dog fights courtesy of the exo abilities. Since BO3 would bring COD veterans back into the battles on ground level as much as possible.
Overall, great effort from Sledgehammer. They just need to fix the bugs. And oh yeah, a more stricter anti-cheat policy would be nice as there are too many suspicious players out there.

As someone who loves games that use their basic movement systems as their core mechanic--games like Dustforce, Mirror's Edge etc; this is one of my favorite releases of 2015. Grapple is one of my dream games finally realized.
The basic mechanics are simple: you are a blob that can attach to the side and underside of platforms, jump, and fire a small string of yourself onto solid objects to grapple and swing past areas where there is no ground to land on. Further mechanics are introduced in the levels themselves, such as red death platforms, ungrapple-able forcefield platforms, white bouncy platforms and pink cannons.
The quality of the levels rollercoasters up and down--some levels make use of brilliant ideas and flesh out the basic mechanics of the game in fresh and clever ways, while others come off as lazy free-form collections of platforms. There are several weak levels and gimmick mechanics--for example, the invisible platform gimmick (platforms that only become visible when you are close enough), which is not at all interesting or fun and results in three of the worst "maze" levels in the game. Later levels fall into the trap of an over-reliance on precision momentum slinging, using long falls, bouncy platforms and cannons. This comes to a head with a level that requires slinging with extreme precision into another cannon, which can require many attempts.
There is plenty to do: collectibles are used to guide the player through the "intended" path of each level and give reasons to return to levels for 100% optimal completion. A time trial mode challenges players to beat individual levels under a predefined par time (which is a useful gauge of performance, since there is no online leaderboard for the game). There is also a speedrun mode that challenges players to beat the game in 1 hour and 20 minutes.
As with all games, there are a few quibbles here and there that you should be aware of:

What a lovely little gem. I almost feel guilty for buying it at such a low price. I was very pleasantly surprised to learn just how fun and... honestly kind of complex this game is.
PROS:
* Great gameplay. Combat can feel a bit repetitive, but being able to cap a zombie in the leg to prevent the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ from jumping you is pretty good. I also really like the skill progression, though it can feel like a grind at times. There's homesteading, zombie shooting, looter shooting, quest taking, micro-management somewhat akin to RTS games, building a huge posse of fellow survivors, exploration... lots of content in this game.
* Content. I'm still kind of baffled just how rich this game is for its price tag. 30 hours in and I still am not done with my first playthrough. I'd say that's pretty impressive. Along the same lines, the RPG elements are pretty solid. I was amused to see that characters respond to just about anything you do to them or others in their community. If you so desired, you could just wiped everyone out with extreme prejudice, or you could be more of a peacemaker and try to recruit as many people as you can... including bandits. I'm somewhere in between. People even remember you being RUDE to them.
*Game design. The author of this game clearly went to great lengths to implement depth and replayability. There are three game winning scenarios that the player can choose from, people to save or not save, quests to take or not take, and just the fact that you can't please everyone in the game makes it so that you can easily boot it back up and try a different path.
-----
CONS:
Honestly... I can't think of many serious problems with this game other than a few minor nitpicks, but there are two things that bother me in particular-
* Ear-bleeding music. UGH. The soundtrack in this game is just hideous. I've played most of it with it muted. It's a minor gripe, I suppose, but still.
*The allied AI can sometimes be a bit bone-headed... like they may wander away from the path of safety just to make a shortcut (and bumping into zombies and looters along the way), they waste time sometimes by wandering around FOREVER looking for food or water when they could just complete their ♥♥♥♥ing jobs and go back to base to eat and drink.
----
All in all, VERY solid game. I highly recommend it. The price tag certainly helps me say that it's worth every penny.

The reason I loved the original Dishonored was because I love games that give you choices, to "play your way," and they combined it with a well told story, beautiful art style, and engaging gameplay. You will find all of these things in Dishonored 2. I never felt as if they sacrificed something for something else. Bethesda stated themselves that it is not an open world game, but they wanted it to feel like one. And it does, to an extent. The level design is fantastic in a way that they managed to create huge levels without any of it feeling pointless. It doesn't exactly feel like open world but your first few playthroughs will result in hours being spent on just one mission if you want to see it all. If you really want to see it all, you'll need to play it multiple times on both playable characters. Replay value feels slightly higher than the last game.
The magic abilities in this game have their own sort of mini upgrade trees and some of them get really interesting. Corvo retains his old powers from the previous game and Emily has her own set of unique abilities. Even though Corvo doesn't have any brand new powers, it was still a refreshing playthrough. Both Emily and Corvo seem to have picked up a small amount of Daud's powers from the original game's DLC, Corvo gaining a "stop time" while aiming blink, and Emily gaining a pull-items-and-bodies-to-me with her Far Reach. The most notable changes are to Dark Vision as it is very different than the original game.  It's less OP and, if you're used to the original, it's a bit annoying to use at first. I adjusted rather quickly and after adjusting it actually makes more sense to work this way.
The passive abilities received some minor changes and a few were added, but I found myself not using any of them besides agility pretty much at all. They're by no means useless but perhaps unnecessary. How good bone charm crafting is completely depends on what you find. If you only find charms you won't use, you won't need to combine any. My first playthrough saw heavy use of the crafting system, but my second playthrough barely even touched it.
The final upgrade of Shadow Kill is amazing for high chaos runs. :)
Enemy AI has seen a large improvement. Guards are smarter when they search for you and have smoother animations. They also act a lot more realistic when they're confused, such as when you inevitably fall on their face because you miss an assassination cue and promptly blink away. Their guard-to-guard banter is just as entertaining as well.
Well, that's about it. The rest you should find out for yourself. It's a worthy successor.

This are fantastic games, and if you haven’t played them yet, or, if you have only played the HD remasters/remakes, then you owe it to yourself to give this version a try.
Serious Sam Classics: Revolution it’s a game that incorporates both the original Serious Sam game, The First Encounter, as well as its sequel, The Second Encounter.
It merges them together in a package filled with technical tweaks that optimize both games for modern systems, adding widescreen resolution support, as well as other settings such as an fov slider.
I didn’t experience any issues other than a weird a common bug that makes it difficult to jump out of the water at times, luckily this can easily be “bypassed” by jumping just before the ledge that you’re trying to climb instead of just walking towards it.
Then there was also some glitching around some walls if I came to close to them, but I think it had to do with me playing with the highest fov setting available, a fair tradeoff in my opinion.
Besides that, no crashes, no framerate drops, and for the most part, flawless performance.
As for the games, the premise is fairly simple, you move through wide and open areas that are surrounded by beautiful “ancient culture” scenery, as you “blast” your way through thousands of enemies that come towards you in hordes.
All of the enemies in Serious Sam are deeply characteristic, and unique, they all have different attacks to keep you paying attention, for the most part all you have to do its dodge the incoming projectiles, or screaming kamikaze enemies.
And that’s pretty much it…
But the game stays fresh and enjoyable.
The first game in my opinion does get a tad bit too repetitive at times, that’s principally because as much as the levels, and areas you go through change in their design, the appearance of this areas doesn’t.
So pretty much the entirety of the first game takes place in Egypt, it’s unique at first and very beautiful aesthetically, but eventually it becomes a bit jarring to look at the same textures, sand, and pillars, over, and over, again.
The second game corrects this by not only changing the environments the levels take place in, but also by adding different obstacles in some cases, or alternatively altering how some rooms work.
At times you find yourself in one that’s a cylinder of sorts, the catch it’s that you can run around the entire area defying gravity in the process as the room keeps filling with dozens of enemies.
The pacing it’s also a lot better in the second game simply because of the way these obstacles are presented into the levels, how some of the levels change in their aesthetic as well as in their design, and also because the weapon distribution its balanced and generous.
The second game it’s divided in three areas that take away your carried weapons at the start of each one of them, it might seem annoying at first but in reality, it’s a brilliant decision that ends up making each area feel new, and each weapon pickup, even when previously carrying every single one of them, feel fresh.
The gunplay it’s also fantastic and probably the principal reason as to why the original games remain superior to the subsequent remakes that came after.
Each and every weapon that you carry its useful in different situations, the rocket launcher it’s great to take down groups of enemies that are closed together, the double-barreled shotgun it’s a nice compromise to take down single enemies that are separated from one an another, the minigun allows you to take plenty of individual enemies at once but smaller ones with low amounts of health at that.
Then there’s a series of other ones that I’m too lazy to describe, but each and every single one of them have a different purpose and a satisfying feel to them.
Pair that up with the enemies blowing into red pieces of meat, shared with the absurd and ridiculous blood effects that you can change to your liking, either for different colors, or simply to disable the entire effect, and you have a gunplay that ends up feeling incredibly satisfying and enjoyable to partake in.
I do recommend this game, and this particular version over the remasters for the simple reason the gameplay it’s significantly superior to those versions, the weapons do just the right amount of damage, the enemies have just the right amount of health, and the levels are as silly and enjoyable as you expect them to be.
In comparison to the other versions that do look significantly better but that sadly both change some aspects of the gunplay, paired with some minor but noticeable changes to the level design, as well as to how many hits certain enemies take to kill, this version remains faithful and balanced to meet the original games idea of trading off realism for silliness and fun.

You play as a blob with the ability to jump, grapple, stick to surfaces, and drop off of them. You have a goal to reach one ach level, and along the way you can acquire collectibles as well as a special collectible. Finding these are of varying difficulty.
The game controls feel okay. Sometimes, the requirement to keep your view focused on your next grapple point interferes with your desire to focus on an objective. I wish you could influence your momentum a bit more while swinging. You can't change your grapple length once attached; it's fixed to the length at which you were from your surface when you grappled.  When you're swinging past a collectible at just slightly longer or shorter lengthy, this can feel frustrating.
There's no real story or narrative here. The ball you control has no real character to speak of either. So it's really just platforming for platforming's sake, which may make this a hard title to stick with once a stage provides a player with any frustration.
The graphics are simple, and unfortunately a tad repetitive. The music is a bit forgettable, as is the sound. This feels a bit more like a tech demo that should get a full game designed around it (story, character, music, etc.), and as is, I don't think I'd recommend this to anyone but the most die-hard of 3D puzzle platformer enthusiasts or someone looking to really play around with a grappling hook mechnanic.

Hello and welcome to this review of Slime Rancher, an adorable FPS RPG about corralling slimes and stealing their poop for sweet sweet profits! Let's get started.
So the meat of Slime Rancher is in its gameplay, where you explore, discover, and...ranch slimes. You can corral them, free-roam ranch them, or let them hang out in their preferred areas and clean up their droppings to your liking.
So first off, there are small slimes that are manageable and come in a simple variety, larger slimes that are a combination of more than one, and giant stationary slimes you have to feed to break apart and get rewards from. Apart from the giant slimes, Gordos, you get plorts from the small and large (Largo) slimes, which are their magical poops that feature a wide variety of uses in technology and are considered quite valuable. As a slime rancher, you collect slimes and feed them so you can collect their plorts.
There's a lot of exploration in Slime Rancher, with 4 huge areas and many sub-areas and passages between them. There's also a lot of content. While the game is simple to play and the goal is simple, there's all manner of upgrades to unlock from teleporters to health and jetpack efficiency increases. You can upgrade your corrals and farms and coops to make things run smoother, too.
Not everything has to be purchased though. Fruit and vegetables grow in the wild, and there's boxes with random goodies and treasure capsules waiting to be discovered, too!
I don't want to say too much, as this is a wonderful and magical feeling title and I'd hate to spoil that for anyone, but it's a great game that's fun even though a lot of the gameplay boils down to sucking things into your vac-pac or shooting them out. This is a case where even though what you're doing may be a boring action, the way you do it and the reasons for doing so make the game a real treat.
So the graphics. My god the graphics. This game is gorgeous, from its great execution of the realistic turned cartoony style to it's crisp design and great use of vibrant and varied color. The whole game is a visual treat full of varied VFX and unique areas with distinct identities. Oh, and did I mention everything everywhere is freaking adorable? Absolutely anyone can find something to enjoy here, gameplay and graphics-wise.
The audio in Slime Rancher is fantastic. Each area has its fair share of unique ambience, but since so much of the game involves the wildlife, each area gets its own sort of unique sound through the foreground noises it produces also. Most sounds are concise and satisfying, and have the feel of a happy birthday celebration. Streamers and confetti shooting off, joyous laughter, plants and wildlife being spit out of the ground with a fun popping sound, plorts clinking around, etc. The music is just as happy, and just as stellar. Maybe after 10 or 20 or 50 or 100 hours you'll get tired of it, depending on your tastes, but until then it's a blast.
So if you somehow didn't see this coming, I can safely recommend Slime Rancher at:
Full price.

Edit #2: I'm putting this first, because quite honestly.. holy crap are people's reading comprehension insanely bad these days. They read something, go full retard and then talk out of their rear while patting themselves on the back like they're some genius's. I never talk about "Story" yet so many people respond with "its sandbox why were you expecting a story?" comments it blows my mind. I'm talking about content, playing mechanics. Not story. Hence why I never even write the word story anywhere in my review... I'm also talking about planned features in the future, which still when they are implimented, still won't be enough in my humble opinion.
So without further ado, onto the actual review..
It's really hard to give this game a thumbs down. Quite honestly. Is it a good game? Absolutely, for the little that it is. The planets are very interesting, the music and atmosphere is spot on, and its a fun little game to be sure without question.
So why the thumbs down?
Quite simply, because it has no depth, or purpose to anything it does. You can scream through the tech in a matter of a few hours, after that.... It's gathering resources, to build more things, to help you gather resources quicker.. That's it.. That's the game.
You build a vehicle to help you gather resources, to help you build construction parts to help you gather more resources, to help you build a spaceship to get to another planet.. where you rinse and repeat.. Build more crafting pods, to help you gather resources faster, to help you build more crafting parts to help you gather more resources, to help you get to a different planet...
Where you rinse and repeat...
Shall I continue or have you gotten the point?
That's all there is to the game.. Literally nothing.. No end game, no point, no reason to craft, or gather, or do anything.
Game is beautiful, the art style is so giggly and fun, the music relaxing and peaceful, everything about the game is great, except that there's no reason to play it...
Edit:
Since a few people don't get what Im' saying "end game" I'll use the controversial No Man's sky as an example. In No Man's Sky you have goals, and free building a base. That's an "end game", simple, but there. This game doesn't even have that.
You're building a solar panel, so you can gather quicker, to build another solar panel on a pod, to gather quicker, to build a part to help you smelt down ore, to build a bigger solar panel to help you craft quicker, to build a piece to let you build a spaceship to go to another planet and do it again from square 1....
That's the game... that's it...

This game is a prime example of why RPG's and MMORPG's are two totally different genres. This is without question an MMO, this is not the same as a stand alone ES game. If that is what you are looking for keep moving.
As MMO's go it is beautifully conceived, with living background a gorgeous visuals. It also has exciting combat that contrasts against the usual cool-down monotony of WOW clones. The quests are original and entertaining. With so much positivity what could be wrong? It isn't Elder Scrolls VI. It's that simple. Emersion is  constantly and consistently broken in over-populated dungeons with scores of other "one of a kind hero’s" slaying spiders. Let's talk about loot for a second, I was so excited when I took out my first enemy, I only got 1 gold, but that was okay it was my first level. At level five, I was still getting the 1 gold coin at level 10 I wasn't even shocked anymore. Any dreams I had of braving the horrors of forgotten dungeons and hauling massive amounts of treasure out where quickly snuffed out.  I could go on about how the feel was off, the backtracking, the horses, and the other nitpicky things that bugged me... but this review will probably never be read and this is just for me to vent my disappointment.
If you are wanting a very expensive MMO where you can say "Oooo I play pretty MMO's" then this is for you. If you want to feel like the Hero of Kvatch, just equip your boots of blinding speed and speed off. That's why I came to the party, and it feels like a member of the Dark Brotherhood has showed up to pick us off one by one with his dagger of disappointment. There is nothing to Fus Do Rah about here...

APB Reloaded is yet another of those games that I truly want to love.... but I don't.  The game is yet another mmo that has been ruined by toxic community and bots, but is also plagued by hackers.  And this is saying something, because it used to be SO much worse than its current state!
The game's premise is that you choose a side of the law: either become a gang member to commit robberies and other crimes or become a freelance law enforcement officer and stop crime... while also using a 'gang' mentality.
Gang mentality is THE key to play in this game.  This is a mmo that you CANNOT solo (which is not neccessarily a bad thing) due to the fact that pvp is open world and also the core aspect of the game.  The starter zone has roving bands of player killers.  And that's the thing with this.  Because it is open world pvp, ganks abound.  Being a criminal is far more rewarding in this game, but also more hazardous as you can be preyed upon by both cops and other criminals whereas being a cop only leaves you open to criminals.  But the only true method of gaining in game currency as a cop is stopping criminals.  Preferrably via arrest and NOT kill.  And so many are out there... in groups...  And it is so easy to kill vs arrest.
Pro's and Con's:
++ nice graphics
++++++ Probably THE BEST character customization engine of ANY mmo out there.  Customization sliders for DAYS.  Ability to create your own unique tattoos in game.  Ability to style your clothes using the same system/methods used to create tattoos.  Can even do this for vehicles!
++ The criminal gameplay is actually pretty fun.  Especially if you can find a sucker that has a vehicle full of loot ready to fence and they aren't able to stop you from stealing the vehicle.
-- Not fun if you are the aforementioned sucker.  If you play alone, this WILL happen... ALOT.
--- Not enough reward in game for actually playing the game's missions.
--- INSANE costs for weapons, gear and customizations.  Seriously, the people running the cash shops in this game are the REAL criminals.
-------- Pay2win.  The best weapons.  Permenant weapons that are not rentals.  The best vehicles.  These are available in the cash shop.
----- While the game sports the best in character customization, if you want a wide variety of options and ability to customize, you're going to have to pay for it via cash shop.

There are many negative reviews about Dishonored 2 and it's performance issues, which are supposedly gonna be fixed soon (hopefully), so for this review let's put aside technical details and delve into the actual game.
When you "press any key" you are greeted by trully artistic (at least in my opinion) menu which makes you even more excited to play the game.
There's a short tutorial for newcomers and for those who have forgotten how Dishonored works.
The story is polished and interesting, the choices well made and make you think about how you want to proceed in game.
Each situation has multiple ways to approach and the ability to choose between Emily and Corvo just enchances that.
For example: you can sneak around like a shadow using Emily's "Shadow Form" then rip apart unaware enemies or "suck" their souls out. Or you can just blast your enemies away with deadly bullets and slice them with your blade.
Visually the game looks really nice and detailed. I spent at least an hour just exploring each map and seeing what they can offer.
In conclusion: I greatly enjoyed each minute of the time I spent on the game so far. It is a great successor to Dishonored 1 (Which is also a really good game). In my opinion once the performance issues are fixed, this might even become a Game of the Year (Maybe not officialy, but for me - for sure).

People often whine about how it's "Pay2win" or infested with hackers, which just isn't true.

APB is definitely a game you want to play with a group of friends, as it is a team game.
It may also be hard to get started, with all the experienced players there.
However, if you can get past that learning curve, it becomes a whole lot of fun :)

See you in San Paro!

This is a review of the actual game, not its optimization issues on various, primarily AMD, builds, though I will say that mine is total AMD, and I have very, very few issues.
I've been playing around 8 hours, as of this review, and this is what I think as of now.
It feels like Dishonored. That really sums it up.
Many sequels, the developer tries to "move forward", or something like that as far as gameplay and design. Dishonored 2 is a true continuation, not, to my mind, a sequel. The game play feels the same, to a point, the appearance, the mechanics, it just feels...right, what I expected.
I love that you can play as Emily or Corvo, that they, over the course of the game, fill in those missing 15 years, explain just what led to the circumstances of the second game, you may have to pay attention, but it's there.
Dishonored 2 is, to me, actualy much harder than Dishonored, even on the easy setting. I'm doing virtually no damage to anyone, but I'm currently on High Chaos. Enemies detect easier than they did in the first game, but, at least on easy, go back to what they were doing quickly. Being detected or having bodies found really counts against you. Compared to other games, though, the fact that its harder doesn't bother me, I actually appreciate it, and understand why.
My biggest problem with the game: I had to relearn to look UP. Lol. My second biggest problem with the game: I'm once again losing whole hours in what feels like the blink of an eye. :p
My first playthrough is as Emily, and while I expect things to change when I play as Corvo, I do not expect how I perceive the game to change, except to possibly get even better.
I hope this helped someone make a decent, informed choice on buying the game.
Also, oh my god, visually, this surpasses the first game, and it was completely stunning. This is...this is unreal beautiful.

Before you downvote this review, note that I'm not evaluating the first two encounters themselves.
I'm a Serious Sam fanatic and I've played all the games of the series--but I still think both the First and Second Encounter suffer from some odd design choices such as the puzzles and platforming. SS3 is my favorite old-school FPS.
That being said, I would not recommend you purchase SS:R anytime soon until there is some major content underway. Unlikely as it may be as this is not a full-time project by CroTeam. You can get this game for free if you own the classic games, but the HD versions are what I would consider the superior remake over SSR.
This review is to evaluate what you are getting with the EA product.
Here is a detailed list of my scale:
1 : A bug-filled mess with zero content or missing many features. Far too early to get into the games. Also, games that get updates infrequently.
2: A game with the beginnings of ideas, yet too soon to invest any time. Check back for updates to see if things improve. (Also, games that play well but do not have all the basic features, such as promised multiplayer modes.)
3: A game that is in a playable state, yet may not have all its technical issues sorted out. Features are all available--all game modes--while they may not be finalized. Games in this section are cautious recommendations to buy, so you should check the updates.
4: A game that is in a playable state, technically competent, and has enough content to be worthy of purchasing right now. Features are all accounted for and the updates for the game are frequent enough to not discourage cautious buyers. Of course, the timing of these updates should be with respect to the size of the development team.
5: A game that could be considered finished. It is in the final stages of development with balancing and other last minute changes to be resolved to be fit for release.
To CroTeam's credit, they do tell people not to buy into SS:R right now unless you want to test out their servers or get early into the game. But I don't understand why they put this through EA to begin with if they had nothing new besides the mutliplayer.
This is an odd thing to state because the game does and doens't have all its content. In one sense, it does have enough to warrant a purchase if you don't own the first two encounters, all of the First and Second encounter are present. And it does have a revamped multiplayer to satiate old-school players.
The final expansion is still not going to be released anytime soon, which besides the updated engine and the 64 player cooperative mode, was the only thing I was interested in playing.
This game plays as good as the classic/HD games.
I marked this down several points not because of the low textures from the classic games which were improved with both HD games. The reason is because they didn't improve the technical faults of the original games.
Most notably, the sound limitations of the original game. Enemies' sound effects do not tell you where their location is, the one major flaw of the classic games when it came to hordes of Kleers and the suicide-bomb runners.
For single-player and local multiplayer purposes, the game runs just fine. I've read on the forums that servers can be a pain to get working properly and have issues for some people.
This product won't be finished anytime soon. CroTeam made this into a fan-project, which I am happy in one sense for them to support a classic series, yet I fail to see any reason to buy this product anytime soon unless they add in the new campaign. (I'll look forward to Serious Sam 4.)
