When I was first asked to do a review for Survivalist, I admit that my expectations were a bit low due to the old-school graphics and the relatively low price on an indie game developed and published by a single individual I hadn't heard of before. Being a veteran of survival, RPG, and all types of strategy games in general I still intended to give a fair review based on the game's content. Twenty minutes into the game all i could say was "Wow!" This game is amazing and so much fun. It masterfully mixes Survival, RPG, RTS, and Action elements into a highly addictive adventure that will entertain you for numerous hours and even at full price I strongly recommend this game to fans of all these genres. Not convinced? Then read on...
In Survivalist the ultimate goal is obviously to survive yet another zombie apocalypse. Except that these zombies offer a greater challenge than typical survival games. The
has multiple strains with varying effects and incubational periods before turning into a zombie yourself. Each will require an antigen specific for that particular type. Another difference is that these zombies are incredibly fast and agile. Don't expect to outrun them. In this game its fight or die.
Surviving will ultimately depend on building a strong community of people working together. You will need to build a strong base able to defend against attacks. It will also need to provide other basic basic needs to survivors like clean drinking water, fresh crops of food, shelter and hygiene. This will require you to recruit people with varying skills, gather an assortment of building materials, and collect items that can be useful. There are many NPC's in the game and most of them can be pursuaded in different ways to join your community. Players can use gifts, perform tasks, or even strong-arm characters into joining. There are countless possibilites based on dialogue and other decisions made over the course of the game. Its really nice how all choices have consequences. And, don't be fooled. Not everybody you encounter is a friendly face ready to welcome you with open arms. There are other survivor communities and bands of looters scattered across the map with their own needs in mind.
Members of your community can be assigned to perform different jobs either by direct control or by using the command feature which will enable you to avoid the hassles of micromanagement. Individuals have a handful of stats that level up through use of that particular skill. They are affected by respect and approval ratings even after being recruited so they can decide to leave your community if they become unhappy with your leadership skills. These are just some of the many challenges that this game offers.
Survivalist is definitely one of those games Steam users won't want to miss. I strongly recommend picking this game up if you're a fan of Survival, RPG, RTS, or Action  games and the price is unbeatable for the content you receive. Forget about the fact that its made by one person on a low budget rather than by an entire development team with studio backing. This game can easily compare to big name titles like State of Decay and hold its own. Yes, the game is that good. I can hardly wait for the sequel.

I've yet to join the fighter's guild or mage guild, yet so I'm not sure how far those take you. But, this game has a deep back history that is revealed in the books you can read and the class/race story line type quests. You can really feel each area is uniquley designed for the races that live there and they are fun to explore. The ambient sound, typical Elder Scrolls voice acting, and great music are all there to draw you in along with some good graphics. I only say good graphics, because I feel they are a little dumbed down to MMO proportions.
Quests: Do you like to group? Go ahead. Do you like to solo? Go ahead. So far, I feel the quests have been a lot of fun and refreshing from the typical MMO grind and collect type quests. I cannot say for sure how it is in higher levels as I have only put 11 hours into the game so far and have tried creating multiple classes/races to get a feel for each one. I keep waiting for the typical quests to pop up, though and I've yet to dive into any PVP action.
Gameplay/Skills: I like the idea of selecting certain skills paths and having those morph and upgrade. Every class can use magicka type spells/skills and/or stamina type weapons skills. The downside is that you can only have so many skills on your skill bar at a time, but this leads to some strategy as to how you want to build and play your character. The other fun aspect is actually fighting in typical Elder Scrolls fashion: click the mouse to attack, hold down for more power, right click to block, and so on. No auto-attack! Also, the mobs move around, dodge, and block. I feel like I am actually playing the game instead of hitting numbers on my keyboard at static enemies.
Crafting: Get ready to loot every box and barrel as there is a whole lot you can do with crafting. From cooking some food to give you stat upgrades, to smithing weapons/armor, and to alchemy, crafting has something for everyone that lends to better equipment, etc. You can also craft/wear any style of armor you want or use any weapon. Each type of armor also has a skill tree that provide help for you character.
Character creation: As in Elder Scrolls fashion, there are almost too many options! But this leads to some cool character designs that can help everyone stand out from each other. Although as I've said and the game description says that you can play any character how you want, there are some drawbacks as each race has certain strengths in certain areas. LIke the Redguard lend themselves to fighting or the High Elves to magicka. But a magicka shooting High Elf could use a two-hander or a Redguard sword and board tank could throw some magicka skills out there.
The only caveat: Pay to play... Sometimes its hard to bite down and pay per month when there are some good free to play MMOs out there, like Rift.
I agree with the metascore at 71/100 and could say that it could go a little higher to 75/100. If you like the Elder Scrolls series and enjoy playing with other people, then give this game a try. If you're new to the series, I think this game will provide a lot of fun and interest for an MMO that lends itself to play a character as you want. Not to mention, a strong history with a series that really laid the groundwork for many RPGs and MMORPGs today. If you're still not sure, wait until it is on sale again and give it a try and if you still don't like it, cancel before the free 30 days is up.

So I have noticed a lot of negative reviews, even before I proceeded to purchase the game for myself and I just want to clear the waters here.
THE PRICE: This seems to be the main concern for people here. "I really don't want to spend this much on a game." You need to understand this game is new, as all new games, the initial price is nothing surprising at all.. On top of the initial $59.99 you will require a credit card for monthly subscription as this is an MMORPG and it is to be expected. Although $15 is quite steep for a subscription, I'm almost certain you will get your play time out of it, which I will adress next.
THE GAMEPLAY: This part reallty impresses me, the customization offered when you start your character is incredible! I feel like I am playing my own unique mer, which is a submerging aspect for a gamer to find in an MMORPG. Once you've created your very own character, you then go through a tutorial which teaches you the basic run down of combat and such, and then you are shipped off to start your life in Tamriel! (which is ABSOLUTELY HUGE) I promise you there is no shortage of quests and things to do! you can spend hours upon hours in a city finding people who need an able bodied adventurer such as yourself!

THE COMMUNITY: The community has been very helpful in guiding me through everything I need to know this far, all you need to do is reach out and ask, there are many guilds based around helping new players. I find that one of the aspects of this game I have the most fun with is that you meet people(other players) throughout your quests and sometimes even get to team up with them! The game was definitely geared toward having a great community rooted in team work. (although you have the option to solo)
OVER ALL CONSENSUS: Bare in mind that every review you read holds bias to the critic. I really enjoy this game and although some people may not be able to dish out a hefty $14.99 monthly to play, I do recommend they give it a taste before throwing it away. The people you will meet are fairly new as well, so you have the opportunity to get in on the game while it's still fresh. My only suggestion is that you don't take the negative reviews so seriously and give the game a try for yourself.
I'll see you in Tamriel!

First things, first.  I did beta test The Elder Scrolls Online, and did not overly care for the game then.  However, I figured I'd give it another go when it finally went on sale.  BIG MISTAKE.
While the game is absolutely beautiful and has an amazing soundtrack, this is not enough to pull this game out of the gutter.   I went into this knowing full well that this was not "Skyrim".  Having played MMORPGs for 15+ years now, I was looking forward to the adaptation of the elder scrolls universe into MMO format.  With all the MMOs that have come and gone, you'd think the newer ones would have noticed what companies did right, and what they did wrong.  Zenimax Online is clueless, utterly clueless.
The biggest problem is, the game does not know what it is trying to be.  Sure, there are lots of people around, but it still feels like a single player game most of the time.  The group finder tool used to put together random parties for dungeons is absurd, it does not check that the right classes are being put into a random group.  Both attempts I had put me in a group without a healer, making the dungeon impossible to complete.
Selling items to other players is a hassle and a real throwback to older MMOs like Everquest.  There is no public auction house like in most MMOs of the last decade.  Instead, there are guild shops.  Items are listed by members, and only available for purchase by other members, severely limiting a customer base.  This in turn has people flooding the zone chats with their wares in hopes of finding a buyer.
The crafting system is decent, however VERY tedious.  You would think that the most effective way to level up a craft would be to actually craft stuff right?  Wrong, in ESO, you get by far the most exp by breaking items apart into their base ingrediants.  This itself isn't a bad thing, however, the experience difference is so big, that it makes leveling through creating items feel like a waste of time.  The crafting can not be automated like in most MMOs, so you are stuck sitting there tapping the "R" key every few seconds (just like in Skyrim).
The combat system is clunky at best for an MMO.  Healing especially is hard to deal with.  After my failed attempts to run a dungeon due to lack of healing, I created a healer and leveled it up enough to do the first dungeon.  It was painful to say the least.  There is no targeting someone and casting a heal spell on them.  Almost all of the heal spells are area of effect based, and target seemingly random wounded allies.  It does not prioritize the most wounded, and with target number limits, more often than not, the people who need healing the most, do not get it.  There are some spells that are single target, however, targeting them is so much more diffficult with this combat system.  Standing still is a no-no in this game, there are always lots of enemy abilities causing you to move.  Casting a spell on another player requires facing them and having your reticule over them when you hit the button.  If they are comstantly moving, it becomes very difficult to actually hit them with your spell.  If they move right as you cast the spell, you instead cast it on yourself, wasting the resources it took to cast it.
Those of you that have played previous Elder Scrolls and Fallout games, will know that bugs were commonplace and usually left for the modders to fix.  Apparently that philosophy carries over to the online version as well.  The game is plagued by so many bugs, you would expect it to still be in beta.  I personally experienced a bug that forced me to log out and back in if I killed an enemy using a specific ability.  It left me unable to interact with anything because it thought I was still in combat.  I skimmed through their customer support forums, lots of reported bugs, but I didn't find a single response from their customer service team.
My verdict, only play this game if you are interested in the lore, as there is tons of it.  All quests and dialogues are voice acted, which is nice, however, all that voice acting does make the game file size insanely large.  They also reuse previous voice actors.  It felt a little odd hearing one of the commonly used voices from Skyrim in ESO.  Even if you find this game on sale again, it is not worth it.  Judging by the number of guilds full of people dying out due to inactivity, this game will go free to play or shut down completely within a year.

After finally picking this game up I have to say, at least for me, the performance issues I experienced at launch are gone. The game runs at a solid 60 when capped on a GTX 1080ti at 1080p and I didn't see it dip once. At 4k I get around 40fps at ultra settings which is better than I expected as well. When uncapped I hit 120 fps almost all the time while at 1080p which is the engines maximum limit.
The game has very few bugs with just the odd gameplay glitch here and there but they are pretty rare now.
The game is a huge step up over the last game in size but also depth and it feels like more effort was put into the level design giving alot more different ways to complete each mission. There's a greater emphasis on exploration as well as alot of new powers, weapons, two playable protagonists and alot more.
Overall I would strongly recommend this game to any stealth gamer or anyone that wants a fun assassin action game. With alot of replayability I would say thats its probably worth full price if you can't wait for a sale but either way its a really good game and worth the money.

I was as close to recommending a game as I might ever get, but ultimately, the game doesn't keep its promises.
The first chapter really was charming, as I am a sucker for old mansions, and I thought the development team really did a great job of creating it. It wasn't hard by any means, but it worked for me. When I reached chapter 2 and finally got the chance to see what's in the cellar, I welcomed the change of pacing. Now, it wasn't as much about taking your time and looking around, but about finding the perfect way so to not fall into the hands of the dark presence down there. The next level was quite the same, and the next level was quite the same, too, and the last level was, again, the same. Not once did I have a feeling of some sort of progression. It just went on and on. Go in there, find this and that, come back, proceed. And it's not that hard, either. Sure, you will get caught by the presence, but I never had the feeling that I outsmarted it by planning my way. I was just running around and, with one level, didn't see it at all.
So while the game starts interesting and builds a decent mytery as to what is going on in the vaults, it does not deliver story- or gameplay-wise.

I recommend this game with mixed feelings.
I bought this on sale, and I think  that is when it should be bought. Lets get the good stuff out of the way, because there is a good bit. The game is gorgeous. The mansion looks creepy and has a definite sense of foreboding. As you explore the mansion, the only soundtrack you get is the thunderstorm happening outside. I loved it. Sadly, the only music soundtrack you get is when you are reading notes, and it is highly repetitive. I feel that it breaks the rhythm of the game. I loved walking through a beautiful mansion at night with no musical accompaniment.  I loved finding and reading all over the place to get the story. There were some light puzzles, but backtracking wasn't a big hindrance. Hindrances came in part 2 of the game but we'll get to that. Part 1 of the game took place in the mansion: reading notes and solving light puzzles until you get to Part 2, which changes locations and feel......and not all for the better.
The bowels of the mansion look great. There are still periodic notes to find and light light puzzles to solve to go deeper underground toward the resolution of the game, but now there is an evil entity chasing us, and the underground cellars are a maze. This is when the game changed for me. What started as a light adventure/creepy walking simulator turns into a very tense cat and mouse maze scramble as you try to flee the evil chasing you. It's not fun. It's taxing. There were notes I know I missed in the cellars but I didn't have the will to go after them all because I didn't feel like dying....again. I died a lot. Fear and anxiety turned it frustration. When I beat the game, I was rewarded with a newspaper front page...and thats it. If this had been a straight walking sim, or light puzzle game in a creepy beautiful mansion, I would have been satisfied. But after 5 underground levels of mazes and evil chasing me....sorry  I want a better resolution than that. The ending felt like a cop out.
Now you are probably wondering why I am still recommending this game! I liked the look of the entire mansion, the first half, and the story. I felt those were strong enough to carry the rest. The second half would probably be more fun with a friend or a group and then you can tense together and laugh at your inability to run away well. I'm glad I played it, but I'm REALLY glad I bought it on sale.

This starts out like an adventure/point and click and turns into a slightly more action/puzzle game.   I won't go into details for the sake of the story.  The theme is set during and after WW1.
The graphics and sound are great.   There's no "low effort retro pixel" junk happening here.   The game is however fairly short, you can sprint through it in about 30 minutes with help of a walkthrough, but it might take an hour or so if you're puzzling it out on your own.
Regardless I'd rather play a 30 minute well made game than an endlessly low effort retro 2D platformer of the sort which infests Steam lately.
Well executed and worth picking up if you enjoy quality.   I hope the developers will go on and get hired by a professional publisher to fully make use of their considerable talent.

The first chapter is great. The game looks nice and has a good sound design, despite obviously low budget. The creepy mansion is fun to explore, with a decent story and clever puzzles providing solid gameplay.
And then the game throws everything out of the window and replaces it with generic dark tunnels and an unimaginative monster chasing you, insta-killing you on touch. Because that's something we've never seen in a horror game, right? Oh wait...
Puzzles are still there but they're mostly the same - you're always looking for missing pieces of a mechanism. The monster is just a nuisance, forcing you to replay the segment over again. Thankfully you don't lose items on death so you don't have to go and pick them up again; this prevents a lot of frustration.
Vernon's Legacy is still a decent game, with fluent gameplay and cool atmosphere. But it's a shame they couldn't resist using all the horror tropes. Had they stayed in puzzle adventure genre like in the first chapter, this could have been a much better game.

It's good to be back on possibly the best action of 2001-2002.
Serious Sam Classics: Revolution is the work of modders, big fans of the original game, that spent time merging the 2 classics into one game, plus something more: - new, third campaign (still not accesible, the game is in Early Access)
- intereting main menu themes
- better multiplayer connection (both LAN and Internet)
- PC, PS and Xbox HUD themes are all accesible through settings
That was it for the changes (mostly).
Now for those who want to get this game, but don't know what it has got to offer.
Serious Sam is an old-school 2001 shooter. It is fast-paced, you won't have much time to think, but mostly to shoot at everything and everyone. Probably doesn't sound as anyone's cup of tea so far. I agree. What makes this game special for me, is the environment. Every level has a unique design, and believe me, for 2001, the game looks amazing. You will fight through antic Egypt temples, dunes, dark sewers, pyramids etc.
Yup, the game action takes place in ancient Egypt. Why? Play the game and see, I don't want to spoil anything from storyline.
The game has also got its fair share of hilarious moments. Remember Duke's viral quotes from 1997? I can't say Sam's ones are the same, but they definitely remain in fans' hearts.
The second Serious Sam game, The Second Encounter, has got the same gameplay of the 2001 classic. It adds a few new weapons (oh, and SUCH weapons!!), but I love it because... you guessed, the environment. This one and Serious Sam 2 are probably the most exotic games in the series. TSE will guide you through Mayan ruins, jungles, volcanos, many more and all locations are filled with memorable puzzles. They are not hard to accomplish, so they won't spoil the lore-fun in any way. However, the game has MANY secrets, and most will require a dose of quicksaves and loads in order to get..
- memorable action!!
- tons of weapons. I haven't insisted on describing them on the review. Instead, just try collecting them all and you will see what I mean;
- tons of levels, massive single campaign with unique locations and enemies;
- 100% Old-school FPS;
- Sam.
- not being able to change difficulty in-game; the balancing seems to get heavy every now and then, making the game a lot harder even on decent difficulties;
- finger muscle soreness due to non-stop clicking...
Personal rating: 92/100 - Amazing

Back when I had my crappy good ol' Pentium 4, the controls lagged like hell.
When I upgraded to a half-decent computer in 2012, the controls lagged like hell.
And now that I upgraded to a pretty decent gaming computer, the controls still lag like hell.
In all seriousness, the game itself is fine. The gunplay is what you'd describe as "good enough", nothing fancy or innovating, but it works. The main problem I had is that the character customization actually lying to you and, as previously mentioned, the car controls. On the topic of characters, once you finish painstakingly customizing your looks (Which you can't change without paying an absurd amount of money I may add), your avatar looks barely like the one you created, which wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for the fact that I tried to replicate Frank West and ended up with Sloth from The Goonies.
And as far as the vehicle controls go, they're bloody awful. The cars themselves handle fine, or at the very least the Not!Audi TT you get at the beginning of the game, but there's an almost one second delay between you pressing a key and the car actually doing something, which obviously results in you driving like you drank half the stash of illegal alcohol you were ferrying around town. Sadly the community isn't very helpful when trying to fix this issue, as most of the replies you get are "You suck", "The game is pretty big, deal with it", or "The game is fine, upgrade your rig" which the latter is kinda hard to do when you're running almost top-of-the-line hardware. I'm not TotalBiscuit, goddammit, I don't have enough money to buy four Titan Xs.
In short, if you can run Crysis 1 at 240 FPS on 4K resolution, I'd give it a shot, otherwise either don't; or get ready to do some cardio, as you'll be running all over the city.

I intended on playing this for an hour to get sufficient exposure to this game, because people are wont to claim a person did not play enough of a game to properly judge it. I'm certainly not beholden to them and can do as I please, but I understand that perspective, and sometimes elements change in a game after a short while, and a rocky start can be forgiven, more than made up for by enjoyable things coming up if you just put up with a few minutes or perhaps even an hour of meh content. I appreciate that, and I also appreciate what this game represented, as it is clearly a great grandfather to some modern RPGs and modern tactical games. If Wasteland 1 played a hand in the ideas that led to games like Shadowrun Dragonfall, the Fallout series, and various other western squad-based games, then "thank you, Wasteland 1!" I am glad its publisher/developer did what it/they did.
But I have nothing more that is favorable to say about this game. Read the other reviews. If you will notice, almost every positive review is from someone who played this game when it came out, and almost every negative review is from someone who never played Wasteland 1 for the first time within the past 2 decades. Furthermore, the positive reviews talk about how much they enjoyed it back then, and do not seem to make any case for the game having aged well. The reason is that this game has aged
. I enjoyed playing Space Quest III when I was a kid and it first came out, but I can fully understand how someone now would not enjoy it. It's nothing wrong with the person, but rather, a problem with having to settle for something so inferior when compared to more recent products. How has this game aged badly? Well, I'll cover what I observed in less than half an hour of playing.
Combat is a rather clunky, involving selecting each character to attack an enemy, and then text scrolls by, telling you if it was a hit or a miss, without any real visual feedback like one might see in more recent games, like red text or a red flash if a player took damage, or different colors of text for evasion and successful hits. The battles feel very airy and detached. I simply don't like the original Final Fantasy, and probably dislike more games from that series than ones I do like, but even I will state that the first FF game does a far better job of giving visual stimuli for combat that this game. I couldn't feel invested in any battle at all, here. FF1 released in Japan in 1987 (and in the U.S. in 1990), while Wasteland 1 released in the U.S. in 1988, so it's not like the technology/ability for Wasteland 1 to have decent visual combat stimuli wasn't there.
One might argue that an entirely text-based game and text-based combat can work, and I would actually agree with that sentiment. I just did not find that it felt good with this game at all. I used to play some text-based RPG in the late 90s and/or early 2000s on a site called netdragons or something like that, and it was actually kinda interesting, with writing used to describe places and battles in a way that made me want to keep playing. With Wasteland 1, however, everything is so bare-bones that the over-reliance on text fails miserably. Heck, in PlaneScape Torment, the text is my favorite part of the game! It's well-written, oozing with lore, and absolutely drew me in until the end. The combat was pretty lame in that game, in my opinion, but it only came up every now and again, thankfully.
Speaking of too-frequent combat being an issue, Wasteland 1 has more combat encounters per steps than Final Fantasy games. I took between 2 steps at times and hit a random battle. Then I took 6 and hit another, 3 and another, and so on and so forth. It appeared that I still had quite a bit more ground left to cover in that area as well. Oh, I know! I could just run away from fights and not have to fight things if I have enough experience...right? Eh...maybe?
Fleeing from battle is done better in the original Final Fantasy games. In this one, you select to run, then have to decide whether to have one character or the entire party run, then have to choose a direction to run in. Then the enemy just follows you and the combat screen comes up again. I did this more than a dozen times trying to escape an encounter with a common enemy (lizard) and I could not. I didn't need to run, but was testing to see how it worked, and my answer is "badly." The only thing I can think of that might make this seemingly non-functioning run function beneficial would be to "run" toward your objectives in the dungeon while the enemy pursues you, hopefully preventing the trigger of another random battle since you're already in one. However, if I need to manipulate the system this badly this early to not be barraged by random battles more frequently than in Final Fantasy, then I find this to be a problem.
The Steam version of this game also tends to flip out and "commandeer" control of your mouse if you Alt + Tab out to try and check anything in Windows, making the screen a smaller window and forbidding your mouse cursor from leaving that window and not permitting me to Alt + Tab out again. This was released on Steam with updates, so it should have been programmed to handle things like Alt + Tabbing out. That's the least of my problems with the game, though; a far cry from where its troubles really lie. I only point it out in case anyone reading really wants to be able to Alt + Tab out while playing.
Oh, and Final Fantasy also handled "boring NPCs" and buildings better, too. I walked to what looked like a town just northwest of my starting position, and all of the little buildings which were in good condition were not able to be entered, nor did it state they were locked or that there were any occupants with whom I could knock on a door and attempt to converse. Instead, I found a single person in the town, at its southwest edge - a boy. I spoke to him and the game does not give me the option of topics to talk about. Instead it lets me freeform type. Cool! That freedom is pretty nice, or so I thought...this just ended up being pretty awful, too.
I saw the town had a river going through it, so I typed "water" to keep it simple, figuring that perhaps he knew something of the town's water source. He shrugged his shoulder and said he didn't know anything. That's fair. So then I typed "Who are you?" to which he replied he didn't know. Fine. Maybe I just need a key word? So then I typed "name" and he said he didn't know. "Parents" but he didn't know. "Town" but he didn't know. "Houses" he didn't know, "dorms" he didn't know, "wasteland" he didn't know, "himself" he didn't know, "weather," "food," and the list goes on. I would rather have stupid stuff like Zelda II's "I AM ERROR" and Final Fantasy's stupidly simple town NPC repeat dialog than something as badly executed as the dialog with the first NPC you can find in this game.
When I'm using games that I do not like to show a way I would have preferred a game handle certain aspects, that's pretty bad. I suppose it's one of those "the enemy of my enemy is my friend" sort of situations, albeit with some loose interpretation. Nostalgia is powerful stuff for many people. If you played this game and loved it in the past, you're probably going to love it now, or say you do. If you didn't play it many years back, then it's probably going to be a miserable experience for you. I was sincerely surprised by how poor it was. I would recommend the original Oregon Trail over this, or the tongue-in-cheek modernized "Organ Trail" instead if you want something retro that isn't an absolute chore to play for those who didn't play Wasteland 1 around the time it came out.

I'e been a fan of TES since finding Morrowind in around 2002, and have been actively playing each installment consistently since then, minus of course the mobile titles.
This is just a shame, the "one huge server" thing doesnt work at all, it's impossible to find people to speak to as most of the time the zone and world chat is like the Tower of Babel, the zone phasing is pointless and serves nothing than to separate you from friends you want to play with.
The game plays like an unresponsive Morrowind, without the charm. The skills in game don't seem to have a decent GCD and you can't "queue" skills to be used in succession, while normally this would be fine in a single player game, in an online game with latency, it's important to have some leeway with timing.
Multiple times I found the music and ambient sounds just stopping for no reason, I found an Argonian blacksmith with the soundbank of an Orc blacksmith and occasionally my weapon wouldnt make any sound whatsoever when in use, not great for a bow user, especially when half of the time my arrows didn't even appear after being shot.
Further to this, the game would often just fail to load an area and I'd be looking at an empty camp for 30 seconds while the game tried to remember who to pop in there, i'd load into an area only to be attacked by enemies that hadn't even rendered on screen yet.
Not to mention missing models in game that are just placeholders of a big red box that says "MISSING" 3 times down either side, way to break immersion by just not including all resources in the initial download, no Zenimax, i'm not going to trawl your support forum looking for files to drop into my directory.
Honestly, if you can bring yourself to download this, which is (I believe) currently one of if not "the" biggest download on Steam right now, then try it just to make sure you don't like it, sort of like you would with pegging or dripping chilli sauce onto your eyeball, just make sure you cancel your subscription before you're charged.
Having said that, if my £50 helps to develop Fallout 4 or TESVI then I can let it slide.
Treat this like you treated Redguard, it just never happened, and we shall never speak of it again.

I have recently started this game and i am enjoying the experience so far, it feels like a multiplayer version of skyrim with a revamped UI to allow most expected MMO interfaces to be added. So far the game experience and play has blended together nicely with the addition of slot attacks and set spells.
I must preface that the games leveling mechanic does not focus on quests but more individual talents and skill honing, for instance there doesn't appear to be quests that are focused around "go kill 20 of X and bring me Y = XP reward". It is more use this ability X times to level your skill in X and apply talent points there to increase damage/range. This is honestly refreshing because it feels like i am working on leveling and investing in skills i truly like and can create a rotation based on my play style. This also is without restriction as far as i can tell there is a huge emphasis on personal choice, meaning you could roll a thief (knightblade) and wear robes and use staffs if you wanted to.
There are outstanding concerns and bugs here and there but none that break the experience for me, i am still enjoying the world and story, and feel like the quality of game play is enhanced by the dialog options and voice acting. One glaring thing that ive noticed is there is no real implementation of morality, in previous ES games you usually had the option to be a♥♥♥♥♥♥or steal from people, in ESO you politely ask questions to quest givers and shop keepers smile at you as you take things off their racks. Which presents a confusing economy if i can loot everything from stores and dont have to actually buy gear/materials.
The All up is that i feel ESO has a lot of great foundation mechanics for an early MMO i think there is an overwhelming surplus of content that can lend itself to expansions or scenario based gameplay, i would love to see these features added over time as content updates or scheduled roll-outs *COUGH*thieves guild*COUGH* but for casual players who enjoy a game that is about the day to day experience ESO has been great so far.

DLC:

Pretty much better in nearly all aspects compared to the main game. Level design is on par with DS1. Although some bosses reuse elements from others, they still feel original. Music is memorable unlike the main game (excluding Smelter Demon, final boss and credits tracks). Interesting lore.

Level design is lazy and boring (like Iron Keep). Enemy swarms by the way of red phantoms, which are unfair (infinite stamina, perfect dodging, animation cancelling; don't do this From). Difficulty relies on ranged enemies attacking you from platforms while tanky melee one are trying to hit you at the same time. New enemy types are not interesting at all.
Bosses are by the most part challenging and fair; expect the reused boss from the original game that uses same attacks as well as slower versions of them, which is in itself already cheap and lazy. You can only figure out the attacks by trial and error, which you never needed to resort in DS1 and DS2 main game. The overall atmosphere is not as gripping as the first dlc.

I sampled this game's early stages, and despite some questionable inventory design and illogical puzzles the atmosphere and plot (the story is told entirely through notes) was really rather engaging.
The beauty of the Unreal Engine 4 shone through, if not exactly the best use of it I'd ever seen, and overall it was looking like a really enjoyable and spooky horror story.
Having played 81 minutes now I've had it refunded - what looked truly like a great little indie game was an ultimate failure, let down by a game design choice which absolutely destroyed it from around 40 minutes of gameplay onwards.
Initially we had a spooky mansion setting, and quite a gripping one at that - foreboding atmosphere and some nice ambience as well as the gothic look of the place made this compelling enough to want to go on. And unfortunately that was where it unravelled - that initial setting was by far the best area, as once you end up deeper in the game and are introduced to the entity which pursues you, it loses every ounce of fun and atmosphere and just becomes a horrible chore.
It has an entire four sections in a row which are basically complete copies of each other, all of whom where you get stalked by literally the most boring, unconvincing enemy you'll ever see and will die time and time again.
What promised so much just turns into a vile grind, and isn't worth your time.
To add insult, there are no configuration options in the menu (forget choosing resolution, folks), and as soon as this game went into retail, the dev simply stopped responding to the forum and presumably took the money and ran.
It's as if they got bored and wanted to wrap it up and gave no real thought to how the game would develop, which is a huge shame because it promised so much and delivered, ultimately, a borefest.
Extremely disappointing and absolutely not recommended.

This game starts out very promising in a well designed, graphically impressive house ca. 1900. There are a bunch of notes which give you an idea of the lives of the people living there and of the strange things they experienced in the basement. The game has a spooky atmosphere and in order to get to the basement you have to solve some fairly clever puzzles. Not really hard, not too ease and they fit in nicely with the overall level design. All the clues you need to solve them are in plain sight and I enjoyed solving most of them. The sound design is sparse, with no voice acting and very little music, mostly when you open up the journal in order to read notes, but what there is helps to set the mood. So far so good.
While I haven't encountered any gamebreaking bugs or glitches and the game has never crashed, there are a lot of small design issues that should've been addressed. The most annoying ones are: gamepad not fully recognised and therefore unusable (I use a wireless Xbox One controller); keyboard commands cannot be rebound, so you have to open your inventory with the 'i' key and open and close the journal with the 'j' key; no brightness, contrast or gamma controls in the options menu. There are also lots of smaller issues like the physics being on overdrive: thrown books bounce like they're made of pure rubber and will clip through walls, you're lantarn sways as if you're watching footage which is sped up four times and all reflective surfaces seem to refract more light than is shone on them. All of the notes you find use the same background with the same white (?!) characters using the same handwritten TTF, giving them little character. Text is sometimes longer than the actual note and doesn't fit unto the page shown. None of this is game breaking, but it annoyed me a lot. TripleBrick needs to put more polish in it's games and not just in it's the graphics.
Unfortunately once you get to the basement (which encompasses about three quarters of the game) everything goes downhill. Instead of clever puzzles you go on fetch quests. Find x items so you can open the next door, rinse and repeat. And the basement is made up of several levels of mazes which all look very much the same. There is the odd room that is slightly more interesting, but most of it looks like it was a cut and past job with a lot of extra rubble added in an attempt to make it look more distinct. Unfortunately all of the rubble also looks alike. To top it all off during most of the basement levels you are haunted by a ghost. A large see through skull that completely fills a hallway. And it's also fast and has no problem finding you at all. It was somewhat scary the very first time I saw it and got the 'YOU DIED' screen for the first time. After that it became a nuissance. You can close doors and gates trying to slow it down or capture it, but the animations for closing doors and gates is very slow so you'll probably die trying to stop the ghost. So the only thing you can really do is run as fast as you can and hope you don't run into one of the many dead ends. Which is difficult if you consider that this ghost sucks up light like a black hole so the closer it gets to you the less you'll be able to see.
The ending was somewhat satisfying but still left a bitter taste.
If more of the game had been like the first part, I wouldn't have minded the bits with the ghost as much. If you could play a game of hide and seek with the ghost like you can in games like Alien:Isolation or Evil Within it would've been a passable game. In it's current state however, I cannot recommend it though. It's too short and has too many issues.
The game does show promise and if you can get it in a Steam sale or as part of a bundle it's worth checking out (especially the first part untill you get to the basement). Hopefully TripleBrick will take these critisism by heart and use it when they design their next game. Because they obviously have the talent and skill necessary to produce a good survival horror game similar to Penumbra or Amnesia. But Vernon's Legacy is nowhere near that level.

is a first person horror based game where you move about collecting notes and other inventory items to progress further along.  It later changes and becomes more of a chase-style game, where you still must collect items, but the chases can make it more difficult, along with the way the map system is done for the second half.
The new game itself opens with some voice acting and a few lines about your uncle dying, and then you enter the manor located in what seems to be an area in post war-torn Germany.
The movement begins with the cliche "find the key" type of scenerio, and then you must do various things to move forward and progress inside the manor.
Later on you realize you have gotten into more than you bargained for, as there is a bit of a twist, and things get a little more difficult and intense.
The element of having to run away and yet still collect various items adds some extra difficulty to things, but it's still not too overly hard.  You can keep anything you collect if you end up dying, but it definitely changes up compared to the beginning once you get beyond a certain point in the game, which I thought was a great thing.  Anyway, my full take on it so far:
Really well done graphics.  I liked the impression I got from this right off the bat.
The theme was very well done too, and everything fit nicely for the setting.  The documents were sometimes interesting, and they were not overly long or too boring, for the most part.  They would generally relate directly to what was going on in the house once you were there.
I thought it was fun gathering items to unlock other areas, or progress further onwards, kind of point and click style.  It was sort of a seek and find, with a few puzzle elements where you had to notice things around you through observation in order to break codes, or find hidden meanings behind things around you.
The later twist in gameplay was quite well done, I thought.  I enjoyed how thrilling and suspenseful it could be with the chase elements.
I'm not really fond of the voice over narration at the very beginning.  I mean, it's not terrible, but it feels strange since it's only the very very beginning part, and nothing else has anything like this once you start to move around and play.
I wish I could do a little bit more with my character, in a general sort of way.  Interact with things more, have more options for my character, or things like that.
Some of the information in the letters was not important to me, or did not seem too relevant, but other letters were directly related to what was going on, explaining things a little further about the events unfolding at the manor.
I would like this to be a good bit longer before it is finished!
I can move through the first statue on the left side.
There is a picture on a table that I can see through in one of the first rooms if I look around the back side of it.
In the kitchen, there is a drawer that moves through a piece of table cloth.
Lots of other clipping issues (putting objects through walls and such).
Well, after playing through the game so far, I thought it was interesting.  Slow start, but the game turned from a point and click kind of first person information and object gathering run - to a literal run for your life, or die game style at moments!
I wasn't really sure what to expect from the game at first, since it was so focused on finding this key or that item to repair or open this door or that other item.  After the first section was cleared though, it got very very interesting...
I liked the suspenseful chases and the rush-like style of having to risk death, or move to escape the later stuff, in the second half, and all in all I like this early access game, and I would recommend this to anybody into the first person style horrors where you have to run for your life or die, to give this one a try! Personally, I am really enjoying this game.
The story is very fluid and there are so many things you can gleam from the story in the environment. Not everything is handed to you and if you want to know more about what you're getting into, what's going on, you get to explore these beautifully put together environments on each level that are so diverse from one another.
A dry near-ruin? Twisted reality? A maze of shifting rooms filled with varying dangers? A city where blood glistens down the steets and corpses are on display for all to see? There's so much to see and explore, and sometimes you just feel like you can drink in the horrors of Karaka with awe.
As for gameplay, it does feel very smooth. Your own mistakes will be your undoing many times over.
Enemies are intelligent. For example, a few times I attempted to take out some dogs with my crossbow behind a barrier while crouched down so I could stealthily enter the room when things calmed down. To my surprise, one of my enemies teleported in behind me and stabbed me in the back despite noone having spotted me.
I find Dishonored 2 difficult, atleast when you're really trying in a high difficulty setting not to kill anyone or be spotted while getting all of your runes/bone charms, or at least all you can. As you do this, you find yourself pressing the quick load button often, and going off on murderous rampages before wiping that slate clean and attempting again. Every time you go through it it's like going through a series of trials to find an answer to a difficult problem.
Once I manuevered through to the roof of a building after shooting out the glass of it and burning down an angry root that slaps me and can somehow see me despite not having eyes when I walked over to the bonecharm or rune I was going for, when dogs came out in a burst of flame as I walked past preoccupied, making me sprint off of the roof and reach for somewhere to Reach only to fall to my death. Fun times.
Anyways, about the frame issues.
I did not play around with the files of the game, and decided to run on the max settings in the options menu.
Dishonored 2 plays at around 60fps for me almost constantly, unless I'm in specific areas filled with guards and amazing design, then it gets a bit choppy. There are few of these places that hurt my fps.
I run with a 750ti and eight gigs of ram along with an i5 processor.
I found that it was difficult to aim your teleporting abilities in slow motion, that 'unfolding the glass' dopped my fps by 15-20, and.... that's really all I have for complaints.
Basically, I'm having lots of fun with this game and it's story and gameplay, much more than I really thought I would to be honest. The game itself is a great experience. I don't know what is with the frame rate issues that so many are having but I am having almost no affect. I still haven't completed a playthrough despite 48 hours of playtime to date, mostly because I've been pouring over all that this game has to offer in the slowest way I could do it.
I reccomend this game, definitely. When you can play this game and work around whatever problems you have with the game I think that this is an astounding work of art worth all the time and money spent deciphering it.

This is a long review so if you just want a brief summary of why I recommend Serious Sam Classics: Revolution.
Alligator Pit manufactures the original in all new light with dazzling new interface and cleaned up visuals. Serious Sam Classics: Revolution revitalizes the classic games taking on similar ideas as the HD remakes by creating a game with cleaner performance.
Serious Sam: Revolution includes the first and second encounters, which means instead of paying $34.00 for both the First and Second Encounter you can get them both for $9.99 (without being on sale). Although, what you are probably wondering is what else is included in Serious Sam Classics: Reovlution? To name a few better graphical options, steam support, new campaigns, new bosses, improved UI, level editors, and much more.
Campaign:
The First Encounter:
For those who already own the first encounter you should probably skip this. This campaign includes thirteen main story levels and two secret levels. All of the levels take place in Egypt and are about the story of how Serious Sam began his quest to save humanity from Metals domination. The original campaign offers hours of gameplay as the levels are incredibly large and filled with secrets. The levels are composed of fighting mass hordes of enemies, solving puzzles, and completing objectives. During the campaign you will fight three bosses: Highlander Aludran Reptiloid, Lava Golem, and Ugh-Zan III. The brilliant group fights and epic boss fights keep you on your toes constantly engaged in a changing environment.
The Second Encounter:
For those who already own the second encounter you should probably skip this. This campaign includes twelve levels (no secret levels), but it also includes the entire campaign from Serious Sam The First Encounter. The campaign is divided across three kingdoms: Mayans, Persia, and medieval Poland. Similar to the First Encounter the second encounter is incredibly long, the levels are large and filled with secrets. The Second Encounter creates even more puzzles, crazier secrets, and throws more enemies at you than imaginable. Not only will you be engaged in all the mysteries abound, but the campaign also provides four bosses: Kukulkan, The Wing God, Exotech Larva, Mordekai the Summoner, and The Ram-God. The Ram-God is from Legend of the Beast DLC, which I assume is going to be implemented into Serious Sam Classis: Revolution.
Bright Island:
I have no information on this campaign, as it is not available in the early access beta.
Space Crusader (Possible Additional Campaign):
This campaign will include the following levels: Water Planet, Lava Planet, Green Planet, Ice Planet, Tropic Planet, and Rock Planet. Although none of this is mentioned, there are hints that this is being implemented based on the screenshots. The screenshots show that they may finally implement the scrapped levels and weapons from the Original Serious Sam. One of the weapons in the screenshots is the Ghost Buster (it looks like it shoots electricity) which was never implemented in the original campaign. it looks like this weapon is being used on the Rock Planet, which is one of the many various planets that was never included in the Serious Sam Campaign. The original campaign would have been over double the size if they finished developing most of the levels they had planned, but for various reasons they were cut. This makes me hope that this edition is finally fulfilling the original dream for Serious Sam and bringing the campaign in its full glory.
Graphical Additions:
The actual quality of the textures is the same as you would see in the HD remakes, although what Serious Sam Classics: Revolution offers is more than just a HD texture experience. It provides modern day graphical elements including: lens flares, fog, object bending, object translucency, smoother particle animation, haze, high resolution reflections, better portal animations, cleaner lighting, higher shading controls, and more. You can see all of these in action by checking out the Technology Test, which provides you with clean visuals of how these will be seen when implemented into the new campaign.
Steam Functionality:
Finally Serious Sam will have access to the workshop, and proper steam servers. The game is supposed to offer up to 42-player multiplayer and even support split screen. The game will come with a level editor, so if they don’t come out with space crusader or sky city someone will. Review Update Serious Sam Classics Revolution has been out now for almost two-half weeks, since then there has been a bundle of added content to the workshop. These include remodeling of textures, multiplayer maps, and even a custom campaign. SSCR has a lot of to offer, and if the community support continues in this fashion this will be an amazing addition to the series.
Results:
At this current point Serious Sam Classic: Revolution is not complete, but lets be honest Croteam and Devlover Digital completed Serious Sam HD in a timely manner; I am sure that you will not be waiting forever, unlike some Early Access Games. This game has a lot of potential with its new graphics engine, level editor, providing the original campaigns, better menu UI, cleaner animations, steam support, and so much more. I would buy this game at full price, but on sale it’s like you are robbing Croteam.
Pros:
+Great new OpenGL shaders and 64-bit support to create a much cleaner and graphic intensive game.
+Steam workshop support
+Steam servers for multiplayer (supports up to 42 players)
+Includes Serious Sam First and Second Encounter
+New Survival Mode
+Already mention of new Bright Island Campaign
+A level editor, so you can go crazy and make your own Serious Adventures
+Loads of enemies and bosses
+Lots of guns to choose from
+Already downloaded my first custom campaign, thanks Workshop support!
Cons:
-Its early access

Wasteland is so awesome. It has been decades since I played - and finished - this game, but I remembered it fondly. Over this last week, I have put tens of hours into playing the game again, and all the old routines came right back.
This game gets better every time you play it. It is designed to be played over and over, with more exploration done each time. It is a deep story, and it has deep game mechanics. It is a difficult game, and the user interface takes a lot of time to learn. Even with all that, I have so much fun making my squad and marching them in the wastes. I feel a sense of connection with the keyboard controls that I do not have with a 3-D first person view type game.
Bottom line, if you are someone who enjoys a deep gaming experience, but you can handle a steep learning curve like Dwarf Fortress, then check out Wasteland.

This is one of the greatest games ever made, but it's definitely from the age of Zork text adventures. I'm not sure anyone under 30 is going to have previous exposure to the interface style and character management, which is a product of what was doable on 6502s with 64 kilobytes of memory and floppy disks for permanent storage.
The updates are cute but I prefer the older animated portaits, and I ended up copying in a bunch of the Fallout 1 and 2 music into it but the new score is OK. Having integrated paragraphs is messing with my head due to the old soft cover book with the spurious entries, but it's a great add-in.
Just a note about the paragraphs -- part of the copy-protection for this game used to be a booklet of a hundred or so short fiction vignettes. If youy didn't have the book, a lot of the game was near impossible to play, but to discourage people from spoiling themselves, about half the entries were from entirely separate stories that had nothing to do with the game.
If your expectations of RPGs are informed by the post-SNES JRPG style this game will probably be frustrating to deal with, but if the old Bards Tale or SSI D&D games were something you enjoyed it's one of the best.

Back in the day I didn't have a lot of disposible income to spend on games, but when I saw the Wasteland box in the Commodore 64 section of Electonics Botique I knew I had to give it a try. Blew my mind - head and shoulders above anything I'd played up until that point. Maybe I'm viewing the game through nostalgia-tinted glasses.
It's not without its flaws, believe me - the control scheme is keyboard only, the balance is wonky, the difficulty is uneven and unforgiving, and there are a lot of artifacts of 1980s game design. But it's fun, if you can deal with the frustrations of autosave and permadeath - there is no game mode other than ironman.
The game has a form of copy protection in that sometimes it asks you to read a paragraph from a booklet that came with the game. I will have to preface this review with this one line:  This is literally the first game in over 2 years I am excited to come home and play.
Survivalist is an RPG/RTS hybrid, with sandbox elements baked in.  You start off as Joe, a financial hedge fund manager who has no practical skills and a boatload of worthless money, who lives in a 3x3 meter concrete bunker.  As you start, the game takes you through its tutorial phase, and I found it to be a quite easy to understand.  It covers most, if not all you need to learn about the game.  In about 1-2 hours you will learn how to build your base, scavenge for loot, and shoot zombies in style.
However, this game shows its detail even in the tutorial, as you can completely skip it, and the game will remember this and assume you know the game, giving you full control over all functions.  It will also remember that you didn't get a certain community member and have certain events unfold!
But this is only the beginning of the game.  From there, you can quest by yourself or with a posse, forgo exploration and build your base and community, or build relations with not only the friendly communities but also the various looter or highwaymen gangs.  I found it a nice touch to be able to recruit what you would expect to be basic "bad guys", and then find out they have personality, and some even have their own story lines!
The quests range from difficult and strategic, mysteries to solve, or easy and borish... but expect the unexpected.  Much like real life, don't take all you hear at face value.  And this is, in my opinion, one of the strongest suits of the game.  Not only do you have multiple approaches to quests, but you'll quickly find out that not all quests are good for you.  I will also note here that the story, or main quest line, is really, really good.  I honestly haven't been engaged in a games story for many years, and this short story for some reason has me coming back for more.
The base building is in the basic RTS style.  You can set your community members out to gather resources, then have some other community members build various structures, while others do your farming, guarding, and exploring.  There aren't too many structures to build, but there is enough variety to work with.  However, the main break away from RTS style games is that your gatherer can also be your builder, soldier, explorer, farmer, doctor, or guard.  However, for veteran RTS players, the controls in Command mode(The RTS mode) are not as extensive as other RTS games.
Combat in this game is simplistic, yet I found it quite fun.  Depending on your firearms skill, you can aim at the torso, legs, or head.  Aiming is heavily based on the firearms skill, with no stars in the skill meaning you cannot hit the broad side of a highway sign, to 5 stars where you can head shot all day long and rarely miss a shot.  The enemies you fight are not the slow type of zombie, these are the "Warp 9 engage!" zombies that can run down a galloping horse on speed.  Seriously, Aim for the legs!  I found this to be a fun, arcade-y style of combat, with reaction time being paramount between being zombie chow or using its skull for a cup.  However, even if they do get ahold of you, don't fret: you can give 'em a swift kick to get them off you.  This will use up your fatigue meter, which is based off of fitness.  Again, no stars = you can kick them off a couple times to 5 stars where you can go all Neo in the matrix, tossing them off repeatedly.  However, there are stronger zombies out there that will require more, if not all your strength to throw off.
The graphics aren't anything to write home about, but I did find them more than passable. For the most part they didn't break me away from the game in any form.  That said... the walking animation is not the greatest, and the sidestep animation reminds me of MC Hammer.  You can't touch this!  The soundtrack has a couple of good tunes in it, but to sum up: "Its good, but not great"  The controls I found to be spot on, and I could always get my character to do what I wanted, when I wanted.
In summery, I love this game.  I imagine I will be playing this for at least another 50 hours, and I spent a whoppin' 5 bucks on it.  I've gotten more enjoyment out of this game than most AAA stuff out there.  And if you are on the fence, you can even download the demo and try it yourself for free.
PS:  This game was made by one guy.  ONE.  Cudos to you, Bob, and thank you for producing a quality FULL game for an amazing price!

Great game. It sits somewhere between Demon Souls and Dark Souls in almost every regard. Personally I felt it fell slightly short of either as a result, but being third best in one of the best game series of recent years still puts it in damn high esteem. It's no one major thing, just lots of little steps back that stop it being quite the experience.
Firstly, it's not as difficult. It's not just that I've beaten both games previously and have the experience to tackle this one, it's that the game has far, far fewer of the fiendish moments that took advantage of the unwary and headstrong. It's better than Demon Souls' attitude of total unfairness in its traps, but far behind Dark Souls throwing bad♥♥♥♥♥♥at you that is completely avoidable if you pay attention and always proceed with caution.
Gone is the interconnected, almost Metroidvania-esque world of Dark Souls with its attiude of "if you can make it here, you deserve to be here." Gone with it is the uniquely organic feel of the world itself telling a story. The tragedy of New Londo makes all the more sense because of where it sits in the world, the feeling of descending endlessly into the Depths, then further still into Blight Town, then down deeper and deeper, it gives a horrifying claustrophobia because you travelled that distance yourself and know just how far underground you are. No more of that. DS2 has a hub-style system with built-in bonfire teleportation from the start. The world feels smaller, there's no interconnection, it's just a series of places you visit in a relatively strict sequence and fails to tell the same story. Head down this spoke and carry on until the end. Now teleport back to the hub and start down another spoke. At least Demon Souls just went all-out with the hub instead of a weak attempt at a hybrid.
Graphically it's technically an improvement. It's a gorgeous game and very easy on the system resources with a steady 60fps. Unfortunately, the consequence of getting that framerate on consoles means they sacrificed the lighting of DS1. Ironic, since this game added in proper dynamic lighting, but gone is the spec mapping or any of the high contrast. There's a really high level of ambient light, nothing shines or gleams or twinkles in the half-light, that dark beauty is replaced by a steady amount of good lighting except a gimmick stage where they remove it. The game as a result looks really flat by comparison. Go watch the April 2013 reveal videos to see what it should have looked like. A game called Dark Souls 2, really well lit.
Bosses. Underwhelming. Very few of the massive, giant terrifying beasts of the previous games. The game is set long after the first one, and there are very few dragons left in the world, so it makes sense in that regard, but so many of the bosses go for a stupid setup of facing multiple enemies instead. The result is that you are forced to co-op a lot more. Don't want to? Tough. They replaced almost all of the big grotesque foes and the majestic, heart-pounding one-on-one duels.
Storyline, eh. Maybe it's too early to judge, but so far it's too tied to the world created by DS1 instead of creating its own. The leap from Demon to Dark Souls worked because they jettisoned Demon Souls' world and systems and started afresh, making it all one great voyage of discovery and slow understanding. DS2 is just a repeat of DS1 in so many ways, oddly frightened of straying from certain concepts whilst trouncing over the ones that people seemed to most enjoy.
Dying reduces your max health until you unhollow now. Demon Souls just straight-up halved your health, so it's not as brutal as that, but it's also not balanced around that, making it quite uneven. Killing an enemy too many times stops it respawning, so if you're patient enough, anyone can beat the game (blasphemy!). PVP balance is still all over the shop, but now you can't avoid it by simply remaining hollowed (in fact, being hollowed increases your chances of invasion).
It may sound like I'm being really negative, but that's not my intention. I'd put this just a tiny notch below the other two games and a must-buy to anyone who likes challenge and serious, intense rewarding games. It's just that it doesn't quite match up to what came before it. If the previous two were 10/10 games, this is a 9.5, can't complain too much about that.

The "Elderscrolls Online" manages to capture the feel and overall lore behind the very popular franchise. When I first became aware of the Elderscrolls it was when Morrowind first came into being, and back then, the Elderscrolls had very much a cult following and wasn't particulary what you would call nowerdays "mainstream". But the principles that governed the early birth of the Elderscrolls stayed true, even when the name became more popular. Now of course the Elderscrolls had been around long before Morrowind hit the stores but unfortunately I wasnt aware of them. But being as I am now an avid follower and self proclaimed "Geek" of what is now THE most popular freeroam RPG's of its time, I had some concerns about the latest chapter of a series of games I have loved for many years being an MMORPG. And, it took me quite a while to build the courage to even play ESOnline in fear of massive dissapointment. BUT, my fears are no more, I am very pleased to say. They have kept true to the overall feel that was so unique to the Single Player titles, and instead of taking the idea and running wild with it, they have somehow managed to make this latest addition still feel like a Single Player game, the only difference is that other players happen to be there too!
If you are a huge Elderscrolls fanatic like me, you HAVE to play this, simply for the storyline alone, which in itself is truly epic and gives you more backstory and delves you deeper into the world than you have been before. If however you are new to the Elderscrolls I would suggest playing the older titles first. Although its not essential to know the backstory to play any of the Elderscrolls titles, you cant help think that if you hadnt been there from the start, there is just so much you wouldnt pick up on.
The Elderscrolls universe has become so huge in recent years, and I hold the games very close to my chest and consider them THE best RPG titles I have ever played (and i've played alot). The Elderscrolls Online extends the complex and beautiful universe of Tamriel and delves you deeper into this gloriously crafted world.
If you haven't got it already, go get it.... NOW!!!

I kept dreading when I would play this game. I knew just by looking at it that I would be mildly bored by it for it's 40 short minutes of play time, and you know what?
I was right in dreading it.
Voices from the Sea is another interactive Japanese-culture-inspired interactive novel. It follows an angsty boy named... Cantus, who lives on an island and is plagued by all the "noise" in his world, like his mom telling him to make more friends, or a kid named Garrio poking fun of him. Honestly, Cantus comes across as a bit of a pr*** in the scenes away from the ocean. Like a moody teenager pouting about how life sucks and no one understands him.
But, unbeknownst to our unlikeable protagonist, he meets a mysterious girl from the ocean named Maris, who is... just strange. Not really charming or enlightening. Just strange. She tries desperately to make him smile in the 7 days they talk, but all of their scenes are as awkwardly-written as everything else in the game. There are SOME points where they start talking like real people (about, you know, real feelings and relationships instead of angsty bullsh**), but they're soon cut off by the pretentious narration. And the blackout with a sentence-ending to close each day is the icing on the pretentious cake.
The game does have a little quality put into the backgrounds, but the actual animation and music are just... bland and cheap-looking. Sure, Everlasting Summer is one of my favorite interactive novels and it looks very similar to Voices from the Sea, but it's the story that made Everlasting Summer such an engrossing game. And Voices from the Sea just doesn't have it. A kid is depressed about vague stuff in life, a girl talks to him in some cringey and awkward scenes, and he realizes he loves his mom out of nowhere at the end... even with how sh**ty he's been treating her up to that point. It just doesn't add up.
But, wait! Voices from the Sea does involve interactivity! REAL interactivity! As in, you can make decisions in this game! Guess what you can choose?
What f***ing seashell looks best.
Are you f***ing kidding me? What is this bullsh**? It's not implemented into the story, save for the end, and it's just a mindless bit where you stare at the same blank screen (Even though you might be moving right or left, according to the game) and you just pick a seashell for the day. It has no impact on the plot. It's just there.
Voices from the Sea is as pretentious as it is artless. As I expected, I was mildly bored while playing, but all those little irritating things culminated into an overall unpleasant 40 minutes that I feel were honestly wasted on this bland interactive novel. It might be free, but I heavily recommend you spend your time on an actually well-written interactive novel, like Everlasting Summer. As for Voices from the Sea, I'm giving it a 3/10. There's a little quality here, but it's so bogged down by the rest of the bullsh** in this game, that I cannot see myself playing it again ever.

Venon's legacy puts you in the shoes of a man named Robert, he learns of his uncles death and returns to the uncles estate Dunkenhof manor.  Upon reaching the manor he notices something is amiss as no one is around to greet him, he finds a letter on the nearby table and this sets you out on a journey to find out what happened at your uncles estate in the years since you've been gone.  The story unfolds via letters left behind by the estates residents who are now conspicuously missing.  The game plays out like many other walking simulators as no combat exist in the game, instead you're greeted by a eerie atmosphere and music, which often times leaves the gamer on the edge of his seat waiting to see what pounces out at him behind the next locked door.
The game can be both frustrating and rewarding at the same time, many of the puzzles are riddles hidden in the pages you've found, others seem to be complete random and require a ton of guess work.  Requiring guess work in a game isn't really the most exciting game play mechanic, but it can be forgiven as Vernon's Legacy has a very interesting story to tell.  The scare factor isn't gained by having strange creatures jump out at you, (although I'm not saying something couldn't jump out at you)  but rather by creating an atmosphere that makes you think something will cause you harm.  The deeper you get in the manor the more nervous you feel with each successive door you unlock or key you find.
The controls and movements were silky smooth, and the controls were spot on, the only issue I had was occasionally the inventory would bug out, normally the RMB would put an item back in your inventory, but occasionally the item wouldn't be placed back in my inventory and I'd be forced to stop playing and reload the game.  That would clear up the issue, I never lost any progress and it conveniently placed me back in the main hallway.  Some of the puzzles were rather frustrating, such as trying to unlock the second safe door, for the life of me I couldn't find any pattern or message in game which gave me a description or hint as to which direction the tabs had to be placed, likewise with the hidden panel which required using the crowbar, it was randomly that I discovered the panel could be interacted with..
Overall the game left me with a very positive feeling, and I felt it was a wonderful experience, not the scariest game ever made, but it certainly had me a bit creeped out at numerous times, like discovering that darkened room on the second floor, it was unnerving going inside and expecting some creepy creature to pounce into your face and end your adventure.  Lucky for me that never happened so I got to continue my journey through the possibly haunted house.
Beautiful graphics
smooth movements
Interesting story told through notes
Challenging puzzles
A great atmosphere
Biggest con was the inventory glitch
Next up was the puzzles solutions which were a little too well hidden, maybe a few additional notes with information helping to show the gamer where those hints are might be helpful.
Vernon's Legacy was a well put together game, the story was interesting, the manor was beautifully put together and the game was fairly challenging to solve without resorting to seeking out a guide or walkthrough.  The only thing that would have been slightly great to add would be something to add tension prior to getting into the tunnels, maybe some noises, some floor creeks, possible even a few shadow figures which disappear as you approach them.  Even without these things the game is well worth a purchase and a play.  If you have a few hours to kill and want to play a game which tells a good story, I'd highly recommend Vernon's Legacy.

This is one of the better horror games that I have played for under $10 on Steam, and I've played a lot of them.
The graphics take advantage of the Unreal4 engine and show off what it can do well, and the game also delivers great sound effects that echo realistically as you explore your uncle Vernon's mansion trying to figure out what exactly happened and why his butler and cook left before you arrive there.
The first part of the game deliver the back story to you via your uncles journal notes and notes written by both his butler and his cook and they are all dated.  This game has a few puzzles and keys that help deliver everything you read in a particular order, but nothing is terribly difficult or should take you more then a few minutes to solve.
Where this game delivers is once some of the back story has been established and you come face to face with what haunts this home of your deceased uncle.  As you try and piece together the whole story, you'll need quick wits and calm nerves keep you from looking like a big scardey cat to anyone who might be watching you play the game in your home.
It's not complete at the time of its launch in early access, but the developer has made that well known and been up front that the rest of the story is coming in the months to come.  If you don't mind waiting to see the resolution of this game, then I highly recommend that all horror game fans not pass this one up.  For the price, it delivers and promises to deliver even more as is completed.  While there are a few random glitches and oddities in the game, the fact that it's in early access excuses these minor set-backs and I'm confident they will be ironed out before this game is released as a final product.
7 out of 10 on early access launch day, much likely a higher score once it see's completely and delivers a full game and more value.
